t: Patients aged over 80 years were significantly less likely to receive a long COVID diagnosis than those aged 18-30 years.
Patients of Asian/Asian British or mixed ethnicity had significantly higher adjusted odds of receiving a long COVID diagnosis than White patients.
Patients whose ethnicity was recorded as 'Other Ethnic Group' had significantly lower adjusted odds of receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Women had significantly higher adjusted odds of receiving a long COVID diagnosis than men.

Patients living in the third and fourth most socio-economically deprived quintiles of areas were significantly more likely to have a recorded long COVID diagnosis than those in the most deprived quintile, while the least deprived quintile showed no significant difference.
Pre-existing anxiety diagnosis before the pandemic was strongly associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing asthma diagnosis before the pandemic was strongly associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing eczema diagnosis before the pandemic was associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing chronic kidney disease before the pandemic was associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing depressive disorder before the pandemic was associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing hypertension before the pandemic was associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing type 2 diabetes before the pandemic was associated with increased odds of subsequently receiving a long COVID diagnosis.
Patients aged 51-60 years received a long COVID diagnosis on average 62.9 days earlier than those aged 18-30 years.
Patients recorded as Asian ethnicity were diagnosed with long COVID significantly earlier in the pandemic than White patients.
Patients recorded as Black ethnicity were diagnosed with long COVID significantly earlier in the pandemic than White patients.
In a multivariate median regression model, patients aged 51-60 years were diagnosed with long Covid on average 62.9 days earlier than those aged 18-30 years.
Patients recorded as Asian ethnicity were diagnosed with long Covid significantly earlier than white patients, by an average of 52.0 days.
Patients recorded as black ethnicity were diagnosed with long Covid significantly earlier than white patients, by an average of 41.3 days.
Women with long Covid waited significantly longer than men to receive a diagnosis, by an average of 22.7 days.

Among the 20 comorbidities examined, only a pre-existing diagnosis of depressive disorder was associated with a significantly longer time to long Covid diagnosis, delaying it by an average of 32.7 days.
Among long Covid patients without a prior anxiety diagnosis, 18.44% received a new anxiety diagnosis after 1 January 2020, compared to 4.06% of the overall population.
Among long Covid patients without a prior depressive disorder diagnosis, 14.99% received a new depressive disorder diagnosis after 1 January 2020, compared to 3.54% overall.
New diagnoses of hypertension after 1 January 2020 were more common among long Covid patients (10.07%) than the overall population (5.91%).
New diagnoses of asthma after 1 January 2020 were more common among long Covid patients (7.14%) than the overall population (1.58%).
New diagnoses of type 2 diabetes mellitus after 1 January 2020 were more common among long Covid patients (4.65%) than the overall population (2.30%).

K-means clustering of pre- and post-pandemic comorbidities showed that long Covid patients grouped into distinct clusters largely centred around common conditions like asthma, hypertension, or T2D, but exhibited a wide range of clinical trajectories in developing new comorbidities after the pandemic onset, with no single dominant trajectory linked to pre-existing conditions.

The frequency of new long Covid diagnoses peaked in early 2021 coinciding with the introduction of long Covid SNOMED codes, then gradually declined, with the initially dominant 'Post-COVID-19 syndrome' code increasingly superseded by other long Covid codes over time.

Patients frequently described severe, disabling fatigue accompanied by post-exertional malaise, where minor exertion caused disproportionate symptom worsening, similar to other chronic post-viral syndromes.
Patients reported bodily pain ranging from diffuse muscle aches to localized, sometimes migrating, joint stiffness that impaired movement and exercise.
Respiratory manifestations such as shortness of breath, chest pressure, and 'air hunger' frequently co-occurred with fatigue and amplified functional limitations.

A heterogeneous secondary symptom pattern (digestive, dermatological, sore throat, headache, fever sensation) affecting only a subset of patients was interpreted as reinforcing a hypothesis of immune-mediated, multi-systemic mechanisms in Long Covid.
Loss of taste (ageusia) and smell (anosmia), along with qualitative distortions like parosmia and phantom odours, persisted for weeks to months and disrupted nutrition and well-being.
Patients reported eye problems including reduced visual acuity, colour distortion, ocular pain, photophobia and nystagmus-like sensations that limited daily activities and screen use.
Tinnitus, described as ringing or buzzing in the ears often intensifying in quiet settings and at night, was commonly reported and interfered with sleep.
Dizziness ranging from mild disequilibrium to severe vertigo requiring support while walking was reported, sometimes sudden and unpredictable.
Cognitive disturbances, especially brain fog, concentration difficulties, and memory lapses, persisted even after other symptoms resolved and profoundly affected daily functioning and work capacity.

Long Covid narratives revealed a coexistence of pervasive negative emotions (fear, stress, anxiety, anger, sadness, abandonment) with positive emotions (hope, relief, gratitude), with fear being most recurrent.
Perceived lack of understanding or empathy from family/friends and feelings of abandonment by the healthcare system contributed to isolation and anger among Long Covid patients.

Heterogeneous experiences with healthcare providers ranged from validating and compassionate to dismissive, with lack of diagnostic recognition associated with emotional distress and diminished trust.
Some patients used self-medication and preventive routines with medications already available at home to try to regain control over their health and reduce symptom burden.
Patients who engaged in moderate adapted physical activity (e.g., cycling) despite fatigue and pain reported it helped maintain functional capacity, mood, and counteract deconditioning.
Formal, prescribed or self-initiated rehabilitation programmes were used by some patients to gradually restore physical endurance and respiratory capacity, helping regain lost function.

Marked heterogeneity in the number, combination, and intensity of Long Covid symptoms across patients (from a few flu-like symptoms to over 50 distinct symptoms) suggests the possible existence of multiple Long Covid phenotypes.
The CLoCk study reported that 66% of children who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 continued to have symptoms at a three-month follow-up, with 30.3% reporting three or more symptoms.
A Swedish study of hospitalised children found that 21% had persistent symptoms after COVID-19, with fatigue being the most common.
In the Swedish BAMSE birth cohort, 16.5% of young adults reported symptoms consistent with long COVID via repeated questionnaires.
A large US study of 5376 children found 36% reported symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, with prevalence and symptom type varying by age group.
A US physician survey found that most physicians recognize long COVID as a problem but few feel prepared to manage it.
Fatigue was described by all interviewed children as a central, pervasive symptom affecting physical, cognitive, and social functioning, and dictated their daily activity choices.
Physical exertion triggered delayed symptom exacerbation, including fever, sore throat, and exhaustion lasting several days, leading children to avoid exercise.
One participant reported near-syncope symptoms requiring her to sit while showering to avoid fainting, alongside subjective reports of a 'rushing pulse' consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
One participant experienced severe motor impairment after acute infection, remaining dependent on crutches and a wheelchair and unable to walk more than a few steps unassisted two years later.
Long COVID caused substantial school absence and required individualized accommodations, with some children out of school for weeks to years.
Children reported losing friendships and social context due to reduced capacity for shared activities, contributing to loneliness.
Family life was affected as parents needed to take time off work to support the child's schooling and healthcare needs, and children reported guilt about the burden placed on parents.
Many children experienced disbelief or dismissal of their symptoms from family members, healthcare providers, and school staff, intensifying feelings of isolation and helplessness.
Some children reported severe psychological distress during the worst phase of illness, including hopelessness and, in one case, doubt about surviving the illness.
Talking with a psychologist helped some children develop hope and acceptance regarding their illness and future, which they associated with improved coping.
Reducing school hours and minimizing physical activity, coordinated between school and healthcare, helped one participant manage exacerbation of symptoms and cope with long COVID.
Some children used online gaming as a compensatory coping strategy to maintain social connection with friends despite physical limitations from long COVID.
Among 190 followed-up children with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, 73 (38.4%) developed long COVID symptoms while 117 fully recovered.
At 1-3 months post-infection, the most commonly reported long COVID symptoms in children were fatigue (52.0%), decreased physical activity (44.1%), and headache (35.3%).
By 12 months, the prevalence of fatigue, decreased physical activity, and headache declined significantly to 19.8%, 13.9%, and 12.3% respectively.
By the end of 12-month follow-up, 32.5% of children continued to experience at least one long COVID symptom.
Full recovery from long COVID symptoms increased progressively over time: 14.0% recovered by 6 months, 43.9% by 9 months, and 67.5% by 12 months.
Neurological symptoms were the most commonly affected system category, reported by 64.6% of children with long COVID, followed by general symptoms (59.8%).
Over 62.2% of children with long COVID reported symptoms affecting more than one organ system, indicating multisystem involvement.
Older age was significantly associated with a higher risk of decreased physical activity as a long COVID symptom.
Older age was associated with headache, memory impairment, difficulty communicating, and difficulty concentrating as long COVID symptoms, with the strongest association for memory impairment.
Older age was significantly associated with lack of energy, neurological symptoms overall, cardiological symptoms, sensory symptoms, and dizziness among children with long COVID.
Younger age was significantly associated with insomnia as a long COVID symptom.
Female sex was significantly associated with a greater likelihood of reporting lack of energy as a long COVID symptom.
Outpatient (non-hospitalized) status was significantly associated with a greater likelihood of muscle pain compared to hospitalized children with long COVID.

Comorbid conditions were identified in 63.0% of children with long COVID, most commonly allergic rhinitis (18.1%), overweight/obesity (16.5%), atopic dermatitis (13.4%), and neurological disorders (10.2%); prevalence of comorbidities did not differ significantly between hospitalized and non-hospitalized groups.
No cases of anosmia, ageusia, or brain fog were reported in the acute phase of illness or during long COVID follow-up in this pediatric cohort.
Neurological symptoms including insomnia, memory impairment, emotional excitability, and concentration difficulties declined significantly over the 12-month study period.
Musculoskeletal complaints, primarily muscle pain, decreased significantly from 27.9% to 10.5% over the 12-month follow-up.

Age and diagnostic method were associated with different spectra of long COVID symptoms; older children diagnosed by IgM serology more frequently reported musculoskeletal, cardiac, respiratory and other symptoms than those confirmed by PCR or rapid antigen test.

The most frequent acute-phase symptoms of pediatric COVID-19 were fever (81.9%), rhinitis/congested nose (59.1%), fatigue (50.4%), cough (43.3%), and decreased appetite (36.3%), with fever present in 100% of hospitalized children.

Fatigue, reduced physical activity, lack of energy, elevated temperature, neurological complaints, muscle pain, tachycardia, and cough were the symptoms most likely to persist beyond 12 months in the 32.5% of children with ongoing long COVID.
In this pediatric cohort, binding anti-IFN-α antibodies were detected in 2.6% (2/78) of children with current or past COVID-19.
Anti-IFN-α antibody prevalence was substantially higher (25%) among children with severe or critical COVID-19 compared with the overall cohort prevalence of 2.6%.
The detection rate of anti-IFN-α antibodies was 4% among all hospitalized COVID-19 patients, compared with 25% among those with severe/critical disease.
Anti-IFN-α antibodies were found in 3.4% (2/59) of children who developed long COVID versus none of 19 children who fully recovered, a difference that was not statistically significant.
Among children hospitalized for long COVID, females predominated significantly (76.9% vs 23.1%), whereas no sex difference was seen in the other study groups.

A case report describes an 11-year-old boy with obesity and allergic rhinitis who had critical COVID-19 pneumonia with marked inflammatory changes (NLR 18.8, CRP 95.5 mg/l, D-dimer 6.7 µg/ml), was found positive for anti-IFN-α antibodies, and subsequently developed long COVID with fatigue, reduced activity, tachycardia, chest pain and abdominal pain.

A second case report describes a 13.8-year-old girl with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (fever, sore throat, anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia) who was positive for anti-IFN-α antibodies and later developed long COVID with fatigue, reduced appetite, insomnia, headaches, cognitive difficulty, weight loss, tachycardia and dizziness.

In adults, high-titer neutralizing autoantibodies against IFN-α2 and IFN-ω were found in about 10% of patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia, versus 0.33% of healthy individuals and none with mild/asymptomatic COVID-19.
In a larger pediatric cohort (168 severe COVID-19, 199 MIS-C, 45 mild SARS-CoV-2), only one patient had high levels of anti-IFN-α2 antibodies, indicating these are rare in children.
A high percentage (24%) of neutralizing anti-IFN-I autoantibodies was noted in vaccinated adults with breakthrough critical COVID-19 pneumonia.

Among ICU COVID-19 patients, 38% were positive for autoantibodies neutralizing IFN-I (5% neutralizing IFN-α2, 33% neutralizing only IFN-ω), and these patients had more severe disease (higher renal failure, ECMO use, prolonged ventilation/ICU stay) though similar mortality to those without such antibodies.

In an Italian adult cohort, binding anti-IFN-α antibodies were found in 7.5% and neutralizing anti-IFN-α antibodies in 3.6% of COVID-19 patients, with higher prevalence in males and those over 60; among ICU patients, 28.6% had binding and 76.9% had neutralizing antibodies, and neutralizing antibodies correlated with higher CRP, LDH, D-dimer and altered hematological parameters.

Nasal IgA1 autoantibodies against IFN-α were present in over 70% of mild/moderate COVID-19 cases at infection onset, peaked after IFN-α production, declined with recovery, and were associated with robust antiviral immunity, fewer symptoms, and better recovery, suggesting a protective role.

In an adult convalescent SARS-CoV-2 cohort of 215 participants (including 121 with long COVID), IFN-α2 antibodies were detected in only 1.6% (2/215), with no significant difference from general population prevalence.
A Danish study of 279 patients with long COVID and 94 controls with prior mild SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID found IFN-I autoantibodies in 1.8% of long COVID patients versus 3.2% of controls.

A German study of 128 post-COVID patients and 38 asymptomatic controls found only 1.56% positive for non-neutralizing binding anti-IFN-β antibodies and none positive for anti-IFN-α antibodies; IFN-stimulated gene activity showed no correlation with fatigue, suggesting IFN-I impairment is unlikely to underlie post-COVID syndrome in adults.
Pooled analysis of 144 studies estimated the global prevalence of long COVID at 36% among individuals with confirmed COVID-19.
Studies restricted to hospitalized patients showed higher pooled long COVID prevalence than those restricted to nonhospitalized patients.
Long COVID prevalence varied substantially by continent, with South America and Africa showing the highest pooled estimates and North America the lowest.
A US-specific meta-analysis of 19 studies estimated long COVID prevalence at 29%, closely matching an independent nationally representative survey estimate.
Long COVID prevalence increased with longer follow-up time since infection, from 35% at under 1 year to 46% at 1-2 years and 43% at over 2 years.
Pooled long COVID prevalence was higher among females than males across 7 sex-stratified studies.
Pooled long COVID prevalence was lower in nonadults than in adults.
The respiratory subtype was the most prevalent long COVID subtype, affecting 20% of confirmed COVID-19 patients.
General fatigue was among the most prevalent long COVID subtypes, affecting 20% of confirmed COVID-19 patients across 119 studies.
The psychological subtype of long COVID had a pooled prevalence of 18% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
The neurological subtype of long COVID, notable for being uncommon after other respiratory viral infections, had a pooled prevalence of 16% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
The dermatological subtype of long COVID had a pooled prevalence of 12% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Memory problems were the most common individual long COVID symptom, with a pooled prevalence of 11%.
Muscle weakness had a pooled prevalence of 11% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Breathlessness or discomfort in breathing had a pooled prevalence of 8% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Dyspnea or observable breathing difficulty had a pooled prevalence of 7% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Joint pain had a pooled prevalence of 7% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Cough had a pooled prevalence of 6% among confirmed COVID-19 patients.
Brain fog was reported with a pooled prevalence of approximately 4% among confirmed COVID-19 patients, contributing to the cognitive burden of the neurological subtype.
Unvaccinated individuals had significantly higher odds of developing long COVID compared to those who received any vaccination, identified as the strongest of the 11 risk factors examined.
Infection with pre-Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha or Delta) was associated with higher odds of long COVID compared to Omicron infection.
Presence of at least one preexisting comorbidity was associated with higher odds of long COVID.
Preexisting cardiovascular disease was associated with higher odds of long COVID.
Preexisting hypertension was associated with higher odds of long COVID.
Female sex was associated with higher odds of developing long COVID across 33 studies.
Intensive care unit admission during acute COVID-19 was associated with higher odds of developing long COVID.
A sensitivity analysis excluding 79 studies with high risk of bias yielded a pooled long COVID prevalence of 35%, consistent with the primary estimate, supporting robustness of the overall findings.

When restricting to the 3 studies that specifically assessed constant, severe, or unusual fatigue rather than general fatigue, the pooled prevalence dropped substantially from 20% to 7%, illustrating sensitivity of estimates to symptom severity definitions.
A Saudi Arabian study found that just over half of surveyed participants experienced hair loss following COVID-19 infection, particularly those who had high fevers.

A cited review of Long COVID literature notes that autonomic dysregulation (dysautonomia) is often misdiagnosed as a psychiatric or psychological condition because anxiety and depression scales include overlapping autonomic symptoms like tachycardia and fatigue.
Experts estimate that more than 65 million people worldwide remain debilitated, disabled, or bedridden due to Long COVID, even though many others have recovered.

Physician-scientist Dr. Ziyah Al-Aly reported that the rate of new Long COVID diagnoses in 2024 remained on par with rates observed in 2022, indicating continued incidence years after the acute pandemic phase.
In Senate testimony, physician-scientist Dr. Ziyah Al-Aly stated that COVID-19 infection can continue to damage multiple organs for years after the initial illness.
Some COVID-19 survivors exhibit irregular, rapid heartbeats detectable on physical exam, echoing cardiac complications historically noted in influenza survivors.
A Long COVID patient narrative (Vanessa Svihla) described months of chest pain, fatigue, tachycardia, brain fog, headaches, and dizziness following COVID-19 infection.
Loss of smell or taste was recognized as an early indicator of COVID-19 infection during the 2020 and early 2021 pandemic waves.
Between 15% and 29% of COVID-19 patients reported at least one gastrointestinal symptom six months after infection.
Decreased tryptophan synthesis was correlated with increased severity of gastrointestinal symptoms in long COVID patients.
GI manifestations of long COVID were not related to the severity of the initial COVID-19 infection and could occur even after mild infection.
Duration of persistent long COVID symptoms was longer in patients who had severe COVID-19 compared to those with mild or moderate disease.
In adults with non-critical COVID-19, 33.1% had digestive disorders at 30 days post-onset, decreasing to 11.5% still affected at 60 days.
In a cohort followed up to 14 months, loss of taste or smell (20.1%) and diarrhea (6.8%) were the most common persistent GI-related manifestations.
COVID-19 has been identified as a potential trigger for new-onset inflammatory bowel disease in a small subset of long COVID patients.
IBS following SARS-CoV-2 infection is thought to be related to severe mucosal inflammation in the GI tract and altered gut-brain axis communication.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a nine-times higher chance of liver steatosis compared to the control group on multiparametric ultrasound.
Increased liver stiffness on ultrasound positively correlated with elevated biomarkers of liver injury, including ALT and GGT, in post-COVID patients.
At three-month follow-up of 55 COVID-19 cases, 25% had residual pulmonary function abnormalities, 71% had radiological abnormalities, and 15% had exertional dyspnea.

In a cohort of previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 81% had dyspnea three months after acute infection, and 24% had persistent abnormal radiographic findings, despite no comorbidities or smoking history.

At four-week follow-up, residual respiratory symptoms persisted in a subset of patients: 29.01% reported cough, 6.11% chest tightness, and 3.82% dyspnea, despite resolution of initial fever, fatigue, and dyspnea.

Patients with severe COVID-19 had reduced diffusion capacity (DLCO), total lung capacity, forced vital capacity, and FEV1 at four-month follow-up, whereas those with mild/moderate disease had normal average pulmonary function.
At six-month follow-up, diffusion capacity remained reduced at 76% of predicted value, along with lower than expected FEV1 and FVC.
Among 165 patients previously hospitalized for COVID-19, fatigue was the most commonly reported neurological symptom, followed by memory complaints and sleep disorders.
Among 1,230 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 in Wuhan, 52% experienced fatigue and muscle weakness six months after infection.
Among 189 participants, 42 experienced chronic insomnia three months after COVID-19 infection, and six had excessive sleepiness.
Among 31 patients evaluated for ongoing neurological complaints at least three months after COVID-19, 29% had mild cognitive impairment and 23% had visual memory impairment.
Increased body temperature during acute COVID-19 infection and decreased SpO2 were predictive factors for later psychological and cognitive impairments.
Female sex was associated with a significantly increased prevalence of symptomatic fatigue and physio-affective symptoms following COVID-19.
In a Chinese cohort, 26% of participants experienced anxiety and depression months after hospital discharge for COVID-19.
Patients with long COVID had significantly different depression (MADRS) and cognitive (MoCA) scores compared to uninfected healthy controls.
Lung diffusion capacity (DLCO) below 80% predicted was significantly reduced in long COVID patients, especially those with severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
At six-month follow-up, DLCO remained reduced at 76% of predicted, with FEV1 and FVC also lower than expected.
Among 165 patients previously hospitalized for COVID-19, fatigue was the most common reported symptom, followed by memory complaints and sleep disorders.
In a Wuhan cohort of 1,230 patients hospitalized with COVID-19, 52% suffered from fatigue and muscle weakness six months after infection.
In a study of 189 participants, 42 experienced chronic insomnia and six had excessive sleepiness three months after COVID-19 infection.
In 31 patients admitted with ongoing neurological complaints at least three months post-COVID, 29% had mild cognitive impairment and 23% had visual memory impairment.
Other neurologic symptoms among hospitalized COVID-19 survivors included tremors and motor deficits.
Memory and attention deficits corresponded to COVID-19 severity and were more common in older patients, whereas peripheral neuropathy was independent of initial disease severity.
Increased body temperature during acute COVID infection and decreased SpO2 were predictive factors for later psychological and cognitive impairments.
Female sex had a significant effect on physio-affective symptoms, with an increased prevalence of symptomatic fatigue reported in women compared to men.
In a Chinese cohort, 26% of participants suffered anxiety and depression months after hospital discharge for COVID-19.
Long COVID patients scored significantly different from healthy controls on MADRS/MoCA and showed increased gray matter volume in the hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia, and frontotemporal regions.
A 62-year-old man developed post-viral cerebellar ataxia and scanning speech after acute COVID-19, with MRI showing mild cerebellar atrophy that improved after steroid treatment.
A 70-year-old male epileptic patient developed post-infectious cerebellar ataxia five weeks after acute COVID-19, presenting with severe imbalance, tremors, and gait difficulty.
Guillain-Barré syndrome, particularly the acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) form, has been reported in association with COVID-19.
A 32-year-old man with confirmed COVID-19 developed severe axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (GBS) after a prolonged ICU stay, confirmed by EMG/NCS and CSF analysis.
A 61-year-old man with diabetes developed severe axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (GBS) after COVID-19, with absent vibration sensation, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and muscle atrophy.
Heart rate variability was significantly lower in long COVID patients compared to normal COVID patients, indicating autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
A significant association was found between long COVID and elevated plasma proBNP concentrations, suggesting increased myocardial strain or heart failure risk.
Long COVID patients were found to be in a procoagulant state with prolonged elevated D-dimer levels.

In a cross-sectional study of 322 post-COVID clinic patients using the COMPASS-31 questionnaire, 73.6% displayed orthostatic intolerance, with GI, secretomotor, and pupillomotor symptoms also commonly severe.
Among 180 patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms, 39 met ESC criteria for acute pericarditis, and those with pericarditis had more frequent palpitations and arrhythmias.
Compared with healthy controls, COVID-19 patients had significantly higher thrombin potential and peak thrombin, indicating persistent endotheliopathy.

COVID-19 infection has been associated with cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome, most often presenting as the acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) subtype with ascending weakness and sensory loss.

A 32-year-old man with confirmed COVID-19 developed severe axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy consistent with Guillain-Barré syndrome, confirmed by EMG/nerve conduction studies and CSF analysis, following ICU admission for ARDS.

A 61-year-old man with diabetes developed severe axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (GBS) roughly two months after COVID-19 admission, with atrophy of intrinsic hand and foot muscles and loss of deep tendon reflexes.
Heart rate variability was significantly lower in long COVID patients compared to patients who recovered from COVID-19 without long-term symptoms, indicating autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
Plasma proBNP concentrations were significantly associated with long COVID, suggesting elevated myocardial strain or increased risk of heart failure.
Long COVID patients were found to be in a procoagulant state, with prolonged elevation of D-dimer alongside other cardiac biomarkers.

In a cross-sectional study of 322 post-COVID clinic patients using the COMPASS-31 questionnaire, 73.6% displayed orthostatic intolerance, with GI, secretomotor, orthostatic, and pupillomotor domains being the most severely affected.

Among 180 patients with persistent or new-onset symptoms at least 12 weeks after a negative COVID-19 test, shortness of breath (52%), heart palpitations (37%), and chest pain (34%) were the most common symptoms.
Of 180 patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms, 39 (21.7%) met ESC criteria for acute pericarditis, and these patients had more frequent heart palpitations and arrhythmias.
COVID-19 patients had significantly higher thrombin potential and peak thrombin compared with healthy controls, indicating persistent endotheliopathy.

Plasma FVIII:C levels remained significantly increased in COVID-19 patients compared with controls, and these levels correlated with peak thrombin formation, implicating FVIII in sustained thrombin generation.
Von Willebrand factor propeptide (VWFpp) levels were significantly elevated in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with endothelial activation.

A previously healthy 31-year-old woman with a mild COVID-19 infection and no comorbidities developed cardiac arrest and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia as a long COVID complication, with imaging showing pulmonary embolism and infarct and elevated D-dimer.

A previously healthy 40-year-old woman developed a left bundle branch block, palpitations, orthostatic intolerance, and sinus tachycardia attributed to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) three months after recovering from COVID-19.

Patients with moderate/severe COVID-19 reported a higher number of cognitive symptoms at follow-up and had an increased risk of memory complaints, confusion, and loss of dependency compared to those with milder disease.

The association between COVID-19 severity and long-term symptoms was only observed for neurological manifestations, not for symptoms such as myalgia and numbness, suggesting the central nervous system may have heightened vulnerability to SARS-CoV-2.
COVID-19 is proposed to stimulate adrenal release of vasoconstricting catecholamines such as norepinephrine, altering vascular resistance and contributing to cardiac autonomic complications.
Arrhythmias occurring in post-COVID-19 patients have been proposed to be associated with right ventricular dysfunction as well as autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

An estimated 71.3% of the post-hospitalization population reported at least one frequently occurring long COVID symptom, and 91.1% reported at least one symptom present at any frequency, six to 24 months after discharge.
39.3% of the population self-reported having long COVID six to 24 months after hospital discharge.
Fatigue was the most prevalent frequently occurring symptom, reported by 34.0% of the whole population and 57.0-63.1% of those self-reporting long COVID.
PEM was frequently reported by 32.3% of the population and 55.6% of those self-reporting long COVID, a novel prevalence finding for Brazil.
Joint pain was frequently reported by 30.1% of the population and 51.6% of those self-reporting long COVID.
Sleep disturbance was frequently reported by 28.4% of the population and 48.1% of those self-reporting long COVID.
Cognitive impairment (brain fog) was frequently reported by 27.5% of the population and 47.6% of those self-reporting long COVID.

About a quarter of menstruating people, and over a third of those who self-reported long COVID, experienced worsening of symptoms right before or during menstruation, a novel finding for Brazilian long COVID research.

Cis women had over three times the odds of cis men of frequently experiencing post-exertional malaise, and were also at greater risk for frequent fatigue, joint pain, sleep disturbance, and cognitive impairment.
Despite greater symptom burden, cis women and cis men did not differ significantly in the odds of self-reporting long COVID.

Working-age individuals (30-39, 40-49, and 50-59 years) had higher risk of frequently occurring fatigue, PEM, and joint pain than other age groups, while age was not a significant predictor of overall symptom burden, cognitive impairment, or self-reported long COVID.
Black individuals had higher risk of frequently occurring sleep disturbance than other race categories, with no other significant race or socioeconomic effects detected.

Pre-existing comorbidities present before COVID-19 hospitalization, including heart disease, diabetes, asthma/bronchitis, chronic liver disease, immunodepression, and pulmonary disease, were positively associated with the risk of long COVID outcomes.

Pre-existing heart disease and cancer were paradoxically associated with lower odds of self-reporting long COVID, despite these patients reporting a high average number of symptoms (6.2 and 5.9, respectively), suggesting attribution bias due to prior diagnosis.

Number of long COVID symptoms, number of pre-existing comorbidities, and use of ventilatory support during COVID-19 hospitalization were each positively associated with self-reported long COVID; ventilatory support was also linked to increased odds of frequent cognitive impairment.

Vaccination status at hospitalization showed no protective effect on long COVID outcomes, but being fully vaccinated or having received a booster dose by the time of interview was associated with a protective effect against long COVID symptoms/self-report.
The seven logistic regression models predicting frequent symptom/self-reported LC outcomes showed moderate discriminative accuracy, with c-statistics ranging from 0.62 to 0.82.
The prevalence of self-reported long COVID decreased modestly from about 44.5% at six and 12 months post-discharge to approximately 39.0% at 18 and 24 months.

Pre-existing asthma/bronchitis was associated with frequent joint pain reporting, which the authors interpret as biologically plausible given known shared inflammatory pathogenesis between osteoarthritis and asthma.
Among 107 farmworkers surveyed, 25 (23.26%) had been diagnosed with COVID-19, a prevalence similar to the estimated 19.20% rate in the general Brazilian population.

Among diagnosed farmworkers, the most frequently reported acute COVID-19 symptoms were tiredness (84%), fever (68%), coughing (68%), loss of sense of taste (68%), headache (68%), and sore throat (64%).
None of the farmworkers diagnosed with COVID-19 required hospital admission.
Persistent symptoms after recovery from COVID-19 were reported by 52% of participants, most commonly tiredness (24%) and shortness of breath (16%).
Farmworkers with hypertension showed a higher prevalence of COVID-19 diagnosis compared to those without hypertension.
Farmworkers with cancer showed a higher prevalence of COVID-19 diagnosis compared to those without cancer.
Obesity showed the strongest positive association with COVID-19 diagnosis among the risk factors assessed in this farmworker sample.
Diabetes was negatively associated with COVID-19 diagnosis in this sample, contrary to the expected direction seen in other populations.
A prevalence ratio for smoking and COVID-19 could not be calculated because none of the smokers in the sample had been diagnosed with the disease.
The most common health problems in the overall farmworker sample were hypertension (38.31%), dyslipidemia (38.31%), and depression (30.28%).
A genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 2 near ACKR3 (CXCR7) was associated with hEDS risk, with lead variant rs2708184 conferring an odds ratio of 1.29.

A second genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 8 (~540kb from KCNV1) showed the strongest statistical association with hEDS, though no clear regulatory features implicating a specific target gene were identified.
Gene-based association testing identified SLC39A13 (zinc transporter ZIP13) as significantly associated with hEDS susceptibility, with a common missense variant p.Thr20Ala predicted to be benign.
Gene-based association analysis identified five Bonferroni-significant genes (including PDGFRL and ACACA) independent of the single-variant GWAS loci, indicating additional risk loci for hEDS.

TWAS combined with Mendelian Randomization showed that higher genetically-predicted CFDP1 expression, consistent across blood, nerve, lung, heart, arteries, colon and skin, causally increases hEDS risk.
TWAS/MR identified increased blood MADD expression as associated with elevated hEDS risk, with high posterior probability (87%) of a shared causal variant.
Decreased genetically-predicted PSMC3 expression in heart and skin was associated with increased hEDS risk, with high posterior probability (>94%) of a shared causal allele across both tissues.
The hEDS risk allele (C) of rs2600746 was associated with reduced ACKR3 expression specifically in tibial nerve, colocalizing with the hEDS GWAS signal.

The hEDS risk allele of rs2600746 creates a novel AHR transcription factor consensus binding site and confers AHR-dependent enhancer activity, confirmed experimentally by luciferase reporter assays in fibroblasts.
hEDS showed a substantial positive genetic correlation with joint hypermobility, its most commonly reported clinical feature.
hEDS showed its most significant comorbidity genetic correlation with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, reported by ~20-30% of patients in the meta-analysis.
hEDS showed a robust positive genetic correlation with chronic pain, reported by 73-91% of patients.
hEDS showed a nominally significant genetic correlation with fibromyalgia.
hEDS showed a significant genetic correlation with irritable bowel syndrome, consistent with the high burden of GI symptoms reported by >80% of patients.
hEDS showed a significant genetic correlation with gastroesophageal reflux disease.
hEDS showed a nominally significant genetic correlation with gastroparesis.
hEDS showed a significant genetic correlation with migraine, a condition reported by 50-68% of patients.
hEDS showed a significant genetic correlation with major depressive disorder, reported by 51-63% of patients.
hEDS showed a nominally significant genetic correlation with autism spectrum disorder, a comorbidity reported by ~10% of patients.
Despite being reported by 64-76% of hEDS patients, anxiety disorders did not show a significant genetic correlation with hEDS.

hEDS did not show significant genetic correlations with structural/vascular manifestations including mitral valve prolapse, tricuspid valve disease, pelvic organ prolapse, or specific hernia subtypes, despite their frequent clinical reporting.
27 of 68 pediatric headache outpatients (39%) were diagnosed with secondary headache as the main illness.
Among secondary headache patients, boys (n=20) significantly outnumbered girls (n=7).
Family history of headache was present in 74% (20/27) of secondary headache patients.
Headache frequency was described as almost daily in 67% (18/27) of secondary headache patients.
Social anxiety disorder (SAD) was the most common cause of secondary headache, diagnosed in 13 of 27 patients, and all SAD patients also had autism spectrum disorder as a comorbidity.
Orthostatic dysregulation (a homeostatic disorder) was diagnosed as the secondary headache cause in 9 of 27 patients, coinciding with adolescent age of onset.
Facial organ-related headache (FORH) was the diagnosed cause of secondary headache in 3 of 27 patients.
Nonvascular intracranial disease was the diagnosed cause of secondary headache in 2 of 27 patients.
Autism spectrum disorder was a comorbidity in 18 of the 27 secondary headache patients.
School refusal was noted as a comorbidity in 8 of the 27 secondary headache patients.
Nine of the autism spectrum disorder patients received their ASD diagnosis only after presenting to the headache outpatient clinic.
All patients diagnosed with social anxiety disorder as their secondary headache diagnosis also had comorbid autism spectrum disorder.
The predominance of adolescent patients in the secondary headache cohort coincided with the typical age of onset for orthostatic dysregulation.

Facial temperature fluctuations are correlated with the emotional and social cognitive states of children with ASD, and consistent thermoregulatory variations across sessions have been linked to improvements in core ASD symptoms and brain connectivity.
Deep-learning emotion-state classifiers trained on thermal imaging datasets of children with ASD achieved accuracy rates exceeding 90% in distinguishing ASD from neurotypical children.
A CNN-based model classified autistic children from thermal facial features with 96% precision.
Two studies combined EEG data with facial thermography to classify ASD patients versus neurotypical individuals, improving detection accuracy and reliability.

Across the 27 included studies, machine learning methods (CNN, linear discriminant analysis, Bayes, Random Forest) applied to IRT data classified emotional or diagnostic mental-health states with accuracy up to 98%.

Across reviewed emotional-disorder studies, anxiety was associated with increased temperature in temporal, frontal, and nasal-tip regions, while depression was linked to higher core body temperature, elevated right periorbital temperature, and reduced thermoregulatory efficiency; both conditions increased periorbital temperature.

The authors note that infrared thermography may lack specificity for detecting emotional changes, as temperature changes are not always directly related to psychologically induced physiological reactions, limiting its stand-alone diagnostic use.

About three-quarters of patients with post-COVID conditions had at least one pre-existing comorbid condition (most commonly hypertension, obesity, and smoking history), and nearly a third had three or more comorbidities.
The most common presenting symptoms at post-COVID follow-up visits were shortness of breath, post-exertional malaise, fatigue, and brain fog.

More than half of patients who underwent physical examination had no abnormal findings at any visit, while 42.6% had at least one abnormality such as hypoxemia, need for supplemental oxygen, sensory loss, rash, hearing loss, or abnormal mental status.

Standardized screening tests for depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, pain, and sleep disorders were abnormal in the majority of the 468 patients screened, whereas PTSD screening was abnormal in only a small minority.
Among imaging modalities used at follow-up, chest CT scans had the highest abnormality rate, while cardiac imaging had the lowest.
Serum glucose was the most frequently abnormal laboratory test among long COVID clinic patients with documented labs.
Serum albumin was abnormal in nearly a third of long COVID clinic patients with documented laboratory tests.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate was abnormal in about a third of long COVID clinic patients with documented laboratory tests.
The single most common diagnosis assigned at post-COVID follow-up visits was post-viral fatigue syndrome, given to 30.1% of patients.

Pulmonary system diagnoses (e.g., pneumonia, fibrosis, restrictive pulmonary disease, pulmonary artery hypertension, pulmonary embolism, and worsening of prior chronic pulmonary disease) were common in this post-COVID clinic population.
Patients attended a median of 3 post-COVID follow-up visits (range 1-46) across a combined 3,914 visits, with 24.1% having only one visit and 5.9% having more than 10 visits.
Nearly two-thirds of patients visited subspecialty care during follow-up, most commonly pulmonology, cardiology, and neurology.
The proportion of patients referred to subspecialty care rose steadily with the number of visits, ranging from about a quarter of single-visit patients to all patients with more than 10 visits.
About 38% of patients had at least one rehabilitation therapy visit during follow-up, most commonly physical therapy, followed by speech therapy and psychotherapy.
Rehabilitation therapy was prescribed more often to patients with 5 or more visits than to those with 1-4 visits.
Nearly 9% of patients were hospitalized at least once during the post-COVID follow-up period.
A cited study suggested that patients with post-COVID conditions may have poorer physical/functional health and greater healthcare utilization than patients in cancer rehabilitation.
Experts reported that post-COVID condition disproportionately affects women, in contrast to severe acute COVID-19 which disproportionately affected men.
Patients racialised as 'migrants' were reported as almost entirely absent from post-COVID specialist clinics despite having been over-represented among those with severe acute COVID-19.

One expert estimated that 2-5% of all children experience post-COVID condition, a burden comparable to concussion, with most recovering spontaneously within months but a subpopulation suffering longer.

Some experts attributed the over-representation of middle-aged women among post-COVID patients to a pre-existing history of unexplained pain/ME, burnout, depression, and anxiety, conditions in which the same demographic is also over-represented.

Some patient advocates and doctors argued that post-COVID represents an ongoing disease process caused by residual virus, rather than a post-infectious sequela, citing patients with prolonged fever lasting years.
Other experts argued post-COVID is not a novel disease but resembles long-lasting fatigue previously observed after other infections such as MERS, SARS, and influenza.

Experts warned that generic exercise recommendations for fatigue and depressed mood, which overlap with burnout and depression treatment, could be harmful for post-COVID patients with underlying heart rate regulation problems, underscoring the need for accurate diagnosis before treatment.

Sweden's 2024 governmental report on post-COVID recommended primary care and rehabilitation as the main approach and emphasised similarities with other post-infectious conditions, a conclusion criticised by some as inconsistent with international policy and evidence.
Experts suggested elderly patients with post-COVID may be underdiagnosed because fatigue and weakness are attributed to normal ageing rather than to a prior COVID-19 infection.

Physical symptoms such as persistent pain, fatigue, and movement difficulty, and mood disorders such as depression, mood swings, hopelessness, and concentration difficulty are described as significant predictors of PASC.

Middle-aged and older adults with chronic health conditions such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory illness, and diabetes are described as facing extreme risk and severe consequences from PASC.
Among 3143 nationally sampled Rwandan COVID-19 survivors, 1076 (34%) met the WHO case definition for PASC.

The most frequently reported PASC symptoms were back pain, headache, dizziness/lightheadedness, fatigue, changes in sexual desire/capacity, limb muscle weakness, vision problems, and confusion or reduced concentration.
Infection during the Delta wave was associated with the highest proportion of PASC (38.9%) compared with the pre-Delta period (23.9%) and the Omicron period (29.5%).
In bivariate analysis, female sex was significantly associated with higher likelihood of PASC.
Older age (35 years and above) was significantly associated with higher likelihood of PASC in both bivariate and multivariate analyses.
Anxiety was the strongest independent predictor of PASC in the multivariate model, with nearly threefold higher odds among those with anxiety.
Current alcohol consumption was associated with lower odds of PASC in the multivariate model.
In the multivariate model, infection during the Delta wave was associated with higher adjusted odds of PASC than pre-Delta infection.
Infection during the Omicron wave was also associated with higher adjusted odds of PASC than pre-Delta infection, though less than Delta.
COVID-19 vaccination status and number of doses received were not significantly associated with PASC in either bivariate or multivariate analysis.
Individuals with hypertension had a higher unadjusted rate of PASC than those without.
Individuals with HIV had a higher unadjusted rate of PASC than those without.
Individuals with chronic kidney disease had a higher unadjusted rate of PASC than those without.
Individuals with rheumatoid arthritis had a higher unadjusted rate of PASC than those without.
Individuals with depression had a higher unadjusted rate of PASC than those without.
In bivariate analysis, individuals with anxiety disorders had a markedly higher rate of PASC than those without.
Higher educational attainment (high school or university) was associated with lower likelihood of reporting PASC compared with no formal education.

PASC caused mild-to-moderate limitations in work, family, and social life for roughly one-quarter to one-third of affected respondents, with about one-fifth reporting marked or extreme disruption, particularly in work and social interactions.
Having more than one COVID-19 episode (reinfection) and hospitalization during acute COVID-19 were significantly associated with higher likelihood of PASC in both bivariate and multivariate models.
Residing in Rwanda's Eastern Province was independently associated with higher likelihood of PASC in the multivariate model.
COVID-19 vaccines are reported to maintain a robust safety profile, with rare adverse events including myocarditis and thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome.
Long COVID (post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection) affects an estimated 10-40% of SARS-CoV-2 survivors, with symptoms including fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and dyspnea.

The review concludes that differentiating vaccine-related adverse events from long COVID relies on timing of symptom onset, detailed symptom characterization, and advanced diagnostic tools, requiring systematic clinical assessment.
During acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and for up to 30 days afterward, beneficial gut commensals were significantly reduced, correlating with elevated inflammatory markers and disease severity.

Hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed decline of Faecalibacterium (inversely correlated with severity) alongside overabundance of Coprococcus, Clostridium ramosum, and Clostridium hathewayi that correlated with disease severity.

Individuals who developed long COVID had a distinct acute-phase gut microbial composition differing from both COVID-19-positive patients who did not develop long COVID and healthy controls, with increased Anaerovoracaceae, Acutalibacteraceae, Blautia, Schaedlerella, Massilimaliae, Faecalimonas, and Ruthenibacterium, and taxa including Eubacterium, Lachnoclostridium, Prevotella, Carnobacterium, Weissella, and Lachnospiraceae predicting subsequent long COVID more strongly than fecal calprotectin.
A three-month follow-up study of post-acute COVID-19 patients found decreases in the Chao index, Simpson index, and overall alpha-diversity, indicating microbial depletion.

Six-month follow-up studies showed persistently reduced gut microbial richness versus uninfected controls, and even mild COVID-19 was associated with significant depletion of the gut-barrier-supporting bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila.

Persistence of a Streptococcus-dominated enterotype (Enterotype-S) at six months was associated with a higher incidence of residual pulmonary abnormalities on CT (55%) compared to a Blautia-dominated enterotype (Enterotype-B, 20%).

In a study of 106 patients with persistent symptoms, F. prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium spp. decreased while Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus increased; F. prausnitzii and B. pseudocatenulatum showed the strongest inverse correlation with long COVID development.
In a large gut metagenomic study of 2871 participants, depletion of Eubacterium rectale was associated with increased COVID-19 mortality.

At phylum level, COVID-19 patients showed increased Firmicutes and Proteobacteria and decreased Bacteroidetes relative to healthy controls; at genus level, Streptococcus and Veillonella were more prevalent in COVID-19 patients while Prevotella was more abundant in non-COVID controls.

A study comparing COVID-19 patients with and without long COVID found enrichment of potentially pathogenic taxa including Campylobacterota, Coriobacteriales, Pseudomonadales, and Campylobacterales in those with long COVID.

In outpatients vaccinated with mixed COVID-19 vaccine regimens, 37% developed long COVID, and these patients had elevated oral Prevotella and Veillonella species (LPS producers); the long COVID oral microbiome resembled that seen in ME/CFS patients.

In a six-month Hong Kong follow-up study, neuropsychiatric symptoms and fatigue were associated with enrichment of C. innocuum and A. naeslundii, while persistent respiratory symptoms were linked to increased Streptococcus and Clostridium species.

An acute-phase microbial cluster with elevated R. gnavus, E. coli, Veillonella, and Streptococcus and decreased F. prausnitzii and Eubacterium was significantly associated with reduced lung function (lower FEV1, FVC, impaired CO2 diffusion) at six months and more severe acute illness with higher ICU admission rates.

Patients with a gastrointestinal symptom cluster in long COVID showed elevated Neisseria, Lautropia, and Agrobacterium along with toxic serum metabolites (4-chlorophenylacetic acid, 5-sulfoxymethylfurfural, estradiol valerate).
Decreased Akkermansia abundance correlated with increased myeloid progenitor inhibitory factor 1 (MPIF-1) and IL-17 in post-acute COVID-19 patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Eubacterium hallii showed a significant negative correlation with circulating MCP-1, MIP-1b, IFN-α2, IL-10, and IL-8, while IL-6 remained elevated throughout a one-year study period in long COVID patients.

Long COVID patients with predominant fatigue and gastrointestinal symptoms displayed persistent IL-6 elevation alongside gastrointestinal barrier dysfunction marked by elevated lipopolysaccharide binding protein (LBP), indicating metabolic endotoxemia.

Gut microbiome-derived L-tryptophan biosynthesis was reduced two-fold in individuals with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms acutely and in those with persistent mental health symptoms post-acutely; serotonin levels were five times lower in patients with long-term neuropsychiatric symptoms than in those with GI symptoms alone.
Serum tryptophan and its microbial metabolite indole-3-propionate negatively correlated with proinflammatory cytokines during both the acute and post-acute phases of COVID-19.

Germ-free mice receiving fecal transplants from long COVID patients developed long-COVID-like symptoms, and subsequent administration of Bifidobacterium longum partially reversed cognitive impairments and respiratory dysfunction, supporting a directly contributory role of dysbiosis.

In the SIM01 trial, six-month supplementation with a Bifidobacterium-based synbiotic improved fatigue, mental fog, and gastrointestinal symptoms in long COVID patients compared to placebo, enriching SCFA-producing bacteria; higher B. longum levels were associated with improved cognitive function.
Three months of a multi-strain synbiotic (L. rhamnosus, L. plantarum, B. lactis, B. longum, fructooligosaccharides, zinc) significantly reduced fatigue during the post-acute phase of COVID-19.
A meta-analysis found gut microbiome alterations were greatest approximately 7–30 days after COVID-19 diagnosis, after which the microbiome began to restore toward a more favorable state.
In severe COVID-19, downregulation of gut ACE2 may contribute to microbial dysbiosis and impaired intestinal barrier function.
Murine studies showed Bacteroides spp. downregulate ACE2 expression in the gut, and their abundance inversely correlates with fecal SARS-CoV-2 viral load.
Studies have shown that microbiome-targeting interventions, particularly with Bifidobacterium, may improve cognitive function in individuals with mild cognitive impairment.

Gut microbiome-derived L-tryptophan biosynthesis was reduced two-fold in individuals with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms during acute COVID-19 and in those with persistent mental health symptoms post-acutely.
Among patients with long-term neuropsychiatric symptoms, serotonin levels were five times lower than in patients with gastrointestinal symptoms alone.
Serum levels of tryptophan and indole-3-propionate negatively correlate with proinflammatory cytokines during both the acute and post-acute phases of COVID-19.

Persistent viral antigens in the gut mucosa may sustain adaptive immune activation, including stimulation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells that can cross-react with the gut microbiota, contributing to ongoing long COVID symptoms.

Autoantibody production has been correlated with a range of post-acute symptoms including respiratory, vasomotor, and neurological manifestations, and may be promoted by persistent viral antigens and SARS-CoV-2 superantigens via molecular mimicry and epitope spreading.
Neurological symptoms in post-acute COVID-19 have been associated with increased CD4+ T cell responses and reduced CD8+ T cell activity targeting the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein.

Oral pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis produce proteases that mimic furin activity and can activate the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, potentially enhancing infectivity and viral persistence in the oral cavity.

In germ-free mice that developed long-COVID-like symptoms after fecal transplants from long COVID patients, administration of Bifidobacterium longum partially reversed cognitive impairments and respiratory dysfunction.
In a one-year follow-up study, alpha diversity metrics were able to differentiate individuals with long COVID from those without, supporting alpha diversity as a candidate biomarker.
The Prevotella-to-Bifidobacterium ratio in saliva and the R. gnavus-to-F. prausnitzii ratio in stool have been proposed as potential microbial biomarkers of long COVID, pending further validation.
In the SIM01 trial, patients showing clinical improvement had fewer gut microbial genes related to antibiotic resistance and greater abundance of genes involved in beneficial metabolite production.

Individuals with higher adherence to the Mediterranean diet had lower levels of gut Oscillobacter and more favorable lactate dehydrogenase concentrations, proposed as a mechanism for reduced inflammation in long COVID.
In murine models, supplementation with the prebiotic inulin improved COVID-19 outcomes by modifying gut microbial composition and increasing levels of deoxycholic acid.

Addition of polyphenols and phytochemicals from fruits and vegetables to probiotic regimens resulted in a two-fold reduction in fatigue, three-fold reduction in cough, and two-fold improvement in quality-of-life scores compared to probiotics alone.

Curcumin treatment (~10 µg/mL) in Vero E6 cell assays demonstrated approximately 99% viral inhibition against both D614G and Delta SARS-CoV-2 variants and suppressed proinflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8 in PBMC assays.

A curcumin-based oro-nasal film spray prevented SARS-CoV-2 infection at low micromolar concentrations (EC5 = 3.15 µg/mL) without causing epithelial cell death, and induced expression of antimicrobial peptides and markers of innate mucosal immunity.

Kaempferol was shown in vitro and in silico to block spike-mediated membrane fusion by disrupting the heptad repeat fusion machinery and viral proteases such as the main protease, and to inhibit oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling (NF-κB, MAPK).

Pinosylvin, a stilbenoid related to resveratrol, has shown antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory actions in other contexts and was identified as a prospective viral protein binder in phytochemical screening, but has limited direct in vitro or animal data for COVID-19.

Three months of supplementation with a synbiotic formulation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus, L. plantarum, Bifidobacterium lactis, B. longum, fructooligosaccharides, and zinc) significantly reduced fatigue during the post-acute phase of COVID-19, accompanied by decreased post-exertional malaise and increased neurotransmitter concentrations in the thalamus and frontal lobes.

Hospitalized COVID-19 patients who received probiotics showed significant increases in beneficial metabolites (arginine, asparagine, lactate) and reductions in 3-hydroxyisobutyrate, with a lower proportion reporting fatigue at follow-up.

Six months of probiotic supplementation increased stool concentrations of dopamine metabolites and butyrate, alongside partial improvements in quality of life and beneficial modulation of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae.

In a trial of encapsulated microbiota transplant for post-COVID-19 fatigue and insomnia, insomnia severity index improved markedly after 12 weeks, with 38% achieving remission versus 10% in controls, along with reductions in blood cortisol and shifts toward donor-like gut microbiota profiles.

In patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 symptoms, microbiota transplantation led to improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, as well as neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression.

In HIV-1-infected individuals, the antiretroviral combination lopinavir/ritonavir has been shown to significantly alter gut microbial composition, including shifts in major phyla and marked reductions in beneficial genera such as Lachnospira, Butyricicoccus, Oscillospira, and Prevotella, raising concerns about confounding in COVID-19 microbiome studies.

Some evidence suggests microbiome imbalances in long COVID may normalize beyond one year post-infection, while other studies indicate dysbiosis can persist 18 months or longer, similar to observations in chronic fatigue syndrome.
A U.S. study found long COVID patients had higher abundances of Bacteroides and Blautia, alongside decreased levels of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium.

Surveys in Saudi Arabia and Egypt found substantial pandemic-related increases in food/snack consumption, weight gain, decreased physical activity, and low Mediterranean diet adherence, which are confounding factors that could contribute to observed gut dysbiosis independent of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The 6-week Adapted Physical Activity (APA) protocol was associated with significant improvement in the physical component of health-related quality of life over time.
The APA protocol was associated with significant improvement in the mental component of health-related quality of life over time.
Anxiety symptoms decreased significantly following the APA protocol, with sustained improvement at medium-term follow-up.
Depression symptoms decreased significantly following the APA protocol, with sustained improvement at medium-term follow-up.
Dyspnea prevalence decreased substantially after the APA protocol, sustained at medium-term follow-up.
Greater dyspnea severity was associated with lower overall quality of life at both baseline and medium-term follow-up.
Non-smokers reported higher physical and mental quality-of-life scores than smokers at certain assessment points.
Smokers exhibited significantly higher anxiety and depression scores than non-smokers.
Quality of life and psychological distress were strongly inversely correlated across all assessment time points, indicating interdependence of physical and mental recovery.
Greater initial COVID-19 severity was associated with worse quality of life and more anxiety/depression outcomes during follow-up.
Patients treated in intensive care units during acute illness had the worst subsequent quality of life and psychological outcomes compared to home care.
Longer hospital stay during acute COVID-19 was associated with worse subsequent quality of life and greater anxiety/depression.
Specific persistent long COVID symptoms, including effort dyspnea, rest dyspnea, myalgia, and memory disorders, were associated with poorer quality of life and greater anxiety/depression.
Common comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension showed only weak, non-significant correlations with HRQOL and anxiety/depression scores.
No baseline demographic or clinical factor (age, sex, BMI, disease severity, smoking) independently predicted anxiety or depression scores at follow-up in multivariate regression.
Individuals with Long COVID had significantly higher COMPASS 31 total autonomic symptom burden scores than recovered COVID comparators.
Individuals with Long COVID had significantly higher orthostatic domain sub-scores than recovered comparators.
A majority of Long COVID participants experienced symptoms during tilt table testing, whereas none of the recovered comparators did.
Higher orthostatic domain scores were associated with greater odds of experiencing symptoms during tilt table testing.
Baseline supine heart rate trended higher in Long COVID participants compared to recovered comparators, though not statistically significant.
Average heart rate across all tilt-table timepoints was significantly higher in Long COVID participants than recovered comparators.
The rate of heart rate change over the course of tilt testing did not differ significantly between Long COVID and recovered participants.
Baseline systolic blood pressure and its change during tilt did not differ significantly between Long COVID and recovered participants.
Diastolic blood pressure and its response to tilt did not differ between Long COVID and recovered groups.
No participants in either the Long COVID or recovered groups met consensus heart rate criteria for POTS during head-up tilt table testing.

Three Long COVID participants exhibited clinically abnormal hemodynamic responses during tilt testing: one orthostatic hypotension, one delayed orthostatic hypotension, and one delayed cardioinhibitory/vasovagal presyncope.
Peak oxygen consumption on cardiopulmonary exercise testing was substantially lower in Long COVID participants than recovered comparators.
Adjusted heart rate reserve, a measure of chronotropic response during exercise, trended lower among Long COVID participants but did not reach statistical significance.
Heart rate recovery at 1 minute post-exercise trended lower in Long COVID participants but was not statistically significant.
Heart rate variability on ambulatory monitoring trended lower in Long COVID participants than recovered comparators, though not statistically significant.
Echocardiographic measures of cardiac structure and function did not differ between Long COVID and recovered participants, arguing against cardiac deconditioning as a mechanism.
Among Long COVID participants, COMPASS 31 total scores did not differ based on whether they reported symptoms with position change.
Orthostatic domain scores did not differ based on self-reported presence of symptoms with position change, suggesting a mismatch between self-report and validated instrument scores.
One Long COVID participant experienced an episode of post-exertional malaise that was triggered by the tilt table test itself.
Beta-testers reported that the reCOVer app increased their awareness of unhelpful boom-bust activity patterns and supported behaviour change through pacing.
Communication and assertiveness tools within the app were reported as valuable by participants experiencing prominent cognitive difficulties associated with long-COVID.
Participants identified areas for improvement in reCOVer, including adding text-to-speech functionality, clarifying goal-setting instructions, and better articulating the app's benefits.

Intermittent hypoxic exposure (IHE) is proposed to alleviate Long COVID symptoms by improving ventilatory function, enhancing cardiopulmonary endurance, modulating immune responses, and reducing inflammation.
Meta-analysis of two studies (post-EBV and post-SARS-CoV-2) found circulating RANTES (CCL5) significantly elevated in PIFS cases compared to recovered controls at 6-12 months post-infection.
Meta-analysis of two post-SARS-CoV-2 studies found circulating TNFα significantly elevated in PIFS/Long COVID cases compared to recovered controls at 6-12 months post-infection.
Meta-analysis of three post-EBV studies found total white blood cell count significantly increased in PIFS cases versus recovered controls at 3-6 months post-infection.

Across 16 studies of circulating cytokines/chemokines, meta-analyses at the 0-1 month and 3-6 month post-infection windows found no significant differences between PIFS cases and recovered controls for most cytokines and chemokines assessed.
Two individual studies (one post-EBV, one post-SARS-CoV-2) found higher neutrophil counts in PIFS cases compared to recovered controls at 12-24 months, though not at earlier timepoints.
Meta-analysis of two post-EBV studies found no significant differences in CD4+ or CD8+ T-lymphocyte subset counts between PIFS cases and recovered controls at 3-6 months.
Meta-analysis of pathogen-specific serology (EBNA IgG, VCA IgG, VCA IgM) found no significant differences between PIFS cases and recovered controls at 3-6 months post-EBV infection.

Across five studies of leucocyte gene expression (RNA sequencing and microarray) in PBMCs, no data were suitable for meta-analysis and no consistent significant differences in gene expression were found between PIFS cases and recovered controls.

Across nine studies investigating immunoglobulin levels and autoantibodies as predictors of PIFS, no consistent significant findings were observed comparing PIFS cases to recovered or healthy controls.

In a study of post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, serum CCL-19 was persistently elevated in PIFS cases compared to recovered controls from baseline through 12 months, and predicted subsequent PIFS development.
In an EBV-triggered cohort, higher baseline high-sensitivity CRP was associated with subsequent development of PIFS at 6 months.
In a SARS-CoV-2 cohort, lower baseline lymphocyte/leucocyte count and IL-7 levels were associated with decreased relative risk of developing PIFS at 6 months.

Among Long COVID studies excluded for lacking a formal PIFS case definition, several found increased frequencies of SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in Long COVID cases, though not consistently across all such studies.

Overall, the systematic review of 30 high-quality studies found largely inconsistent or negative immunological findings across biomarker categories, with only WBC count, RANTES, and TNFα showing significant elevation in PIFS versus recovered controls, providing only cautious support for a persistent immune activation hypothesis.
Long COVID participants had higher Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores than short COVID and COVID-negative participants.
Long COVID participants had 1.58-fold higher odds of clinically significant excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS>10) compared with the reference group.
Long COVID participants had higher Fatigue Severity Scale scores than short COVID and COVID-negative participants.
Long COVID participants had 2.22-fold higher odds of severe fatigue compared with the reference group.
Long COVID cases reported more excessive quantity of sleep (≥10 hours per 24h) than COVID-negative participants.
During the pandemic, long COVID participants reported greater worsening of excessive daytime sleepiness, fatigue, sleep inertia, and napping than other groups.
Pooled analysis found anxiety was among the most common mental health symptoms of long COVID, with a prevalence of 31% and the longest average duration among mental health symptoms at 3.8 months.
Depression was one of the most common long COVID mental health symptoms, with a pooled prevalence of 31% and mean duration of 3.5 months.
There was no statistically significant difference between the pooled prevalence of depression and anxiety among long COVID patients.
Somnipathy (sleep disorder) in the mental health symptom category had a mean reported duration of 3 months in long COVID patients.
Diarrhoea was the only digestive symptom reported in the meta-analysis, with a pooled prevalence of 12.7% and low heterogeneity, persisting for a mean of 2 months.
The two digestive-symptom studies did not differ significantly from each other in reported prevalence.

Shortness of breath was the most influential respiratory symptom in the pooled analysis (59.7% weighting), with a prevalence of 24% and the longest respiratory symptom duration, averaging 6.52 months across 10 studies.
Chest distress had a pooled prevalence of 23% among long COVID patients, persisting for a mean of 2 months.
Persistent cough was reported by 11% of patients in a single included study, lasting up to 2 months.
Fever-like/influenza symptoms were reported by 16-17% of individuals across two studies in long COVID.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported neurological symptom of long COVID, carrying the highest weight (47.2%) in the pooled analysis, with a prevalence of 34% and a mean duration of 5.5 months.
Cognitive/memory/attention impairment was a common neurological symptom of long COVID, with a prevalence of 36% and mean duration of 6.34 months.
Olfactory dysfunction (loss of smell) was reported in 21% of long COVID patients, with a mean duration of 6.25 months.
Taste disorders were reported in 20% of long COVID patients, with the longest average duration among neurological symptoms at 8 months.
There was no significant difference in prevalence among the pooled neurological symptom subgroups (fatigue, cognitive impairment, olfactory, taste, sleep).
Sleep disturbance, classified under neurological symptoms, had a mean duration of 5.57 months in long COVID patients.
Musculoskeletal/joint pain, including headache and chest pain, was the most frequently reported symptom in the 'other symptoms' category, with a prevalence of 15% and mean duration of 5 months.
Loss of appetite was the most common symptom in the 'other symptoms' category, with a prevalence of 22% and a mean duration of 4 months, higher (though not significantly) than the prevalence of pain.
Activity barriers and word-finding difficulties were the longest-lasting long COVID symptoms identified, persisting up to 12 months, though based on single studies only and not meta-analysed.
Weight loss was reported as a long COVID symptom with a shorter duration of impact, lasting about 2 months, based on a single study.

Overall, approximately 13-28% of long COVID patients experienced persistent symptoms lasting 2-12 months after diagnosis, including fever, sore throat, cough, muscle/body pain, loss of taste or smell, and diarrhoea.

SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers sustained secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in lung alveoli, activating fibroblasts and driving collagen/fibronectin deposition and pulmonary fibrosis.
Chronic lung inflammation drives secretion of TGF-β1, which stimulates fibroblasts to upregulate collagen gene expression, causing stiffening and remodeling of lung tissue.
Imaging studies show that DLCO remains reduced for months after recovery in Long COVID patients, confirming ongoing impairment of gas exchange.
Elevated factor VIII, D-dimer, fibrinogen, and sICAM-1 levels have been reported in Long COVID patients, reflecting a hypercoagulable state that drives alveolar capillary microthrombosis.
Long COVID patients often show elevated von Willebrand factor, ICAM-1, and E-selectin, markers of endothelial activation, together with reduced nitric oxide availability promoting vasospasm.
Cardiac MRI in Long COVID patients shows increased T2-weighted signal intensity indicating myocardial inflammation and late gadolinium enhancement indicating fibrosis and necrosis.
Some Long COVID patients develop autoantibodies targeting cardiac antigens, causing sustained immune-mediated injury to myocardial cells resembling virus-induced inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

Long COVID patients with reduced heart rate variability have a higher risk of dysautonomia and arrhythmias, reflecting impaired autonomic hemodynamic control.

The risk of developing new-onset hypertension after COVID-19 is higher than after other viral illnesses including influenza, with hypertension-related disorders remaining common even in previously normotensive individuals.
