Among 6,572 surveyed participants, 85.91% reported testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 following relaxation of China's zero-COVID policy.
Among SARS-CoV-2 positive participants, 96.79% reported symptoms, with fever, cough, fatigue, pharyngeal discomfort, and body soreness being most common.
A subset of infected individuals experienced long COVID symptoms, with palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath most likely to persist beyond 90 days.
The number of vaccine doses received significantly affected SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate, with positivity increasing across 1-3 doses but lowest among those who received 4 doses.
After adjustment for confounders, receiving 3 or 4 vaccine doses was associated with significantly reduced risk of dyspnea compared to ≤2 doses.
Receiving 3 or 4 vaccine doses was associated with significantly reduced risk of eye soreness and fatigue compared to ≤2 doses.
Receiving 3 or 4 vaccine doses was associated with significantly reduced risk of gastrointestinal discomfort compared to ≤2 doses.
Vaccination with 3 or 4 doses also significantly reduced the occurrence of shortness of breath, decreased sense of smell, chest distress, headache/dizziness, and fever.
Compared to 2 doses of inactivated vaccine, receiving 3 doses of protein vaccine significantly reduced shortness of breath, runny nose, nasal congestion, and eye pain/fatigue.
Vaccination with 3 doses of inactivated vaccine plus 1 dose of protein vaccine significantly reduced decreased smell, decreased taste, and gastrointestinal discomfort.
SARS-CoV-2 positivity was significantly lower among participants vaccinated within the previous 6 months compared to those vaccinated longer ago.

Compared to vaccination within 3 months, vaccination more than 12 months prior significantly increased the risk of multiple long COVID-associated symptoms including decreased smell, palpitations, chest distress, decreased taste, fatigue, eye pain/fatigue, full body soreness, gastrointestinal discomfort, headache/dizziness, and fever.
Vaccination with 3 or 4 doses significantly reduced the duration of cough, decreased smell, and eye soreness/fatigue beyond 1 week.
Vaccination with 3 doses of protein vaccine significantly reduced cough duration beyond 1 week.
Compared with vaccination within 12 months, vaccination more than 12 months prior significantly increased duration of decreased smell, palpitations, decreased taste, and headache/dizziness.
Vaccination with 3 or 4 doses significantly reduced decreased smell and joint pain lasting more than 2 weeks.
Vaccination more than 12 months prior significantly increased the likelihood of decreased smell, decreased taste, and full body soreness lasting more than 2 weeks.
Vaccination more than 12 months prior significantly increased fatigue and headache/dizziness lasting more than one month.
Among surveyed healthcare workers, 75% reported long-term symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with approximately 37% (279/783) experiencing more than three symptoms.
Long COVID symptom scores were significantly positively correlated with PHQ-9 depression scores in the cohort.
Long COVID symptom scores were significantly positively correlated with GAD-7 anxiety scores in the cohort.
Healthcare workers aged 55 years or older were significantly less likely to report more than three long COVID symptoms compared with younger age groups.
Married healthcare workers were significantly less likely to report more than three long COVID symptoms compared with single respondents.
Divorced or widowed healthcare workers were significantly more likely to report more than three long COVID symptoms compared with single respondents.
Healthcare workers with a current or past history of mental health problems were much more likely to report more than three long COVID symptoms than those without such a history.
Healthcare workers infected with SARS-CoV-2 were significantly more likely to report more than three long COVID symptoms than those not infected.
In multivariate logistic regression adjusting for confounders, absence of a mental health history remained independently associated with lower odds of reporting more than three long COVID symptoms.
In multivariate logistic regression, SARS-CoV-2 infection remained independently associated with higher odds of reporting more than three long COVID symptoms.
Female healthcare workers were disproportionately represented among those reporting more than three long COVID symptoms, consistent with published sex differences in Long COVID.
Moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were substantially more common among those with more than three long COVID symptoms compared with those with fewer symptoms.
Moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms were substantially more common among those with more than three long COVID symptoms compared with those with fewer symptoms.

Non-infected healthcare workers also reported a notable burden of long-COVID-like symptoms, with a median symptom score of 1 (IQR 1-3) compared with 3 (IQR 1-6) among infected participants, suggesting symptom reporting is not exclusive to confirmed infection.
Among 200 Long COVID clinic patients, 87% reported at least one sleep complaint (unrefreshing sleep, insomnia, or lethargy) on the general intake screening questionnaire.
Insomnia, defined by an ISI score ≥15, was the most common specific sleep complaint, affecting 42.5% (85/200) of the cohort.
Excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS ≥10) affected 28.5% (57/200) of the cohort, exceeding most previously published rates in Long COVID.
Subjective sleep-related breathing complaints (loud snoring, snorting/gasping, apneic events) were reported by 57.5% of the Long COVID cohort.
Restless legs syndrome complaints, based on the ASQ RLS probability score, were present in 15.5% of the Long COVID cohort.
Parasomnia activity (e.g., sleepwalking, sleep eating, dream enactment) was self-reported by 14.5% of patients.
An extreme circadian phenotype (definite morning or evening type on rMEQ) was present in 11% of the cohort.
Only 7% of the cohort had a documented history of sleep complaints prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection, more than ten-fold lower than the rate of sleep complaints reported after developing Long COVID.

Gaussian mixture modeling of latent symptom factor scores identified two overlapping clusters; Cluster 1 (n=105) showed higher BMI, higher ISI and ESS scores, and lower functional sleep quality (FOSQ) than Cluster 0.
The latent insomnia/unrefreshing-sleep factor (Factor 1) from principal component analysis strongly correlated with Insomnia Severity Index scores.
Cross-validated logistic regression models using latent factor scores discriminated insomnia cases (ISI ≥15) with good accuracy.
Latent factor scores also predicted excessive daytime sleepiness (ESS ≥10) with good discrimination.
Latent factor scores were poor at predicting extreme circadian phenotype, in contrast to their good performance for insomnia and daytime sleepiness.
Patients self-identifying as Multiracial had over three times greater odds of reporting insomnia compared to those identifying as White.
Patients hospitalized during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection had 4.4 times the odds of experiencing insomnia compared to non-hospitalized patients.

Age, illness duration, sex, race, and BMI were not significantly associated with insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep-related breathing complaints, parasomnia activity, or extreme circadian phenotype in this cohort, contrasting with some prior literature.
Most patients in the Long COVID clinic reported functional impairment, with over a third exhibiting severe impairment.

Factor analysis of symptom items revealed a multidimensional structure with domains spanning insomnia/unrefreshing sleep, sensory changes (smell/taste), respiratory complaints, GI symptoms with headache/lightheadedness, anxiety/depression, post-exertional malaise/fatigue/brain fog, and lethargy/lightheadedness linked to cortisol.
Colchicine did not significantly improve 6-minute walk test distance from baseline to 52 weeks compared to placebo in adults with long COVID.
Colchicine was associated with a small, statistically significant but not clinically relevant difference in FEV1/FVC ratio change compared to placebo at 52 weeks.

Colchicine did not improve inflammatory markers or patient-reported outcomes including quality of life, anxiety, depression, fatigue, and dyspnea compared to placebo across all predefined secondary outcomes except FEV1/FVC ratio.
Sixty-eight percent of chronic hemodialysis patients who survived acute SARS-CoV-2 infection developed long COVID, defined as at least one persistent symptom two to three months post-infection.
Diabetes mellitus was the risk factor independently and significantly associated with long COVID in hemodialysis patients after multivariate adjustment.
Diabetes was independently associated with persistent post-COVID fatigue in hemodialysis patients.
Female sex was independently associated with increased risk of persistent post-COVID fatigue in hemodialysis patients.
Obesity approached but did not reach statistical significance as a risk factor for persistent post-COVID fatigue.
Diabetes was independently associated with persistent post-COVID anxiety symptoms in hemodialysis patients.
Obesity was independently associated with persistent post-COVID anxiety symptoms in hemodialysis patients.
Obesity was the only variable independently associated with persistent dyspnea after extensive multivariate adjustment.
Diabetes was significantly associated with persistent post-COVID cough after multivariate adjustment.
Obesity was significantly associated with post-COVID weight loss in hemodialysis patients.
Vaccination status was not significantly associated with the occurrence of long COVID in this hemodialysis cohort, contrasting with some prior evidence of a protective vaccine effect.

In bivariate analysis, long COVID frequency was significantly higher among diabetic and obese patients, and among those requiring hospitalization, oxygen therapy, hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids, or anticoagulation, suggesting acute illness severity drives persistence of symptoms.
The most common persistent long COVID symptoms had characteristic durations, with anxiety lasting longest (median 11 weeks) and anosmia shortest (median 7 weeks).
Among 945 chronic hemodialysis patients over the 36-month study period, 17.2% were infected with SARS-CoV-2 and survived the acute phase, with 11% requiring hospitalization.
At baseline, patients who ultimately completed only 12 PRP sessions had significantly higher absolute FVC than those who required 24 sessions.
At baseline, FEV1 was significantly higher in the 12-session group compared to the 36-session group.
At baseline, the 6-minute walk distance was significantly higher in the 12-session group than in the 36-session group.
At baseline, the number of repetitions in the sit-to-stand test was significantly higher in the 12-session group than in the 36-session group.
At baseline, the physical FAS score was significantly lower (less fatigue) in the 12-session group compared to both the 24- and 36-session groups.
At baseline, the total FAS score was significantly lower in the 12-session group than in the 24-session group.
At baseline, the PCFS functional status score was significantly lower (less impairment) in the 12-session group compared to the 36-session group.
At baseline, the mMRC dyspnea score was significantly lower in the 12-session group compared to both the 24- and 36-session groups.
At baseline, the Borg dyspnea/fatigue scale score was significantly lower in the 12-session group than in the 24-session group.
At baseline, the role-emotional (RE) domain of health-related quality of life was significantly higher in the 36-session group.
The prevalence of diabetes mellitus was significantly higher in the 12-session group at baseline (17/68.00%).
Individualized pulmonary rehabilitation significantly increased 6-minute walk distance from baseline in all three dosage groups, and this improvement was sustained at the 1-year follow-up.
The number of repetitions in the sit-to-stand test increased significantly with PRP in all three groups, an improvement that was maintained at 1-year re-evaluation.
Right and left hand-grip strength increased significantly after PRP in all three dosage groups, with the increase maintained at 1 year in the 12-session group.
Maximum inspiratory pressure increased significantly after PRP in the 12-, 24-, and 36-session groups, with improvements maintained at 1 year in the 36-session group.
FVC and FEV1 increased significantly with PRP in the 24- and 36-session groups, and these gains persisted at the 1-year re-evaluation.

Physical, mental, and total FAS fatigue scores decreased significantly with PRP across the three groups; in the 12-session group the mental fatigue improvement was not further sustained but overall fatigue reduction persisted at 1 year in all groups.
The PCFS functional limitation score decreased significantly with PRP in all three dosage groups, and this improvement was sustained at the 1-year follow-up.
The mMRC dyspnea score decreased significantly with PRP across the three groups, and the reduction was sustained at the 1-year follow-up.

Several SF-36 HRQoL domains (physical functioning, physical role, bodily pain, vitality, mental health in the 12-session group; physical functioning, vitality, social functioning, mental health in the 24- and 36-session groups) improved significantly after PRP and remained improved at the 1-year follow-up.

At the 1-year follow-up, there were no significant differences among the 12-, 24-, and 36-session groups in spirometric variables, exercise capacity, or quality of life, except for the bodily pain domain, regardless of the number of sessions performed.
At the 1-year follow-up, physical and total FAS fatigue scores remained significantly lower in the 12-session group compared to the 36-session group.
At the 1-year follow-up, the PCFS score remained significantly lower in the 12-session group compared to the 24-session group.

At the 1-year follow-up, the bodily pain HRQoL score was significantly higher (better) in the 12-session group compared to the 24-session group, with bodily pain persisting as a problem in the 24-session group.
The prevalence of diabetes mellitus remained significantly higher in the 12-session group at the 1-year follow-up.
The most commonly affected organ system was General disorders and administration site conditions (75.67%), with fatigue/malaise the predominant symptom, affecting 69.93% of patients.
Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders were the second most affected organ system (60.34%), led by cough (50.64%) and dyspnea (24.83%).
Impairments in activities of daily living (Social circumstances SOC) were reported in 44.21% of patients.
Nervous system disorders affected 40.26% of patients, most commonly headache (23.24%) and attention disturbance (13.85%).
Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders affected 27.70% of patients, mainly myalgia (24.63%) and arthralgia (13.06%).
Psychiatric disorders were noted in 22.95% of patients, most frequently sleep disturbance (13.55%) and anxiety (13.25%).
Inpatient management during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with an increased likelihood of developing General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
Inpatient management during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with an increased likelihood of Social circumstances impairments (daily activity limitations) in long COVID.
Prior COVID-19 vaccination was protective against developing Nervous system disorder manifestations of long COVID.
Prior COVID-19 vaccination was protective against developing Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder manifestations of long COVID.
Female gender was associated with an increased likelihood of developing General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
Female gender was associated with increased likelihood of Social circumstances impairments (ADL limitations) in long COVID.
Female gender was associated with increased likelihood of Psychiatric disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Female gender was associated with increased likelihood of Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Female gender was associated with reduced likelihood of Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Increasing age was associated with a higher risk of General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
Increasing age was associated with a higher risk of Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Non-smokers had a reduced risk of Nervous system disorder manifestations of long COVID compared to current smokers.
Non-smokers had a reduced risk of Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder manifestations of long COVID compared to current smokers.
Pre-existing COPD was associated with increased likelihood of Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Pre-existing asthma was strongly associated with increased likelihood of Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorder manifestations in long COVID.
Hypertension was associated with increased likelihood of General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
Hypertension was associated with increased likelihood of Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder manifestations of long COVID.
History of coronary artery disease was associated with increased likelihood of General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
History of autoimmune disease was associated with increased likelihood of General disorders and administration site conditions manifestations of long COVID.
History of stroke was associated with increased likelihood of Psychiatric disorder manifestations in long COVID.
History of cancer was associated with increased likelihood of Psychiatric disorder manifestations in long COVID.
LC-Plasma intake did not significantly change the total severity score or VAS score for eight COVID-19 symptoms compared with placebo over the 14-day observation period, the study's primary endpoint.

Reduction in respiratory symptom VAS scores from baseline was significantly greater in the placebo group than the LC-Plasma group on day 3, indicating slower symptomatic improvement in the LC-Plasma group at this timepoint.

The decrease in cough VAS score was significantly greater in the placebo group than in the LC-Plasma group at early time points (days 2 and 3), indicating cough improved more slowly in patients taking LC-Plasma.

A post hoc analysis showed a significantly higher proportion of patients free of smell and taste disturbances in the LC-Plasma group compared with placebo at day 13, indicating faster resolution of these symptoms.
The proportion of patients without smell disorder was significantly higher in the LC-Plasma group than placebo at day 10.
Nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load decreased significantly by day 4 only in the LC-Plasma group, whereas the placebo group showed no significant decrease until day 8.
At baseline (day 1), peripheral pDC counts were significantly lower in the LC-Plasma group than the placebo group despite randomization.
Peripheral pDC counts increased by day 8 in the LC-Plasma group while decreasing in the placebo group, consistent with LC-Plasma-induced pDC activation and mobilization.
The proportion of pDCs among lineage-negative cells was better maintained in the LC-Plasma group through day 8, whereas it declined markedly in the placebo group.
pDC activation markers HLA-DR and CD86 increased over the study period in both groups, with no significant between-group differences in adjusted percent change.
Serum anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgM and IgG antibody levels increased over time in both groups with no between-group differences.
Serum interleukin-6 and MCP-1 levels decreased over time in both groups without between-group differences.
mRNA expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISG15, RSAD2, OAS1, MxA, IRF9, IFIT1) declined from day 1 to day 8 in both groups with no significant between-group differences.
PBMC IFN-alpha mRNA expression change on day 4 was significantly lower (relatively suppressed) in the LC-Plasma group compared with a significant increase in the placebo group.
IFN-beta mRNA expression did not change significantly within either group, and there were no between-group differences; IFN-lambda was undetectable in all patients at all timepoints.
Peripheral lymphocyte percentage decreased from day 1 to day 8 in both groups with no significant between-group difference.

Adverse events occurred in a small number of patients in both groups (diarrhea, cough-variant asthma, and urticaria in LC-Plasma; rib fracture in placebo), with no serious adverse events and no significant between-group difference in AE frequency, confirming LC-Plasma's safety.

A diminutive atrial septal defect with a left-to-right shunt (Qp/Qs 1.8) was discovered co-existing with severe aortic root dilatation and moderate aortic regurgitation in a Marfan syndrome patient, an uncommon combination.
The patient showed severe aortic root dilatation with a root diameter of 67 mm, consistent with the aortic pathology typical of Marfan syndrome.
Moderate aortic regurgitation was demonstrated with a pressure half time of 430 m/s, alongside peripheral signs (Corrigan pulse, Hill's sign, water hammer pulse).
A grade 2 mitral valve prolapse predominantly involving the anterior leaflet was noted in the patient.
Slit lamp examination revealed supero-temporal lens subluxation (ectopia lentis) in the right eye, a classic ocular feature of Marfan syndrome.

The patient had disproportionate skeletal measurements (arm span/height ratio 1.05, lower/upper segment ratio 0.8) plus positive wrist and thumb signs, pes cavus, pectus carinatum, thoracolumbar kyphosis, and reduced elbow extension, together supporting a clinical diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.
Aortic root dilatation is reported as the most common cardiovascular manifestation of Marfan syndrome, occurring in 60-80% of affected individuals.
Mitral valve prolapse, with a preponderance for anterior leaflet involvement, is the second most common cardiovascular manifestation of Marfan syndrome, with prevalence 40-77% depending on age.
Pulmonary valve prolapse is reported in 5.3% of Marfan syndrome patients.
Up to 7% of Marfan syndrome patients may exhibit left ventricular dilatation without features of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, reflecting heterogeneous cardiovascular involvement.

The patient was managed with a multi-drug regimen for heart failure and cardiovascular risk reduction (beta blocker, angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, antiplatelet agent, and lipid-lowering therapy) while awaiting surgical referral for aortic valve replacement.
Children with ASD experience gastrointestinal symptoms at substantially higher rates than children without ASD.
Food allergies are more common in children with ASD than in children without ASD.
The authors' own cross-referencing of GWAS-catalog ASD-associated genes with GTEx-defined enteric nervous system gene expression data identified 387 genes shared between the two lists.
GO and PANTHER cellular-component analysis showed enrichment of ASD-associated ENS-expressed genes in neuronal projection and synapse-related components.
Biological pathway enrichment of ASD-associated ENS-expressed genes highlighted antigen presentation via MHC class II and regulation of neurogenesis/axonogenesis as top pathways.
In ASD, the sympathetic branch of the ANS is overactive largely due to a parasympathetic deficit, producing autonomic imbalance that disturbs the gut-brain axis.
Elevated brain IL-6 during pregnancy from maternal immune activation crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes excitatory/inhibitory synaptic imbalance mediating autistic-like behaviors.

iPSC-derived cortical neurons from four ASD-associated mutant lines (SHANK3, GRIN2B, UBTF, 7q11.23 duplication) showed hyperexcitability and early maturation compared to control neurons from unaffected family members.

iPSC-derived forebrain neurons homozygous for the gain-of-function ASD-associated KCNT1 P924L mutation showed hyperexcitable network activity, elevated post-action-potential hyperpolarization amplitude, and shortened action potential duration.

iPSC-derived dentate gyrus granule neurons carrying the ASD-associated IQSEC2 A350V mutation were hyperexcitable when immature but became hypoexcitable and less viable upon maturation, with reduced synaptic gene expression and AMPA receptor surface expression.
iPSC-derived oligodendrocyte progenitor cells carrying the ASD-associated SHANK3 InsG3680 mutation showed impaired glutamate signaling (lower calcium activity) and impaired myelination.
Enterocytes from individuals with Phelan-McDermid syndrome (22q13 deletion, ASD-associated) showed decreased ZIP2 and ZIP4 zinc transporter expression at mRNA and protein levels.

In a FOXP1 mutant mouse model, the FOXP1 target proteins Rbms3, Nexn, and Wls are decreased in the esophagus, disrupting nitric-oxide-mediated lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and causing esophageal achalasia, impaired colonic contractions, prolonged GI transit, and muscle atrophy.

The ASD-associated SEMA5A S956G missense mutation impairs SEMA5A function in embryonic rat gut-derived ENS cultures, reducing enteric axon complexity and synaptic density and altering SYNAPSIN-1 phosphorylation, thereby decreasing synaptic vesicle release and neuronal firing.

A DYRK1A loss-of-function mutation in Xenopus tropicalis reduced the migration area of ENS progenitor cells and expression of the neural crest marker SOX10, and inhibiting DYRK1A in mature tadpoles decreased defecation, indicating reduced gut motility.
Treatment with an SSRI or a 5-HTR6 receptor agonist restored normal gut motility in tadpoles with inhibited DYRK1A activity to levels similar to control tadpoles.

Reducing expression of the ASD-related chromatin remodelers CHD2 and CHD8 significantly reduced SOX10 expression and ENS progenitor migration in the Xenopus tropicalis model, mirroring the DYRK1A phenotype.

Reduction of SYNGAP1, an ASD-related synaptic regulatory gene, moderately reduced SOX10 expression in the Xenopus ENS progenitor model, showing a convergent but weaker phenotype than DYRK1A/CHD2/CHD8.

SHANK3B knockout mice show altered intestinal epithelial morphology, increased GI permeability, a denser myenteric plexus with more mature neurons, and slower/shorter-propagating colonic contractions resulting in slower GI transit, with heterozygotes showing milder changes.
SHANK3A or SHANK3B knockout zebrafish exhibit more gut goblet cells as adults, and fewer serotonin-expressing enteroendocrine cells as larvae, compared to wild-type zebrafish.
Mice homozygous for CASPR2 (CNTNAP2) knockout show colonic repetitive contractions 31% shorter than wild-type mice and accelerated colonic transit.

NLGN3 R451C knock-in and NLGN3 knockout mice show faster small intestinal and colonic motility, more responsive colonic enteric neuron GABAA receptors, more myenteric neurons, and a longer colon diameter compared to wild-type mice.

Mice with the ASD-related SLC6A4 Gly56Ala knock-in mutation show increased crypt epithelial cell proliferation, ENS hypoplasia, a less active peristaltic reflex, and slower GI transit compared to wild-type mice — an opposite motility phenotype to several other ASD gene models.
A comparison of behavioral phenotypes across 86 individuals with GRIN2B variants found substantial phenotypic diversity despite a shared genetic mechanism.

Food neophobia and/or selectivity is reported far more often in children with ASD (58-67% by parents, 22.9-69.1% by caregivers) than in children without ASD (8.4-57.89% by parents, 1-37.1% by caregivers).
About 90% of children with ASD exhibit atypical sensory responses compared to about 33% of children without ASD.
A systematic review found a positive correlation between food selectivity and impaired sensory processing in ASD.

In 279 patients with ASD and severe food selectivity, at least 67% did not eat vegetables and 27% did not eat fruits, with a preference for ultra-processed, calorie-dense foods and over 50% having significant nutritional deficiencies, particularly in calcium, fiber, and vitamins D and E.
Zinc deficiency is significantly more common in individuals with ASD than in peers without ASD.

Children with ASD have lower retinal dehydrogenase 1 enzyme levels and lower serum retinoic acid levels than controls, and vitamin A deficiency is associated with more severe ASD symptoms and GI problems, especially constipation.

In a VPA-induced rat model of ASD, gestational vitamin A deficiency worsened autistic-like behavior and caused longer GI transit time and ENS dysplasia compared to VPA-exposed rats with normal vitamin A levels.

Children with ASD and digestive disorders show lower transcript levels of disaccharidases and hexose transporters and lower CDX2 mRNA in intestinal biopsies compared to children with digestive disorders without ASD, indicating impaired carbohydrate digestion/transport.

Urine samples of children with ASD show increased intermediate products of several amino acids, including arginine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, and methionine, compared to control children, reflecting neurotransmitter pathway imbalances.
Mice homozygous for CASPR2 (CNTNAP2) knockout show colonic repetitive contractions that are 31% shorter and accelerated colonic transit compared to wild-type mice.

Mice with NLGN3 R451C knock-in or NLGN3 knockout exhibit faster small intestinal motility, more responsive colonic GABAA receptors, and altered myenteric neuron numbers and colon diameter compared to wild-type mice.

Mice with an ASD-related SLC6A4 Gly56Ala knock-in mutation show increased crypt epithelial cell proliferation, ENS hypoplasia, a less active peristaltic reflex, and slower GI transit compared to wild-type mice.

Food neophobia and/or selectivity is reported far more often in children with ASD (58-67% by parent report, 22.9-69.1% by caregiver report) than in children without ASD (8.4-57.89% and 1-37.1% respectively).

Approximately 90% of children with ASD exhibit atypical sensory responses compared to about 33% of children without ASD, and a systematic review found a positive correlation between food selectivity and impaired sensory processing.

In a study of 279 patients with ASD and severe food selectivity, at least 67% did not eat vegetables and 27% did not eat fruits, with a preference for ultra-processed calorie-dense foods, and over 50% had significant nutritional deficiencies especially in calcium, fiber, and vitamins D and E.
Zinc deficiency, which is important for GI development and ENS synaptic plasticity, is significantly more common in individuals with ASD than in peers without ASD.

Children with ASD have lower retinal dehydrogenase 1 activity and lower serum retinoic acid levels compared to controls, and vitamin A deficiency exacerbates core ASD symptoms and is associated with GI problems, especially constipation.

In a VPA-induced rat model of ASD, gestational vitamin A deficiency led to more severe autistic-like behavior, longer GI transit time, and ENS dysplasia compared to ASD rats with normal vitamin A levels.

Children with ASD and digestive disorders have lower transcript levels of disaccharidases and hexose transporters in intestinal biopsies compared to children with digestive disorders without ASD, associated with low levels of CDX2 mRNA, a transcription factor regulating carbohydrate transporter/enzyme genes.

Blood and urine analyses of children with ASD reveal abnormalities in amino-acid pathways (arginine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, methionine intermediates elevated in urine) associated with neurotransmitter imbalances compared to control children.

Loss-of-function mutations in BCKDK in families with ASD, epilepsy, and intellectual disability cause lower plasma branched-chain amino acid concentrations, and BCKDK knockout mice exhibit tremors, epileptic seizures, hindlimb clasping, and dysregulated brain amino acid transporter pathways.
Disrupted tryptophan metabolism is associated with elevated urinary reactive oxygen species markers 7,8-dihydroneopterin and neopterin in 40 children with ASD compared to controls.

Blood samples of children with ASD exhibited decreased levels of antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase, and 4-hydroxyphenyllactate compared to controls, indicating excessive oxidative stress.

Urinary serotonin was reported higher in children with ASD, while blood melatonin (a serotonin product) was lower, and melatonin deficiency is associated with sleep-wake rhythm disturbance and mutual association between ASD symptoms, sleep disturbance, and digestive issues.

Children with ASD have lower blood levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids and higher sphingosine-1-phosphate, suggesting abnormal lipid and sphingomyelin metabolism linked to disrupted neuronal structure and white matter development.

Lipid peroxidation perturbations elevate advanced glycation end products and dityrosine in the plasma of children with ASD leading to proteotoxic stress, with dityrosine increase linked to increased dual oxidase (DUOX) activity as a mucosal immune response to reduced colonic barrier permeability.

Maternal immune activation (MIA) animal models, in which immune signaling molecules disrupt fetal neural development, show variable phenotype severity depending on immunogen type, timing, dose, delivery mode, mouse strain, maternal responsiveness, and offspring sex.
Pre-conception microbiota transplantation improved neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the MIA model by inhibiting interleukin-17A (IL-17A) signaling during pregnancy.

Fecal microbiota analysis of children with ASD shows overgrowth of pathogenic strains and imbalance in the Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio, with considerable heterogeneity in the affected microbial populations across studies.
Adults with ASD exhibited lower alpha diversity in fecal microbiota composition and higher abundance of three bacterial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequence variants compared to adults without ASD.

75% of duodenal biopsies from children with ASD showed reduced expression of barrier-forming tight junction components (CLDN1, OCLN, TRIC), while 66% showed increased mRNA and protein levels of pore-forming claudins (claudin-2, -10, -15), compared to controls.

Transferring fecal supernatants from adult ASD model mice to naïve mice led to reduced colonic barrier permeability compared to transfers from wild-type mice, attributed to lower tight junction proteins (JAM-A, cingulin, ZO-2) and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNF-α in the proximal colon.

Transfer of fecal supernatants from adult humans with ASD to mice reduced expression of glial and neuronal connectivity proteins in the ENS, such as βIII-tubulin and synapsin, compared to transfer from adults without ASD.
Esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy in 36 children with ASD versus 26 controls showed Paneth cells in ASD patients were frequently enlarged with an increased number per crypt compared to controls.

In an ileocolonoscopy study of 148 children with ASD and 30 controls, 90% of ASD children had ileo-colonic lymphoid nodular hyperplasia (LNH) versus 30% of controls, and 68% of ASD children with LNH had moderate-to-severe LNH versus 15% of controls; no correlation was found between LNH severity and diet or age.

Lymphocytic colitis in children with ASD is less severe than classical IBD but shows significantly increased basement membrane thickness and mucosal γδ T cell density compared to children with IBD without ASD.

A study found significant increases in CD3+CD4+ intraepithelial lymphocytes and CD19+ lamina propria B cells in the duodenum, ileum, and colon of children with ASD compared to children with IBD without ASD.

Transcriptome profiling of GI mucosal biopsy tissue revealed that gene expression profiles of autistic children with GI problems and children with IBD (without ASD) show distinctive features despite significant overlap.
Cross-referencing ASD-associated genes from the GWAS catalog with genes expressed in the ENS (GTEx data) identified 387 shared ASD-associated genes expressed in the ENS.

A comparison of behavioral phenotypes in 86 individuals with variants in the ASD-related gene GRIN2B found highly diverse phenotypes, illustrating that even a shared genetic mechanism can produce variable clinical presentations.

Prior literature cited in this paper reports that damage to the vagus nerve is associated with alterations in cognitive behavior and neurochemical adaptations.
In long COVID, mitochondrial biogenesis is reduced relative to normal physiological levels.
Respiratory chain (electron transport chain) activity is reduced in long COVID.
Reactive oxygen species production is increased in long COVID.
MFN2 (mitochondrial outer-membrane fusion protein) expression/activity is reported as decreased in long COVID.
OPA1 (inner-membrane fusion protein, cristae maintenance) is reported as decreased in long COVID.
PGC-1α (master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis) is reported as decreased in long COVID.
PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy is described as defective in long COVID.
The SARS-CoV-2 accessory protein ORF9b binds host TOM70 and disrupts MAVS/TOM70-dependent antiviral signaling, altering mitochondrial protein import and innate immunity.

Persistent mitochondrial stress in long COVID is proposed to drive systemic inflammation resembling the 'inflammaging' pattern seen in aging, sustaining a cycle of immune activation and tissue damage.
Persistent mitochondrial dysfunction in long COVID is proposed to underlie fatigue, myalgia, and cognitive deficits resembling mitochondrial disease phenotypes.
Aging-associated mitochondrial dysfunction is proposed to contribute to the development of long COVID, particularly in individuals with pre-existing metabolic disorders or older age.

In long COVID, a Warburg-like shift from oxidative phosphorylation toward glycolysis is proposed to worsen fatigue and impair tissue repair because dysfunctional mitochondria cannot meet recovery energy demands.
Brain fog reported by long COVID patients (and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder) is proposed to stem from mitochondrial dysfunction in neurons.

The authors propose mitochondrial transplantation (introducing healthy donor mitochondria) as a potential therapy to restore energy production, reduce oxidative stress, and modulate immune responses in long COVID, though this remains preclinical/conceptual for this condition.
In long COVID, cytokine storms and persistent fatigue, muscle pain, and brain fog are associated with reduced mitochondrial biogenesis (lower PGC-1α) and endothelial/epithelial dysfunction.

High-content screens in human airway organoids identified HIF-1α-driven glycolysis and fatty-acid biosynthesis as actionable metabolic vulnerabilities for blocking SARS-CoV-2 replication, and HIF-1α-driven reprogramming in monocytes/macrophages enhances glycolysis while impairing T-cell responses and epithelial survival.

SARS-CoV-2 alters host folate and one-carbon metabolism, causing glucose and folate depletion in infected cells while enabling de novo purine synthesis, and viral replication is highly sensitive to folate metabolism inhibitors such as methotrexate.

In a longitudinal study, 25% of pregnant women with COVID-19 developed fatigue at six months post-infection, and fatigue was more common among those with symptomatic infection than among those testing positive only at delivery or not infected.

A pilot study found 88% of women experienced fatigue during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (mild 8.2% to extreme 26.4%), and 46% still had fatigue at 12 months postpartum, with 30% describing it as very challenging or extremely burdensome.

Among 56 symptomatic individuals followed over time, 30.4% had persistent symptoms and fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among those symptomatic for six months or more (60%), followed by myalgia, olfactory disorders, and cough.

In a prospective study, fatigue was the second most common symptom four weeks post-infection (15%, after cough at 12%), and remained the most prevalent symptom at eight or more weeks post-infection (9.7%, followed by cough at 4.5%).

In a cross-sectional study of pregnant (n=111) vs non-pregnant women (n=181), fatigue prevalence was nearly identical (71.2% vs 71.8%) with no significant difference in prevalence or severity, attributed to young age and absence of pre-existing conditions.
Fatigue was the second most common PASC symptom (76.3% of patients), with post-exertional malaise being the most frequently reported symptom (77.7%).
Long COVID in pregnancy was associated with risk factors including obesity, pre-existing depression and anxiety disorders, economic hardship, and need for oxygen therapy during acute infection.

Using two national EHR networks, the incidence of post-acute sequelae involving cognitive, fatigue, and respiratory symptoms among individuals infected during pregnancy was 4.86 per 100 persons in PCORnet and 6.83 per 100 persons in N3C within 180 days of infection.

Pregnant individuals had a significantly lower adjusted hazard of developing Long COVID compared with non-pregnant controls, though fatigue remained one of the most frequently coded components of post-COVID syndrome.
Acute-phase cough was associated with a significantly elevated risk of persistent fatigue (HR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.07-2.96).
Acute-phase myalgia was associated with a significantly elevated risk of persistent fatigue (HR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.01-2.44).
Acute-phase anosmia acted as a protective factor, reducing the risk of prolonged fatigue (HR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.40-0.88).

Maternal comorbidities such as hypertension, heart disease, and lung disease did not independently influence the risk of persistent fatigue, and no correlation was found between fatigue duration and trimester of pregnancy.
No statistically significant difference in maternal age was found between women who experienced Long COVID and those who did not, nor between pregnant and non-pregnant women in a separate study.
Pregnant women who smoke were found to be at significantly higher risk of experiencing post-viral fatigue compared with non-pregnant women.
No statistically significant differences were observed between smokers and non-smokers regarding overall Long COVID symptoms, and fatigue frequency was not influenced by alcohol consumption.

None of the four prespecified primary comparisons (BrainHQ vs active comparator, PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs active comparator, tDCS-active+BrainHQ vs tDCS-sham+BrainHQ, and PASC-CoRE+BrainHQ vs BrainHQ alone) showed a significant difference in change in the modified ECog2 score from baseline to end of intervention.

All five treatment arms, including the active comparator, showed an improvement of approximately half a rating point on the modified ECog2 from baseline to end of intervention, indicating nonspecific improvement not attributable to any specific rehabilitative intervention.

Across the entire cohort, improvement in modified ECog2 score was inversely related to the duration of long COVID prior to randomization, with each additional year of illness duration associated with less improvement.

Neither participant-reported secondary outcomes (sleep, fatigue, cognition, depression, anxiety) nor neuropsychological test scores showed differential benefit for any treatment arm compared with the respective control arm.

Participant-reported secondary outcomes including sleep, fatigue, cognition, depression, and anxiety, as well as some neuropsychological test scores (word list learning, symbol digit test, fluency), improved from baseline to end of intervention across all treatment arms including the active comparator.

The proportion of participants reporting postexertional malaise decreased from 76% at baseline to 56% at end of intervention, and none of the interventions, including active tDCS, worsened postexertional malaise or caused premature discontinuation.

Among the modified intention-to-treat population, 11 participants experienced treatment-emergent serious adverse events, and one participant receiving active tDCS experienced a minor thermal injury under an electrode one month after randomization.

At baseline, most participants with subjective cognitive complaints did not have objective cognitive impairment: 60.9% had no test scores 1.5 SD or more below normative expectations, while only 8.7% showed impairment on two or more cognitive domains.

At end of intervention, 74% of participants across all treatment arms reported that the intervention helped their cognitive functioning, and a majority reported improved overall functioning, while 7% reported feeling somewhat or much worse.
Adherence to intervention protocols was excellent across all arms, with over 90% of participants completing more than 80% of intervention activities.
There was no significant interaction between treatment assignment and the time elapsed from initial COVID-19 infection to randomization on the primary outcome.

Multiplexed imaging of post-mortem lung tissue from 12 individuals showed viral persistence in the lungs of Long COVID patients up to 359 days after acute infection, even in those with negative nasopharyngeal swabs.

In 48 children with Long COVID, SARS-CoV-2 was detected in at least one nasal or tonsillar specimen in 27% of children, with IHC for NSP-16 indicating active viral replication in 53.8% of infected tissues, identifying tonsils and adenoids as major reservoir sites in children.

In a longitudinal study of 113 patients, fecal shedding of SARS-CoV-2 vRNA persisted in 12.7% of patients at 4 months and 3.8% at 7 months post-infection, correlating with the severity of gastrointestinal symptoms.
Persistent vRNA reservoirs were detected at autopsy throughout the brain in Long COVID patients, extensively distributed as late as 230 days and up to 7 months following symptom onset.
Reservoirs of vRNA were detected in the gut mucosa approximately 7 months after mild acute COVID-19 in 32 of 46 patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

Multimodal molecular imaging in 24 participants showed tissue-based T cell activation and vRNA persistence for up to 2 years after COVID-19, with T-cell hyperactivation in the spinal cord and gut associated with Long COVID symptoms.
Spike protein and vRNA were detected in 30% of patients with Long COVID, while none of the control individuals without Long COVID had detectable Spike protein or vRNA.

Using the Simoa single-molecule array platform in a large cohort of pandemic-era Long COVID patients versus pre-pandemic controls, 25% of participants had one or more detectable residual SARS-CoV-2 antigens up to 14 months after acute infection, with Spike protein the most commonly detected antigen.
MMP-9 was significantly elevated in the serum of patients with Long COVID compared to healthy controls, and Spike protein stimulated microglia in vitro to produce MMP-9.

Computational sequence analysis revealed a superantigen-like motif in the Spike protein S1 subunit highly similar to a Staphylococcal enterotoxin B fragment, with high predicted affinity for T cell receptors and MHC Class II, supporting a hypothesized autoimmune mechanism in Long COVID.
The Spike protein S1 subunit contributes to lung inflammation via activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and release of IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-18.

In an endoscopy study of 46 IBD patients 219 days after confirmed COVID-19, viral nucleoprotein persisted in the gut epithelium of 24 patients despite inability to culture replicating virus, and LC symptoms correlated with residual antigen persistence.

Patients with Long COVID exhibited persistent systemic inflammation 12 months after acute COVID-19, with elevated circulating organ-damage markers including C3 protein and anti-nuclear autoantibodies.

Tocilizumab administration was associated with improvement in Long COVID symptoms, particularly in patients with elevated inflammatory markers.
JAK inhibitors have shown promise in clinical trials for modulating the immune response and reducing the severity of persistent Long COVID symptoms.

In a cohort followed for 10 months, fecal shedding of SARS-CoV-2 RNA persisted in a subset of Long COVID patients and was correlated with the severity of gastrointestinal symptoms.

A study of inflammatory bowel disease patients found persistent viral RNA reservoirs in the gut mucosa in the majority of patients approximately 7 months after mild acute COVID-19.

Females are significantly more likely than males to develop severe Long COVID symptoms, though the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms driving this sex difference remain undetermined.

Among 2,989 patients screened after symptomatic Omicron-era SARS-CoV-2 infection, 38.6% (1,155) had persistent or new long COVID symptoms three months after infection.
The most frequently reported persistent symptoms at 3 months were memory loss (49.8%), fatigue (46.4%), other unclassified symptoms (37.2%), headache (25.2%) and muscle pain (25.1%).

Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of long COVID symptoms identified three distinct phenotypic clusters: Cluster 1 (39.7%, dominated by memory loss and concentration difficulties), Cluster 2 (47.5%, dominated by fatigue and 'other' symptoms with fewest symptoms overall), and Cluster 3 (12.7%, the highest symptom-burden cluster with a broad multi-system symptom profile).

Cluster 3 patients had the highest symptom burden (median 8 symptoms, IQR 7-10) including high rates of dyspnea (55.1%), anxiety (64.6%) and depression (46.3%), compared with much lower rates in Clusters 1 and 2.
Presence of COPD was associated with lower odds of belonging to Cluster 1 (memory/concentration-predominant phenotype) relative to the asymptomatic reference group.
Male sex was associated with increased odds of belonging to Cluster 2 (fatigue/'other symptoms'-predominant, lowest symptom burden phenotype).
COPD was associated with increased odds of belonging to Cluster 3, the highest symptom-burden, worst quality-of-life phenotype.
Cardiovascular disease was associated with substantially increased odds of belonging to Cluster 3, the highest symptom-burden phenotype.

Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-3L utility score) at 3 months was lowest in Cluster 3 (0.59) compared with Cluster 2 (0.73) and Cluster 1 (0.75), with Cluster 3 also showing the poorest scores across all individual EQ-5D domains.

In an adjusted model (accounting for sex, age, comorbidity burden, and study cohort), Cluster 3 showed the largest quality-of-life decrement relative to asymptomatic patients, followed by Cluster 2 and Cluster 1.

Compared to patients without persistent symptoms at 3 months, those with long COVID symptoms were more likely to be female, older, White, and have obesity and other comorbidities (CCI ≥ 1), while vaccination status did not differ between groups.

No significant association was found between vaccination status and cluster membership, hospitalization, healthcare worker status, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or cancer for any of the three clusters in the adjusted logistic regression.
7.0% of US adults reported experiencing long COVID in 2022, with 43.7% reporting acute COVID and 49.3% reporting no COVID.
A higher percentage of females than males reported long COVID (8.7% vs. 5.2%).
Long COVID prevalence varied by age, being highest among those aged 45-54 and 55-64 (9.2% each) and lower among those 18-44 (6.1%) and 65+ (5.8%).
Long COVID prevalence differed by race/ethnicity, being highest in non-Hispanic White adults (7.9%), followed by Hispanic (6.7%) and non-Hispanic Black adults (4.5%).
Unadjusted average total healthcare expenditures were substantially higher for adults with long COVID than for those without COVID (USD 11,305 vs. USD 7162).
Unadjusted average payer (third-party) expenditures were higher for adults with long COVID than those without COVID (USD 9983 vs. USD 6097).
Unadjusted average out-of-pocket expenditures were modestly higher for adults with long COVID than those without COVID (USD 1322 vs. USD 1065).
After adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, health, and lifestyle covariates, adults with long COVID had 1.54 times greater total healthcare expenditures than adults without COVID.
After adjustment, adults with long COVID had 1.58 times greater payer (third-party) healthcare expenditures than adults without COVID.

Adjusted mean total healthcare expenditures were highest for long COVID (USD 11,641), intermediate for acute COVID (USD 8361), and lowest for no COVID (USD 7543), yielding excess total expenditures of +USD 4098 for long COVID versus no COVID.
Most of the excess healthcare cost associated with long COVID was borne by third-party payers, with an adjusted excess of +USD 3705 versus no COVID.
The adjusted excess out-of-pocket expenditure for long COVID versus no COVID (+USD 236) was small and not statistically significant.

In stratified two-part models, excess total expenditures for long COVID versus no COVID were USD 3737 among adults with multimorbidity and USD 2603 among those without multimorbidity, indicating comorbidity burden does not fully explain the cost difference.
Excess third-party (payer) spending attributable to long COVID was greater among adults with multimorbidity (+USD 4192) than those without multimorbidity (+USD 1216).
Cited prior research found long COVID patients had a higher Charlson comorbidity index than those without long COVID (1.2 vs. 0.9), indicating greater baseline health burden.
Fatigue was significantly more common among long COVID participants older than 40 years compared to younger participants.
Fatigue and breathlessness were the most commonly reported persistent symptoms among the 210 long COVID participants, followed by cognitive difficulties and musculoskeletal complaints.

Patients who had moderate-to-severe acute COVID-19 illness were significantly more likely to report persistent long COVID symptoms, particularly respiratory and neurological complaints, compared with those who had mild initial illness.
CRP levels were significantly higher in symptomatic long COVID participants compared to asymptomatic recovered participants.
IL-6 levels were significantly higher in symptomatic long COVID participants compared to asymptomatic recovered participants, supporting a role for ongoing systemic inflammation.

Among the 90 participants with persistent respiratory complaints, fibrotic changes and ground-glass opacities were the most common radiological abnormalities on chest imaging, supporting chronic pulmonary involvement after clinical recovery.
Fatigue is described as among the most disabling and defining symptoms of Long COVID, present in over half of cases.

A subset of Long COVID patients experience post-exertional malaise (PEM), a pathological worsening of symptoms after physical or cognitive exertion that may share mechanisms with other post-viral syndromes such as ME/CFS.
A conservative global estimate suggests at least 65 million cases of Long COVID, with the true burden likely higher due to underreporting and undocumented infections.
Prevalence estimates of Long COVID vary substantially by hospitalisation and vaccination status.

People with Long COVID may exhibit skeletal muscle abnormalities including mitochondrial and endothelial dysfunction and a shift toward anaerobic metabolism and glycolytic muscle fibres, which can reduce movement capacity and potentially trigger post-exertional malaise.

Potential causes proposed for Long COVID-related skeletal muscle abnormalities include deconditioning, local tissue hypoxia, autoimmunity, electrophysiological changes and central (neurological) fatigue.

The risk of developing long COVID after Omicron infection is similar to that after Delta variant infection, per cited prior literature.
Over 30% of long COVID sequelae persist at 2-year follow-up even among patients who were not hospitalized during the initial infection, according to cited literature.

Prior evidence cited in the protocol suggests that receiving antiviral treatment for acute COVID-19 has some protective effect against developing long COVID, alongside healthy lifestyle and vaccination.
Early treatment with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir during acute COVID-19 has been shown in prior studies to prevent hospitalization and death from COVID-19.

Among 149 pregnant individuals with acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, 24% were classified as Symptoms Absent, 27% as Symptoms Present, and 6% as Symptoms Resolved based on retrospective EHR symptom documentation.
Using the 2023 NIH RECOVER PASC scoring model adapted for this cohort, 89% of participants were classified as PASC Zero and 10% as PASC Indeterminate.
Using the 2024 NIH RECOVER PASC scoring model, 85% of participants were classified as PASC Zero, 15% as PASC Indeterminate, and one participant as PASC Positive.
Participants in the Symptoms Present and Symptoms Resolved subcohorts had substantially higher rates of declined or post-diagnosis SARS-CoV-2 vaccination than the Symptoms Absent subcohort.
PASC Indeterminate participants had markedly higher rates of declined or delayed vaccination than PASC Zero participants under the 2023 scoring model.
PASC Indeterminate participants had higher rates of declined or delayed vaccination than PASC Zero participants under the 2024 scoring model.
Fatigue, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms were the most frequently documented persisting symptoms among participants classified as Symptoms Present.
Most participants had no EHR documentation of pain or skin color change following acute COVID-19, suggesting these symptoms were rarely captured or experienced in this cohort.

Loss or change in sense of taste or smell, a hallmark acute COVID-19 symptom and highly weighted PASC score item, was infrequently documented as a persistent symptom in this pregnant cohort, possibly confounded by pregnancy-related changes in taste and smell.
The Symptoms Absent subcohort had a greater proportion of first-time pregnancies compared to the Symptoms Present subcohort.

Antithrombolytics were the most frequently prescribed medication during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection among Symptoms Absent participants, while antivirals were the most frequently prescribed among Symptoms Present participants.
Antithrombolytics were the most prescribed medication for PASC Zero subcohorts in both 2023 and 2024 models, while antivirals predominated in PASC Indeterminate subcohorts.
Severe acute COVID-19 (requiring hospitalization or ventilation) was more frequently documented in the Symptoms Absent subcohort than the Symptoms Present subcohort.
Cesarean delivery rates trended higher in the Symptoms Present subcohort than the Symptoms Absent subcohort, and both were elevated relative to national rates.

Persistence of at least one of 26 Long COVID-associated symptoms was observed in 26.7% of the overall cohort, using a conservative definition requiring documentation at both 30+ days post-infection and at the final encounter.
The majority (78%) of participants with persistent symptoms had only a single persisting symptom rather than multiple.

Only 2 of 149 patients with EHR-documented persistent symptoms consistent with Long COVID had an explicit Long COVID diagnosis recorded in their chart, indicating substantial underdiagnosis or underdocumentation.

Of the 26 evaluated Long COVID-associated symptoms, 22 were documented as persisting in at least one participant and 23 were documented as resolving in at least one participant, indicating broad symptom heterogeneity.
The rate of long COVID symptoms increased with severity of prior acute COVID-19 infection, being lowest in asymptomatic and vaccinated cohorts and highest in those with prior severe infection.
Overall, 21.1% (36/171) of evaluable patients had self-reported long COVID symptoms a median of 2.1 years after acute COVID-19 infection.
Modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea scores were increased (≥1) in 24 of 36 long COVID patients, most frequently in those with prior severe infection.
Eight of 36 long COVID patients had chest HRCT abnormalities considered possibly or probably related to COVID-19, occurring significantly more often in those with prior severe infection.

Spirometric flow-volume loop patterns were normal in 25 of 35 evaluable long COVID patients, with obstructive changes in 5, restrictive in 3, and mixed obstructive/restrictive in 2, with no significant differences between cohorts.
Six-minute walk distance was reduced (below predicted normal) in almost all long COVID patients tested, with only three achieving normal distance and nine achieving ≥80% of predicted.

Reduced FEF25-75% with bronchodilator reversibility was observed in several long COVID patients despite normal FEV1/FVC, but similar abnormalities were also seen in asymptomatic control patients, suggesting this is not specific to long COVID.
Females made up the large majority (89%) of long COVID patients in this cohort, consistent with prior reports of higher self-reported long COVID prevalence in women.
Patients with long COVID symptoms had a high mean body mass index, with a non-significant trend toward highest BMI in those with prior severe infection.
Hypertension was a common comorbidity among long COVID patients, with a non-significant trend to be more frequent among those with prior severe COVID-19 infection.

Most long COVID patients maintained oxygen saturation above 95% during the six-minute walk test, with significant desaturation occurring in only three patients (one in cohort 2, two in cohort 3), none of whom had HRCT changes compatible with COVID-19.
The most common primary and secondary symptoms reported by long COVID patients were tiredness/fatigue, shortness of breath and cough.

By study completion on 20 December 2022, 9781 long COVID patients had been invited to use the digital health intervention 'Living With COVID Recovery', of whom 7679 (78.5%) registered across 33 NHS clinics.
Long COVID was reported to be extremely debilitating, with fatigue and health-related quality of life impact comparable to that seen in stage IV lung cancer.
Social disadvantage was reported to influence the severity of long COVID symptoms, indicating care and rehabilitation should account for socioeconomic factors.
Medical record integration was identified as a barrier deterring some NHS clinics from adopting the digital health intervention.
At three months post-infection, plasma ICAM-1 levels were higher in hospitalized than non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, indicating greater endothelial activation.
VCAM-1 levels at three months post-infection were higher in hospitalized than non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
IL-6 levels at three months post-infection were higher in hospitalized than non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
At three months post-infection, no significant differences in D-Dimer, E-Selectin, ICAM-1, or VCAM-1 levels were found between asymptomatic (Never LC) and symptomatic (Ongoing LC) individuals.
At twelve months, ICAM-1 levels were higher in Never LC subjects compared to those whose long COVID symptoms had resolved (Resolved LC).
D-dimer levels increased significantly from three to twelve months post-infection, indicating progressive coagulation/endothelial involvement over time.
E-Selectin levels increased significantly from three to twelve months post-infection.
VCAM-1 levels increased significantly from three to twelve months post-infection.
ICAM-1 levels rose significantly from three to twelve months post-infection.
IL-6 levels declined significantly from three to twelve months post-infection, while IL-1β, IL-8, and TNF-α showed no significant longitudinal change.
TNF-α levels showed no significant change from three to twelve months post-infection.
Spike- and nucleocapsid-specific T-cell responses did not differ between Never LC and Ongoing LC subjects at three months, nor at twelve months in Resolved LC.
The spike-specific T-cell response was significantly higher in hospitalized than non-hospitalized patients at three months post-infection.
The elevated spike-specific T-cell response in hospitalized patients declined markedly by twelve months post-infection.
Across the whole cohort, spike-specific T-cell response was significantly reduced at twelve months compared with three months post-infection.
Nucleocapsid-specific T-cell response was similar between hospitalized and non-hospitalized subjects at three months but declined significantly by twelve months in both groups.
Within the long COVID group at three months, male patients showed significantly higher E-Selectin, VCAM-1, and ICAM-1 than female patients, a difference that did not persist at twelve months.
TNF-α levels were significantly higher in female Ongoing LC patients compared with Never LC females at three months post-infection.
IL-8 levels were significantly higher in male long COVID patients than female long COVID patients at three months post-infection.

Among long COVID patients, males exhibited a significantly stronger spike-specific T-cell response than females at three months, a difference proposed to relate to greater protection against long COVID in males.
At three months post-infection, older age was positively correlated with E-Selectin, VCAM-1, and IL-1β levels, suggesting greater endothelial activation and inflammation with increasing age.
At twelve months, older age was inversely correlated with the spike-specific T-cell response, suggesting sharper waning of adaptive immunity with age.
The prevalence of long COVID in this unvaccinated post-COVID cohort was 34%, with respiratory symptoms, fatigue, and neuropsychological complaints being the most frequent manifestations.

Among symptomatic long COVID patients, the most frequently reported symptoms were dyspnea/cough/shortness of breath, followed by fatigue, other symptoms, neuropsychological symptoms, anosmia/ageusia/dysosmia/dysgeusia, and arthromyalgias.
Almost all responders (94.1%) had not fully recovered from long COVID as measured by the Post-COVID Functional Status scale, with functional impact ranging from negligible to severe.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported ongoing symptom among those not fully recovered from long COVID.
Cognitive dysfunction was the second most common ongoing symptom in long COVID patients who had not fully recovered.
Breathlessness or wheezing was commonly reported among unrecovered long COVID patients.
Joint and muscle pain was reported by over a third of unrecovered long COVID participants.
Nearly a third of unrecovered long COVID participants reported a mental health impact, combining anxiety and depression.
Vocational status was severely affected, with only about one-fifth of participants working in the same capacity as before their initial COVID-19 infection.
Six-month recovery trajectory measured by the Global Rate of Change scale showed most patients at a plateau, some improving, and a fifth worsening, indicating a non-linear recovery course.
Among those reporting recovery, provision of information/advice, medication, and onward referrals from the LC clinic were identified as aiding recovery.
Over half of participants who remained symptomatic were not currently receiving any care or support for long COVID.
Among those not working in the same capacity as before COVID-19 infection, the majority were not receiving care or support.
44.3% of participants who had not fully recovered from long COVID reported unmet care needs, the largest of four identified care-status groups.
Participants who were no longer working or working with adjustments reported a higher frequency of unmet care needs compared to those working in the same capacity as before long COVID.
Unmet care needs were slightly greater in younger participants and those with longer duration of long COVID, and in those whose initial infection was managed in the community.
The mean duration of long COVID symptoms among the surveyed cohort exceeded 3 years, with the majority of initial infections managed in the community rather than hospital.
Patients with long COVID at 36 months had a higher prevalence of asthma as a comorbidity compared with asymptomatic patients.
Cardiovascular disease as a comorbidity was less prevalent in patients with long COVID at 36 months compared with asymptomatic patients.
Use of mechanical ventilation during acute illness was more common among patients who developed long COVID than those who did not, though ICU admission rates did not differ.
Reinfection rate did not differ significantly between the long COVID and asymptomatic groups.
Fever at 36 months was reported more frequently among patients who had a documented reinfection than among those without reinfection.
The overall proportion of patients reporting any long COVID symptom decreased progressively from 46.2% at 3 months to 26.8% at 36 months post-diagnosis.
Between 12 and 36 months, the proportion of patients reporting 5–9 symptoms increased rather than decreased, unlike other symptom-count categories.
Fatigue, dyspnea, muscular weakness, alopecia, and cough persisted over time and remained among the most common long COVID symptoms at 36 months, unlike olfactory/taste symptoms which declined.

Patients in the multiple symptoms cluster (defined by symptoms at 3 months) had the highest symptom counts, lowest QOL score, and highest presenteeism impairment among all clusters at follow-up, and these symptoms tended to persist to 36 months.
Unlike at 12 months, no sex difference in long COVID prevalence was observed at 36 months, suggesting the impact of sex on long COVID risk diminished over time.

Patients who received at least one COVID-19 vaccination had a lower prevalence of long COVID symptoms at 3 months than unvaccinated patients, though no difference was seen between fewer than three versus three or more vaccinations.
Patients with five or more long COVID symptoms had worse subjective economic conditions, higher absenteeism, and lower SF-36 QOL scores than those with one to four symptoms.
Subjective economic condition worsening was most prevalent in the continuous long COVID symptom subgroup, followed by relapse and recovered subgroups.
Absolute presenteeism scores were lower (indicating worse work productivity) in the continuous and relapse symptom groups compared with the recovered group.
Absolute absenteeism worsened specifically in the continuous symptom group compared with the relapse and recovered groups.
In the anosmia and dysgeusia cluster, both symptoms remained elevated at 12 months but declined substantially by 36 months.
In the fatigue and dyspnea cluster, fatigue decreased between 12 and 36 months, but dyspnea increased over the same period, suggesting divergent trajectories within the cluster.

COVID-19 patients showed significant gut dysbiosis with reduction of beneficial bacteria like Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium and enrichment of pathogenic bacteria such as Enterococcus, Klebsiella, and Streptococcus.

In COVID-19 patients, F. prausnitzii and several Bacteroidota species were inversely correlated with disease severity, while opportunistic bacteria like Clostridium hathewayi and Clostridium ramosum were associated with more severe disease.

16S rRNA sequencing of 22 COVID-19 patients vs 15 healthy controls found significantly altered oral and gut microbiome diversity with increased abundance of pathogenic and commensal genera including Bacteroides, Escherichia, Shigella, Enterococcus, Bifidobacterium, Megamonas, Streptococcus, Rothia, Klebsiella, and Veillonella.
Analysis of stool and oral microbiome composition could determine COVID-19 disease severity form with an accuracy exceeding 80%, outperforming clinical biomarkers and comorbidity data.

In 35 COVID-19 convalescents followed for one year, gut microbial diversity gradually increased with rising SCFA/butyrate-producing bacteria and Bifidobacterium and declining LPS-producing microorganisms, accompanied by a significant rise in serum sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) that aided endothelial function restoration and reduced inflammation.

Post-COVID gut microbiota characterized by decreased SCFA-producing bacteria (Faecalibacterium, Ruminococcus, Dorea, Bifidobacterium) and increased opportunistic bacteria (Corynebacterium, Streptococcus, Enterococcus) correlates with elevated CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α, supporting gut-mediated systemic inflammation in long COVID.

SCFAs such as butyrate and propionate can regulate regulatory T cell differentiation, inhibit NF-κB activation, and lower IL-6, representing a mechanism by which gut dysbiosis influences immune activation in post-COVID.
COVID-19 survivors with an altered gut microbiota profile showed elevated IL-17, TNF-α, and IL-1β, suggesting persistent mucosal and systemic inflammation in post-COVID.

Elevated levels of the inflammatory cytokine IL-6 are associated with post-COVID symptoms including loss of appetite and weight loss.

Variants of the IL-2 gene influence markers of systemic inflammation and vascular regulation in post-COVID patients, with specific polymorphisms linked to differences in inflammatory profile and long-term outcomes.
The rs2268616 variant in the placental growth factor (PGF) gene has a stronger effect on COVID-19/post-COVID outcomes in men and people with type 2 diabetes.

SARS-CoV-2-induced defective ACE2 receptor function leads to impaired mTOR pathway activation, decreased antimicrobial peptide secretion, and dysbiotic gut changes, contributing to gut-brain axis dysfunction in post-COVID.

A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs involving 1198 COVID-19 patients found that probiotic supplementation increased rates of overall symptom improvement and shortened symptom duration and hospitalization length compared with controls.
The same meta-analysis found no clear effect of probiotic supplementation on fever, headache, or weakness in COVID-19 patients.
Probiotic supplementation reduced serum C-reactive protein concentrations by lowering the inflammatory response in COVID-19 patients.

The incidence of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) has risen sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic, with an estimated 6-7 million new U.S. cases, compared to a pre-pandemic prevalence of 0.5-1%.
Polymorphisms in the IL-2 gene, which controls an immune system component, are associated with variation in systemic inflammation markers and vascular regulation among post-COVID patients.
The rs2268616 variant in the placental growth factor (PGF) gene shows a stronger effect on COVID-19/post-COVID severity in men and in people with type 2 diabetes.

In a placebo-controlled RCT of 38 post-COVID patients, four weeks of the multi-strain probiotic VSL#3 significantly decreased Chalder Fatigue Scale scores compared with no change in the placebo group.

Two weeks of supplementation with ProbioSEB CSC3 combined with ImmunoSEB systemic enzymes resolved fatigue symptoms in 91% of participants, with significant reduction in physical and mental fatigue versus controls.
Among symptomatic COVID-19 patients, about 6.2% develop long COVID symptoms, with respiratory symptoms affecting 3.7% and significantly impacting quality of life.
About 10-13% of hospitalized and non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients continue to experience persistent or new symptoms beyond 4 weeks post-infection.
In a follow-up study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 26% and 12% of patients experienced anxiety or depression at 1 and 2 years after discharge, respectively.
At 2-year follow-up, quality-of-life assessments of COVID-19 survivors remained lower compared to uninfected controls.

A study on return to work found that 6.6% of hospitalized patients and 36% of ICU patients had not resumed work 6 months after discharge; another cohort found 45% had not returned to full-time work at 1 year and 49% self-reported memory or concentration difficulties.
Approximately 40-45% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients continue to experience dyspnoea at 1 year, and 44% still exhibit an mMRC score of 2 or higher at 2 years.
Risk factors for post-COVID-19 dyspnea include socioeconomic deprivation, a history of anxiety or depression, advanced age, female gender, ICU admission, and prolonged hospital stay.
Omicron infection was associated with reduced pneumonia severity and lower ICU admission/death risk compared with Delta, and long COVID incidence was 24-50% lower with Omicron than Delta.
Reinfection with the Omicron variant is significantly more common in long COVID patients than those without long COVID, and reinfection is associated with increased incidence of dyspnoea.

Impaired lung diffusion capacity (DLCO % predicted <80%) is the most prevalent pulmonary function abnormality in COVID-19 recovery, more common than restrictive (7%) or obstructive (3.8%) ventilatory dysfunction, with 39.7% showing impaired diffusion at 1 year.
Age, female sex, BMI, and ferritin levels during hospitalization were factors associated with impaired lung diffusion capacity at 1-year follow-up.
In a 3-year follow-up of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, pulmonary diffusion dysfunction declined from 49% at 6 months to 38% at 3 years, though it remained higher than in healthy controls.
Corticosteroid therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation initiated within 6 weeks after discharge have been shown to enhance pulmonary function recovery.
Residual lung abnormalities on chest CT declined from 46% at 6 months to 36% at 3 years, with non-fibrotic lesions resolving while fibrotic-like lesions remained largely stable.

Several months after mild COVID-19 infection, some patients showed marked CD4+ T lymphocyte infiltration around the small airways in lung tissue, together with elevated IL-1β in bronchoalveolar lavage, suggesting ongoing small airway inflammation.

Lung tissue analysis showed that early COVID-19 deaths were characterized by predominant inflammation-related gene expression, while late deaths showed significantly increased fibrosis-associated gene expression with histological fibrosis, indicating time-dependent progression from inflammation to fibrosis.

In vitro, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in a simulated COVID-19 infection environment induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition in lung epithelial cells, and patients with abnormal lung findings 3-6 months post-recovery had higher NET-associated proteins in blood and upper respiratory samples than fully recovered patients.

In a 20-month longitudinal follow-up of long COVID patients, levels of inflammatory cytokines IFN-α2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α remained elevated compared to healthy controls, suggesting sustained chronic inflammation.

Fineschi et al. observed continued upregulation of JAK3 and STAT1/3 in some long COVID patients even 28 months after infection, despite absence of detectable viral remnants, indicating inflammation not driven by persistent virus.
Compared with fully recovered COVID-19 patients, long COVID patients show significant upregulation of ICOS and S1PR1, genes associated with T cell activation and inflammatory responses.
Chemokines CCL3 and CCL19 were markedly elevated in patients with impaired lung function and correlated with decreased DLCO, suggesting a role as biomarkers of chronic pulmonary inflammation.
