Cardiopulmonary symptoms in long COVID have been linked to elevated levels of inflammatory markers IL-1R2, MATN2, and COLEC12.

In COVID-19 convalescent patients, significant increases in γ/δ T cells, B cells, and CD8+ T cells were observed in BAL samples, closely associated with impaired lung function and radiographic abnormalities.

In some patients with post-COVID-19 conditions, abnormal B cell activation and autoantibody formation were observed, with autoantibody titers remaining elevated and new autoantibody types emerging as long as 1 year after infection; 55% of patients with elevated plasma inflammatory markers were positive for autoantibodies, versus fewer in those with normal inflammation.

Phetsouphanh et al. found that immune activation (elevated antibodies and T cell activation markers) seen 3-8 months post-infection in some long COVID patients had largely resolved by 2 years, with most patients experiencing significant improvement in quality of life.
Microthrombi were identified in the plasma of long COVID patients along with significantly elevated α2-antiplasmin, which impairs microthrombi dissolution.
A study on viral pneumonia patients requiring ECMO support showed COVID-19 patients had a 12-fold higher risk of thrombosis compared to patients with other viral pneumonias.

Convalescent COVID-19 patients may exhibit structural damage to the RBC membrane, morphological alterations, reduced deformability, and increased aggregation, which impair microvascular circulation and may relate to persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms.
Even non-hospitalized patients with mild or asymptomatic COVID-19 infection exhibit a higher risk of thrombosis compared to uninfected controls.
SARS-CoV-2 can directly damage alveolar epithelial cells by binding ACE2 receptors, or indirectly through immune-mediated mechanisms, contributing to pulmonary fibrosis.

COVID-19-related lung injury shows a time-dependent progression from inflammation to fibrosis, with early deaths showing inflammation-gene expression predominance and late deaths showing increased fibrosis-gene expression and histological fibrosis.

In a surgical lung biopsy study of COVID-19 patients with persistent interstitial lung disease findings, about 50% showed a histological pattern consistent with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), often in patients with pre-existing lung disease.

Transbronchial cryobiopsy in COVID-19 survivors with persistent symptoms identified three histological patterns: a chronic fibrosing/UIP-like pattern, an acute/subacute injury-repair pattern (organizing pneumonia, fibrosing NSIP, diffuse alveolar damage), and a vascular-dominant pattern with capillary/venule proliferation.
A 2-year follow-up study of severe COVID-19 patients found a significant overall decline in fibrosis severity over time, suggesting partial resolution rather than progressive fibrosis.

In vitro, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in a simulated COVID-19 environment induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in lung epithelial cells, a potential mechanism of pulmonary fibrosis; NET-associated proteins were higher in blood and upper respiratory samples of patients with abnormal lung findings 3-6 months post-recovery than in those fully recovered.

A 20-month longitudinal study found that levels of inflammatory cytokines IFN-α2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α remained elevated in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, suggesting sustained chronic inflammation.

Continued upregulation of inflammation-related genes JAK3 and STAT1/3 was observed in some long COVID patients even 28 months after infection, despite absence of detectable viral remnants, indicating inflammation not driven by persistent viral infection.
Compared with fully recovered COVID-19 patients, long COVID patients showed significant upregulation of genes ICOS and S1PR1, associated with T cell activation and inflammatory responses.

Chemokines CCL3 and CCL19 were markedly elevated in patients with impaired lung function and correlated with decreased DLCO, suggesting their potential as biomarkers of chronic pulmonary inflammation.
Cardiopulmonary symptoms of long COVID have been linked to elevated levels of inflammatory markers IL-1R2, MATN2, and COLEC12, offering potential therapeutic targets.

In COVID-19 convalescent patients, significant increases in γ/δ T cells, B cells, and CD8+ T cells were observed in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples, closely associated with impaired lung function and radiographic abnormalities.

Several months after mild COVID-19 infection, some patients showed marked T lymphocyte infiltration, particularly CD4+ T cells, around small airways in lung tissue, along with elevated IL-1β in BAL samples, suggesting the small airways as a key site of ongoing inflammation.

In some patients with post-COVID-19 conditions, abnormal B cell activation and autoantibody formation were observed, with autoantibody titers remaining elevated and new autoantibody types emerging as late as 1 year after infection.

Phetsouphanh et al. found that some long COVID patients exhibited marked immune activation (elevated antibody levels and T cell activation markers) 3-8 months post-infection, but by 2 years these alterations had largely resolved with most patients showing significant quality-of-life improvement, suggesting immune dysregulation can be transient.

In Woodruff et al., 55% of patients with elevated plasma inflammatory markers were positive for autoantibodies, significantly higher than in patients with normal inflammation levels, suggesting a bidirectional relationship between chronic inflammation and autoantibody production.
Microthrombi were found in the plasma of long COVID patients with significantly elevated levels of α2-antiplasmin, which impairs microthrombi dissolution.
COVID-19 patients requiring ECMO for viral pneumonia exhibited a 12-fold higher risk of thrombosis compared to patients with other viral pneumonias.
The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein can bind fibrinogen, forming pro-inflammatory, plasmin-resistant thrombi that lead to systemic thrombosis and inflammation.

Convalescent COVID-19 patients may exhibit structural damage to the RBC membrane and morphological alterations, with reduced deformability and increased aggregation, impairing microvascular circulation.

Elevated levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) have been observed in COVID-19 patients, potentially reflecting a compensatory response to hypoxia, but this compensation may be insufficient and may instead aggravate RBC injury.

Even non-hospitalized patients with mild or asymptomatic COVID-19 exhibit a higher risk of thrombosis compared to uninfected controls, indicating hypercoagulability is not restricted to severe disease.
Elevated IL-6 levels during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection are associated with persistent viral infection, which can extend PCR positivity for up to 400 days in some patients.

A significant association was found between persistent SARS-CoV-2 viral presence and long COVID symptoms, with patients having higher viral copy numbers being more likely to develop long-term symptoms.

Two-dose COVID-19 vaccination compared to no vaccination was associated with a 36% reduction in risk of long COVID, and a 40% reduction compared to one-dose vaccination, though vaccination did not significantly alleviate symptoms in patients already experiencing long-term symptoms.

Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) can enhance exercise capacity, alleviate persistent symptoms, and improve quality of life in long COVID patients, although effects on dyspnoea and fatigue vary across studies.
Corticosteroid treatment enhanced lung function and alleviated dyspnoea in patients with persistent chest CT abnormalities, with similar efficacy between high-dose and low-dose prednisolone regimens.
N-acetylcysteine and suboxide have demonstrated potential in mitigating post-COVID-19 inflammation and endothelial dysfunction by modulating inflammatory and fibrinolytic factors.
For COVID-19 patients discharged with high thrombosis risk, extended rivaroxaban thromboprophylaxis significantly improved clinical outcomes.
Preliminary evidence suggests that Paxlovid (antiviral) reduces the risk of developing long COVID and alleviates pulmonary burden.

Patients who underwent bilateral orthotopic lung transplantation for severe COVID-19-related lung damage showed significant improvements in activities of daily life and functional mobility after pre- and post-transplant rehabilitation.
People with severe mental illness had elevated prevalence of 11 of 15 neurological conditions at all time points and 13 of 15 at the time of SMI diagnosis compared with matched non-SMI controls.
Other/secondary parkinsonism showed the strongest association with SMI of any neurological condition studied at the time of SMI diagnosis.
Other movement disorders (choreiform, dystonic) were significantly elevated in SMI at time of diagnosis.
Dementia prevalence in people with SMI increased over time, becoming most markedly elevated 5 years after SMI diagnosis.
Parkinson's disease prevalence in people with SMI increased over time, becoming most markedly elevated 5 years after SMI diagnosis.
Motor neuron disease was the only one of 15 neurological conditions studied that was never significantly elevated in people with SMI compared with matched controls at any timepoint.
Epilepsy prevalence was elevated compared with matched controls in all three SMI subtypes (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, other psychoses) as early as 5 years before SMI diagnosis.
Cerebral palsy prevalence was elevated compared with matched controls in all three SMI subtypes as early as 5 years before SMI diagnosis.
At the time of SMI diagnosis, dementia and Parkinson's disease prevalence were also elevated in all three SMI subtypes, unlike at earlier timepoints.

In patients with schizophrenia specifically, multiple sclerosis, paralysis, disorders of nerve root/plexus/peripheral nerves and spinal cord disorders were not significantly elevated compared with matched controls at any timepoint, despite being elevated in bipolar disorder and other psychoses.
Additional adjustment for BMI, smoking status, alcohol misuse and substance misuse did not substantially alter the association between neurological conditions and SMI.
Within 5 years after SMI diagnosis, mortality was higher among people with SMI compared with the matched non-SMI comparator group.
At the time of first SMI diagnosis, epilepsy was the most common comorbid neurological condition, followed by cerebrovascular disease, dementia, Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis.

Disorders of the autonomic nervous system were rare enough (fewer than 100 people without SMI at all timepoints, <0.04%) that subtype-specific stratified analysis by SMI diagnosis could not be conducted for this category.

The authors note that genome-wide association studies have found substantial overlap in genetic variants predisposing to psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, cognitive and other neurological conditions, proposed as a possible shared genetic cause of SMI-neurological comorbidity.

The authors cite evidence that by the time motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease appear, 68-82% of striatal dopamine has already been lost, arguing against SMI diagnosis being a direct cause of subsequent neurodegeneration.
The authors propose that psychosis may represent a common prodromal feature of dementia, consistent with dementia rates diverging sharply from controls only around the time of SMI diagnosis.
A survey of 475 ASMR viewers found that the large majority reported using ASMR videos for relaxation (98%), to aid sleep onset (82%), and to reduce stress or anxiety (~70%).
Participants who experienced ASMR tingles reported lower state-anxiety and improved mood for up to thirty minutes after listening to ASMR audio.

In a within-subjects comparison, tingling segments of ASMR videos produced reliable heart rate deceleration (3-5 bpm) and a 5-8% increase in high-frequency heart rate variability relative to non-tingling segments.

ASMR videos produced greater reductions in pulse rate than nature videos and were associated with increased pulse wave amplitude, indicating peripheral vasodilation and parasympathetic vascular effects.

In a large online study (N=1,037), ASMR viewing improved relaxation and mood in both insomniac and non-insomniac participants, but response magnitude did not differ significantly between the two groups despite tingle-experiencers showing the strongest improvements.
Skin conductance responses increased during ASMR tingling segments compared to non-tingling control periods, indicating concurrent sympathetic activation.
ASMR experiences are accompanied by pupil dilation, a marker of sympathetic/LC-noradrenergic orienting activity.
C-tactile afferents fire optimally at stroking velocities of 1-10 cm/s (peak ~3 cm/s), and their firing rate correlates with subjective pleasantness ratings with near-unit slope.

Higher pleasantness ratings of C-tactile stroking predicted greater reductions in concurrent pain ratings, with each one-point increase in pleasantness producing an additional 0.9-point decrease in pain rating.
Five minutes of scalp massage at CT-optimal velocity produced a significant increase in HF-HRV and a reduction in self-reported anxiety on the Spielberger state-anxiety test.
A 45-minute relaxation massage before bed enhanced sleep efficiency in individuals with insomnia.

During moments of ASMR tingling, fMRI showed elevated BOLD activation in auditory and somatosensory regions as well as the nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex, implicating reward and affiliative circuitry.
ASMR experiencers score higher on trait Empathetic Concern and on neuroticism/anxiety measures than non-experiencers.
ASMR experiencers show reduced functional connectivity in the prefrontal cortex and default mode network, implying diminished top-down inhibition of sensory-affective stimuli.
Physical touch was the most commonly endorsed and most intense ASMR trigger (98% of participants), with minimal inter-individual variation compared to auditory/visual triggers.
Gentle social touch enhanced the intensity and pleasantness of ASMR responses, but only in individuals who were ASMR-experiencers.
Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) produces heart rate deceleration and a rise in HF-HRV within five minutes of stimulation.
Nightly sessions of taVNS significantly enhanced sleep quality, reduced insomnia severity, and increased total sleep duration in individuals with chronic insomnia in controlled trials.
A brief taVNS protocol significantly reduced anxiety symptoms in university students, with effects persisting up to two weeks after stimulation, in a double-blind RCT.
Eight weeks of taVNS significantly reduced anxiety and depression symptoms (HAMA/HAMD) and improved sleep quality (PSQI) in a randomised clinical trial.
ASMR experiencers with higher baseline state anxiety showed a significant reduction in STAI-S scores after viewing an ASMR video, whereas non-experiencers showed no change.

Autistic individuals show altered tactile sensitivity and hedonic perception to CT-innervated skin stimulation, with diminished CT-evoked responses in social brain regions (orbitofrontal cortex, superior temporal sulcus) that scale negatively with autistic trait load.

The coupling between subjective pleasantness reports and central neural representations of touch is weaker in adolescents with autism, suggesting a disconnect between afferent input and hedonic experience.

Some anxious or autistic individuals find deep pressure touch (e.g., weighted blankets, squeeze devices) more calming than light touch, with reductions in arousal, anxiety, and insomnia observed in certain responders.

Multisensory neurons in the ventral intraparietal area fire more vigorously to broadband sounds moving toward the head (70cm to 10cm) than to the same stimuli in far space, in macaque electrophysiology.
A meta-analysis found a modest 15 ms reduction in tactile reaction times when sounds occurred near the body versus farther away, with variability and small effect sizes noted.
MEG recordings showed beta-band desynchronisation in secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) in response to realistic haircut and water-dripping sounds resembling ASMR triggers.
Viewing a virtual stick stroking a forearm associated with one's own body in VR produced tingling sensations in 89% of users despite zero actual skin input.

In the original survey study, pleasantness ratings strongly predicted ASMR classification (each 1 SD increase in pleasantness increased odds of reporting ASMR by ~8-fold), while arousal showed a non-significant negative trend.
Arousal was not a significant predictor of ASMR classification, and the pleasantness-by-arousal interaction did not improve model fit.
Across 136 ASMR-positive trials, tingle intensity increased linearly with pleasantness but not with arousal in the linear mixed-effects model.

A follow-up interaction model showed pleasantness remained a strong positive predictor of tingle intensity while arousal became a significant negative predictor, and the pleasantness-by-arousal interaction was significant, indicating the pleasantness-tingle relationship steepened at higher arousal.
EEG studies found increased alpha, gamma, and sensorimotor rhythm (SMR) power in ASMR experiencers relative to non-experiencers during auditory ASMR triggers.

Engelbregt et al. (2022) reported reductions in alpha and theta with elevated beta, including alpha decreases over temporal-parietal sites, during ASMR exposure, consistent with an early sensory orienting phase.
Scalp massage in office workers significantly reduced cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate, and self-reported stress.
Early apoptosis (Annexin V+/PI-) in PBMCs was significantly higher in elderly post-COVID individuals than in age-matched controls.
Late apoptosis (Annexin V+/PI+) in PBMCs was significantly elevated in post-COVID elderly individuals compared to controls.
CD4+ T cells from post-COVID elderly individuals showed significantly increased apoptosis compared to controls.
CD8+ T cells from post-COVID elderly individuals showed significantly increased apoptosis compared to controls.

JC-1 assay showed significantly greater mitochondrial depolarization (green/red fluorescence ratio) in post-COVID elderly individuals than controls, indicating activation of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.
Bax (pro-apoptotic protein) expression was significantly elevated in PBMCs of post-COVID elderly individuals compared to controls.
Bcl-2 (anti-apoptotic protein) expression was significantly decreased in PBMCs of post-COVID elderly individuals compared to controls.
The Bax/Bcl-2 ratio was significantly higher in post-COVID elderly subjects than controls, indicating a strong pro-apoptotic shift.
Active Caspase-3 levels were significantly increased in PBMCs of the post-COVID group, indicating execution-phase apoptosis.
Among post-COVID participants, higher apoptotic indices positively correlated with the severity of initial COVID-19 infection (mild, moderate, severe).
Apoptotic indices were inversely correlated with time since recovery (<9 months), suggesting partial normalization of apoptosis over time in some post-COVID individuals.
Among post-COVID donors, female donors showed a modest but statistically significant increase in early apoptosis of CD4+ T cells compared to male donors.
Female post-COVID donors showed a higher Bax/Bcl-2 ratio than male donors, suggesting a greater pro-apoptotic tendency, but this trend did not reach statistical significance.
No significant sex-based differences were observed in late apoptosis or mitochondrial depolarization within the post-COVID group.
T cell proportions in PBMCs progressively declined with increasing COVID-19 disease severity from Healthy to Hospitalized states.
Macrophages, neutrophils, and secretory cells were significantly enriched (by R_o/e ratio) in severe COVID-19 disease states while T cells were depleted.
IL32 was among the top expressed cytokines and showed the highest expression across all disease groups, suggesting a pivotal pro-inflammatory role.
LTB was among the top 10 highly expressed cytokines in pathological COVID-19 states.
MIF was among the top 10 highly expressed cytokines in pathological COVID-19 states.
T cells exhibited the highest cytokine module scores among all cell types, constituting 34.7% of the spatial distribution of cytokine activity.
Myeloid cells had the highest contribution to the inflammatory module score (35.4%), followed by T cells (31.2%).
T cell cytokine and inflammatory module scores were significantly elevated compared to Healthy controls, with the greatest increase in the Hospitalized group.

Naive T cells predominated in Healthy individuals, whereas effector and memory T cells were significantly enriched in diseased groups, with Memory CD8+ T cells showing the strongest enrichment in Hospitalized patients.
Effector CD8+ T cells displayed the highest cytotoxic module scores among T cell subtypes, reflecting critical killing functions during disease progression.
Memory T cell subsets showed elevated exhaustion and inflammatory module scores, suggesting functional impairment during prolonged immune responses in COVID-19.
Memory CD4+ T cells showed elevated regulatory effector scores, indicating an immunomodulatory role.
CellChat cell-cell communication analysis identified Memory CD8+ T cells as the subset with the highest interaction intensity with other T cell subtypes, acting as a central communication hub.
Memory CD8+ T cells showed prominent expression of MHC-I-related genes (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C), consistent with their central role in the MHC-I antigen presentation communication network.

KEGG pathway analysis showed Memory CD8+ T cells were significantly enriched in immune-related processes including natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity, antigen processing and presentation, chemokine signaling, and COVID-19-related pathways.

Memory CD8+ T cells also showed enrichment of metabolic pathways including oxidative phosphorylation and ribosome-related processes, indicating immunometabolic coordination during active immune states.

Cross-group differential expression analysis of Memory CD8+ T cells identified seven key genes (RPS26, RPS29, RPL36, RPL39, CD3E, RPS28, RPS21) that were substantially upregulated in Hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
Among nine machine learning algorithms tested, XGBoost achieved the highest and most stable average AUC in both training and testing datasets, and was selected as the final diagnostic model.
SHAP-based interpretability analysis of the XGBoost model identified RPS26, RPS29, and RPL36 as the genes with the greatest contribution to COVID-19 diagnostic predictions.
Citing prior literature, the authors note that RPS26 regulates specific mRNA translation and maintains T cell development and homeostasis, with knockout causing peripheral T cell deficits.
The authors propose that downregulation of CD3E, a core T cell receptor complex component, may impair immune recognition efficiency in COVID-19.

The authors propose that persistent MHC-I-mediated communication involving metabolically active but functionally exhausted memory CD8+ T cells, alongside sustained cytokine expression and myeloid enrichment, may drive low-grade continuous immune activation and unresolved tissue inflammation underlying Long COVID.
Pooled analysis of five RCTs showed that pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved six-minute walk distance compared to usual care in patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Pooled analysis of four RCTs found that pulmonary rehabilitation did not significantly improve dyspnea scores (mMRC scale) compared to control in PASC patients.
Pooled analysis of four RCTs showed a significant reduction in fatigue among PASC patients receiving pulmonary rehabilitation compared to controls.
Pooled analysis of five RCTs demonstrated significant improvement in health-related quality of life following pulmonary rehabilitation compared to controls.

Pooled analysis of three RCTs showed a significant improvement in maximal inspiratory pressure (a measure of pulmonary/respiratory muscle function) in the pulmonary rehabilitation group compared to controls.

Subgroup analyses comparing telerehabilitation versus face-to-face pulmonary rehabilitation found no statistically significant differences in exercise capacity, dyspnea, fatigue, or health-related quality of life outcomes.
Nearly 80% of PASC/PVS patients showed impairment in at least one of four assessed cognitive domains (attention, working speed, verbal fluency, working memory).
Nearly a third of patients had multi-domain cognitive impairment, defined as three or more tests below average.
Over half of the total sample scored below the age-adjusted norm on the d2 Test of Attention.
The majority of the sample scored below the age-adjusted norm on working speed in the d2 Test of Attention.
Nearly half of the sample scored below the norm on the formal lexical (phonemic) verbal fluency subtest.
About a third of the sample scored below average on the digit span backwards task, indicating reduced short-term/working memory.
No statistically significant differences in cognitive performance were found between PASC and PVS patients in any assessed domain.
Nearly two-thirds of the sample met the cut-off for probable clinically relevant depression.
The vast majority of patients reported clinically relevant fatigue.
A significantly higher proportion of men than women performed below average on formal lexical verbal fluency.
No significant gender differences were found in attention, working speed, or working memory performance.
Patients performed significantly worse than healthy control normative data in attention, working speed, and formal lexical verbal fluency, with particularly large effect sizes in older patients.
Elevated CRP was significantly associated with below-average attention performance.
Elevated CRP was significantly associated with below-average working memory performance.
Elevated CRP was significantly associated with multidomain cognitive impairment.
The proportion of patients with elevated CRP did not differ significantly between PASC and PVS groups.
Higher education level was consistently associated with decreased odds of cognitive impairment across all assessed domains in PASC patients.
Older age increased the risk of impairment in attention and working speed but was inversely related to risk of impairment in lexical fluency.
Longer time since acute infection was associated with greater risk of impairment in attention, working memory, and multidomain impairment, but not with working speed or lexical fluency.
Clinically relevant depressive symptoms were significantly associated with increased odds of cognitive impairment across all four cognitive domains.
Clinically relevant fatigue was significantly associated only with impairment in the working speed domain, not other cognitive domains.

A BMI of 30 or above was associated with increased risk of impairment in lexical verbal fluency and working memory, whereas smoking status was not significantly related to impairment in any cognitive domain.
Smoking status was not significantly associated with cognitive impairment in any domain.

In a subgroup of PASC patients without clinically relevant depression, subclinical depressive symptoms remained significantly associated with impairment in attention and multidomain functioning, indicating cognitive impairment is not solely attributable to clinical depression.
Among participants who had been infected with SARS-CoV-2, 29.5% met the study's criteria for PASC (new symptom onset within 3 months, persistence >2 months, and at least some functional limitation).
Women showed a higher prevalence of PASC (35.3%) than men (24.2%).
Younger adults aged 18-29 showed the highest PASC prevalence (34.0%) compared with older age groups (29.4% for 30-45; 27.6% for 46-65).
Individuals with university or higher education had higher PASC prevalence (32.8%) than those with secondary or lower education (28.4%), contrary to prior literature.
Participants reporting high financial hardship had higher PASC prevalence (31.6%) than those with low financial hardship (27.8%).
Fatigue and lack of energy was the most commonly reported PASC symptom, affecting over three-quarters of participants with PASC, with an average duration of about 9 months.
Decreased physical performance was reported by approximately two-thirds of PASC participants, with an average duration of about 8 months.
Muscle and joint pain was reported by nearly half of PASC participants, with an average duration of about 7 months.
Difficulty concentrating or remembering was among the longest-lasting PASC symptoms, averaging nearly 11 months in duration and affecting nearly 40% of PASC participants.
Sleep disturbances were reported by over a third of PASC participants and were among the longest-lasting symptoms, averaging about 10 months.
Pre-pandemic BMI category showed no significant association with PASC status, contrasting with prior studies identifying obesity as a PASC risk factor.

Smoking status was significantly associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection status overall (non-smokers proportion lowest among non-infected), but no significant difference in smoking was found specifically between the infected-no-PASC and PASC groups.

Pre-pandemic sufficient physical activity was lowest in the infected-no-PASC group, while PASC and non-infected groups had similarly higher rates of sufficient activity, suggesting physical activity was associated with reduced infection risk but not protection against developing PASC once infected.
Individuals with PASC reported significantly higher perceived stress than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC.

Individuals with PASC reported significantly higher depressive symptom severity than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC, with the largest effect size among the ill-being measures.
Individuals with PASC reported significantly higher generalized anxiety symptom severity than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC.
Individuals with PASC reported significantly lower emotional well-being than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC.
Individuals with PASC reported significantly lower psychological well-being (sense of purpose, self-acceptance, personal growth) than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC.
Individuals with PASC reported significantly lower social well-being than both non-infected individuals and those infected without PASC, with the smallest effect size among the well-being measures.
Severe post-COVID-19 symptoms were strongly associated with reduced functional capacity in unadjusted analysis.
Mild post-COVID-19 symptoms did not show a significant association with functional capacity.
Severe post-COVID-19 symptoms were strongly linked to higher depression scores.
After adjusting for depression, severe post-COVID-19 symptoms remained significantly associated with reduced functional capacity but with a smaller effect size.
Depression was independently associated with reduced functional capacity after adjusting for other factors.
Bootstrapped mediation analysis confirmed post-COVID-19 symptom severity was significantly associated with reduced functional capacity partly through depression.
The interaction between depression and post-COVID-19 symptom severity on functional status was not significant, indicating depression did not moderate this relationship.
Individuals with PASC had significantly reduced functional capacity compared with those without PASC.
PASC was associated with higher depression scores.
In an adjusted model, both PASC and depression were independently and significantly associated with reduced functional capacity.
Bootstrapped mediation analysis showed depression significantly mediated the relationship between PASC and functional capacity, accounting for 51% of the overall association.
No significant interaction was found between depression and PASC on functional capacity, indicating depression did not moderate this relationship.

Longer duration since COVID-19 infection (3-6 and 6-12 months) was associated with higher depression, which was linked to reduced functional capacity, with depression partially mediating and moderating this relationship.
In longitudinal analysis, depression was significantly associated with deterioration of functional capacity over time.
PASC was significantly associated with changes (deterioration) in functional capacity over time, with depression accounting for 44% of the overall longitudinal association.
A sensitivity analysis excluding the fatigue item from the PHQ-9 confirmed that depressive symptoms still mediate the relationship between PASC/symptom severity and functional capacity.
VanderWeele's sensitivity analysis showed the mediation effect of depression remained robust to unmeasured confounding at ρ=-0.5.

Non-vaccinated individuals showed a larger (marginally significant) reduction in functional capacity associated with moderate/severe symptoms compared with vaccinated individuals, who showed a weaker but significant effect.
PHQ-9 scores were significantly associated with reductions in DASI scores in both vaccinated and non-vaccinated subgroups.

Among depression subscales, trouble concentrating, little energy and little interest were most strongly associated with reduced functional capacity, and somatic symptoms accounted for the largest proportion of variance and poorer functional recovery over time.
Depressive symptoms were highly prevalent among the PERCEIVE cohort, with little energy, sleep disturbances and appetite changes being most commonly reported.
Among participants with severe depression, a high proportion also reported fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain and palpitations.

Individuals later diagnosed with long COVID had a significantly higher frequency of depression than matched controls before the pandemic (2019), 12 months before, and 6 months after long COVID diagnosis.
Depression was not significantly associated with long COVID in men in 2019, unlike in women and unlike the other time points.
Individuals later diagnosed with long COVID had a significantly higher frequency of anxiety than matched controls across all three time points examined.
Headache diagnoses had the highest significant association with subsequent long COVID diagnosis across all time points and in both sexes.

Unlike the other diagnoses, post-viral fatigue syndrome was not significantly associated with later long COVID diagnosis in 2019 (pre-pandemic), only becoming significant in the 12 months before and 6 months after diagnosis.

In women with long COVID, the odds of a post-viral fatigue diagnosis rose sharply from before the pandemic to shortly before long COVID diagnosis, then declined slightly after diagnosis while remaining far above pre-pandemic levels.

In men with long COVID, the odds of a post-viral fatigue diagnosis increased sharply from before the pandemic through 12 months before diagnosis and continued to increase further at 6 months after diagnosis, unlike the pattern in women.
In men, the odds ratio for headache was lower at 6 months after long COVID diagnosis compared to 12 months before diagnosis, but remained significantly elevated relative to pre-pandemic controls.
About two-thirds of individuals diagnosed with long COVID in this population were women, consistent with prior evidence that female sex is a risk factor for developing long COVID.

A parallel study on the same cohort found the post-COVID group had a significantly higher pre-pandemic prevalence of respiratory diagnoses, including asthma, than controls, suggesting a possible confounding role of respiratory disease in mental health assessment.

The authors propose that chronic systemic inflammation linking depression and anxiety may be a shared pathway predisposing individuals to both pre-pandemic mental health symptoms and subsequent long COVID.

The authors note a potential diagnostic overlap between the ICD-10 code used for post-viral fatigue syndrome (G93.3) and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which could affect interpretation of fatigue-related associations, though they judge substantial impact unlikely given the study period's diagnostic patterns.
Among working-age adults who ever had COVID-19, 27.5% reported long COVID symptoms lasting 3 months or longer.
Among respondents with long COVID symptoms, 22.6% reported severe activity limitations.
In fully adjusted models, Hispanic respondents reported long COVID symptoms at higher rates than other racial-ethnic groups.
Respondents with household income below $25,000 were substantially more likely to report long COVID symptoms than those earning $200,000 or more.
Medicaid-insured respondents were more likely to report long COVID symptoms compared to those with employer-sponsored insurance.
Uninsured respondents were more likely to report long COVID symptoms compared to those with employer-sponsored insurance.
Living in more rural U.S. states was associated with a higher adjusted probability of reporting long COVID symptoms.
Concurrent anxiety symptoms were associated with a higher adjusted probability of reporting long COVID symptoms.
Concurrent depressive symptoms were associated with a higher adjusted probability of reporting long COVID symptoms.

Long COVID participants showed no significant differences from healthy controls on pulmonary function testing or 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures including ventilation defect percentage and gas exchange ratios.
Long COVID participants reported significantly reduced perceived cognitive function in everyday life on the PROMIS questionnaire relative to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated fatigue scores on PROMIS compared to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated anxiety scores compared to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated depression scores compared to normative expectations.
Long COVID participants had significantly elevated sleep disturbance scores compared to normative expectations.

Despite subjective cognitive complaints, objective cognitive testing (NIHTB-CB) showed total cognition composite and most domain scores within normal limits, revealing a discordance between subjective and objective cognition.
Reduced 129Xe pulmonary gas exchange (RBC:mem and RBC:gas) was negatively correlated with cerebral perfusion measured by ASL.
Reduced 129Xe gas exchange (RBC:mem and RBC:gas) was inversely correlated with self-reported sleep disturbance severity.
Cerebral perfusion measured by ASL showed a strong positive relationship with severity of sleep disturbance.
Higher 129Xe RBC:mem gas exchange was positively correlated with better executive function and showed a trend toward better total cognitive composite score.
129Xe pulmonary MRI gas exchange measures were not associated with subjective (PROMIS) report of everyday cognitive difficulties.
Initial associations between lobar brain volumes and 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures were no longer significant after adjusting for age.
White matter hyperintensity volume and diffusion tensor metrics (FA, MD, RD) were not significantly associated with 129Xe pulmonary MRI measures after controlling for age.
Fibromyalgia was a pre-existing comorbidity in 2 of 11 (18%) Long COVID participants with available medical records.
The most commonly reported Long COVID symptoms in the cohort were fatigue, dyspnea, and headache, with cognitive impairment, joint pain, and neuropathy also frequently reported.
At 12 weeks, patients receiving primary care pulmonary rehabilitation showed a significantly greater increase in 6-minute walk distance than controls receiving no rehabilitation.
The improvement in 6-minute walk distance in the pulmonary rehabilitation group persisted and remained significantly greater than controls at 24 weeks.
A per-protocol analysis restricted to patients with adequate compliance (≥25 sessions) confirmed a similar treatment effect on 6-minute walk distance at 12 weeks.
The overall treatment effect on 6-minute walk distance across the study period was estimated at 55 m in favour of the intervention group.
Health status measured by the CAT questionnaire improved significantly more in the pulmonary rehabilitation group than in controls at 12 weeks.
CIS-fatigue scores decreased significantly more in the pulmonary rehabilitation group than in controls at 12 weeks.
CIS-activity subscale scores improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation than control at 12 weeks.
CIS-total score improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation at 12 weeks in an unadjusted model, but this effect lost significance after adjusting for confounders.
Dyspnoea, measured by the mMRC scale, improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation than control at 12 weeks.
After covariate adjustment, dysfunctional breathing symptoms (Nijmegen questionnaire) improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation.
Inspiratory muscle strength (MIP) improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation after covariate adjustment.
Expiratory muscle strength (MEP) improved significantly more with pulmonary rehabilitation after covariate adjustment.

No significant between-group differences were found for health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L utility index and VAS), post-COVID functional status, anxiety/depression, handgrip strength or daily step counts.
Patients in the pulmonary rehabilitation group were nearly six times more likely to achieve a minimal clinically important improvement in 6-minute walk distance than controls.
Patients in the pulmonary rehabilitation group were more likely to achieve a clinically significant improvement in CIS-fatigue than controls.
Patients in the pulmonary rehabilitation group were more likely to achieve a clinically significant improvement in mMRC dyspnoea score than controls.
Patients in the pulmonary rehabilitation group were more likely to achieve a clinically significant improvement in MIP than controls.
The early improvement in CIS-fatigue seen at 12 weeks with pulmonary rehabilitation was not sustained at 36 weeks, with fatigue levels rising again after the initial improvement.
A significant time-by-group interaction for MIP was observed, with a treatment effect evident at week 24.
The pulmonary rehabilitation intervention was associated with a small number of adverse events, mostly mild, and one unrelated serious adverse event of Staphylococcus epidermidis sepsis.

Only a small proportion of patients reported postexertional malaise during the stepwise rehabilitation programme, and none discontinued treatment because of it, suggesting the programme is feasible despite PEM concerns.

Both the cognitive and affective psychoeducation interventions were associated with a significant reduction in executive/attentional complaints from baseline to 2 months, with no difference between arms.
Both intervention arms showed significant improvement in self-reported memory complaints from baseline to 2 months, with no group-by-time interaction.
Reliable change indices showed that just over a third of patients in each arm improved beyond what would be expected from measurement error alone on BRIEF-A and MMQ.
Improvements in cognitive complaints were maintained at 8 months, with a larger sustained effect in the cognitive arm than the affective arm for both BRIEF-A and MMQ.
Both arms showed a moderate reduction in overall fatigue from baseline to 2 months, with no group interaction.
A significant group-by-time interaction showed that psychosocial fatigue improved only in the cognitive arm, not the affective arm.
A time effect on sleep difficulties was observed at 2 months, driven mainly by the cognitive group, with no significant improvement in the affective group.
A sex effect on sleep complaints was observed, with men reporting more sleep difficulty at short-term follow-up but women reporting more sleep difficulty at 8-month follow-up.
Symptom distress improved significantly over time in the cognitive group but not the affective group.
An interaction effect showed that interpersonal relations improved significantly only in the affective arm, aligning with its focus on behavioural activation and communication.
Quality of life measured by the QLSI improved significantly over time in both arms, with a sex effect showing men reported lower quality of life.
EQ-5D-5L VAS scores improved over time, mainly driven by a moderate effect in the cognitive group.
Overall work impairment decreased over time in both arms, with the affective arm showing a faster (2-month) effect than the cognitive arm (which showed effect mainly by 8 months).

MoCA scores remained unchanged across all three time points, unlike the more detailed neuropsychological measures, suggesting this brief global screening tool is insensitive to Long COVID cognitive changes.
Objective attention performance (worst Z-score) improved significantly only in the cognitive arm at 2 months, and improvement was maintained through 8 months.
Objective long-term memory performance improved significantly only in the cognitive arm at 2 and 8 months.
Objective working memory performance improved significantly only in the affective arm at 2 months, but this effect was not maintained at 8 months.
No significant improvement in objective executive function performance was observed in either arm at 2 or 8 months.
Time elapsed since first SARS-CoV-2 infection did not predict changes in self-reported cognitive complaints, arguing against spontaneous recovery as the sole explanation for observed improvements.

Despite statistically significant improvements, a majority of patients remained above clinical thresholds for fatigue, sleep difficulties, psychological distress and quality of life after intervention.

Both interventions had high feasibility, low dropout, and no reported adverse events, with equal satisfaction between arms despite the cognitive intervention being rated more useful and credible pre-randomization.
Contrary to the study hypothesis, the cognitive intervention did not show superior effects over the affective intervention on the primary outcome of perceived cognitive difficulties.
Female sex was one of the biopsychosocial variables predicting a long COVID diagnosis, with women more likely to be classified as having long COVID.
Higher stress was one of the biopsychosocial variables that classified participants as having a long COVID diagnosis.
Social support was one of the biopsychosocial variables that classified participants as having a long COVID diagnosis.
Symptom clustering revealed that phenotypes combining both mental and physical health symptoms were predictive of brain fog in long COVID.
Phenotypes with only sleep-related symptoms were not predictive of brain fog, unlike combined mental/physical symptom phenotypes.
Phenotypes with only physical symptoms (without mental health symptoms) were not predictive of brain fog.
Brain fog in long COVID was marked by slower reading and typing speed measured during home-based tasks.
Slower reaction times on cognitive tasks were identified as a marker of brain fog in long COVID.
Changes in information processing speed and decision-making thresholds were identified as markers of brain fog in long COVID.
Long COVID participants with brain fog showed slower typing speeds during home-based cognitive/behavioral tasks.
Participants with brain fog showed slower reaction times on cognitive tasks compared to those without brain fog.
Brain fog in long COVID was associated with changes in information processing speed measured via cognitive tasks.
Brain fog in long COVID was associated with changes in decision-making thresholds during cognitive choice tasks.
At one-year follow-up, the large majority (82.4%) of participants who had long COVID at timepoint 1 had still not remitted.
Older age was independently associated with increased odds of mortality in hospitalized Omicron patients.
ICU admission during hospitalization was a strong independent predictor of mortality.
Diabetes was independently associated with increased mortality risk in hospitalized Omicron patients.
Antibacterial use during hospitalization was associated with reduced odds of mortality.
Higher lymphocyte count was associated with reduced odds of mortality (i.e., lymphopenia increased mortality risk).
At 6 months post-discharge, 86.0% of hospitalized Omicron survivors reported at least one persistent symptom.
At 1 year post-discharge, symptom persistence declined slightly to 83.5% of patients reporting at least one symptom, with symptom counts decreasing significantly over time.
Fatigue, cough, and snoring were the most commonly reported persistent symptoms among post-discharge Omicron patients.
The number of persistent symptoms per patient decreased significantly between the 6-month and 1-year follow-up visits.
Patients with persistent symptoms had significantly longer hospital stays than those without persistent symptoms.
Symptomatic patients had lower lymphocyte counts (lymphopenia) compared with asymptomatic patients.
Symptomatic patients had significantly elevated C-reactive protein levels compared with asymptomatic patients.
A CRP threshold of 15.38 mg/L or higher was identified as an optimal cutoff predicting greater risk of long COVID symptom persistence.
The proportion of CYP meeting Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFQ) case-ness increased from 35.0% at 3 months to 40.2% at 24 months post-infection.
Among the 943 CYP, 15.9% persistently met CFQ case-ness at all four follow-up time-points, while smaller proportions met it once, twice, or three times.
Female sex was associated with a higher likelihood of ever meeting CFQ fatigue case-ness during follow-up compared to males.
Older age at infection was associated with a higher likelihood of ever meeting CFQ fatigue case-ness.
CYP who ever met CFQ case-ness were far more likely to retrospectively report frequent tiredness before the pandemic than never-cases.
Ever-cases were more likely than never-cases to retrospectively report tiredness/fatigue as a main symptom at their acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Meeting the research definition for Post-COVID Condition at 3-months post-infection was strongly associated with ever meeting CFQ fatigue case-ness during follow-up.
Overall CFQ total fatigue scores increased modestly over 24 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection, rising by an average of 0.019 points per month, equating to a 0.448 point increase over 24 months.
The physical fatigue subscale of the CFQ increased over time at a rate of 0.012 points per month.
The mental fatigue subscale of the CFQ increased over time at a rate of 0.007 points per month.
Fatigue trajectories over 24 months differed by sex, with females showing a worsening trajectory and males showing a relatively flat trajectory.

Fatigue trajectories diverged by whether participants met the PCC definition at 3-months: scores decreased over time in those meeting the definition but increased in those who did not, with PCC-positive participants having nearly double the predicted fatigue score at 24 months.

Among those who reported fatigue/tiredness as a main symptom at acute infection, fatigue scores decreased over follow-up, while scores increased among those who did not, resulting in convergence of trajectories over time.

A single-item question on fatigue (mild/severe combined) showed moderate-to-good sensitivity and specificity for detecting CFQ case-ness across follow-ups, with higher negative than positive predictive value.
When restricted to 'severe fatigue' responses only, the single-item had low sensitivity but very high specificity for CFQ case-ness.
Among participants reporting no unusual fatigue/tiredness on the single-item, 12.1-19.4% were nonetheless identified as CFQ cases, indicating the single-item under-detects borderline fatigue cases.
The CFQ demonstrated good internal reliability at each follow-up time-point in this cohort.

Post-infection fatigue prevalence in this cohort (35-40%) closely resembled pre-pandemic adolescent fatigue prevalence reported in a 1999 UK study (34.1-38.1%), raising questions about the diagnostic specificity of fatigue for Post-COVID Condition.
Mean CFQ scores among CFQ cases in this Long COVID cohort were comparable to mean CFQ scores reported in a specialist paediatric chronic fatigue syndrome clinic sample.
Among CFQ ever-cases, the items relating to lacking energy, feeling sleepy/drowsy, needing to rest more, and problems with tiredness had the highest prevalence across all follow-ups.

Never-cases had consistently low mean total CFQ scores (less than 1 point) across all follow-ups, while ever-cases scored between 4 and 5 points, reflecting a clear separation in fatigue severity between the two groups.
During the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, musculoskeletal pain, weakness, and excessive tiredness were the most frequently reported symptoms in this Italian cohort.
Compared with the acute phase, mean excessive tiredness scores decreased by 0.43 points at the persistent (post-COVID) phase, but remained clinically relevant.
Muscle weakness scores decreased by 0.52 points from the acute to the persistent phase, reflecting a small-to-moderate but incomplete recovery.
Muscle/joint pain scores decreased by 0.54 points from acute to persistent phase, the largest reduction among symptoms assessed, yet remained clinically relevant.
Fatigue/asthenia scores decreased by 0.40 points from the acute to persistent phase, the smallest reduction among symptoms measured.
Headache scores decreased by 0.41 points from acute to persistent phase, indicating incomplete resolution.
Excessive tiredness, fatigue/asthenia, and muscle weakness showed moderate inter-item correlations, suggesting they represent related but distinct symptom constructs within the validated instrument.
Women reported significantly higher persistent fatigue than men, though the difference was small and may attenuate after adjustment for confounders.
Symptom persistence was comparable between participants aged ≤30 years and those older than 30 years.
A small proportion of participants (4.4%) reported at least one chronic comorbidity, most commonly hypertension, indicating a largely low-comorbidity cohort.

Only 3.6% of participants were hospitalized during acute infection and 2.8% required oxygen therapy, indicating the cohort represented largely community-managed, mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19 cases who nonetheless developed Long COVID.
HRQoL remained significantly reduced compared with pre-COVID-19 levels at 6, 9, 12, and 15 months after a positive PCR test, with the magnitude of reduction diminishing over time.
Participants reporting any COVID-19-related symptoms had significantly reduced HRQoL compared with those without symptoms.
Participants reporting fatigue had a markedly larger reduction in HRQoL than those without fatigue.
Older age was associated with significantly higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Lack of COVID-19 vaccination was associated with significantly higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures.
Presence of any COVID-19-related symptoms was associated with higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures.
Older age was associated with significantly higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Lack of COVID-19 vaccination was associated with significantly higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures.
Having any COVID-19-related symptoms was associated with significantly higher odds of experiencing catastrophic health expenditures.
Experiencing a pay cut or reduced income due to COVID-19-related symptoms was strongly associated with higher odds of catastrophic health expenditures.
Severe or critical acute SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly increased the odds of experiencing catastrophic health costs.
Fatigue was associated with significantly increased odds of experiencing catastrophic health costs.
Better health-related quality of life was associated with significantly decreased odds of experiencing catastrophic costs after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Social support was associated with significantly decreased odds of experiencing catastrophic costs after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Fatigue prevalence among COVID-19 survivors decreased gradually over the year, from 50% at one month to 36% at twelve months post-discharge.
Participants with persistent fatigue performed fewer repetitions on the 1-minute Sit-to-Stand Test than those without fatigue at 1, 4, and 12 months, though not significantly at 6 months.
Physical performance in the fatigue group remained stable over the 12-month follow-up, showing no significant change from baseline.

In the fatigue group, predicted FVC values gradually increased between 1 and 6 months and between 1 and 12 months, with the fatigue group only reaching significant improvement and normal-range values by 12 months, later than the non-fatigue group.
Other pulmonary function measures (FEF, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio) did not show statistically significant changes over the 12-month follow-up.

Possible or probable anxiety was more prevalent in the fatigue group across all timepoints and increased from 48% at 1 month to 56% at 12 months, with significant group differences and worsening HADS-A scores over time.
Depressive symptoms were significantly more common in the fatigue group at all timepoints, rising from 47% at 1 month to 66% at 12 months, with worsening HADS-D scores over time.

A decision tree model combining depressive symptoms with predicted FVC greater than 75% at 30 days post-discharge significantly predicted long-term fatigue persistence in 19% of the sample, with overall model accuracy of 79%.

A secondary decision tree node identified that the combination of depressive signs, predicted FVC below 75%, and impaired physical performance (fewer than 12 sit-to-stand repetitions per minute) characterized 10% of the sample within the fatigue group.
A Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 7 or greater one month after hospital discharge was associated with long-term persistence of fatigue symptoms according to the predictive model.
The fatigue group was predominantly female, but the decision tree model did not identify gender as a significant discriminative predictor of long-term fatigue persistence.

Patients in the fatigue group had BMI values exceeding 30 kg/m2, consistent with obesity-related reductions in diaphragm excursion and chest wall mechanics contributing to reduced FVC and long COVID fatigue.
Among participants in the fatigue group, 81% had been admitted to the ICU and 61% had required invasive mechanical ventilation during acute COVID-19 hospitalization.

Days with higher daily stress scores were significantly associated with increased severity of all 8 Long COVID symptoms on the same day, independent of effortful activities and demographic/medical factors.
High daily stress (8/10) was associated with anxiety severity 4.9 points higher on the same day compared with mean stress levels, the strongest association observed.
High daily stress (8/10) was associated with depression severity 3.2 points higher on the same day compared with mean stress levels.
Higher daily stress predicted more severe anxiety symptoms one day later.
Higher daily stress predicted more severe depression symptoms one day later.
Higher daily stress predicted more severe anxiety symptoms two days later.
Higher daily stress predicted more severe dizziness symptoms two days later.
Higher daily worry about one's illness (8/10) was associated with increased fatigue severity on the same day compared with mean worry levels.
Higher daily worry was associated with increased anxiety severity on the same day.
Higher daily worry was associated with increased depression severity on the same day.
Higher daily worry was associated with increased cognitive dysfunction severity on the same day.
Higher daily worry was, unexpectedly, associated with reduced anxiety severity one day later, suggesting a delayed protective effect distinct from stress.
Higher daily worry was associated with reduced depression severity one day later.
Higher daily worry was associated with reduced pain severity two days later.

Daily rumination about one's illness showed limited impact on Long COVID symptoms, with evidence of association for only 2 symptoms across all analyses, contrasting with the broader effects of stress and worry.

Subgroup analyses testing effect modification by gender and by preexisting mental health condition found that associations between stress/worry/rumination and symptom severity were broadly consistent across subgroups, with only a small number of exceptions.
Men reported higher average symptom scores than women across most domains, including stress, worry, rumination, anxiety, and depression.
Dual use of combustible cigarettes and heated tobacco products was more prevalent among participants with a history of COVID-19 (13.5%) than among those without (7.3%).

Among current tobacco users (dual, CC, or HTP combined) with a history of COVID-19, adjusted odds of persistent arthralgia, chest pain, dyspnea, and dysosmia were significantly increased compared with never-users without COVID-19 history.
Among current tobacco users with a history of COVID-19, aORs for dysgeusia, memory impairment, and loss of concentration were not significantly increased.
Among former tobacco users with a history of COVID-19, aORs for arthralgia and headache were significantly increased, while aORs for dyspnea and dysosmia were significantly decreased.
Among dual users with a history of COVID-19, adjusted odds of persistent arthralgia, chest pain, dyspnea, dysgeusia, and dysosmia were significantly elevated.
Among dual users with a history of COVID-19, the adjusted odds of persistent sexual dysfunction were significantly decreased.
Among exclusive combustible cigarette (CC) users with a history of COVID-19, adjusted odds of persistent chest pain, dyspnea, and fatigue were significantly increased.
Among exclusive heated tobacco product (HTP) users with a history of COVID-19, adjusted odds of persistent dyspnea and sexual dysfunction were significantly increased.

Dual users with a history of COVID-19 showed a greater number of significant associations with persistent long-COVID-type symptoms than exclusive CC or HTP users, suggesting dual use may negate any risk reduction expected from HTP substitution.

A cited in vitro study found that dual exposure to combustible cigarette and heated tobacco product emissions significantly increased oxidative stress and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis compared with either exposure alone, offered as a possible mechanism for the greater symptom burden seen in dual users.

The authors conclude that, despite headache and arthralgia increases likely reflecting nicotine withdrawal, former smokers with a history of COVID-19 did not show the elevated dysgeusia, dysosmia, or chest pain seen in current smokers, suggesting smoking cessation may confer overall protection against characteristic long-COVID symptoms.
Unbiased proteomics revealed a reduction in lung basement membrane proteins 21 days after influenza infection in mice that had symptomatically recovered, suggesting lingering tissue damage.
Peptide location fingerprinting revealed structure-associated changes in collagen IV, particularly within its NC1 domains, in lungs of mice after resolution of influenza infection.
Structure-associated changes were also identified in laminin components of the lung basement membrane after influenza infection resolution.

Non-infected, aged mice show similar structure-associated changes in laminin and collagen IV as seen post-influenza, suggesting inflammation-driven basement membrane degeneration contributes to tissue ageing.
Macrophages localized to basement-membrane-deficient lung regions were found to express collagen IV and laminin chains, suggesting a compensatory or reparative role.

Peak oxygen consumption (VO2peak) showed a small but statistically significant reduction after COVID-19 infection compared to pre-infection cardiopulmonary exercise testing in highly active individuals.
Oxygen consumption at the second ventilatory threshold (VT2) was slightly but significantly reduced post-COVID-19 compared to pre-infection values.
The peak ventilatory equivalent for carbon dioxide (VE/VCO2) increased significantly after COVID-19 infection, indicating a slight decline in ventilatory efficiency.

Respiratory rate at the second ventilatory threshold (VT2) showed a slight statistically significant reduction post-COVID-19, but this was not considered clinically or biologically relevant and could not be definitively attributed to COVID-19 effects versus reduced training volume.
Spirometric parameters (FVC and FEV1) showed no significant changes between pre- and post-COVID-19 assessments.
Only a minority of highly active individuals (14%) experienced a VO2peak reduction exceeding the clinically meaningful critical difference threshold after COVID-19.
Only a small minority of participants (4.7%) showed an increase in peak VE/VCO2 exceeding the clinically meaningful critical difference threshold after COVID-19.

Overall, highly active individuals demonstrated notable cardiopulmonary resilience after COVID-19, with all observed changes remaining below clinically significant critical difference thresholds, suggesting no meaningful cardiopulmonary impairment from mild COVID-19 infection.
In the standing posture, cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, and thoracolumbar kyphosis were significantly lower in females than males.
C7-SVA and T1 pelvic angle showed significant positive correlations with age in the standing position.
Cervical lordosis in the standing position negatively correlated with BMI, suggestive of BMI-related cervical kyphosis.
At 45° recline, cervical lordosis, T1 spinopelvic inclination, and T1 pelvic angle were negatively correlated with sex.
T1 spinopelvic inclination demonstrated a significant positive correlation with height at 25° and 35° recline, with a weaker positive trend at 45°.
Changes in thoracic kyphosis and thoracolumbar kyphosis from standing to reclined postures (25°, 35°, 45°) were significantly positively correlated with sex, being greater in females.
Changes in T1 pelvic angle at 35° and 45° recline showed a significant negative correlation with sex.
The change in lumbar lordosis at 25° recline was significantly positively correlated with age.
Changes in T1 spinopelvic inclination across all three recline angles were significantly positively correlated with body height.

Lap belt X-value (horizontal displacement) and Z-value (vertical displacement) showed strong positive correlations with BMI across all reclining angles, meaning higher-BMI individuals had greater anterior and superior displacement of the lap belt.
Lap belt angle was negatively correlated with BMI at all reclining angles, with higher BMI shifting the belt cranially and closer to the pelvis, increasing seat belt syndrome risk.

Lumbar lordosis and sacral slope progressively decreased while pelvic tilt increased with greater car seat recline angle, with the magnitude of LL and SS reduction being greater than reported in conventional chair-sitting studies.
BMI had no significant effect on spinal alignment changes during reclining at any angle, unlike its strong effect on seat belt positioning.
The 24-hour HF ratio (maximum HF/minimum HF), reflecting diurnal variation in parasympathetic tone, was significantly lower in the OD group than in healthy controls.
Adolescents with OD had a prolonged total sleep duration compared with healthy controls.
Sleep efficiency was lower in OD patients compared with healthy controls.
Total energy consumption measured by accelerometer was lower in OD patients than in healthy controls.
During the morning standing test, OD patients showed a higher heart-rate ratio (standing-to-supine) than healthy controls.
Across the full sample, the standing-test heart-rate ratio correlated strongly with average HF power.
The standing-test heart-rate ratio correlated strongly with average LF power across the full sample.
The standing-test heart-rate ratio correlated with the natural log of maximum HF power across the full sample.
The standing-test heart-rate ratio correlated with SDNN across the full sample.
No significant correlation was found between the standing-test blood pressure ratio and any HRV measure.

The correlation between standing-test HR ratio and average HF power seen in healthy controls (r = 0.581, p < 0.05) was not present in the OD group, suggesting a breakdown of normal autonomic coupling in OD.
Internet addiction test (IAT) scores positively correlated with average HF power, contrary to prior reports linking internet dependence with decreased HF.
Internet addiction test (IAT) scores positively correlated with maximum HF power.
No significant correlation was found between depression self-rating scale (DSRS) scores and any HRV measure.
Neither STAI trait (r=0.035) nor STAI state (r=0.002) anxiety scores significantly correlated with maximum HF power.
Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) scores did not significantly correlate with maximum HF power in this adolescent sample.

No significant correlation was found between depressive symptoms and total sleep time, contrasting with prior literature linking later sleep onset/shorter sleep duration to greater adolescent depressive symptoms.
Of the 19 OD patients, POTS could be confirmed by prior physician diagnosis or the study standing test in only 6 cases; the remainder were classified as OD based on clinical symptoms alone.
POTS predominantly affects adolescent girls, with a cited prevalence of 6.8%.
A large self-report survey of over 4800 patients with POTS found the most common age of symptom onset was 14 years.

School refusal behavior is reported in over half of Japanese children with OD symptoms, and 30-40% of children with school refusal behavior are found to have OD, indicating substantial bidirectional comorbidity.
Proposed POTS mechanism involves abnormally increased sympathetic activity, circulating catecholamine excess, and peripheral sympathetic denervation leading to central hypovolemia.
Alveolar macrophages express high levels of TCF4 compared with T cells and peritoneal macrophages, with minimal expression of other TCF/LEF family members.
Combined GM-CSF and TGF-β stimulation induces robust TCF4 expression in cultured alveolar macrophages.
GM-CSF plus TGF-β also induces TCF4 expression in bone marrow-derived monocytes.

Myeloid-specific TCF4 deletion (Tcf7l2cKO) causes defective alveolar macrophage maturation, loss of Siglec Fhigh AMs, emergence of a Siglec Flow population, and significantly lower AM numbers in BAL, with elevated BAL protein.
TCF4-deficient AMs show reduced expression of PPARγ, the master transcription factor for AM development and maturation.
HIF-1α, which drives AM inflammatory programs, is upregulated in TCF4-deficient AMs.

TCF4 deficiency impairs the AM and pre-AM populations at postnatal day 3 without significantly affecting fetal monocyte or fetal macrophage populations, indicating TCF4 acts at the pre-AM-to-AM developmental transition.
Mixed bone marrow chimera experiments show that WT-derived AMs outcompete Tcf7l2cKO-derived AMs, demonstrating a cell-intrinsic requirement for TCF4 in mature AM development.
Myeloid-specific TCF4 knockout mice have greatly increased morbidity and mortality after sublethal influenza A infection compared to controls.
Mafb and c-Maf, repressors of macrophage stemness, are highly upregulated in TCF4-deficient AMs, suggesting impaired self-renewal.
Colony-forming unit assays show WT AMs form colonies efficiently while TCF4-deficient AMs yield very few colonies, indicating impaired self-renewal capacity.
TCF4 deletion reduces the proliferative (Ki67+) capacity of AMs and renders them unresponsive to GM-CSF stimulation, associated with downregulation of GM-CSF, Siglec F and TGF-β receptor genes.

Inducible (adult-onset) TCF4 deletion does not change AM numbers acutely but produces decreased CFU capacity, decreased AM numbers by day 40, emergence of Siglec Flow cells, and reduced Ki67 expression, showing TCF4 is required for ongoing self-renewal independent of developmental effects.
Deletion of β-catenin in AMs increases TCF4 expression, indicating β-catenin negatively regulates TCF4.
Active β-catenin and its binding partner HIF-1α are increased in TCF4-deficient AMs, especially after Poly(I:C) stimulation.
Wnt pathway genes Fzd2, Ctnnb1, Wnt1 and Wnt4 are upregulated in TCF4-deficient AMs upon Poly(I:C) treatment, and conversely suppressed upon TCF4 overexpression.

β-catenin and HIF-1α inhibitors (XAV939 and LW6) dampen inflammatory cytokine gene expression (Il1β, Il6, Tnf, Ccl2) in TCF4-deficient AMs, indicating TCF4 represses inflammation via antagonizing β-catenin/HIF-1α.
TCF4-deficient AMs show decreased basal and maximal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR), which is rescued by β-catenin or HIF-1α inhibition after Poly(I:C) stimulation.

ChIP assays show TCF4 and β-catenin co-occupy the same regulatory regions of glycolytic genes (Eno1, Hk2) and mitochondrial genes (Ndufs1, Ndufa4), suggesting competitive binding that determines metabolic fate.
TCF4 expression in AMs is transiently suppressed at the peak of inflammation during acute influenza (day 7) and SARS-CoV-2 (day 4) infection, recovering to near-baseline afterward.
TLR ligands (Poly(I:C), LPS, R848) and cytokines (IFNα, IFNγ, TNF) significantly reduce TCF4 expression in AMs in vitro.
In vivo neutralization of IFNγ restores TCF4 levels in AMs after IAV infection more effectively than IFNAR1 blockade, implicating type II interferon as the dominant driver of TCF4 suppression.
TCF7L2 gene expression is reduced in both total lung macrophages and the AM compartment in severe COVID-19 BAL samples but not in moderate disease, compared to healthy controls.
CD68+ macrophages from acute COVID-19 autopsy lungs show markedly reduced TCF4 protein expression compared to non-COVID-19 controls.
Inducible myeloid-specific TCF4 deletion (Tcf7l2icKO) led to significantly greater weight loss and mortality compared to controls after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Tcf7l2icKO mice showed a decreased frequency of alveolar macrophages in BAL at 10 days post SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to controls.
Tcf7l2icKO mice showed extensive lung inflammation and increased disrupted lung area on H&E staining compared to WT after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Tcf7l2icKO mice infected with influenza A virus lost more weight and the majority succumbed to infection after day 9, compared to WT.
Tcf7l2icKO mice had decreased AM frequency and numbers in BAL 14 days after influenza infection compared to WT.
Lungs of Tcf7l2icKO mice showed significantly greater inflammation and damage than WT counterparts after influenza infection.
Deleting TCF4 starting on day 4 after infection (during ongoing IAV infection) also caused failure to recover, with lower AM frequency/number at day 14 compared to controls.

scRNA-seq of lungs at day 9 post-influenza showed AMs from Tcf7l2icKO mice were enriched for p53 pathway genes consistent with cell-cycle arrest/senescence, along with inflammatory signatures (complement activation, IL-12 production, type I interferon responses).

AMs from WT (Tcf7l2fl/fl) mice showed enrichment of active cell-cycle programs, stem cell modules, and DNA repair pathways, with higher S-phase enrichment and Mki67 expression than Tcf7l2icKO AMs after influenza infection.

Whole-lung GSEA showed broad enrichment of type I and type II interferon responses in Tcf7l2icKO mice, whereas WT lungs displayed enrichment of epithelial proliferation, wound-healing, and myeloid differentiation pathways after influenza infection.

In long-term post-infection models (21 d.p.i for SARS-CoV-2, 42 d.p.i for IAV), AMs from Tcf7l2icKO mice were predominantly the immature Siglec F-low subset, indicating impaired repopulation of mature AMs.
Immunofluorescence showed markedly increased accumulation of dysplastic KRT8-high transitional epithelial cells in Tcf7l2icKO mouse lungs after SARS-CoV-2 or influenza infection, compared to WT.
Masson trichrome staining revealed increased lung fibrosis in Tcf7l2icKO mice compared to WT after acute SARS-CoV-2 or influenza infection.

TCF7L2 expression was reduced in lung macrophages of patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 with pulmonary fibrosis (PASC-PF), confirmed by both public dataset analysis and immunofluorescence of CD68+ macrophages compared to healthy controls.
Siglec F+ AMs from aged mice with chronic post-viral lung fibrosis (a PASC-PF mouse model) showed persistently reduced TCF4 expression compared to naïve mice.
Adenoviral overexpression of TCF4 (Adv-Tcf7l2) in WT AMs significantly increased proliferation, Ki67 co-expression, and colony-forming unit number/size in vitro.
TCF4 overexpression significantly downregulated inflammatory cytokine gene expression (Il1β, Tnf, Il6, Ccl2) in AMs stimulated with Poly(I:C).

Mice transduced with Adv-Tcf7l2 prior to high-dose influenza infection (600 PFU) showed reduced weight loss, increased AM frequency/number and Ki67+ AM proportion, and reduced lung inflammation compared to Adv-control mice.
Adv-Tcf7l2-transduced mice recovered after lethal-dose influenza (1000 PFU), whereas the majority of Adv-control mice succumbed to infection.
Depleting AMs with intranasal clodronate abolished the protective effect of TCF4 overexpression on survival after lethal influenza infection, demonstrating the benefit is AM-dependent.
TCF4 expression was impaired in aged alveolar macrophages compared to young AMs.
TCF4 overexpression in aged mice diminished the immature Siglec F-low AM population while increasing the mature Siglec F-high population and Ki67+ AM frequency.
TCF4 overexpression significantly improved morbidity and mortality outcomes in aged mice after influenza infection, and reduced morbidity after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Post-acute TCF4 overexpression initiated 28 days after influenza infection in aged mice increased mature AM presence, decreased KRT8+ transitional cell accumulation, increased AT1/AT2 cell numbers, and reduced collagen deposition/lung inflammation by day 60.

TCF4 overexpression restored lung function parameters (Rrs, Crs, Rn, tissue resistance G, tissue elastance H, Ers) toward near-basal levels in aged mice with chronic post-influenza lung disease at 60 days post-infection, as measured by FlexiVent.
The point prevalence of hEDS in the N3C EHR cohort was estimated at approximately 1 in 800 patients, substantially higher than prior clinical estimates of about 1 in 3,100.
Confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis was only modestly more common in patients with hEDS than in matched controls.
Patients with hEDS had substantially higher odds of being classified as a possible COVID-19 case based on symptoms/testing history than matched controls.
Long COVID diagnosis was over four times more prevalent among patients with hEDS than matched controls.
Patients with hEDS had over six times the odds of attending a Long COVID specialty clinic compared to matched controls.
Patients with hEDS had over 2.5 times higher odds of receiving Paxlovid than matched controls.
