Case-control studies found that classical mast cell degranulation markers tryptase (TPSB2) and carboxypeptidase A3 (CPA3) are not universally elevated in Long COVID patients.

In severe COVID-19, hyperactivated myeloid-derived suppressor cells may drive destructive inflammation in secondary lymphoid organs, collapsing T-cell development and causing the profound T-cell lymphopenia seen in severe disease.

In murine models of severe COVID-19, depletion of inflammatory monocyte-macrophages or ablation of type I interferon signaling prevented death despite unchanged viral loads, indicating immune-mediated damage rather than viral replication drives pathology.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein impairs lysosomal acidification and autophagosome-lysosome fusion in monocytes, reducing their ability to degrade internalized viral antigen, an effect amplified in CD16+ non-classical monocytes with inherently lower lysosomal enzyme content.
Intermediate and non-classical monocytes express high levels of CCR5 and CX3CR1, promoting their migration to and retention in previously inflamed tissues and vasculature.

SARS-CoV-2 disruption of gut homeostasis is associated with microbiome dysbiosis marked by overgrowth of Gram-negative Clostridia and depletion of commensals like Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, with increased intestinal permeability promoting microbial translocation and systemic inflammation.
Activated MAIT cells upregulate CD40L (CD154), which engages CD40 on macrophages and dendritic cells, promoting further activation and amplifying the inflammatory loop.
SARS-CoV-2 spike protein interacts with neuropilin-1 (NRP1), a surface molecule required for regulatory T-cell stability and suppressive function, contributing to Treg dysfunction in Long COVID.

Direct engagement of TLR2 and TLR4 by spike protein, along with inflammatory properties of lipid nanoparticle adjuvants in mRNA vaccine platforms, may compound macrophage epigenetic reprogramming and sustained pro-inflammatory cytokine release.

Patients treated with interferon-alpha for hepatitis C developed persistent fatigue with clinical and immunological parallels to ME/CFS, suggesting that exaggerated interferon signaling can induce chronic fatigue-like illness in susceptible individuals.

Chronic stimulation pushes MAIT cells into functional exhaustion, characterized by reduced cytokine secretion and upregulation of inhibitory receptors like PD-L1 and TIM-3, preventing mucosal healing and perpetuating systemic inflammation.
A recent publication highlighted that interferon-gamma is suppressed in some Long COVID cases, suggesting MAIT cells may become exhausted and lead to poor mucosal immunity.

Case-control studies showed that classical mast cell degranulation markers such as tryptase (TPSB2) and carboxypeptidase A3 (CPA3) are not universally elevated in Long COVID, though this does not exclude mast cell activation via non-degranulating pathways.

Proteomic analyses have shown that fibrinolysis-resistant microclots in Long COVID contain misfolded fibrinogen with amyloid-like properties, potentially triggered by an oxidative and inflammatory macrophage-driven environment.

Under sustained inflammatory stimulation, macrophages release macrophage extracellular traps (METs) that act as scaffolds for platelet adhesion and coagulation factor activation, contributing to fibrin-rich microthrombi and thromboinflammation in Long COVID.

Imaging studies reveal hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy, particularly in axillary lymph nodes, persisting long after vaccination or infection, indicating chronic macrophage and antigen-presenting cell activation.
Retinal microvascular abnormalities in Long COVID further confirm vascular involvement with central nervous system linkage.
Neuroinflammatory signatures have been localized to the dorsal inferior medulla in patients with POTS and Long COVID, linking symptom clusters to autonomic nuclei in this brainstem region.

The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle, the largest in the brain and located near the medulla and pons, may act as an immunological interface whose inflammation could disproportionately affect brainstem autonomic and cardiorespiratory control regions in Long COVID.

The paper proposes mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines, and leukotriene receptor antagonists as potential targeted treatments for a subset of Long COVID patients with mast cell sensitivity, as a secondary amplification loop rather than primary driver.
The cumulative signal of all specific EBNA1 peptides on the microarray was 2.2-fold higher in post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) samples than in convalescent (CC) samples.
Seven of 158 EBNA1 peptides on the microarray were more frequently recognized (specific) by PCS samples than CC samples.
Of 37 EBNA1 peptides showing differential signal intensity between cohorts, 29 had higher signals in PCS samples compared to CC.
Peptide E-169, from the glycine-alanine repeat region of EBNA1, showed clearly higher antibody reactivity in PCS samples compared to CC samples on the peptide microarray.

Peptide E-405, located in an EBNA1 region previously linked to multiple sclerosis autoantibodies, showed higher reactivity in a subset of PCS samples exceeding the maximum CC signal, more selectively than the overlapping peptide E-401.
Full-length EBNA1 ELISA showed slightly higher seropositivity and a non-significant trend toward higher overall IgG signal in PCS versus CC samples.
No samples in either cohort had detectable IgM against EBV VCA, and only a small minority in each cohort had IgG against EBV EA-D, indicating no evidence of recent EBV reactivation or new infection.
Peptide-ELISA validation confirmed that E-169 and E-405 were the only tested peptides distinguishing PCS from CC samples at p<0.05, with high correlation to the microarray results.
Antibody signals against the CRYAB peptide (proposed molecular mimicry target for MS-associated anti-EBNA1 antibodies) did not differ between PCS and CC samples.

BLASTp analysis of the E-405 EBNA1 peptide sequence revealed strongest homology (up to 9/14 or 8/10 residues) to human immunoglobulin heavy chain junction region sequences, raising the possibility of antibody cross-reactivity.
The overall frequency of HEp-2-reactive (ANA/cytoplasmic) autoantibody-positive samples did not differ significantly between PCS (20.8%) and CC (12.5%) cohorts.

Antibodies against beta-2-glycoprotein I were undetectable in all samples, and only two samples per cohort had detectable anti-cardiolipin IgG, indicating thrombotic-risk-associated autoantibodies could not distinguish PCS from CC.
Convalescents (CC) had significantly higher levels of anti-IFN-alpha2 and anti-IL-15 IgG autoantibodies than patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Unlike anti-IFN-alpha2 and anti-IL-15, anti-IFN-omega autoantibody levels were not among the significantly differing analytes between CC and PCS cohorts.
There was a non-significant trend toward higher plasma IFN-alpha2 and IL-15 concentrations in convalescents compared to PCS patients.
Anti-cytokine autoantibody levels did not correlate with the corresponding plasma cytokine concentrations for either IFN-alpha2 or IL-15.
Adjustment for confounders (age, sex, HEp-2 autoantibody status, number of vaccinations) in binary logistic regression did not diminish the association between higher E-169/E-405 reactivity and PCS.

After Benjamini-Hochberg correction and effect-size/ROC analysis, the discriminative power of E-169 and E-405 reactivity for distinguishing PCS from CC was found to be statistically modest and of small effect size.

Subgrouping PCS patients by predominant clinical phenotype (cardio-respiratory, cognitive, fatigue, mixed-type) revealed no robust differences in EBNA1 peptide reactivity, anti-cytokine antibody levels, or cytokine concentrations across subgroups.

Reanalysis of a prior peptide microarray dataset from a chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) cohort showed a trend toward higher reactivity for a peptide overlapping E-169 in CFS patients versus healthy donors, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Reanalysis of the same prior CFS dataset showed higher median E-405 signal in CFS versus healthy donors, but the difference was not statistically robust.

In 170 PASC patients with cognitive complaints, brain fog was associated with objective impairment in attention and episodic memory, correlated with but separate from central fatigue, with depression's effect on brain fog mediated indirectly through central fatigue.

In 71 Irish PASC patients self-reporting brain fog, key indicators were word-finding difficulties, memory impairment, reduced cognitive response times, dizziness, myalgia, reduced grip strength, reduced gait speed, and poorer Chalder Fatigue Scale scores.
Small studies show PASC patients with brain fog exhibit lower functional connectivity in multiple brain regions on MRI.
Small studies show hypometabolism of the cingulate cortex on FDG-PET in PASC patients with brain fog.
PASC patients showed changes in their quantitative EEG profile compared with pre-PASC recordings.

Among 139 newly diagnosed PD patients, subjective cognitive decline (SCD) prevalence was 28%, most commonly affecting memory (28% of SCD patients) and attention/working memory (26%), with anxiety and depression as overlapping symptoms.

In 90 non-demented PD patients comparing subjective (PDCFRS) and objective (MoCA) cognitive measures, 32% were classified as 'underestimators' with subjective decline but no objective impairment; Fatigue Severity Scale and Beck Depression Inventory scores distinguished underestimators from other groups.

Among 18 PD patients with subjective cognitive decline, greater self-reported concern about cognition correlated with greater hypometabolism in middle frontal, middle temporal, and occipital regions and the angular gyrus on FDG-PET.

In an online assessment of 612 individuals with PD, confusion more than quadrupled the odds of poor quality of life and memory loss more than tripled it, as measured by the McGill Quality of Life Questionnaire.
In a study of 139 PD patients, confusion and memory problems were significantly correlated with poor quality of life on the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39.

Mice with mild respiratory COVID-19 showed elevated reactivity of microglia and macrophages in subcortical and hippocampal white matter, persisting for 7 weeks post-infection, resembling chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment mechanisms.

CCL11 levels remained persistently elevated in murine cerebrospinal fluid after COVID-19 infection, and CCL11 was elevated in plasma of PASC patients but only those with cognitive symptoms; CCL11 has previously been causally linked to cognitive impairment in normal aging.

A case-control PET study found that PASC patients with depressive symptoms and/or cognitive impairment had higher translocator protein levels (a microglial activation marker) in cortex, hippocampus, and other brain regions compared with healthy controls.
In 28 patients with multiple sclerosis, translocator protein levels in white matter and cortex correlated with decreased information processing speed and greater neurologic disability.

Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in monocytes and microglial cells by alpha-synuclein is well documented in Parkinson's disease, and can also be triggered by dopaminergic degeneration even without alpha-synuclein aggregates.
Serum NLRP3 levels are elevated in PD patients and correlate linearly with alpha-synuclein levels.
Serum interleukin-1β, a potent proinflammatory cytokine, is elevated in PD patients.

The Fatigue and Altered Cognition Scale (FACs) two-factor structure and internal consistency (alpha 0.91-0.97) has been validated in TBI, MS, and PASC, with no item overlap with cardinal symptoms of depression or anxiety.
Preliminary research indicates methylphenidate, a dopaminergic psychostimulant, is associated with subjective improvement in memory and concentration in PASC and alleviates fatigue in MS and PD.

Carnosic acid, a rosemary derivative, is hypothesized as a therapy for brain fog in PASC, Alzheimer's disease, and PD via KEAP1/NRF2 pathway activation attenuating NLRP3-driven inflammation, though no clinical study has yet been published.
Amantadine, used off-label for MS fatigue, has also improved cognitive function in some studies, possibly via interference with dopamine transmission.
Many patients receiving disease-modifying (largely anti-inflammatory) treatment for MS report improvements in fatigue, cognition, or both.

Case studies of growth hormone replacement therapy, based on a model of brain fog as pituitary dysfunction, have been promising in patients with TBI and PASC, but randomized clinical trials are needed.

Multimodal non-invasive electrodiagnostic testing detected neurophysiological evidence of small fibre neuropathy (SFN) in three of nine (33%) individuals with long COVID-19 and neuropathic/autonomic symptoms.
Two of nine individuals had bilaterally absent lower limb sympathetic skin responses, indicating sudomotor small fibre dysfunction.
Two individuals had a prolonged cutaneous silent period onset latency (with normal duration) in both upper and lower limbs, indicating small A-delta fibre dysfunction.
Two individuals had reduced electrochemical skin conductance on Sudoscan, consistent with sudomotor small fibre dysfunction.

Two individuals had abnormal quantitative thermal threshold testing in the lower limbs, one with abnormal cold and warm detection thresholds and the other with abnormal cold but preserved warm detection thresholds.
Five of nine patients had a positive NASA Lean Test indicating orthostatic intolerance, although none had a significant (>20 mmHg) postural blood pressure drop.

There was no significant difference in symptom/disability scores (EQ-5D-5L, MFIS, PHQ-9) between individuals with and without electrodiagnostic evidence of SFN, with both groups scoring highly on disability measures.
All patients reported significant fatigue, with frequent additional complaints of brain-fog (89%), limb paraesthesias (66%), dizziness/light-headedness (56%) and postural light-headedness (33%).
Routine nerve conduction studies (assessing large fibre function) were normal in all nine individuals, despite high neuropathic and autonomic symptom scores.

The Small Fibre Neuropathy Screening List (SFNSL) score was considerably higher than the >10 sensitivity cut-off even among individuals without electrodiagnostic evidence of SFN, indicating it lacks specificity in this population.

The 33% detection rate of SFN via non-invasive multimodal electrodiagnostic testing compared favourably with, but was lower than, the approximately 50% rate reported using skin biopsy in other long COVID-19 cohorts.

A variety of pharmacologic treatments including naltrexone, pyridostigmine, ivabradine, pregabalin and tricyclic antidepressants had been trialled for participants' neuropathic and autonomic symptoms, with no efficacy outcomes reported.
Piloerector muscle nerve fiber density (PMNFD) was significantly reduced in patients with painful long COVID compared with healthy controls.
Sweat gland nerve fiber density (SGNFD) was significantly reduced in patients with painful long COVID compared with healthy controls.

In the subgroup of long COVID patients with normal intraepidermal nerve fiber density, PMNFD remained significantly reduced compared with healthy controls, indicating autonomic damage independent of somatic small fiber loss.

In the subgroup of long COVID patients with normal intraepidermal nerve fiber density, SGNFD remained significantly reduced compared with healthy controls, indicating autonomic damage independent of somatic small fiber loss.
PMNFD did not correlate with total COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score in patients with painful long COVID.
SGNFD did not correlate with total COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score in patients with painful long COVID.
No association was found between autonomic skin biopsy fiber density measures and disease duration in patients with painful long COVID.
No association was found between autonomic skin biopsy fiber density measures and the interval from infection to symptom onset in patients with painful long COVID.
No association was found between autonomic skin biopsy fiber density measures and COVID-19 disease severity in patients with painful long COVID.
Among 31 patients with painful long COVID, 23 (74%) had normal intraepidermal nerve fiber density while 8 (26%) had reduced IENFD and met Besta criteria for small fiber neuropathy.
Orthostatic intolerance was the most frequently reported autonomic symptom, occurring in 77% of patients with painful long COVID.
Gastrointestinal autonomic symptoms were reported by 52% of patients with painful long COVID.
Secretomotor autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, dry eyes, abnormal sweating) were reported by 52% of patients with painful long COVID.

Both verum and sham groups showed significant time-on-task increases in subjective mental exhaustion (VASexhaustion) and decreases in mental fitness (VASfitness) during the AX-CPT at baseline, confirming successful induction of state fatigue.
Anodal tDCS over the left dlPFC did not significantly alter the trajectory of subjective exhaustion (VASexhaustion) or fitness (VASfitness) ratings across assessments compared to sham stimulation.
Behavioral metrics during the AX-CPT (accuracy, RT, RT SD) showed no significant time-on-task change at baseline and no modulation by tDCS stimulation condition or assessment time point.

Frontal theta power (Fz) increased significantly over the course of the AX-CPT at baseline in both stimulation groups, consistent with increased compensatory cognitive effort during fatigue induction, but this was not significantly modulated by tDCS or assessment time point.
tDCS stimulation condition and assessment time point did not significantly affect frontal theta power slopes across the AX-CPT.

Occipital alpha power (POz) increased over time-on-task in both groups at baseline, and a significant stimulation-by-assessment interaction showed that the post-intervention increase in alpha power was significantly greater in the sham group than in the verum (tDCS) group, with the sham effect diminishing by follow-up.

Auditory p50 sensory gating showed no significant overall stimulation, assessment, or interaction effects, but a trend-level time-by-stimulation interaction reflected a significant reduction in p50 suppression ratio after the AX-CPT in the sham group only, not in the verum group.

Adaptive task difficulty in the gamified Go/No-Go task increased progressively across the four stimulation sessions in both groups, indicating a learning/practice effect, with no significant effect of stimulation condition.

Go/No-Go accuracy showed significant effects of session and session-by-difficulty interaction with only trend-level stimulation-by-session interaction, and no significant main effect of stimulation condition.
Reaction times in the Go/No-Go task were significantly affected by session and task difficulty, but not by stimulation condition.

d′-prime in the Go/No-Go task showed significant main effects of stimulation condition and session, with a significant session-by-condition interaction: task difficulty improved d′-prime in the first session for both groups, but this effect reversed to a significant negative association with difficulty in the verum (tDCS) group during sessions 3 and 4.

Blinding integrity assessment showed no significant difference in the rate at which participants correctly guessed their stimulation assignment between the verum (70%) and sham (50%) groups, supporting adequate blinding.
Peak oxygen uptake during maximal CPET did not differ between Long COVID and control groups in either females or males.
Long COVID females showed consistently lower heart rate than control females at multiple post-exercise recovery time points (3, 5, 10, 30, 60 min and 24 h).
SBP responses during maximal exercise and recovery showed no significant group×time interaction between Long COVID and control participants, with sex differences dominating instead.
DBP patterns across CPET and recovery were homogeneous with no significant differences between Long COVID and control groups.

PWV showed homogeneous patterns with no significant group×time interactions between Long COVID and control groups, indicating Long COVID did not alter arterial stiffness trajectories; sex differences seen in controls were absent in the Long COVID group.
Long COVID females showed lower AIx@75 than control females at 10 min, 60 min, and 24 h post-exercise, though temporal trajectories were similar overall.
TVR showed a main effect of sex but no group effect or group×time interaction, indicating Long COVID did not alter peripheral vascular resistance regulation.
PVR after exercise showed a main effect of sex without a significant influence of Long COVID status.
Cardiac output showed a predominant sex effect with no group×sex interaction, but the typical male-female CO gap seen in controls was attenuated in the Long COVID group.
At rest, Long COVID females had significantly higher HF (parasympathetic) HRV power than Long COVID males, a sex difference not present in the control group.
The LF/HF ratio at rest showed a significant overall condition (Long COVID vs control) effect, though not a sex effect, with no meaningful group×time interaction during recovery.
24-hour mean ambulatory SBP was significantly lower in Long COVID females compared with control females, while male groups showed no difference.
All groups exhibited nocturnal systolic BP dipping within the normal physiological range (10-20%), indicating preserved circadian autonomic regulation regardless of Long COVID status.
During the acute COVID-19 phase, participants who later developed Long COVID reported a significantly higher number of symptoms than controls, in both females and males.
Persistent Long COVID symptoms differed by sex: fatigue and hair loss were most prevalent among females, while memory loss and fatigue predominated among males.

The overall study concluded that Long COVID was not associated with clinically meaningful impairment of hemodynamic, autonomic, or vascular responses to maximal exercise in young, physically active adults, despite females having greater acute symptom burden and shorter infection-to-assessment interval.

Both groups showed a reduction in the physical subdomain of fatigue over time (39.1% in the intervention group vs 16.7% in controls), but the group×period interaction was not statistically significant.
The cognitive subdomain of the MFIS showed no significant main effects or interaction between groups over time.
The psychosocial subdomain of the MFIS improved significantly more in the intervention group than in controls, with a significant group×period interaction.
Total MFIS score decreased over time in both groups with no significant group effect or interaction, and the control group showed a slightly larger percentage reduction than the intervention group.
Total EQ-5D-5L scores improved over time overall but showed no significant between-group difference or interaction.
Self-perceived health status (EQ-VAS) improved significantly more in the intervention group than in controls, with a significant group×period interaction.
Body weight did not change significantly within or between groups over the 12-week program.
Total body fat percentage did not change significantly within or between groups during the intervention.
Regional fat percentages in the right/left arms, right/left legs, and trunk showed no significant changes within or between groups.
Total body water percentage did not differ significantly between groups or across time.
Total and segmental (arms, legs, trunk) muscle mass percentages showed no significant within- or between-group changes over the 12-week program.

None of the five EQ-5D-5L dimensions showed statistically significant between-group differences at pre- or post-intervention, though the usual activities dimension approached significance post-intervention.
Fatigue is reported to affect approximately 32% to 71% of patients with Long COVID across several longitudinal cohorts.
A total MFIS score of 38 or higher is generally considered indicative of clinically significant fatigue.
83% of long COVID patients exceeded the study-defined threshold for dyspnea indicating need for pulmonary rehabilitation.
78% of long COVID patients exceeded the study-defined threshold for fatigue.
74% of long COVID patients exceeded the study-defined threshold for frailty.
58% of long COVID patients exceeded the study-defined threshold for posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms.
Quality of life was impaired in 80% of long COVID patients.
Anxiety was prevalent in 42% of long COVID patients.
Depression was prevalent in 36% of long COVID patients.
About one quarter of long COVID patients showed a clinically significant (≥25%) reduction in 6-minute walk distance.
More than half of long COVID patients showed a clinically significant (≥50%) reduction in sit-to-stand performance.
Nearly all patients (98%) exceeded at least one predefined test threshold indicating a need for rehabilitation, and 85% qualified for more than one type of rehabilitation service.
Pulmonary rehabilitation was the most frequently required rehabilitation service, needed by 83% of long COVID patients.
Mental health support was required by 78% of long COVID patients based on predefined thresholds.
Neurorehabilitation was required by 70% of long COVID patients based on predefined thresholds.
Two-thirds of the long COVID cohort had required hospitalization during their acute infection.

Long COVID, defined as at least one self-reported symptom persisting four weeks or more after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, was found in 64% of a nationally representative sample of Tunisian COVID-19 survivors.
Female COVID-19 survivors had a higher prevalence of long COVID than males, with a prevalence of 73% among females.
Compared to respondents under 18 years old, those aged 18-64 years had a significantly higher prevalence of long COVID.
Being a woman of childbearing age was independently associated with a higher prevalence of long COVID in both univariable and multivariable (adjusted) analyses.
Residence in the Center region of Tunisia was independently associated with a higher prevalence of long COVID compared to the southern region.
Being a healthcare worker was associated with a higher prevalence of long COVID in univariable analysis but was not retained in the final multivariable model.
Being symptomatic during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a significantly higher prevalence of long COVID.
Having intense COVID-19, defined as four or more symptoms during the acute phase, was independently associated with higher long-COVID prevalence in both univariable and multivariable analyses.
Experiencing severe COVID-19 during the acute phase (requiring oxygen, hospitalization, or ICU) was associated with higher long-COVID prevalence in univariable analysis.
Being vaccinated against COVID-19 (at least one dose) was associated with higher long-COVID prevalence in univariable analysis.
After adjustment for confounders in multivariable analysis, COVID-19 vaccination status was no longer significantly associated with long COVID.
Having received specific treatment during the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with higher long-COVID prevalence in univariable analysis.
Long COVID prevalence was not significantly associated with the SARS-CoV-2 variant of concern circulating at the time of infection (wild-type, Alpha, or Delta periods).

Tobacco consumption, severity of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, and pre-existing conditions including obesity, diabetes, asthma, and cardiovascular disease were not significantly associated with long-COVID prevalence.
The median duration of long-COVID symptoms among affected participants was 11 months.
Among participants with long COVID, general symptoms (mainly fatigue and myalgia/arthralgia) were most prevalent, followed by cognitive symptoms (memory loss and concentration problems).
A genome-wide association study identified variants in FOXP4 as being associated with increased risk of developing Long COVID.
Anti-type I interferon autoantibodies, though key drivers of acute COVID-19 severity, do not appear to predispose patients to developing Long COVID.
High circulating levels of IL-6 during acute COVID-19 do not appear to predispose patients to developing chronic fatigue syndrome afterward.

Early antiviral treatment with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with reduced risk of developing post-acute sequelae, suggesting a potential Long COVID prevention strategy.
SARS-CoV-2 infection has been reported to downregulate ACE2, which in enterocytes can reduce B0AT1/SLC6A19-mediated tryptophan uptake and subsequent antimicrobial peptide production.
Reduced peripheral serotonin (5-HT) levels were reported in acute COVID-19 and in Long COVID, attributed to impaired tryptophan absorption downstream of ACE2 changes in the intestinal epithelium.
Circulating spike/S1 antigen has been detected in plasma months to a year after infection in some Long COVID cohorts, positioning spike as a potential LC biomarker.
Intracellular spike protein has been identified in non-classical (CD14low/CD16+) monocytes independent of vaccination status, persisting up to 15 months post-infection.

More severe Long COVID profiles were associated with higher spike-specific IgG levels and constrained memory CD8+ T-cell expansion, whereas lower spike-specific IgG with increased spike-specific CD8+ T-cell frequencies correlated with better prognosis.

Observation of double-stranded RNA in gut lamina propria near macrophages/monocytes suggests ongoing viral replication or replication intermediates in immune-monitored intestinal niches in Long COVID.

Long COVID is associated with persistent gut dysbiosis at 6 months post-infection, including increased Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus, decreased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and reduced short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and butyrate levels.
People with Long COVID show elevated plasma zonulin, a tight junction protein marker, indicating intestinal barrier compromise.
Long COVID patients show elevated plasma LPS-binding protein (LBP) and β-glucan, markers of bacterial and fungal microbial translocation respectively.
Higher levels of soluble CD14 (sCD14) have been detected in Long COVID cohorts, indicating monocyte activation in the context of LPS exposure.

Hypoxia inducible factor 1 alpha pathway dysregulation is implicated in Long COVID, with differing effects in lung epithelium versus endothelium potentially supporting a vascular-proliferative phenotype linking acute COVID to Long COVID.
Individuals with Long COVID maintain detectable SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell clonotypes for more than two years after infection, indicating persistent virus-specific immune memory.

Inhibitory receptors PD-1 and TIM-3 were modestly increased on SARS-CoV-2 non-spike-specific CD8+ T-cells in individuals with Long COVID compared to controls, despite minimal overall differences in virus-specific T-cell frequencies.

Long COVID and severe COVID-19 have been linked to expansion of T-bethi/CD11c+ age-associated B-cell populations reflecting extra-follicular responses, poor affinity maturation, and propensity toward autoreactivity.

Some Long COVID cohorts show lower SARS-CoV-2-neutralizing antibody titers alongside evidence of autoreactivity, with inverse relationships between autoantibody levels and virus-specific antibodies in some studies.

Biomarkers of neuroinflammation and neuroaxonal injury including glial fibrillary acidic protein, tau, and neurofilament light chain have been found elevated in cerebrospinal fluid in some Long COVID cohorts and can be increased in blood among patients with neurocognitive symptoms.

Fibrin has emerged as a predictor of Long COVID-related cognitive deficits, being deposited at sites of vascular damage/BBB disruption, and it binds SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to potentiate neuropathology and microglial activation even without systemic infection.

In mouse experiments, intravenously administered spike protein crossed the blood-brain barrier likely via adsorptive transcytosis and reached brain parenchyma, and intracerebral spike infusion triggered neuroinflammation and long-term cognitive deficits through TLR4-dependent pathways.

Fecal microbiota transplantation from individuals with Long COVID into germ-free mice caused impairments in memory, cognition, and spatial learning, supporting a gut-brain axis link between intestinal dysbiosis and neurological symptoms.
Epidemiological studies indicate that SARS-CoV-2 infection increases the risk of subsequently developing ME/CFS for up to four years following acute infection.
A machine-learning classifier based on a panel of 11 microRNAs discriminated ME/CFS from fibromyalgia in a research setting.
Circulating soluble SMPDL3 was found increased in ME/CFS, potentially related to monocytic activation.

POTS in Long COVID is characterized by vasomotor dysregulation and reduced cardiac preload with compensatory tachycardia, and typical associated symptoms include dizziness, cognitive dysfunction, and fatigue.
Imaging studies in Long COVID report reduced gray-matter thickness, overall brain volume loss, and neurovascular abnormalities involving both central and autonomic nervous systems.

In a mouse model of mild SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infection, reactive microglia and pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines persisted in the brain and CSF 7 weeks post-infection, accompanied by reduced hippocampal neurogenesis and loss of myelinating oligodendrocytes; a comparable mild H1N1 infection did not cause the sustained oligodendroglial deficit.
Large Long COVID cohort studies have not demonstrated an increased incidence of multiple sclerosis to date, although longer-term follow-up may be warranted.

In severe COVID-19, soluble CD163, ferritin, and IL-18 associate with worse outcomes and with neurological symptoms; sCD163 is also linked to HIV-associated neurocognitive impairment, suggesting a shared myeloid activation signature across post-infectious conditions.

EBV and CMV reactivation have been reported after COVID-19, with EBV more consistently linked to Long COVID and neurological features; EBV is also a well-supported risk factor for multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases.
Varicella-zoster virus reactivation appears increased post-COVID and in Long COVID, and in individuals with comorbidities has been associated with rheumatic and cardiorenal complications.

Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome can persist for at least six months after Borrelia burgdorferi infection, with autonomic dysfunction among the prominent neurological complaints, and neuroimaging has shown microglial activation in some cohorts.

Across meta-analyses, frequently reported risk factors for Long COVID include pre-existing comorbidities, female sex, older age, high body mass index, and smoking, but not the presence of inborn errors of immunity.
Vaccination reduces both the risk and severity of Long COVID but does not fully prevent its development, nor does it consistently eliminate viral persistence when present.

Early antiviral treatment with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection has been associated with a reduced risk of developing post-acute sequelae, suggesting a potential Long COVID prevention strategy.
Individuals with a history of COVID-19 had a higher prevalence of at least one long-covid-associated symptom than individuals without a COVID-19 history.
The mean number of symptoms reported was higher in individuals with a history of COVID-19 than those without.
Insomnia was the most prevalent symptom overall but did not differ significantly between individuals with and without a COVID-19 history.
Individuals with a history of COVID-19 had significantly increased odds of fatigue compared with those without, after adjusting for sex and age.
Individuals with a history of COVID-19 had significantly increased odds of concentration impairment compared with those without.
COVID-19 history was associated with significantly increased odds of sore throat/pharyngeal inflammation.
COVID-19 history was associated with significantly increased odds of skin rashes.
Among females, COVID-19 history was associated with significantly increased odds of fatigue.
Among males, fatigue prevalence did not differ significantly between those with and without COVID-19 history.
Among females, COVID-19 history was strongly associated with concentration impairment.
Among males, concentration impairment prevalence was comparable between those with and without COVID-19 history.
Females with a COVID-19 history had a significantly higher risk of reduced sense of taste than females without.
Fatigue risk was significantly elevated in individuals infected both before and after emergence of the Omicron variant, compared with never-infected individuals.
Concentration impairment risk was significantly elevated in individuals infected both before and after emergence of the Omicron variant, compared with never-infected individuals.
Headache risk was significantly elevated only in individuals infected before the Omicron variant, compared with never-infected individuals.
Sore throat/pharyngeal inflammation risk was significantly elevated in individuals infected during the Omicron phase, compared with never-infected individuals.
Skin rash risk was significantly elevated in individuals infected during the Omicron phase, compared with never-infected individuals.
Males infected before Omicron had significantly higher odds of headache compared with males without COVID-19 history.
Females infected before Omicron had markedly higher odds of reduced sense of taste compared with females without COVID-19 history.
Females infected before Omicron had significantly higher odds of fatigue than females without COVID-19 history.
Females infected before Omicron had markedly higher odds of concentration impairment than females without COVID-19 history.
Women infected during the Omicron phase had significantly higher odds of fatigue than women without COVID-19 history.
Women infected during the Omicron phase had significantly higher odds of concentration impairment than women without COVID-19 history.
Women infected during the Omicron phase had significantly higher odds of sore throat than women without COVID-19 history.
Individuals infected most recently (within the last 14 months, Omicron phase) showed the highest fatigue prevalence and risk among all COVID-19 subgroups.

Only 3.6% of the sample received a formal clinical diagnosis of long covid despite the high population prevalence of symptoms, and only three individuals were followed up at dedicated long covid centres.
Insomnia was the most prevalent symptom overall but did not show a significant difference in prevalence between individuals with and without a history of COVID-19.

Individuals whose most recent infection occurred during the Omicron phase within the last 14 months showed markedly higher prevalence of fatigue and concentration impairment, with the highest adjusted odds ratios among all COVID-19 subgroups.

Among individuals with one or more concurrent diseases, those with a history of COVID-19 had significantly higher prevalence of concentration impairment than non-COVID-19 counterparts with comorbidities.
In individuals with concurrent diseases, a history of COVID-19 was associated with a significantly increased probability of memory loss, along with fatigue, concentration impairment and sore throat.

Self-reported health status showed a mild negative correlation with fatigue, dyspnoea, joint pain and muscle pain regardless of COVID-19 history, with fatigue remaining negatively correlated even after accounting for Omicron variant status and comorbidities.
A strong positive correlation emerged between reduced sense of taste and reduced sense of smell specifically in individuals with a pre-Omicron history of COVID-19.
Males infected with COVID-19 in the pre-Omicron period had significantly higher odds of experiencing headaches compared with males with no history of COVID-19.
Females infected in the pre-Omicron phase showed significantly higher odds of reduced sense of taste, fatigue, and concentration impairment compared with females without a history of COVID-19.
Females infected during the Omicron phase had significantly higher odds of fatigue, concentration impairment and sore throat compared with females without a history of COVID-19.

Multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, smoking, BMI, comorbidities, COVID-19 history and vaccination status confirmed that a positive history of COVID-19 remained significantly associated with fatigue, concentration impairment, skin rashes and sore throat.
Elevated kappa free light chains (>19.4 mg/L) were significantly associated with elevated eosinophil cationic protein (>20 ng/mL) in allergic long COVID patients.
Elevated kappa free light chains (>19.4 mg/L) were significantly associated with elevated total IgE (>200 kU/L) in allergic long COVID patients.
Elevated lambda free light chains (>26.3 mg/L) were significantly associated with elevated ECP (>20 ng/mL) in the cohort, though the effect was smaller than the kappa-ECP association.
Among allergic long COVID patients, fatigue, dyspnea, cough, and cognitive difficulties were the most commonly reported persistent symptoms.
Total IgE levels showed wide interindividual variability among allergic long COVID patients, with a mean of 165.4 kU/L and a range of 5–844 kU/L.
ECP levels showed marked fluctuation among allergic long COVID patients, with a mean of 64.2 ng/mL, consistent with heightened eosinophilic activity in many subjects.
The kappa/lambda free light chain ratio varied widely across the cohort, suggesting some degree of immune imbalance in allergic long COVID patients.
Patients with elevated blood eosinophil counts and total IgE were more likely to report prominent respiratory symptoms, including persistent dyspnea and chronic cough.

Elevated ECP and free light chain levels were more frequently associated with broader systemic symptomatology, including increased frequency of upper respiratory infections and worsening of allergic baseline symptoms.

Individuals with higher ECP and free light chain levels tended to have longer recovery trajectories, with some reporting persistent fatigue, cognitive fog, and respiratory discomfort beyond six months post-infection.
Fatigue was the most common persistent symptom reported at baseline among COVID-19 survivors discharged from hospital.
Exertional dyspnoea was the second most prevalent persistent symptom at baseline following hospital discharge for COVID-19.
Insomnia was reported as the third most common persistent symptom at baseline in this post-hospitalisation COVID-19 cohort.
Mental confusion was the least common of the four persistent symptoms assessed at baseline.
Female sex was consistently associated with both the baseline presence and the persistence of all four assessed symptoms (mental confusion, exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, insomnia).
Older age was linked to baseline mental confusion and to persistence of exertional dyspnoea and fatigue over the 12-month follow-up.

Markers of greater acute COVID-19 severity, including ICU admission, longer hospital stay, and higher WHO severity score, were associated with symptom improvement over the 12-month follow-up rather than persistence.
Pre-existing coronary heart disease independently predicted persistence of dyspnoea and fatigue after COVID-19 hospitalisation.
Pre-existing cancer independently predicted persistence of dyspnoea and fatigue after COVID-19 hospitalisation.
Pre-existing hypertension appeared to be protective against persistent symptoms following COVID-19 hospitalisation.
At 4-8 months postinfection, adjusted risk of any new-onset long-COVID symptom was roughly twice as high in SARS-CoV-2-infected participants compared with contemporaneous uninfected controls.

At 9-12 months postinfection, infected participants continued to have a significantly higher risk of new-onset long-COVID symptoms than uninfected controls, though the excess risk was smaller than at 4-8 months.
Infected participants had consistently higher risk of new-onset neurological symptom cluster manifestations than uninfected controls at both 4-8 and 9-12 months postinfection.
Infected participants had consistently higher risk of new-onset autonomic symptom cluster manifestations than uninfected controls at both 4-8 and 9-12 months postinfection.
Infected participants had consistently higher risk of new-onset exercise intolerance symptom cluster manifestations than uninfected controls at both 4-8 and 9-12 months postinfection.
Among 1097 long COVID patients tested, low random ACTH levels (≤10 pg/mL) were found in 12.3% of patients.
Low random cortisol levels (<4 μg/dL) were found in 9.8% of the 1097 screened long COVID patients.
Baseline serum prolactin was elevated above normal in nearly half of the 15 long COVID patients, suggesting possible hypothalamic impairment.
Serum IGF-I levels showed only a slight, statistically non-significant decrease (mean −0.8 SD) in long COVID patients.
Pituitary MRI revealed an empty sella in one of 15 long COVID patients, with no other structural abnormalities detected in the remaining 14.
Peak ACTH response to CRH stimulation was delayed beyond 60 minutes in 2 of 15 (13.3%) long COVID patients, though overall peak responses were preserved.
Peak LH response to GnRH stimulation was delayed beyond 60 minutes in 5 of 15 (33.3%) long COVID patients.
Peak FSH response to GnRH stimulation was delayed beyond 60 minutes in 13 of 15 (86.6%) long COVID patients, the most frequently delayed hormone tested.
TSH levels remained significantly elevated (4.1-fold above baseline) at 120 minutes after TRH stimulation, indicating sustained hormone secretion.
LH levels showed the largest sustained elevation of all hormones tested, remaining 9.3-fold above baseline at 120 minutes after GnRH stimulation.

Delayed and sustained gonadotropin/TSH/PRL responses to stimulation testing persisted even after excluding patients with prior systemic glucocorticoid exposure, suggesting the pattern is not attributable to steroid use.
GH responses to GHRP-2 stimulation were preserved, with a significantly elevated mean peak of 35.5 ng/mL in 11 tested patients, indicating intact GH axis function.
In two patients already on steroid replacement for presumed post-COVID adrenal insufficiency, glucocorticoid tapering was successfully achieved after evaluation.
Following endocrine work-up, a small dose of hydrocortisone was newly initiated in two patients and androgen supplementation was started in one patient among the 16 studied.

Despite low random ACTH/cortisol levels used for enrollment, peak ACTH and cortisol responses to CRH and their 120-minute recovery levels were nearly normal, failing to reveal a clear HPA axis abnormality.
Men with long COVID not infrequently experience late-onset hypogonadism (LOH) syndrome, characterized by decreased testosterone, as previously reported by this group.
Approximately 20% of women with long COVID experience menstrual cycle abnormalities, which can be associated with depressive mood, as previously reported by this group.
The most common chief complaints among the 15 long COVID patients studied were fatigue (100%), insomnia (66.7%), headache (60.0%), anorexia/nausea (40.0%), and brain fog (40.0%).
Long COVID patients had a higher number of comorbidities than SARS-CoV-2-infected controls without persistent symptoms.
The higher comorbidity burden in Long COVID was driven specifically by females, with no difference observed between male patients and male controls.

In Long COVID patients, females showed a relative increase in the frequency of endocrine/metabolic/nutritional and psychological comorbidities compared to the pattern seen in controls, where males had higher comorbidity frequency overall.
Female Long COVID patients reported a significantly higher overall symptom burden than male patients.
Persistent fatigue was positively associated with female sex among Long COVID patients.

Among female Long COVID patients, symptom frequency, including persistent fatigue, was highest in those aged 61-70 years, with fatigue positively associating with age, while younger females reported fewer symptoms; no clear age-related pattern was seen in males.
The most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms were persistent fatigue (76%), drowsiness/concentration difficulties/insomnia (71% each), forgetfulness (68%), dizziness (65%), and anxiety (62%).
Among the 30 patients who responded regarding employment, most reported negative impacts on work capacity due to Long COVID, and over half of those affected had to stop working entirely.
The frequency of CD8+ T cells was slightly increased in Long COVID patients overall, an effect driven primarily by male patients.
Production of granzyme K by CD8+ T cells was decreased in Long COVID patients, a change driven primarily by females, though this did not reach statistical significance after adjustment.
NKG2D expression on CD8+ T cells was reduced in Long COVID patients, an effect attributable mainly to females, though not statistically significant after adjustment.
Total CD4+ T cell frequency, activation status, and memory subsets (effector memory, central memory, TEMRA) were similar between Long COVID patients and controls.
Long COVID patients showed a trend toward reduced CD8+ central memory T cells compared to controls, but this did not reach statistical significance.
NK cell frequency and cytotoxic marker expression (granzyme B, granzyme K, perforin, NKG2D) showed no significant differences between Long COVID patients and controls, nor between sexes.

Total B cells, memory B cells, and plasmablasts, along with IgA, IgG, and IgM titers against SARS-CoV-2 Spike and Nucleocapsid, showed no significant differences between Long COVID patients and controls, indicating intact humoral immunity.
Plasma TNF-α levels were elevated overall in Long COVID patients compared with controls.
When disaggregated by sex, TNF-α elevation was present in both sexes but more pronounced in males with Long COVID, though this sex difference did not reach statistical significance.
Plasma IL-10 levels did not differ significantly between Long COVID patients and controls, overall or by sex.
Plasma sCD40L, a marker linked to inflammation and vascular risk, was elevated in Long COVID patient serum, an increase predominantly seen in females, though not statistically significant.
Plasma sFAS levels were modestly increased in Long COVID patients, driven primarily by females who showed higher circulating sFAS than female controls, though not statistically significant.
Plasma perforin was reduced in Long COVID patients, an effect driven by females, while plasma granzyme A and B levels remained unchanged across groups and sexes.

Plasma perforin levels showed a modest positive correlation with disease duration, increasing in patients with longer time since diagnosis; other markers (TNF-α, IL-10, sCD40L, sFAS, granzyme A) showed no such correlation.
TNF-α, IL-10, sCD40L, sFAS, and granzyme A plasma levels showed no correlation with the time elapsed since Long COVID diagnosis.
Plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, IFN-γ, MCP-1, IL-18, and IL-23 were similar between Long COVID patients and controls.
In regression analysis adjusted for sex, age, and time since infection, the number of comorbidities was not found to be associated with Long COVID status.
A single session of transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS) successfully relieved severe dyspnea in a patient with long COVID, with no recurrence at 6-month follow-up.
85.7% of nursing home care providers reported experiencing Long COVID, with an average of about six persistent symptoms.
The most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms among nursing home care providers were cough, fatigue, sore throat, lethargy, and headache.
Burnout was positively and significantly correlated with the number of Long COVID symptoms reported by care providers.
Higher work stress related to infectious diseases was significantly correlated with higher burnout among nursing home care providers.
Higher infection control fatigue was significantly correlated with higher burnout among nursing home care providers.
Coping was not significantly correlated with burnout among nursing home care providers.
In multivariate regression, work stress related to infectious diseases was a significant independent predictor of higher burnout.
The infection control fatigue subdomain reflecting complexity of nursing duty and staff shortages was a significant independent predictor of higher burnout.
The infection control fatigue subdomain reflecting conflicts from uncertain situations and lack of support was a significant independent predictor of higher burnout.
Despite being included as a theoretically important mediator, coping was not a statistically significant predictor of burnout in the multivariate regression model.
Burnout levels differed significantly by education level, with those holding a college degree or higher reporting higher burnout than those with a middle school education.
Burnout levels differed significantly by job type, with nurses reporting higher burnout than caregivers.
Care providers who had five or more symptoms at the time of COVID-19 diagnosis had higher burnout levels than those with two or fewer symptoms.
Patients requiring adjacent segment disease revision surgery were significantly older than those who did not require revision.
Higher lower dermal (LD) layer echogenicity on ultrasound was associated with increased risk of adjacent segment disease revision surgery.
Higher upper dermal (UD) layer echogenicity on ultrasound was associated with increased risk of adjacent segment disease revision surgery.
Higher average dermal (AD) layer echogenicity on ultrasound was associated with increased risk of adjacent segment disease revision surgery.
An optimal lower dermal echogenicity cutoff of 124.3 was identified to predict adjacent segment disease revision risk with moderate diagnostic accuracy.

Across 32 planned nights of home-based nocturnal HRV monitoring using a wearable garment-type device, 25 nights (78%) yielded usable paired physiological and behavioral data, indicating feasibility of long-term home monitoring in a child with ASD.
One of the two initially enrolled preschool boys with ASD could not tolerate the wearable garment device due to severe sensory hypersensitivity and was unable to continue participation.
Total sleep duration did not significantly differ between nights preceding days with reported problem behaviors and nights preceding days without problem behaviors.
Time-domain HRV indices (AVNN, SDNN, rMSSD, pNN50) measured the night before did not significantly differ between nights preceding problem-behavior days and non-problem-behavior days.
Mean nocturnal heart rate did not significantly differ between nights preceding problem-behavior days and non-problem-behavior days.

Frequency-domain HRV parameters (LF, HF, normalized LF, normalized HF, and LF/HF ratio, an index of sympathetic/parasympathetic balance) did not significantly differ between nights preceding problem-behavior days and non-problem-behavior days.

Despite comparable caregiver-reported sleep duration across nights, several HRV measures (SDNN, rMSSD, pNN50) showed substantial night-to-night variability, fluctuating by roughly 50-70 ms for SDNN and rMSSD and by more than 20 percentage points for pNN50, whereas heart rate itself varied minimally.
The participant's Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2) total raw score of 93 and T-score of 85 indicated severe difficulties in social interaction consistent with ASD.
The participant's Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) total problems score of 44 fell within the clinical range, while internalizing (5) and externalizing (9) scores were within the normal range.
Among the 25 nights included in analysis, problem behaviors—specifically biting, hypersensitive responses to sounds, and inappropriate defecation (failure to use the toilet)—were reported on 5 days.
Across multiple actigraphy studies, children with ASD showed reduced total sleep time, lower sleep efficiency, and longer sleep latency compared to typically developing peers.
Children with ASD showed diminished heart rate variability and increased heart rate compared to typically developing children.
Toddlers with ASD showed increased SDNN and coefficient of variation in cardiac activity compared to typically developing children during a joint attention task.
Wearable-derived heart rate was the most significant predictor of challenging behaviour in children with ASD in a machine learning model.
Preceding biosensor data (heart rate, heart rate variability, motion) could predict aggressive episodes in youth with ASD up to one minute before onset.
Machine-learning analysis of wearable-derived peripheral physiology predicted aggressive behaviour onset in youth with ASD in an inpatient setting.
Low electrodermal activity during parent-child compliance interactions was related to higher parent-reported externalizing problems in children with ASD.
Electrodermal activity peak frequency and amplitude correlated with autonomy, responsiveness, mood, and adaptive behaviour in children with ASD.
Using fNIRS, young children with ASD showed higher medial prefrontal cortex activation to social stimuli than typically developing children, and this activation correlated with ASD symptom severity.
Children with ASD did not differ from typically developing children in overall social attention (eye gaze to partner's eyes) or overall electrodermal activity during a conversational task.
Wearable accelerometer data could detect self-injurious behaviour in individuals with ASD with high accuracy and specificity using machine learning.
Total sleep time was negatively associated with challenging and repetitive behaviours during treatment in children with ASD.
Heart rate in children with ASD correlated with ASD symptoms during one interactive activity but not during other activities, suggesting context-dependent autonomic-symptom coupling.
In children with ASD, heart rate increased and heart rate variability decreased during a stress task compared to a rest task, supporting the validity of wearables for measuring psychosocial stress.
In young children with ASD, increases in heart rate but not heart rate variability were associated with onset of challenging behaviours.

The majority of studies (17 of 22) in children with ADHD reported group differences in sleep parameters compared to typically developing children, most consistently longer sleep onset latency and lower sleep efficiency.
Five studies found no differences in diverse sleep parameters between children with ADHD and typically developing children.

Longer total sleep time was found in children with bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, major depressive disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder, and longer sleep onset latency was found in bipolar disorder, OCD, MDD, and GAD.
Lower sleep efficiency and shorter sleep duration measured by actigraphy at age two predicted more aggressive behaviour at age three in a community toddler sample.
Actigraphic daytime sleep duration was positively associated with delinquency in adolescents with externalizing behavioural symptoms.
Children with PTSD in residential care showed higher sleep fragmentation than controls, correlating with PTSD symptom severity, insomnia, and post-traumatic nightmare severity.
A wrist-worn biosensor combined with machine learning could detect OCD episodes in adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder with 70% accuracy, driven largely by blood volume pulse features.

Wearable device wear was generally feasible and tolerated across paediatric mental health studies, including in autism samples where sensory sensitivity was a concern, though some participants refused to wear devices or removed sensors.

This scoping review found no studies that used wearables as part of an active mental health intervention for children or adolescents; wearables were used only for monitoring/assessment or to track outcomes of separate interventions.

Machine learning models using wearable-derived heart rate and other biosensor signals predicted challenging behaviour in children with ASD with high precision and accuracy, with heart rate as the strongest predictor and heart rate variability correlating with behaviour occurrence.
Wearable biosensor data (blood volume pulse, inter-beat interval, heart rate, heart rate variability, motion) predicted aggressive episodes in youth with ASD up to one minute before they occurred.
Machine learning analysis of wearable peripheral physiology data predicted aggressive behaviour in youth with ASD approximately 3 minutes before onset.
Children with ASD showed diminished heart rate variability and increased heart rate compared to typically developing children, measured via wearable devices.

Toddlers with ASD showed increased SDNN and coefficient of variation of heart rate compared to typically developing toddlers, with low-frequency power decreasing from baseline to a joint-attention task.
Lower electrodermal activity during parent-child compliance interactions was associated with higher parent-reported externalizing problems in children with ASD.

Frequency and amplitude of electrodermal activity peaks correlated with behavioural outcomes in children with ASD, including autonomy, responsiveness, negative mood, emotion dysregulation, and adaptive behaviour.
Heart rate in children with ASD correlated with ASD symptom severity during one interactive activity but not during other activities.
A model combining galvanic skin response and heart rate variability data reliably predicted emotional states in children with ASD.
A method using ECG-derived R-R interval data detected physiological arousal associated with anxiety in children with ASD with high sensitivity and specificity.
An increase in heart rate was associated with the onset of challenging behaviours in young children with ASD, while heart rate variability was not a significant predictor.

During a psychosocial stress task, children with ASD showed increased heart rate and decreased heart rate variability compared to a rest task, supporting the validity of wearables for measuring stress.
Machine learning algorithms applied to wearable accelerometer movement data detected a range of self-injurious behaviours in children with ASD with high accuracy and specificity.

Wearable fNIRS recordings showed that medial prefrontal cortex activity was significantly higher in children with ASD than typically developing children during social video viewing, and this activity correlated with ASD symptom severity.
Children with ASD did not differ from typically developing children in overall social attention to a conversational partner's eyes or in overall electrodermal activity during social interaction.
A wearable heart rate-based framework for recognizing affective states in children with ASD showed wide intra-subject variability in classification accuracy.
Heart rate variability data was found to be more effective than raw ECG data for capturing valence states (positive/negative internal states) in children with ASD.
Wearable ECG monitoring during naturalistic clinician-child interactions showed that cardiac activity in children with ASD was influenced by changing social engagement states.
Elevated heart rate values were observed around emotional outbursts in preschoolers with ASD, as well as during other moments of therapy sessions.

Despite increased sensory sensitivity often reported in autism, most children with ASD across the reviewed studies were willing to wear wearable devices, although a minority refused or removed sensors.
Autistic children exhibited more regular (lower entropy) postural control than typically developing children across standing, sitting, and sitting-with-fine-motor-task conditions.
Postural control regularity significantly differed across the three task conditions (standing, sitting, sitting with fine motor task) in both groups.
There was no significant group-by-task interaction, indicating that the difference in postural control regularity between autistic and TD children remained consistent regardless of task condition.
Autistic children had lower entropy in postural control, indicating more predictable but less adaptable postural patterns compared to typically developing children.
Fibromyalgia prevalence was significantly higher among mothers of children with ADHD than among mothers of typically developing children.
Mothers of children with ADHD reported markedly elevated anxiety symptoms compared with control mothers.
Mothers of children with ADHD reported markedly elevated depressive symptoms compared with control mothers.

In univariate analysis, higher maternal autistic traits were associated with fibromyalgia, along with higher anxiety, depression, and history of psychiatric disorder, although this association did not remain significant in the adjusted model.
In the fully adjusted multivariable model restricted to the ADHD group, higher maternal anxiety and older child age remained independent predictors of maternal fibromyalgia.
Older age of the child with ADHD was an independent predictor of maternal fibromyalgia in the fully adjusted model.
In the full combined sample analysis, having a child with ADHD was independently associated with maternal fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia symptom severity was moderately positively correlated with both anxiety and depressive symptom severity.

Individuals with two SARS-CoV-2 infections had a higher absolute and relative risk of a hospital-diagnosed long COVID than those with only one infection across all follow-up landmarks (180 days, 1 year, 2 years), though the risk difference declined over time.
The association between reinfection and long COVID risk was robust across major SARS-CoV-2 variant periods, with somewhat higher hazard ratios in the earlier Wildtype/Alpha period than Delta/Omicron.

A negative-control analysis using hip fracture as an outcome showed no increased risk among individuals with prior SARS-CoV-2 infections, supporting that the reinfection-long COVID association is not driven by differential healthcare-seeking or ascertainment bias.
Absolute risk of long COVID decreased with an increasing number of prior SARS-CoV-2 vaccine doses, with the lowest risk observed among individuals who had received three doses.
The absolute risk increase in long COVID attributable to primary infection was larger than the incremental risk increase attributable to reinfection.
Differences in the effect of reinfection on long COVID risk by sex or socioeconomic status (income quartile) did not reach statistical significance.

The relative association between reinfection and long COVID diagnosis was stronger among individuals who had received three vaccine doses compared with those with zero or two doses, despite this group having the lowest overall absolute risk of long COVID.
Reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 was associated with a marginally elevated risk of a fatigue diagnosis compared with primary infection at the 1-year landmark, though the absolute difference was small.
The association between SARS-CoV-2 reinfection and headache diagnosis did not reach statistical significance.
Primary SARS-CoV-2 infection (relative to no infection) was not associated with an increased risk of a fatigue or headache diagnosis, except for a small increase in fatigue risk.
Plasma sST2 was significantly elevated in hospitalized patients during acute COVID-19 compared to healthy controls.
sST2 returned to baseline concentrations during the post-acute phase and remained stable across follow-up timepoints at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months in long COVID patients.
sST2 concentrations were not associated with the initial severity of acute COVID-19 infection.
sST2 concentrations were not associated with persistent fatigue in long COVID patients.
sST2 concentrations were not associated with persistent dyspnea in long COVID patients.
sST2 concentrations were not associated with reduced DLCO in long COVID patients.
sST2 concentrations were not associated with abnormal pulmonary function test results in long COVID patients.
No correlation was found between sST2 and VEGF-A concentrations in long COVID patients.
Plasma sST2 concentrations did not correlate with VEGF-A levels in long COVID patients.
Plasma sST2 concentrations did not correlate with circulating endothelial cell (CEC) counts in long COVID patients.
Plasma sST2 concentrations did not correlate with von Willebrand factor antigen (VWF:Ag) levels in long COVID patients.
Plasma sST2 concentrations did not correlate with D-dimer levels in long COVID patients.
The authors conclude that IL-33/sST2-independent mechanisms may underlie the chronic vascular injury observed in long COVID, since sST2 did not track with persistent endothelial dysfunction.
Nearly one-third of the pediatric cohort developed post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), with higher rates at both extremes of the age range.
In the full cohort clustering, a distinct group of predominantly hospitalized, unvaccinated young children showed acute fever and post-acute respiratory sequelae (rhinorrhea and persistent cough).
A cluster of older children with no acute symptoms generally did not go on to develop PASC.

Vaccinated adolescent girls with comorbidities formed a high-risk cluster with acute headache, myalgia, fatigue and anosmia/ageusia, and subsequently high PASC rates with persistent headache, fatigue and insomnia.
Among children who developed PASC, young unvaccinated children formed a cluster characterized by persistent respiratory sequelae (rhinorrhea and cough).
Among PASC patients, older children (mostly male) reporting full recovery formed a cluster with mild headache and abdominal pain sequelae.
Among PASC patients, vaccinated adolescent girls with comorbidities and perceived incomplete recovery formed a cluster with persistent insomnia and fatigue.
Acute symptom prevalence differed significantly by age group, with headache, sore throat and muscle pain becoming more common with increasing age, while fever was more frequent in young children.

COVID-19 vaccination coverage and hospitalization rates during the acute phase differed markedly by pediatric age group, with vaccination more common in adolescents and hospitalization more common in young children.

Symptom clusters identified in this Italian pediatric cohort only partially overlapped with those reported in the U.S. RECOVER pediatric long COVID study, agreeing on adolescent fatigue/insomnia and older-child gastrointestinal sequelae but diverging elsewhere.
Among patients who visited a specialized long COVID outpatient clinic believing they had long COVID, only 2.2% were ultimately found to have an alternative diagnosis explaining their symptoms.
Among the 14 patients ultimately diagnosed with alternative conditions, weakness or difficulty with movement was the most common presenting symptom, followed by numbness or pain, and fatigue.

Oxidised LDL, fungal (1,3)-β-d-glucan, and the intestinal permeability marker zonulin were elevated in long COVID individuals, indicating disrupted gut barrier integrity and fungal translocation.

Nearly two-thirds of patients discussed in calls to the long COVID RACE line were female.
The most common age group of patients discussed in long COVID RACE line calls was 40-49 years old.

RACE line calls originated overwhelmingly from urban/suburban regions, with Greater Vancouver and the Fraser Valley accounting for more than three-quarters of consultations, while rural/remote regions were underrepresented.
Subacute symptom queries (2-12 weeks post-diagnosis) and vaccination-related questions were the most common reasons for RACE line calls.
Call volume to the long COVID RACE line increased substantially over the study period, rising from 18% of calls in August-December 2020 to 40% and 42% in the subsequent two quarters of 2021.
The number of RACE line queries increased markedly after the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines, coinciding with the start of the vaccine rollout in early 2021.
Among symptom-related RACE line calls, shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and fever were the most frequently reported symptoms of long COVID.
Respiratory symptoms were the single largest category of symptoms reported to the long COVID RACE line, comprising 40% of all reported symptoms.
Neurological symptoms including dizziness, light-headedness, numbness, vertigo, and paresthesia were commonly described by primary care providers regarding long COVID patients.
Beyond 12 weeks post-infection, the most commonly reported chronic long COVID symptoms were shortness of breath, chest pain, and fatigue.
Oral microbiota alpha- and beta-diversity did not differ between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
Salivary interleukin-6 levels did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
Salivary TNF-alpha levels did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and healthy controls.

Valeric acid showed the strongest uncorrected association, trending higher in long COVID patients relative to controls, but this did not remain statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple SCFAs.

Long COVID patients had higher Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS) scores than healthy controls, indicating greater fatigue burden.

Vaccination significantly reduced mortality risk in COPD patients who also had cardiovascular disease comorbidity.

History of lower respiratory tract infection was associated with reduced risk of prolonged post-COVID-19 symptoms in the same COPD cohort.

A Japanese study identified asthma as an independent risk factor for persistent fatigue in patients with long COVID.

mRNA vaccines such as BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 have demonstrated efficacy in reducing the risks of SARS-CoV-2 infection, hospitalization, and death in COPD patients.

Co-administration of ritonavir with fluticasone-containing ICS may increase systemic steroid exposure, risking adrenal suppression, with alternative ICS such as budesonide or mometasone preferred due to lesser CYP3A4 metabolism.

Montelukast, though primarily metabolized by CYP2C8, is potentially affected by ritonavir's effect on CYP3A4.

Self-reported autonomic dysfunction was significantly more common in females than males with HSD.
Females with both hEDS and HSD self-reported more nausea, constipation, and vomiting than males.
Dyspepsia and hemorrhoids were uniquely more common in females than males among hEDS patients.
Lower abdominal pain/cramps, diarrhea, and bowel cramps were uniquely more common in females than males among HSD patients.
Irritable bowel syndrome was significantly more common in females than males among HSD patients.
