Females with HSD self-reported more insomnia and sleep disturbances than males with HSD.
Anxiety was self-reported more often in females than males with HSD, but showed no sex difference in hEDS.
History of abuse and sexual abuse were self-reported more often in females than males with both hEDS and HSD.
Females with HSD self-reported more post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) than males with HSD.

When restricting analysis to females only, autonomic dysfunction was found more often in HSD than hEDS patients, differing from the authors' previous study that included males and did not show this diagnosis difference.

A separate cohort study of 703 patients referred for mast cell activation symptoms found only 4.4% met formal MCAS diagnostic criteria, far lower than the 5-17% of hEDS/HSD patients in this study who self-reported having MCAS.

Only ≤1% of hEDS/HSD patients self-reported a tryptase mutation, which is part of the diagnostic criteria for hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), a condition defined by increased TPSAB1 gene copy number and elevated serum tryptase.

Cardiac mast cell degranulation in males has been reported to drive extracellular matrix remodeling that promotes fibrosis and progression to chronic heart failure, illustrating organ- and sex-specific mast cell function.

Heightened mast cell activation near sensory neurons has been linked to symptom severity in chronic pain disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome, migraine, and fibromyalgia, all of which occur more often in females and are prevalent among hEDS/HSD patients.

The authors propose that greater testosterone-associated muscle mass in males may reduce joint hypermobility and subsequent subluxation/dislocation risk, potentially explaining lower musculoskeletal symptom burden in males, though this hypothesis does not readily explain non-joint symptoms such as migraine or GI issues.

Females with HSD self-reported significantly more symptoms/comorbidities than males for 48.4% of the 122 items examined, compared to 25.4% for females with hEDS, roughly a two-fold difference in the magnitude of sex-based symptom disparity between diagnoses.

The authors suggest that fewer sex differences in hEDS symptoms/comorbidities compared to HSD may indicate a greater genetic contribution driving hEDS pathology, whereas HSD symptom burden may be more influenced by factors such as sex hormones.
Awareness that a confederate could co-perceive the same stimulus (public vs private) had no significant effect on perceptual decision accuracy.
Confidence ratings did not differ significantly between public and private co-perception conditions.
Reaction time did not differ significantly between public and private co-perception conditions.
Weibull psychometric function threshold and slope parameters for the motion discrimination task did not differ between public and private conditions.
Metacognitive efficiency, measured as ROC AUC, did not differ significantly between public and private perception conditions.
Mean amplitude of the EEG centro-parietal positivity (CPP), an evidence-accumulation signal, did not differ between public and private co-perception conditions.
Mean pupil size during the 1-second post-response window did not differ significantly between public and private conditions.
Pupil diameter during a post-stimulus time window was slightly but reliably larger in public (co-perceived) trials than private trials, interpreted as a marker of social-vigilance-linked arousal.

Multivariate EEG activity (RSA) encoded the public/private social context distinction in a pre-stimulus and early post-stimulus temporal cluster, even though this was not detected by univariate ERP amplitude analysis.

Drift diffusion model fits showed no differences between public and private trials in decision starting-point bias or drift rate, indicating that the anticipatory neural/pupil signatures of co-perception did not translate into decision-criterion or evidence-accumulation changes.

The authors speculate, without presenting new data, that covert neural/pupillometric markers of social vigilance could help characterize atypical responses to social presence previously reported in clinical groups such as autism and social anxiety.
Before acute sleep deprivation, LF power increased after acupuncture compared with before acupuncture.
Before acute sleep deprivation, HF power increased after acupuncture compared with before acupuncture.
After acute sleep deprivation, heart rate was decreased compared with before sleep deprivation (prior to acupuncture).
After acute sleep deprivation, RMSSD (root mean square of successive R-R interval differences) decreased compared with before sleep deprivation.
After acute sleep deprivation, HF power decreased compared with before sleep deprivation.
After acute sleep deprivation, LF power decreased compared with before sleep deprivation.
After acute sleep deprivation, acupuncture treatment reduced psychomotor vigilance task reaction time compared with pre-acupuncture measurements, indicating improved attention.

After acute sleep deprivation, acupuncture increased the proportion of adjacent heartbeat interval differences exceeding 50 ms (pNN50%), alongside SDNN, RMSSD, HF and LF increases, suggesting enhanced parasympathetic/vagal tone.
Patients with a positive COVID-19 PCR test had more than double the risk of a subsequent chronic rhinosinusitis diagnosis compared to matched COVID-19-negative patients.
During the pre-Delta variant period, COVID-19-positive patients had a 44% increased risk of subsequent chronic rhinosinusitis diagnosis compared to COVID-19-negative patients.
During the Delta variant period, COVID-19-positive patients had a 20% increased risk of subsequent chronic rhinosinusitis diagnosis compared to COVID-19-negative patients.
During the Omicron variant period, COVID-19-positive patients had more than double the risk of subsequent chronic rhinosinusitis diagnosis compared to COVID-19-negative patients.
Prior COVID-19 vaccination did not significantly modify the risk of developing chronic rhinosinusitis among patients with a positive COVID-19 PCR test.
Of 24 candidate symptoms, 13 were significantly more prevalent in ancestral SARS-CoV-2-infected healthcare workers than in uninfected controls, defining them as PASC-specific.
Fatigue was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Loss of smell/taste was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Brain fog was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Joint pain was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Hair loss was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Headache was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Chest pain was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Muscle pain was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Shortness of breath was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Dizziness was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Cough was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Burnout or exhaustion was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Runny nose was significantly more common in aSCV2-infected participants than in uninfected controls at baseline.
Subjective long COVID was reported far more often by aSCV2-infected participants than by uninfected controls at baseline.
Among HCWs with PASC-specific symptoms, those who self-identified as having long COVID reported a substantially higher symptom burden than those who did not.
Fatigue prevalence was much higher among participants with subjective long COVID compared to those without.
The number of PASC symptoms per participant declined significantly over roughly four years of follow-up, though a majority still reported at least one symptom at the final survey.
Sensitivity analysis restricted to participants with complete follow-up data confirmed the decline in symptom count over time.
Fatigue prevalence decreased significantly from baseline to the final follow-up survey.
Loss of smell/taste prevalence decreased significantly from baseline to the final follow-up survey.
Brain fog prevalence did not significantly change from baseline to the final follow-up survey, suggesting persistent cognitive impairment.

Once established, subjective long COVID rarely resolved over the follow-up period; nearly all resolutions occurred only at the first follow-up, and most remaining respondents still reported ongoing long COVID at the final survey.
Among participants with subjective long COVID, functional limitations measured by the PCFS were mostly mild at baseline and remained stable over the follow-up period.
Participants with a higher initial number of PASC symptoms tended to also report higher symptom counts at the final follow-up survey.
There was a non-significant trend for participants with moderate or severe functional limitations at baseline to still report limitations at final follow-up.

The baseline prevalence of PASC symptoms in this healthcare worker cohort (40.8% at ~18.5 months post-infection) was higher than reported in most prior studies and higher than a recent meta-analysis's pooled 3-year estimate.
PASC prevalence was 26% at both 15 months and 3 years after severe/critical COVID-19 ALI/ARDS, similar to the 21% prevalence observed in the RECOVER cohort at 6 months.

No biomarkers of inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, or complement activation (IL-6, IL-8, sTNFR-1, GDF-15, ADAMTS13, angiopoietin, sICAM-1, sVCAM-1, C2, C4b, C5) were significantly associated with PASC at 15 months or 3 years in either unadjusted or adjusted analyses.
IL-8 was associated with brain fog at 3 years in unadjusted analysis and remained significant after adjusting for confounders.
sTNFR-1 was associated with brain fog at 3 years in unadjusted analysis, but this association did not remain significant after adjusting for confounders.
C4b levels at 4 months and 15 months were significantly associated with PEM at 3 years in unadjusted models but the association was not significant after adjusting for confounders.
GDF-15 was significantly associated with frailty category at 3 years cross-sectionally in unadjusted analysis, but this did not remain significant after adjusting for confounders.

PASC, PEM, brain fog, and fatigue were significantly associated with greater frailty, lower short physical performance battery (SPPB) scores, and reduced 6-minute walk distance at 15 months; at 3 years these physical function measures remained significantly associated only with PEM.
At 15 months, participants with PASC were significantly older, more likely to be female, and had a higher BMI than those without PASC; at 3 years, PASC was associated with higher BMI only.
Post-exertional malaise prevalence was 43% at 15 months and 47% at 3 years, brain fog prevalence was 22% and 27%, and fatigue prevalence was 27% and 41%, respectively, in the cohort.
No biomarkers were consistently associated with any specific symptom phenotype (PEM, brain fog, fatigue) after adjusting for multiple comparisons.
No biomarkers were consistently associated with frailty phenotype categories in either unadjusted or adjusted analyses.

The authors note their finding of no persistent inflammatory biomarker elevation is consistent with a prior meta-analysis showing that initial severity of acute COVID-19 illness is a major risk factor for developing PASC.
Myocarditis following COVID-19 remains relatively uncommon but occurs at a significantly higher rate than before the pandemic.
Persistent viral antigen or RNA in cardiac tissue is hypothesized to cause chronic immune activation contributing to myocardial injury in Long COVID.
Autoimmunity, including anti-heart antibodies, is proposed as an immune-mediated mechanism of cardiac damage in Long COVID myocarditis.
Microvascular endothelial dysfunction with impaired myocardial perfusion is proposed as a mechanism underlying cardiac involvement in Long COVID.
Maladaptive inflammatory responses are described as contributing to myocardial injury in Long COVID.

Patients with Long COVID myocarditis can present with atypical features including exercise intolerance, orthostatic tachycardia, or unexplained fatigue in addition to typical chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations.
Exercise restriction for 3-6 months is recommended as a management approach in confirmed cases of Long COVID myocarditis.
Corticosteroids may be used as anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapy in fulminant myocarditis cases or those overlapping with multisystem inflammatory syndrome.
NSAIDs and colchicine are used to target pericardial involvement when present in Long COVID myocarditis.
Anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive therapy, such as corticosteroids, may be used in specific scenarios including fulminant myocarditis or cases overlapping with multisystem inflammatory syndrome.
Therapies targeting pericardial involvement, such as NSAIDs and colchicine, are recommended when pericardial involvement is present in Long COVID myocarditis.
Advanced age (>60 years) was identified as a risk factor for long COVID in an Ethiopian cohort study by Seyoum et al.
Elias et al. found that older age (as a continuous variable) increased the risk of persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
Dryden et al. reported that patient age ≥65 years was a risk factor for long COVID occurrence.
Zulu et al. did not find age to be a risk factor for long COVID, though the median age of participants with persistent symptoms was 33 years.
Female sex was found to increase the risk of developing post-acute COVID-19 syndrome in one included study.
Being a woman was found to be a factor associated with the persistence of symptoms after acute COVID-19 in a second study.
Some studies did not find sex to be a significant risk factor for long COVID, although a majority (63%) of symptomatic patients in the population studied were female.

Crankson et al. found that risk of long COVID decreased with increasing patient education level, with primary, secondary/vocational, and higher education all associated with reduced risk compared to no formal education.
Multiple studies (Mendelsohn, Malambo, Osikomaiya, Ogoina) found that the occurrence of long COVID increased with the initial severity of acute COVID-19 disease.
A table finding indicated that occurrence of persistent COVID-19 symptoms was significantly increased specifically in relation to mild initial COVID-19 disease severity.
Elias et al. found that longer hospital stay increased the chances of developing persistent long COVID symptoms.
Malambo et al. specified that hospitalization duration of ≥15 days strongly increased the risk of developing persistent long COVID symptoms.
Dryden et al. found that ICU admission during acute COVID-19 increased the chances of presenting persistent long COVID symptoms.
Zulu et al. found that individuals with five or more symptoms at symptom onset were nearly three times more likely to report persistent long COVID symptoms.
Zulu et al. found that participants with loss of appetite at symptom onset had higher odds of reporting persistent long COVID symptoms.
Nuamah et al. found that patients who experienced chest pain during acute infection had 98% higher odds of having persistent symptoms beyond 14 days.
Malambo et al. showed that presence of comorbidities including HIV was longitudinally associated with increased odds of long COVID.

Crankson et al. found that COVID-19 patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus spent longer in hospital and had a four-fold higher risk of long COVID compared to those without these comorbidities.
Kinge et al. found hypertension to be the most frequently reported comorbid condition among long COVID patients, especially among workers aged 45-55 years.
Long COVID prevalence varied substantially across the 15 included SSA studies, ranging from 2% in Ghana to 66.7% in South Africa, reflecting differences in definitions, populations, and follow-up.
Fatigue was the most consistently reported long COVID symptom across the included SSA studies, documented in 12 of 15 studies with a prevalence of 25-66% among long COVID patients.
Dyspnea was reported as a persistent long COVID symptom in 10 of the included SSA studies, with prevalence of 15-45%.
A single case report described polyphagia as an atypical long COVID presentation in a Ugandan woman.

In Malambo et al.'s study, a smaller proportion of vaccinated patients (21.9%) had persistent COVID-19 symptoms compared to unvaccinated patients (78.1%), suggesting a possible protective association of vaccination.

In Elias et al.'s study, the proportion of patients presenting persistent COVID-19 symptoms was similar between vaccinated (34.1%) and unvaccinated (39.7%) patients, showing little apparent vaccination effect.
Self-reported fatigue decreased significantly by 51% in the ECES-treated group compared with a non-significant 22.6% decrease in the placebo group, with a significant between-group difference.
Treatment with ECES significantly increased quality of life as measured by a visual analog scale, whereas the placebo group showed a non-significant change.
A VAS sub-analysis showed significant improvement in dyspnea/fatigue in both groups, but the improvement was larger in the ECES group than placebo.
Pain/discomfort was significantly lower in the ECES-treated group compared with placebo.
Depression/anxiety scores were significantly lower after treatment in both the ECES and placebo groups.
In men, ECES treatment significantly increased dominant-hand grip strength, whereas placebo showed a non-significant decrease, with a significant between-group difference.
In women, ECES treatment significantly increased dominant-hand grip strength while placebo showed no change, with a significant between-group difference.
Serum IL-1β significantly decreased in the ECES-treated group after 3 months, while it decreased in the placebo group without reaching significance.
Serum IL-6 significantly decreased with ECES treatment and also significantly decreased in the placebo group.
Serum TNF-α significantly decreased in the ECES-treated group, while the placebo group showed a non-significant reduction.
Serum syndecan-1, a marker of endothelial glycocalyx damage, significantly decreased in the ECES-treated group while showing a non-significant modest increase in the placebo group.

A meta-analysis of 51 RCTs with 4,026 participants found that rehabilitation interventions (physical training, respiratory muscle strengthening, telerehabilitation) improved functional capacity, cardiorespiratory performance, reduced dyspnea and fatigue, and enhanced quality of life in long COVID patients.
The same meta-analysis found no consistent effects of rehabilitation interventions on spirometric parameters, global fatigue (MFIS), or anxiety and depression symptoms.

A randomized, double-blind trial of 70 patients with post-COVID fatigue found that HD-tDCS applied over the left primary motor cortex for 10 sessions over 5 weeks significantly reduced fatigue, including cognitive and psychosocial dimensions, compared to sham.

In 56 adults who underwent mechanical ventilation for ARDS, HD-tDCS applied over the left diaphragmatic primary motor cortex in a 4×1 montage significantly increased ventilator-free days within the first 28 days compared to controls.

In 47 post-COVID patients with persistent fatigue (>6 months), eight sessions of tDCS over the left DLPFC (2 mA, 20 min) significantly reduced physical fatigue immediately post-treatment and at 1-month follow-up, along with reduced depressive symptoms, compared to sham.
In the same DLPFC tDCS study of post-COVID fatigue, cognitive fatigue and quality of life did not show significant improvements with active stimulation.

A case series of six patients with persistent post-COVID respiratory sequelae found that combining HD-tDCS with inspiratory muscle training enhanced respiratory muscle strength and efficiency, and increased inspiratory capacity, ventilation, lung volumes, and maximal inspiratory pressure.
A case report demonstrated that tDCS contributed to reducing anxiety and depression symptoms in a post-COVID patient, supporting a potential adjunctive role for neuromodulation in rehabilitation.

A randomized study of post-COVID patients with fatigue and cognitive impairment lasting nearly 3 years found that tDCS combined with cognitive training (15 sessions), delivered over either M1 or DLPFC, improved fatigue, cognitive performance, anxiety, depression, pain, and sleep quality, with M1 stimulation showing slight superiority for fatigue and sleep.

A pilot study of adults with persistent post-COVID cognitive complaints (mostly women, mean age 43) randomized to 20 sessions of active or sham tDCS combined with cognitive training found modest but significant improvements in inhibitory control, processing speed, and divided attention, plus reduced anxiety and depressive symptoms in both groups.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of tDCS targeting the medial prefrontal cortex for neuropsychiatric symptoms in long COVID (20 sessions of 30 min) found no significant improvement in cognitive function, suggesting tDCS monotherapy may be insufficient.

A two-phase study of non-invasive neurostimulation targeting olfactory structures (olfactory bulb, tract, and piriform cortex) for persistent post-COVID anosmia found that participants with more severe initial olfactory deficits showed better outcomes, though statistical significance was limited by small sample size.

tDCS is proposed to reduce persistent neuroinflammation in long COVID by modulating microglial activation and cytokine levels, creating more favorable conditions for neuroplasticity and functional compensation of deficits.
Impairment of the blood–brain barrier in long COVID is proposed to increase glutamate levels, which in turn promote oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and hypercoagulability.
Reduced activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection is proposed to contribute to a hyperinflammatory state in long COVID.
Hospital laboratory-measured CRP levels did not differ significantly between long-COVID patients and recovered controls.
IL-6 measured by MSD electrochemiluminescence assay was marginally higher in long-COVID patients than controls but did not reach statistical significance.
TNF-α measured by MSD electrochemiluminescence assay was marginally higher in long-COVID patients than controls but did not reach statistical significance.
NULISA ultrasensitive assay showed nominally higher CRP in long-COVID patients versus controls, but this did not survive FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
NULISA assay showed nominally higher TNF-α in long-COVID patients versus controls, but this did not survive FDR correction.
NULISA assay showed nominally higher IL-6 in long-COVID patients versus controls, but this did not survive FDR correction.
Plasma TREM2, elevated in acute severe COVID-19, showed no statistically significant difference between long-COVID patients and recovered controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Plasma neurofilament light, a marker of neuronal damage, showed no significant difference between long-COVID patients and controls.
Plasma GFAP, a marker of astroglial neuroinflammation, showed no significant difference between long-COVID patients and controls.
Plasma IL-1β showed no significant difference between long-COVID patients and controls, with a negligible mean difference.
Inflammatory and neurological biomarkers (NfL, GFAP, TREM2, CRP, TNF-α, IL-6) did not correlate with symptom severity scores in long-COVID patients.
35.9% of participants (506/1408) reported at least one long COVID symptom 9–15 months after their initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of developing long COVID in multivariable logistic regression.
Absence of pre-existing comorbidities was independently associated with lower odds of long COVID.
Higher frequency of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Occurrence of other pathogenic respiratory infections during the post-acute recovery period was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Acute-phase shortness of breath/chest distress was independently associated with increased odds of subsequent long COVID.
Acute-phase dyspnea was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Acute-phase palpitations were independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Acute-phase skin rash was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID, showing the largest effect size among the acute symptom predictors.
Acute-phase back or spine pain was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Acute-phase brain fog/problems thinking or concentrating was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.
Acute-phase forgetfulness was independently associated with increased odds of long COVID.

A nomogram built from nine demographic and acute-phase predictors showed good discrimination for identifying individuals at risk of long COVID, with internal bootstrap validation confirming stability.
Among long COVID patients, the most common persistent symptoms with incidence ≥5% were fatigue, cough, decreased activity tolerance, shortness of breath, expectoration and forgetfulness.

Compared to the recovered group, the long COVID group had significantly worse quality of life (lower EQ-VAS), reduced functional independence (lower Barthel ADL index), greater disability (higher WHODAS), and poorer scores across all five EQ-5D dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, depression).
The long COVID group had significantly higher Cognitive Failure Questionnaire scores than the recovered group, indicating adverse effects on cognitive function even one year after infection.
Acute-phase symptoms during SARS-CoV-2 reinfection (second infection) were generally less frequent than during the initial infection, including fever, cough, fatigue, and sore throat.

Individuals with multiple SARS-CoV-2 infections exhibited a higher incidence and greater severity of long COVID symptoms than those with a single infection, with 25 of 48 symptoms significantly more common in the multiple-infection group (e.g., fatigue 24.1% vs 12.4%).
Patients with other pathogenic respiratory infections during recovery had lower rates of perceived complete recovery and more/severe long COVID symptoms than those without such infections.
Hospitalization due to acute COVID-19 was associated with higher univariable odds of long COVID but did not remain significant after multivariable adjustment.
Advanced age, a risk factor widely reported in prior long COVID studies, showed no significant association with long COVID in this cohort's comparative or regression analyses.
Vaccination dose number was not significantly associated with long COVID in this cohort's multivariable model, contrasting with a prior meta-analysis showing vaccination reduces long COVID risk.
Conservative estimates put the global incidence of long COVID at approximately 10%, corresponding to at least 77.8 million affected people.

Risk factors reported for long COVID include older age, female gender, multiple comorbidities, prior chronic respiratory disease (e.g., COPD), severe acute illness requiring hospitalization or mechanical ventilation, high viral load, and smoking.
Reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus and human herpesvirus 6 is listed among risk factors that may predispose individuals to long COVID.
Autoantibodies directed against various organs and against type I interferon are cited as a risk factor for long COVID.
Neurological symptoms are present in approximately 33% of long COVID cases, most commonly fatigue, followed by headaches, polyneuropathy, neuropsychiatric problems, and cognitive impairment.
A meta-analysis found that approximately 20% of long COVID patients experience no respiratory symptoms, with fatigue and dyspnea being the most prevalent respiratory sequelae among those affected.
Cited research indicates a markedly elevated risk of cardiovascular disease while recovering from long COVID.
Multiple studies indicate an elevated risk of developing chronic kidney disease following COVID-19, which may represent a manifestation of long COVID.
Long COVID gastrointestinal symptoms are associated with both pre-existing and post-COVID-19 mental health disorders, although the underlying mechanism is unclear.
Autopsy findings showed that individuals infected with the Alpha variant died substantially earlier than those infected with the wild-type strain during the same period.
The Alpha variant (B.1.1.7), the first designated VOC, carries 17 mutation sites including 9 on the spike protein and shows 50-100% increased transmissibility relative to the wild-type strain.
The Omicron variant (B.1.1.529) carries over 60 mutation sites, including multiple RBD amino acid substitutions, conferring high transmissibility and immune evasion.
Compared to previous variants of concern, Omicron infection resulted in fewer long COVID symptoms and the lowest prevalence of long COVID.
No differences in viral persistence have been found to differ between SARS-CoV-2 variants.
Outpatients who developed long COVID had higher peak nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral loads within the first 21 days of infection compared to those who fully recovered.
TNF-alpha and IL-1beta were significantly elevated in the early stages of long COVID.
IL-1beta was significantly elevated, together with TNF-alpha, in the early stages of long COVID.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a manifestation of autonomic dysfunction in long COVID, is thought to be causally driven by inflammation, tissue hypoxia, and autoimmunity, arising from direct or indirect neuronal injury that alters vascular tone.
A meta-analysis found that early antiviral treatment for acute COVID-19 can reduce hospitalization rates and mortality risk, and may lower the population incidence of long COVID.

Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid), which selectively inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, has shown particular efficacy against the Omicron variant, reducing risk of severe and persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
COVID-19 patients treated with dexamethasone had a lower risk of developing long COVID symptoms, with dexamethasone reducing systemic inflammation and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
The monoclonal antibody combination amubarvimab/romlusevimab reduced hospitalization or death risk by 79% but has not been shown to reduce the risk of long COVID.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies may be a viable treatment for chronic long COVID headaches, potentially lessening psychological effects and improving headache-related quality of life.

A systematic review and meta-analysis found that receiving at least one dose of SARS-CoV-2 vaccine provides protection against long COVID, with two doses before infection or one dose after infection reducing risk, and no direct evidence that vaccines exacerbate long COVID.
A meta-analysis indicates that long-term physical exercise enhances quality of life for long COVID patients, particularly benefiting those with musculoskeletal discomfort.

Epipharyngeal abrasive therapy (EAT) cleared residual SARS-CoV-2 RNA from the epipharynx and, by reducing pharyngeal inflammation, was reported to alleviate systemic symptoms associated with long COVID.
Fatigue was the most common long COVID-19 symptom, reported by 72.67% of participants.
Breathlessness on walking up a flight of stairs was reported by 64.96% of participants, the second most common symptom.
Sleep problems, including difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or oversleeping, were reported by 62.95% of participants.
The mean symptom severity subscale score was 8.63 (SD 6.21) out of a possible 30, indicating moderate persistent symptom burden after COVID-19.
The mean functional disability subscale score was 1.47 (SD 2.15) out of a possible 15, indicating mild functional impairment overall.
The mean overall health score was 6.9 (SD 2.16) out of a possible 10, reflecting a moderate reduction in perceived overall health after COVID-19.
Cognition problems (concentration, memory, or planning difficulty) were the most severe common symptom, with a mean score in the moderate range affecting daily life to some extent.

Difficulty with other activities of daily living (household work, leisure/sporting activities, paid/unpaid work, study, or shopping) was the most common functional limitation, reported by 31.03% of participants.
Other symptoms such as fever (21.99%), hair loss (20.43%), dry eyes/redness of eyes (18.83%), and change in appetite (15.47%) were common among the 25 additional symptoms assessed.
Female participants showed higher symptom, functional, and other-symptom impairment and worse overall health after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with male participants.
Rural residence was associated with worse rehabilitation status and overall health after COVID-19, potentially due to limited healthcare access and lower health literacy.
Participants infected with SARS-CoV-2 two or more times showed higher prevalence and severity of long COVID-19 symptoms than those infected only once.

Participants whose most recent SARS-CoV-2 infection occurred more than 12 months prior showed the highest prevalence and severity of symptoms across most measures, followed by those infected 7-12 months prior.
Scores for symptom severity, functional ability, and other symptoms subscales were significantly positively correlated with each other.
Overall health scores were significantly negatively correlated with symptom severity, functional ability, and other symptom subscale scores.
In the discrete choice experiment, a longer medical distance (60 minutes) was the strongest negative predictor of healthcare-seeking preference among long COVID-19 patients.
Western medicine as a medical service type was significantly less preferred than traditional Chinese medicine for managing long COVID-19.
Higher out-of-pocket costs per visit were significantly associated with lower preference for a given healthcare option among long COVID-19 patients.

Attendance at tertiary hospitals, rehabilitation training, nutrition support, and integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine were all significantly positively preferred attribute levels for long COVID-19 healthcare choices.
The positive preference for integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine was not statistically significant among participants infected with SARS-CoV-2 two or more times.

Among participants whose most recent infection was ≥10 months prior, preferences for tertiary hospital, nutrition support, and integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine were no longer statistically significant, and rehabilitation training preference was also non-significant among those infected more than 12 months ago.
All common symptoms and functional limitations assessed were more severe after COVID-19 infection than participants' recalled pre-COVID baseline.

The discussion cites prior literature suggesting X chromosome-linked genes are associated with susceptibility to viral infection and autoimmune disease, supporting a proposed autoimmune mechanism underlying the female predominance in long COVID-19.
The discrete-time quantum walk (QW) algorithm outperformed random walk with restart (RWR) in predicting Long COVID-associated proteins, achieving a higher area under the precision-recall curve.

Long COVID proteins located in deep regions of the SARS-CoV-2-induced protein network were enriched for complement regulation and thromboinflammatory pathways, considered mechanistically central to Long COVID.
Long COVID proteins located in shallow (proximal) regions of the network were enriched for gamma-carboxylation and ECM organization pathways, reflecting acute COVID-19-related processes.

Quantum walk analysis uniquely prioritized CISD1, CISD2, and CISD3, iron-sulfur binding proteins implicated in reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, as top candidate proteins for Long COVID, with probabilities far higher than assigned by RWR.

VDAC1, a voltage-dependent anion channel involved in mitochondrial calcium transport, is significantly reduced in Long COVID patients and was identified via the QW subnetwork as a potential therapeutic target.

Cannabidiol was identified via DrugBank as the only FDA-approved compound targeting VDAC1, positioning it as a candidate repurposed therapeutic for Long COVID given its anti-inflammatory and neuropsychiatric properties.
IL-6 was the top-ranked node identified by the RWR algorithm and is linked, via peripheral inflammation, to Long COVID; it was the sole RWR-identified pathway with a known Long COVID association.

QW-identified key proteins were enriched in pathways linked to neuronal inflammation, metabolic inflammation, glycosylation disorders, glycosaminoglycan metabolism, and FGF signaling dysregulation, collectively associated with autoimmune responses characteristic of Long COVID.
Coagulation and fibrin clot formation pathways, enriched among deep Long COVID proteins, are closely associated with hallmark Long COVID symptoms such as fatigue and post-exertional malaise.

WFS1, CISD2, BCL2, VDAC1, and CANX are involved in calcium regulation within mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), and dysregulated mitochondrial Ca2+ handling can cause mitochondrial collapse or trigger mitophagy relevant to Long COVID.

BECN1 promotes autophagosome formation at MAMs while PRKN facilitates mitochondrial ubiquitylation and recruitment of ubiquitin-binding receptors, both regulating mitophagy implicated in Long COVID mitochondrial dysfunction.

Mitochondrial dysfunction links the QW-derived Long COVID subnetwork to Parkinson's disease via PRKN, a gene whose mutations are a known cause of Parkinson's disease, aligning with evidence that COVID-19 may raise Parkinson's disease risk through shared mitochondrial and immune mechanisms.

Gene Ontology enrichment of the CISD1/2/3 subnetwork proteins revealed significant enrichment in autophagy, mitophagy, ROS metabolism, and endoplasmic reticulum stress response, supporting a strong link between this subnetwork and mitochondrial dysfunction in Long COVID.

Long COVID proteins (LCPs), based on 6-month proteomic data, were predominantly located in deep regions of the SARS-CoV-2-induced protein network, with 60% classified as deep (distance>2) versus 40% shallow (distance≤2), indicating that most Long COVID-associated proteins reside distant from direct SARS-CoV-2 interactors.

Among the top 947 key proteins, QW identified more deep Long COVID proteins than RWR (27 vs 5), while RWR identified more shallow Long COVID proteins than QW (43 vs 24), demonstrating QW's superior ability to capture proteins mechanistically distant from SARS-CoV-2 interactors.

The paper-based immunoassay with dendrimer signal amplification and on-chip mass spectrometry achieved a limit of detection of 2.4 pM (161.2 pg/mL) for recombinant SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein, with excellent linearity between 5 and 40 pM.

Plasma samples from 10 long COVID patients showed MS signal intensity up to two orders of magnitude higher than samples from 10 healthy controls, with no overlap between groups and a statistically significant difference.

Detection of residual nucleocapsid antigen in convalescent plasma samples supports the hypothesis that persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigenemia may contribute to chronic immune activation and prolonged symptomatology in long COVID.

The completed paper-based immunoassay (ionic probe-dendrimer-antibody complex) retained a strong analytical signal after 30 days of ambient storage, with only a 16.7% signal reduction compared to day 1 and signal-to-noise remaining above 5.

The capture-antibody-functionalized paper chip (bioactive paper chip) remained functional after 30 days of ambient storage, showing only about a 12% signal drop relative to day 0 when assayed with 100 pM N protein.
Negative control samples containing 1% BSA without N protein produced a much lower m/z 87 signal than positive samples, indicating minimal nonspecific binding in the assay.

A global estimate puts the prevalence of self-reported fatigue, respiratory symptoms, and cognitive decline lasting at least 3 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection at 6.2%, with wide uncertainty reflecting heterogeneous data.
Persistent tissue reservoirs of SARS-CoV-2 have been hypothesised as a pathobiological driver of long COVID.
Inflammation-triggered tissue damage and immune dysregulation are proposed mechanisms underlying organ dysfunction in long COVID.
Mitochondrial dysfunction has been proposed as one of the pathobiological drivers of long COVID.
Reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus or other latent viruses has been proposed as a contributing mechanism to long COVID.
Lung remodelling following ARDS-related diffuse alveolar damage has been hypothesised to progress to long-term pulmonary fibrosis, contributing to chronic hypoxia and fatigue.

Mechanical ventilation can cause volutrauma (ventilator-induced lung injury from overdistension), releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines that may induce or worsen lung injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing comorbidities such as COPD.

Persistent SARS-CoV-2 reservoirs in extrapulmonary tissue may increase circulating spike protein, enhancing endothelial and blood-brain barrier dysfunction and contributing to the emergence or worsening of COVID-driven fatigue.
Disseminated pulmonary micro-immunothromboses have been proposed to contribute to alveolar-capillary dysfunction and impaired gas exchange, producing dyspnea and fatigue.

In the paper's own qualitative causal Bayesian network, the modelled probability of persistent organ dysfunction (P1) increased with COVID-19 severity and with symptom reporting: 1% given mild disease, 7% given severe disease, 3% given symptoms reported at t1, and 36% given symptoms reported at both t1 and t3.

The ADAPT study's operational long COVID case definition includes ongoing physical symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue/malaise) and/or neuropsychiatric symptoms lasting longer than three months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, and was used to validate the framework's periods and language.
The mean levels of the median value of studied GPCR autoantibodies showed a non-significant trend toward being higher in Long COVID patients compared to asymptomatic post-COVID individuals.
Anti-β2 adrenergic receptor autoantibody showed the largest numerical difference between LC and APC groups, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Mean total Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score was significantly higher in LC patients than in APC individuals.
Physical fatigue subscale score of the FAS was significantly higher in LC than APC.
Mental fatigue subscale score of the FAS was significantly higher in LC than APC.
Morning blood cortisol was significantly lower in LC patients compared to APC individuals, suggesting altered HPA-axis regulation.
SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cell (IFN-γ ELISpot) responses to Spike and Nucleocapsid antigens trended weaker in LC patients than in APC individuals, particularly for the Spike antigen.
A distinct, intercorrelated cluster of GPCR- and endothelial-directed autoantibodies formed an autoimmune signature positively associated with several Long COVID symptoms and overall fatigue score.
Age and hormonal variables correlated negatively with both the autoimmune autoantibody cluster and symptom clusters, suggesting a regulatory influence on the autoimmune-fatigue relationship.
Using a 95th-percentile cutoff derived from the APC autoantibody distribution, the authors correctly identified a subset of Long COVID patients with no apparent false positives.
LC patients had received significantly fewer SARS-CoV-2 vaccine doses than APC individuals, consistent with a proposed protective effect of vaccination against developing Long COVID.
C2 complement protein levels were elevated in long COVID patients six months after infection compared with controls.
C5 complement protein levels were elevated in long COVID patients twelve months after infection.
No significant differences in C3, C4, and C5 complement component levels were found between long COVID survivors and controls at one and two years post-infection.
C4a and C4b activation products were elevated in long COVID patients compared with pre-infected controls without long COVID at one year post-infection.
C4d activation product levels did not differ between long COVID patients, non-previously infected individuals, and pre-infected controls without long COVID six months after infection.

Wei et al. found significant dysregulation of C1qA, C1qC, and C4a activation products as well as C3 and C5 components in long COVID subjects compared with patients without long COVID, but did not specify direction of change.
Baillie et al. found increased levels of the C1s/C1-inhibitor complex in long COVID individuals compared with matched infected controls without long COVID one year after infection.

Hurler et al. found no differences in C1-INH product, C1s/C1-INH complex, or pentraxin 3 (PTX3) levels among long COVID patients, previously infected controls without long COVID, and non-infected controls at approximately 90 days post-infection.
Studies reported contradictory results for C1q in long COVID: one found elevated levels, another found lower levels, and a third found no significant difference.
Patients with post-COVID fatigue had increased C2 levels one year after infection.
Survivors with post-COVID fatigue or dyspnea showed decreased C3 and C5 levels two years post-infection.
C1qA activation product levels were increased in individuals with gastrointestinal or cognitive post-COVID symptoms, but not in those with fatigue or cardiorespiratory symptoms.
Higher CH50 levels (functional activity of the classical complement pathway) were significantly associated with post-COVID brain fog but not with fatigue or dyspnea, at three months post-infection.
MBL levels, a central lectin pathway component, did not differ between long COVID individuals and infected or non-infected controls.
No significant difference in MASP1-C1INH complex levels was found between long COVID and control groups.
MBL levels were lower in long COVID patients with brain fog than in long COVID survivors without brain fog and in healthy controls.
Long COVID individuals had higher levels of Ba and iC3b activation products and higher Factor D and properdin regulators compared with infected controls, while Factor B levels were similar.
C3f, a fragment of C3 cleavage, decreased gradually following a first or second SARS-CoV-2 infection during the recovery period.
COLEC12, which activates the alternative complement pathway independent of C3b, was elevated in people with post-COVID fatigue and cardiorespiratory symptoms.

Terminal pathway markers C5bC6 complex were increased while C7 protein was decreased in long COVID patients at six months post-infection; age and vaccination status were not associated with C7 levels.
C5a activation product, C9 component, and terminal complement complex (TCC) levels were higher in long COVID patients than in infected controls without long COVID.
C7 protein levels showed no overall difference between long COVID survivors and controls at two years post-infection, but patients with post-COVID dyspnea had lower C7 than those without dyspnea.
C1q levels were increased during the acute/active phase of infection (days 0 and 14) but not at days 28 or 90 post-infection, suggesting temporal fluctuation of complement activation.

Across the reviewed studies, abnormalities were more consistently reported in the classical, alternative, and terminal complement pathways than in the lectin pathway, though responses varied by study and timepoint.

In background reference data (not the long COVID cohorts), females exhibited lower C3 and properdin levels and higher Factor D concentration than males, with no sex difference in classical pathway activity.
Aging has been associated with increased classical and alternative complement pathway activity (but not lectin), potentially raising activation products (C3a, C5a) and components (C3, C4, C5).

A cited reference study found that healthy females exhibit lower levels of C3 and properdin and higher factor D concentrations than males, with no sex difference in classical pathway activity, illustrating known sex effects on complement biology.

Only one included study adjusted for sex, age, and BMI as confounders and found these factors did not affect the observed differences in the alternative complement pathway between individuals with and without long COVID.

Aging has been associated with increased activity of the classical and alternative complement pathways, but not the lectin pathway, potentially raising levels of activation products such as C3a and C5a.
Obesity induces chronic low-grade inflammation that activates the complement system, particularly the classical pathway, by triggering production of C3 and C1q.
Reduced levels of the C1q complement component have been associated with autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, cited as context for interpreting lower C1q findings in long COVID.

Hurler et al. found that C1q product levels were increased during the active phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection (days 0 and 14) but not at days 28 or 90 post-infection, suggesting complement activation fluctuates over the disease course.
The long-COVID group had a significantly higher proportion of female participants than the post-COVID recovery group.

Long-COVID participants showed significantly higher prevalence of fatigue, sleep disorders, muscle weakness, concentration difficulties, and neurological complaints compared to post-COVID participants.
Post-COVID participants presented predominantly with respiratory symptoms, notably dyspnea and cough, more often than long-COVID participants.
Post-COVID participants had significantly lower blood oxygen partial pressure than long-COVID participants at rehabilitation admission.
Vital capacity was markedly reduced in post-COVID participants compared to long-COVID participants.
Diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide was markedly reduced in post-COVID participants compared to long-COVID participants.
The 6-minute walk test result was significantly lower in post-COVID participants than long-COVID participants, indicating reduced cardiovascular/pulmonary performance.
Total leukocyte count was higher in post-COVID participants than in long-COVID participants, without significant differences in lymphocyte, eosinophil, or basophil counts.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly higher in post-COVID participants than in long-COVID participants.
D-dimer levels, reflecting coagulation activation, were significantly higher in post-COVID than in long-COVID participants.
CRP was only slightly elevated in post-COVID and normal in long-COVID, without a statistically significant difference between the groups.
Targeted proteomic profiling identified 92 of 180 analyzed OLINK proteins as differentially expressed among PC, LC, and pmC groups, with distinct clustering patterns separating the groups.
Neutrophil chemoattractants CXCL1 and CXCL5 were increased in both long-COVID and post-COVID participants relative to the post-mild-COVID control group.
Macrophage activation markers MCP-1 and CSF-1 were increased in both long-COVID and post-COVID participants relative to the post-mild-COVID control group.
Lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 3 (LAMP3) was the most upregulated protein in post-COVID participants and is implicated in dendritic cell-mediated immune regulation.
Programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1), an immune-inhibitory protein and previously reported COVID-19 severity marker, was upregulated in post-COVID participants.
Integrin alpha-11 (ITGA11), a profibrogenic myofibroblast membrane protein, was among the most upregulated proteins in long-COVID participants, suggesting possible mild pulmonary fibrosis.

Plexin A4 (PLXNA4), involved in Toll-like receptor-induced cytokine release and semaphorin-plexin immune signaling, was upregulated in long-COVID participants, suggesting persistent immune reactivity.

C-type lectin domain family 4 members A and C (CLEC4A, CLEC4C/BDCA2), interferon-inhibitory proteins on plasmacytoid dendritic cells, were upregulated in long-COVID participants, potentially reflecting compensatory suppression of interferon overexpression.

A random forest machine learning model using a 184-protein OLINK panel differentiated long-COVID from post-COVID participants with approximately 89% accuracy, with LAMP3, CKAP4, and KRT19 as the most important discriminating features.
A significant correlation was found between BMI below 30 and elevated integrin beta 6 (ITGB6) levels among the tested protein biomarkers.
Levels of CD83, CKAP4, IL-10RB, IL-15RA, ITGB6, and JUN showed a clear positive correlation with worsened (decreased) lung diffusion capacity in post-COVID participants.
Matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1), keratin 19 (KRT19), and CSF-1 showed a positive association with reduced pulmonary diffusion capacity.
Post-COVID participants had a much larger number of upregulated OLINK proteins than long-COVID participants, with substantial but incomplete overlap between the two groups' upregulated protein sets.
Kamikihito, a Kampo herbal formula, was prescribed to alleviate anxiety and support neurogenesis in a patient with Long COVID brain fog.
Saireito and Saikokaryukotsuboreito, Kampo formulas containing Scutellaria root and Bupleurum root, were added to target neuroinflammation via suppression of microglial activation.
After the integrative Kampo regimen, the patient's quality-of-life and mental health scores improved substantially and he returned to work within 2.5 months.
At baseline, the patient showed significant impairment in quality of life and high psychological distress, with elevated depression and anxiety scores.
Brain fog is described as a refractory symptom of Long COVID that currently lacks established standard treatments.
Kamikihito was prescribed based on the pharmacological rationale that it supports hippocampal neurogenesis, targeting the neurogenic component of brain fog.

Saireito and Saikokaryukotsuboreito, which contain Scutellaria root and Bupleurum root, were added to the regimen with the rationale of suppressing microglial activation underlying neuroinflammation in Long COVID brain fog.
After initiating the integrative Kampo regimen, the patient's symptoms improved sufficiently to allow return to work within 2.5 months.

At baseline five months post-COVID-19, the patient presented with a triad of persistent brain fog, fatigue, and anxiety alongside significant quality-of-life impairment and high psychological distress.
The principal component built from inflammatory biomarkers (PC_Inflam) was the best predictor of fatigue (FFtotal) scores in long COVID patients.
PC_Inflam was the best predictor of anxiety (HAMAtotal) scores in long COVID patients.
PC_Inflam was the best predictor of depression (HAMDtotal) scores in long COVID patients.
The principal component of insulin resistance biomarkers (PC_IR) had a lower predictive value for neuropsychiatric symptoms than PC_Inflam.
Long COVID patients showed elevated inflammatory biomarkers (IL-1β, IL-10, IL-18, CRP) alongside neuropsychiatric symptoms and insulin resistance markers.
Insulin resistance biomarkers (HOMA2IR, HOMA%S, HOMA%B) were altered in long COVID patients and associated with neuropsychiatric symptoms.

The principal component built from insulin resistance biomarkers (PC_IR) was a weaker predictor of neuropsychiatric symptom scores than the principal component built from inflammatory biomarkers (PC_Inflam) in Long COVID patients.
The authors conclude that inflammation plays a significant role in the main neuropsychiatric symptoms observed in Long COVID.
Among 283 ICU-treated COVID-19 ARDS patients, 29% died within 30 days of ICU admission.
Cumulative all-cause mortality at 4 years after ICU admission for COVID-19-related ARDS was 44.5%.
Older age at ICU admission was independently associated with higher odds of 30-day mortality in COVID-19-related ARDS.
Higher white blood cell count at ICU admission was independently associated with increased 30-day mortality.
APACHE II score, though strongly associated with 30-day mortality univariably, lost statistical significance after adjustment for age and WBC.
Baseline LDH was significantly higher in patients who died within 30 days compared with 30-day survivors.
Baseline D-dimer was significantly higher among 30-day non-survivors compared with survivors.
Platelet counts were lower in 30-day non-survivors compared with survivors.
Type 2 diabetes was more prevalent among 30-day non-survivors than survivors.
CRRT use during ICU admission was more frequent among 30-day non-survivors than survivors, though this variable had substantial missingness.
Among 30-day survivors, older age was the only factor independently associated with late mortality (occurring between day 30 and year 4).
Baseline troponin was markedly higher among patients who later died (day 30 to year 4) compared with long-term survivors.
Coronary heart disease, chronic kidney disease, and COPD were each more frequent among patients experiencing late mortality than among long-term survivors.
Among 4-year follow-up responders, 30% reported at least some functional limitation on the Post-COVID-19 Functional Status scale, including 3.7% with moderate or worse limitation.
Insomnia was reported by nearly half of 4-year follow-up responders.
Clinically relevant fatigue was present in over a quarter of 4-year follow-up responders.
Subjective cognitive complaints were reported by nearly 40% of 4-year follow-up responders.
Among participants employed pre-COVID, 15.2% had not returned to full-time work by 4 years after ICU admission.
Rehabilitation uptake among 4-year follow-up responders was low, with only 39.2% reporting any rehabilitation received during the four years after ICU discharge.
More than one third of 4-year follow-up responders reported at least one rehospitalization during follow-up.
The estimated median quality-adjusted life years (QALY) at 4 years among follow-up responders was 3.7 out of a possible 4.
Patients with clinically relevant fatigue (FAS ≥ 12) had significantly lower 4-year QALY than those without.
Subjective cognitive complaints (CFQ ≥ 3) were associated with lower 4-year QALY compared with no/mild cognitive complaints.
Not returning to full-time work after the ICU stay was associated with markedly lower 4-year QALY than returning to work.
Patients who reported receiving rehabilitation had lower 4-year QALY than those who did not, likely reflecting confounding by indication rather than harm from rehabilitation.
Clinically relevant dyspnoea (mMRC ≥ 3) was associated with lower 4-year QALY than milder dyspnoea.
Insomnia status was not significantly associated with 4-year QALY.
A composite cumulative impairment score built from six post-ICU sequelae domains showed good discrimination for distinguishing lower versus higher 4-year QALY.
Approximately one in five follow-up responders reported moderate or severe pain/discomfort on the EQ-5D-5L, and nearly 30% reported anxiety/depression symptoms.
EMDR sessions are associated with reduced heart rate and increased heart rate variability, consistent with enhanced parasympathetic tone and reduced sympathetic arousal during bilateral stimulation.
Cerebrospinal fluid flow is significantly driven by arterial pulsations, suggesting rhythmic physiological inputs can directly modulate CSF clearance dynamics.
Meningeal lymphatic vessels drain cerebrospinal fluid, solutes, and immune cells from meningeal compartments toward deep cervical lymph nodes, contributing to CNS immune surveillance and homeostasis.
Regulatory T cells contribute to continuous CNS immune surveillance and constrain excessive microglial reactivity via cytokine-mediated and contact-dependent mechanisms, promoting synaptic stability.
Transmembrane protein 119 is a molecular marker used to distinguish homeostatic microglia from inflammatory activation states.
Purinergic receptor P2RY12 is a molecular marker used to distinguish homeostatic microglia from inflammatory activation states.
Altered immune regulation and microglial activation have been linked to atypical synaptic pruning and network instability in autism spectrum disorder.

Clinical observations from non-controlled settings suggest bilateral rhythmic stimulation is associated with gradual improvements in sensory tolerance, emotional stability, attention, and adaptability in autism, with secondary improvements in language use and social engagement.
Chronic stress exposure and post-traumatic stress disorder are associated with sustained autonomic imbalance, reduced parasympathetic tone, and persistent low-grade inflammation.
Paigen (high-fat, atherogenic) diet feeding in Mdr2−/− mice enriched Staphylococcus, Bacteroides, and Akkermansia in the gut while reducing commensal Lactobacillus compared to control diet.
Paigen diet feeding increased intestinal (gut) barrier permeability in Mdr2−/− mice, correlating with the observed gut dysbiosis.

Small numbers of Staphylococcus xylosus, S. sciuri, and Enterococcus faecalis were isolated from the brains of Paigen diet-fed Mdr2−/− mice, but not from blood, meninges, or CSF, ruling out meningitis.
Bacteria including S. xylosus were isolated from the cervical vagus nerve but not from the spinal cord of Paigen diet-fed Mdr2−/− mice, indicating specific vagal localization.
Unilateral right cervical vagotomy reduced brain bacterial CFU by ~20-fold in Paigen diet-fed Mdr2−/− mice compared to sham controls, and a third had no detectable brain bacteria.

Whole genome sequencing showed that S. xylosus, S. sciuri, and E. faecalis isolates from the brain were nearly identical (~99.998% average nucleotide identity) to isolates from the feces and ileum of the same mouse, confirming a common gut origin.

Antibiotic treatment during Paigen diet feeding shifted the enriched gut bacterium from Staphylococcus species to Paenibacillus cineris, which correspondingly became the predominant species found in the brain instead of Staphylococcus.

Wild-type C57BL/6 mice fed Paigen diet also showed enrichment of S. xylosus and E. faecalis in feces/ileum and detectable translocation of these bacteria to the brain, extending the phenomenon beyond the Mdr2−/− model.

In wild-type B6 mice, unilateral right cervical vagotomy reduced the proportion of mice with detectable brain bacteria (47% vs 75% in sham) and reduced bacterial levels ~3-4-fold in those still positive.

In a kinetic study of B6 mice fed Paigen diet, bacteria appeared in the vagus nerve at days 2-4 before first being detected in the brain at day 6, temporally supporting the vagus nerve as the conduit for translocation.

Paigen diet-fed B6 mice showed disruption of the ileal mucosal lining with an approximately two-fold reduction in goblet cells per crypt/villus compared to control diet, providing a mechanistic basis for increased gut permeability.

Exogenously gavaged, barcode-marked Enterobacter cloacae (strain JC96) was cultured from the brains of 40% of antibiotic-treated, Paigen diet-fed mice, with the specific barcode confirmed in brain isolates, directly demonstrating gut-to-brain translocation.

In germ-free mice monocolonized with E. cloacae, bacterial translocation to the vagus nerve and brain occurred only when mice were also fed Paigen diet (which increased gut permeability), not when fed control diet despite equal gut colonization, showing intestinal colonization alone is insufficient without barrier permeability.

Droplet digital PCR specifically detected the barcoded JC96 Enterobacter DNA in brain samples of colonized, Paigen diet-fed Mdr2−/− mice, corroborating culture-based detection with molecular evidence, while control diet and negative-strain samples were negative.

Reversion from Paigen diet back to control diet reduced intestinal barrier permeability roughly four-fold and reduced brain bacterial detection to below detectable limits in most mice, showing that bacterial brain localization is a reversible process.

Without dietary intervention, mouse models of Alzheimer's (APP/PS1), Parkinson's (LRRK2), and autism spectrum disorder (BTBR) all exhibited altered gut microbiome composition and increased intestinal barrier permeability compared to wild-type mice, along with detectable bacterial translocation to the brain and vagus nerve.

BTBR mice, a genetic model of autism spectrum disorder, showed broad gut bacterial enrichment (Firmicutes, Lachnospiraceae, Corynebacterium, Anaeroplasma, and other taxa) compared to wild-type B6 mice, alongside increased gut barrier permeability and bacterial translocation to the brain and vagus nerve, with translocated bacteria matching those found in the gut.

Dose-dependent DSS-induced gut permeability revealed a threshold effect: low-dose (1%) DSS caused bacterial translocation to the brain without bacteremia, while high-dose (5%) DSS caused much greater permeability, resulting in both bacteremia and a >10-fold increase in brain bacterial recovery.

Despite bacterial translocation to the brain in all models studied (diet-induced and Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and autism models), blood-brain barrier permeability was not increased compared to controls, indicating translocation occurs independently of BBB breakdown.
Myhre syndrome is caused by recurrent heterozygous gain-of-function variants in SMAD4, a key regulator of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix homeostasis.

MYHRS presents with a progressive fibrotic phenotype affecting the skeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and integumentary systems, including short stature, joint contractures, cardiac valve defects, subglottic stenosis, and skin thickening.
Neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder, may occur in individuals with Myhre Syndrome.
Despite carrying recurrent, similar pathogenic mutations, individuals with MYHRS exhibit significant phenotypic variability.
Current management of MYHRS is symptomatic only, and no disease-modifying therapies are currently available.
Individuals with Myhre Syndrome commonly present with short stature, joint contractures, and skin thickening as part of the multisystem fibrotic phenotype.
Cardiac valve defects and subglottic stenosis are recognized features of the Myhre Syndrome fibrotic phenotype affecting the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.
Despite the recurrent nature of the causative SMAD4 variants, individuals with Myhre Syndrome show significant phenotypic variability.
The authors identify unmet needs regarding clinical and biochemical endpoints critical for evaluating future disease-modifying therapies in Myhre Syndrome.
Adolescents with acute EBV infection had significantly higher preinfection hair cortisol levels than age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
Hair cortisol levels in EBV-infected adolescents were significantly lower at six months postinfection compared to their own preinfection levels.
During acute EBV infection, there was a non-significant trend toward a positive association between preinfection hair cortisol and concurrent fatigue.
At six months postinfection, the association between preinfection hair cortisol and fatigue became significantly negative.
No association was found between hair cortisol and fatigue among healthy controls.
Preinfection hair cortisol concentration did not predict chronic fatigue at six months after acute EBV infection.

The shift from a positive to a negative association between hair cortisol and fatigue over time suggests HPA-axis alterations are more likely a consequence rather than a cause of chronic fatigue following EBV infection.
MA30-infected mice had a 40% mortality rate compared to 0% mortality in PR8-infected mice, though both groups showed similar ~20% acute weight loss with recovery to 90-95% baseline by 28 DPI.
In MA30 infection, male mice showed significantly greater body weight loss and higher mortality than female mice.
PR8 (influenza) infection showed no sex difference in body weight loss or survival between male and female mice.
Viral RNA became undetectable by qPCR at 14-28 DPI in both MA30- and PR8-infected lungs, but IHC showed low-level viral antigen persistence up to 28 DPI.
Both MA30- and PR8-infected lungs showed widespread, persistent immune cell infiltration on H&E staining through 28 DPI, indicating unresolved inflammation beyond the acute phase.
Both MA30 and PR8 infections induced ongoing collagen deposition and fibrotic remodeling in the lung interstitium at 14, 21, and 28 DPI with no evidence of resolution.
KRT5+ progenitor cell migration and pod-structure formation in consolidated lung regions occurred in PR8-infected mice but was absent in MA30-infected mice at 14, 21, and 28 DPI.

At 21 DPI, MA30-infected lungs showed upregulated complement genes (C1qa, C1qb, C1qc, C6, C3ar1), coagulation factors (Fga, Fgg, Alb), and pro-inflammatory markers (Cxcl10, Tnf) compared to non-infected mice.

At 21 DPI, PR8-infected lungs showed upregulated interferon-responsive genes (Ifit1, Stat1, Ifng, Irf7), epithelial regeneration markers (Krt5, Krt15, Krt4), and pro-inflammatory chemokines compared to non-infected mice.

Pathway analysis of subchronic (21 DPI) MA30-infected lungs showed upregulation of complement/coagulation, ECM receptor interaction, chemokine, cytokine, and PPAR signaling pathways, with downregulation of tight junction signaling suggesting epithelial barrier dysfunction.

Pathway analysis of subchronic (21 DPI) PR8-infected lungs showed upregulated cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, IFN gamma/beta, ECM regulation, and TLR signaling pathways with downregulated muscle contraction and PPAR signaling.

A micro-choice based concentrated rehabilitation program did not significantly change the proportion of patients reporting no anxiety/depression problems on EQ-5D-5L.
A micro-choice based concentrated rehabilitation program significantly improved overall quality of life on EQ-5D-5L index scores.
Enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) significantly reduced fatigue as measured by PROMIS fatigue score.
Enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) significantly improved disease-specific quality of life on SAQ-QOL.
A subset of EECP-treated patients self-reported improved cognition (memory, focus, concentration/brain fog).
Pooled meta-analysis across five studies showed a statistically significant moderate effect of non-pharmacological interventions on reducing mental health symptoms in AYA long COVID.
Pooled meta-analysis across three studies showed a large but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on reducing fatigue in AYA long COVID.
Pooled meta-analysis across three studies showed a substantial but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on improving quality of life in AYA long COVID.
Pooled meta-analysis across three studies showed a large but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on reducing cognitive difficulties in AYA long COVID.

In a waitlist-controlled before-after study, a micro-choice based concentrated group rehabilitation program significantly improved overall quality of life in young adults with long COVID as measured by the EQ-5D-5L index score.
Enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) significantly reduced fatigue in long COVID patients as measured by the PROMIS fatigue score compared to baseline.
EECP treatment was associated with improved quality of life scores in long COVID patients as measured by the Seattle Angina Questionnaire-Quality of Life scale.
A subset of long COVID patients treated with EECP self-reported improved cognition, including memory recall, focus, and concentration, often described as brain fog.
A pooled meta-analysis of five studies found a statistically significant moderate effect of non-pharmacological interventions in reducing mental health symptoms in AYA with long COVID.
A pooled meta-analysis of three studies found a large but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on reducing fatigue in AYA with long COVID.
A pooled meta-analysis of three studies found a substantial but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on improving quality of life in AYA with long COVID.
A pooled meta-analysis of three studies found a large but statistically non-significant effect of non-pharmacological interventions on reducing cognitive difficulties in AYA with long COVID.
Hair loss was more commonly reported after wave 2 community-diagnosed COVID-19 compared with matched comparators without COVID-19.
Mobility impairment was significantly more common after wave 2 COVID-19 and its increased reporting persisted at 6-12 months.
Fatigue was significantly more common after wave 2 COVID-19 and its increased reporting persisted at 6-12 months.
Cognitive impairment was significantly more common after wave 2 COVID-19 and its increased reporting persisted at 6-12 months.
Loss of taste or smell was significantly more common after wave 2 COVID-19 compared with matched comparators.
New prescriptions for NSAIDs were modestly more common in the year after community-diagnosed COVID-19 (wave 2) compared with matched comparators.
New prescriptions for drugs to treat infections were modestly increased after community-diagnosed COVID-19 (wave 2) compared with matched comparators.
New prescriptions for musculoskeletal problem treatments were modestly increased after community-diagnosed COVID-19 (wave 2) compared with matched comparators.

Elevated reporting of mobility impairment, fatigue and cognitive impairment persisted 6-12 months after community-diagnosed COVID-19 compared with matched comparators, unlike other symptoms which resolved earlier.

Associations between COVID-19 and long-COVID symptoms/prescribing were generally weaker in the later wave 4 cohort (Omicron era) than in the earlier wave 2 cohort, suggesting reduced long-COVID burden with less severe illness.
Among 3,155 Brazilian nurses with confirmed COVID-19, 60.9% reported symptoms persisting for four weeks or longer after diagnosis.
Self-reported memory loss was the strongest independent predictor of symptom persistence four weeks or longer after COVID-19 diagnosis among Brazilian nurses.
Self-reported fatigue was independently associated with higher odds of symptom persistence for four weeks or more after COVID-19 diagnosis.
Dyspnea was significantly associated with higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence.
Palpitations were significantly associated with higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence, potentially reflecting autonomic dysregulation.
Loss of smell (anosmia) was positively associated with long COVID symptom persistence.
Self-reported anxiety was independently associated with symptom persistence, possibly via prolonged neuroinflammatory activation and psychological burden of fatigue/cognitive impairment.
Hair loss was independently associated with higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence.
Presence of a pre-existing chronic disease was associated with significantly higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence in nurses.
Absence of chronic disease was protectively associated with lower odds of long COVID symptom persistence.
Obesity was significantly associated with higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence, potentially via chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation.
Rhinitis was significantly associated with higher odds of long COVID symptom persistence, possibly reflecting predisposition to heightened inflammatory/allergic responses.
Need for oxygen therapy during the acute phase of COVID-19 was the strongest clinical predictor of symptom persistence for four weeks or longer.

Among nurses with persistent COVID-19 symptoms, fatigue (70.0%) and memory loss (68.8%) were the most frequently reported, followed by anxiety, hair loss, cough, insomnia, loss of smell, loss of taste, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia and depression at progressively lower frequencies.

A neurocognitive-psychological symptom cluster (memory loss, fatigue, anxiety, cough, hair loss) showed strong pairwise co-occurrence by Jaccard index, suggesting a shared underlying process such as neuroinflammation.
A cardiorespiratory symptom cluster (tachycardia, palpitations, dyspnea, depression) showed strong pairwise co-occurrence, suggesting shared autonomic/cardiovascular involvement in long COVID.
A chemosensory/sleep symptom cluster (loss of taste, loss of smell, insomnia) showed strong pairwise co-occurrence in nurses with persistent post-COVID symptoms.
Among 1052 surviving COVID-19 hospitalized patients followed up approximately three years post-infection, 14.25% reported developing a new disease after initial COVID-19 infection.
51 patients (4.85%) of the surviving cohort were still undergoing treatment for post-COVID-19-related illness at the time of follow-up.
COVID-19 vaccination status was not significantly associated with the development of new post-COVID-19 disease.
COVID-19 vaccination dose status was not significantly associated with ongoing treatment for post-COVID-19 symptoms.
Lung disease was the most frequently reported new post-COVID condition among survivors three years after infection.
Chronic body pain was the second most common new post-COVID condition reported by survivors.
Coronary artery disease/angioplasty was newly reported in 1.61% of survivors following COVID-19 hospitalization.
New diabetes mellitus diagnosis was reported in 1.61% of survivors following COVID-19 hospitalization.
Hypertension was newly reported in 1.52% of survivors following COVID-19 hospitalization.
General fatigue was reported as a new post-COVID complication in 1.24% of survivors.
Mortality was slightly higher among females than males in this hospitalized COVID-19 cohort, but the difference was not statistically significant.
17.0% of participants reported at least one hospital follow-up visit during post-COVID recovery, indicating modest healthcare utilization among long COVID survivors.
SARS-CoV-2 spike S1, RBD, and nucleocapsid IgG antibody levels were significantly higher in LTCS patients than in healthy controls.
No significant difference in SARS-CoV-2-specific antibody levels was found between LTCS and convalescent (CONV) individuals.
Plasma IL-10 was markedly decreased in LTCS patients compared with both healthy controls and convalescent individuals.
IFN-γ was significantly downregulated in LTCS patients relative to healthy controls and convalescent individuals.
TNF-α was significantly downregulated in LTCS patients relative to healthy controls and convalescent individuals.
IL-6 was significantly downregulated in LTCS patients relative to healthy controls and convalescent individuals.
