IL-8 (CXCL8) was significantly downregulated in LTCS patients relative to healthy controls and convalescent individuals.
IL-1RA was significantly increased in LTCS compared with convalescent individuals.
IL-7 was significantly decreased in LTCS compared with healthy controls, but not with convalescent individuals.
IP-10 (CXCL10) was significantly reduced in LTCS compared with convalescent individuals.
IFN-α2 tended to be lower in LTCS compared with healthy controls, but this did not reach statistical significance.
No significant differences were observed across groups for G-CSF, MCP-1 (CCL2), MIP-1α (CCL3), or IL-2.
CD56+CD16+ classical NK cells were significantly reduced in LTCS patients compared with healthy controls by flow cytometry, with no difference vs convalescent individuals.
CD56+CD3+ NKT cells were significantly reduced in LTCS patients compared with healthy controls, with no difference vs convalescent individuals.
CD16-CD14- myeloid monocytes were significantly decreased in LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals.
The frequency of CD3+ T cells was significantly increased in LTCS patients relative to healthy controls.
Activated memory CD4+CD38+CCR7+ T cells were significantly elevated in convalescent participants compared with healthy controls, but not in LTCS.
Activated CD8+CD38+CCR7+ and CD8+HLA-DR+CCR7+ T cells were significantly reduced in convalescent participants compared with healthy controls.
Single-cell RNA-seq showed that NK I cells (cluster C4) were significantly reduced in LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals.
CD4-CD8- double-negative T cells (cluster C6) were significantly increased in LTCS patients compared with healthy controls.
Memory B cells (cluster C16) were significantly increased in LTCS patients compared with healthy controls.
Intermediate B cells (cluster C21) showed a non-significant decrease in LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals.

Differential expression analysis of NK cells identified 455 significantly altered genes in LTCS compared with convalescent individuals, with 115 genes (25%) upregulated and 340 genes (75%) downregulated.
PDCD4 was significantly upregulated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals, and has been linked to impaired autophagy in Parkinson's disease models.
CHD1 was significantly upregulated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals, and has been linked to IL-6 transcription and myeloid-derived suppressor cell recruitment.
CXCR4 was significantly upregulated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals, potentially reflecting tissue trafficking.

Among 114 LTCS patients, the most common reported symptoms were dyspnea (55%) and fatigue (54%), followed by dizziness, ageusia, headache, neuropathy, anosmia, anxiety, and myalgia, while diarrhea and sleep disturbances were rare.
Gender-specific analysis of the LTCS cohort showed that concentration deficits, anosmia, and ageusia were more common in men, whereas headache was more common in women.
Flow cytometry validation showed no significant difference in perforin and granzyme B protein levels in NK cells between LTCS patients and healthy controls.
The frequency of TNF-α-producing NK cells was reduced in LTCS patients, supporting functional impairment of NK-cell cytokine production at the protein level.

NK cells from LTCS patients showed downregulated pathways related to olfactory receptor activity, chemical stimulus detection, fatty acid elongation, and saturated fatty acid metabolism when compared with healthy controls.
Pathways involving histone H3K9me/H3K9me2 demethylase activity and circadian regulation of translation were activated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with healthy controls.
Genes involved in muscle cell projection—PLEKHO1, ARPC2, and ARPC1A—were significantly upregulated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals.
Circadian translation regulatory genes CLOCK, HNRNPD, RBM4, PER1, and PER2 were upregulated in NK cells of LTCS patients compared with convalescent individuals.

CXCR4, CXCR5, and CCR6 chemokine receptors, previously reported as enriched in SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells, were also highly expressed in NK cells from the LTCS cohort, suggesting potential NK-cell trafficking from blood to inflamed tissues.
The LTCS cohort was disproportionately female (60% women, 40% men), consistent with previously reported epidemiological trends in long COVID.
Correlation analysis in LTCS patients showed that histidine and glutamine were uniquely associated primarily with pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Triglycerides and apolipoproteins Apo-A1 and Apo-A2 in LTCS patients showed alterations resembling those seen in acute COVID-19 compared with healthy controls.
LTCS and acute COVID-19 patients were distinguished by differing phenylalanine, 3-hydroxybutyrate, and glucose concentrations, pointing to imbalanced energy metabolism in long COVID.

The authors link their observed reduction in IFN-α2 and IFN-γ in LTCS patients to a proposed mechanism whereby viral RNA-driven type I interferon activity reduces serotonin production, potentially contributing to cognitive impairment.

Clarithromycin (CAM) 800 mg/day or 400 mg/day for 7 days did not significantly improve the primary endpoint of overall symptom severity score compared with standard care, though CAM 800 mg/day showed a nonsignificant trend toward earlier symptom resolution.
CAM 800 mg/day led to significantly earlier improvement in fatigue severity compared with the control group.
Serum G-CSF showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 4.
Serum IL-15 showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 8.
Serum TGF-α showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 8.
Serum FGF-2 showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 14.
Serum IL-7 showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 14; IL-7 has been proposed as a marker of immune recovery in critical COVID-19.
Serum TNF-α showed a significantly greater reduction from baseline in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls at day 14.
Nasal IL-8 levels decreased significantly in both the CAM 800 mg/day group (days 4 and 14) and CAM 400 mg/day group (days 4, 8, and 14) compared with controls.
Nasal IFN-γ decreased significantly in the CAM 800 mg/day group at day 4 and in the CAM 400 mg/day group at day 8 compared with controls.
Serum IgA levels at day 8 were significantly higher in controls than in the CAM 800 mg/day group, indicating lower IgA responses with CAM treatment.
Serum IgG levels at days 4 and 14 were significantly higher in controls than in the CAM 400 mg/day group.

At day 4, the control group showed a significantly larger percentage reduction in nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load than either CAM 800 mg/day or CAM 400 mg/day groups, suggesting CAM did not accelerate (and may have slowed) viral clearance.
Prothrombin time increased significantly more from day 1 to day 14 in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls.
eGFR (creatinine-based) increased significantly more from day 1 to day 14 in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls.
Blood sugar levels increased significantly more from day 1 to day 8 in the CAM 800 mg/day group than in controls.

No COVID-19 disease progression occurred in either CAM-treated group, whereas two control-group patients (11.8%) experienced progression (hypoxemia in one, systemic inflammation exacerbation in another); however, gastrointestinal and liver-related adverse events occurred exclusively in the CAM 800 mg/day group, with no AE deemed causally related to CAM and no deaths in any group.
Incidence of oxygen requirement during the clinical course was numerically lower in the CAM 400 mg/day group than in controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Chest radiography scores improved (decreased) in all three groups over the study period, with no significant between-group differences at any time point.
VPA-induced ASD-like rats showed significant spatial learning and memory deficits in the Morris water maze compared to control rats.
Six weeks of voluntary wheel running exercise improved spatial learning and memory in VPA rats, shortening escape latency and increasing platform crossings and target-quadrant time/distance.
VPA rats exhibited significantly prolonged self-grooming duration and increased marble-burying compared to controls, indicating heightened repetitive/stereotypic behavior.
Voluntary wheel running exercise substantially reduced grooming duration and the number of buried marbles in VPA rats.
VPA rats showed reduced spontaneous locomotion and reduced central-zone exploration in the open field test compared to controls, indicating impaired exploratory behavior and anxiety-like phenotype.
In the three-chamber test, VPA rats showed impaired sociability (preferring the empty cage over Stranger 1) and defective social novelty recognition compared to controls.
Voluntary exercise significantly ameliorated sociability deficits and social novelty recognition impairments in VPA rats.
Beta-diversity analysis showed VPA rats had a distinct gut microbiota structure from controls, and exercise shifted the VPA-EX microbiota toward a CONN-like configuration.

At the genus level, VPA rats showed elevated Ligilactobacillus and reduced Alloprevotella and Romboutsia relative to controls; exercise partially normalized these taxa and increased beneficial Lactobacillus.

VPA rats had markedly reduced fecal and plasma short-chain fatty acids (acetate, butyrate, caproate, isocaproate, and total SCFAs) compared to controls; exercise restored these to near-control levels, with the most pronounced increase in butyrate.
Exercise-induced elevations in fecal/plasma butyric, caproic, and isocaproic acids correlated with reduced marble-burying and improved social contact time in VPA rats.

Hippocampal neuroactive substances including betaine aldehyde chloride, leucine, methionine, threonine, tyramine, tyrosine, and glutathione were reduced, while 3-hydroxybutyric acid was elevated in VPA rats versus controls; exercise broadly modulated these levels.

In the prefrontal cortex, VPA rats showed elevated glycine, ethanolamine, epinephrine, dopamine, 3-hydroxybutyric acid, 5-HTP, 5-HIAA, choline, aspartic acid, tyramine, xanthurenic acid, and kynurenine compared to controls; exercise significantly reduced most of these.

VPA rats showed increased Iba1+ microglia and M1 (iNOS+/Iba1+) polarization with reduced M2 (Arg-1+/Iba1+) polarization in hippocampus and PFC compared to controls; exercise attenuated microglial reactivity and shifted polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype.

VPA rats showed increased GFAP+ astrocyte reactivity and reduced NeuN fluorescence (neuronal marker) in hippocampal subregions and PFC compared to controls; exercise reduced GFAP+ cells and partially restored NeuN in DG and PFC.
Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy abolished the exercise-induced improvements in spatial memory, repetitive behaviors, locomotion/exploration, and sociability seen in sham-operated exercised VPA rats.

Vagotomy blocked exercise's ability to reduce pro-inflammatory microglial polarization (iNOS+/Iba1+), increase anti-inflammatory Arg-1+/Iba1+ cells, reduce GFAP+ astrocyte reactivity, and restore NeuN neuronal integrity, whereas sham-operated exercised rats showed these benefits.

Exercise-mediated restoration of fecal and plasma SCFAs (acetate, butyrate, caproate, isocaproate) persisted even after vagotomy, indicating this SCFA elevation is largely vagus-independent; however, this SCFA restoration was not associated with behavioral improvement in vagotomized rats.

Vagotomy blunted exercise-induced normalization of hippocampal and prefrontal neuroactive substances, with the PFC showing more pronounced blunting (no significant changes in VPA-SDV-EX vs VPA) than the hippocampus.

Elevated iNOS levels in hippocampus and PFC were negatively correlated with social interaction time with unfamiliar rats, and NeuN expression was positively correlated with spatial memory performance (target quadrant duration).
Hippocampal glutamic acid levels were negatively correlated with the number of buried marbles, suggesting reduced glutamatergic signaling may underlie increased stereotypic behavior in VPA rats.

LEfSe analysis identified Lactobacillus murinus as the top discriminative biomarker of the VPA group gut microbiota (26 dominant biomarkers), while Romboutsia was the top biomarker in controls and exercise induced a distinct 5-taxon signature dominated by Bacteroides acidifaciens.
Youth with MDD showed a smaller heart rate increase in response to the Trier Social Stress Test compared to healthy controls.
Youth with MDD exhibited a blunted parasympathetic stress response, shown as a smaller increase in RespHRV during the TSST compared to healthy controls.
Youth with MDD showed a blunted sympathetic stress response, indicated by a smaller reduction in PEP during the TSST compared to healthy controls.
Youth with MDD reported higher levels of psychological stress in response to the psychosocial stress task than healthy controls, despite showing blunted physiological ANS responses.
No effects of sex were found on ANS stress reactivity differences between MDD and healthy control youth.
Depression showed the highest one-step expected influence (centrality) of all nodes in the long COVID symptom network.
Cardiologic/respiratory symptoms showed the second-highest node centrality in the network, after depression.
Anxiety showed the third-highest node centrality in the long COVID symptom network.

Cardiologic/respiratory symptoms, neurological symptoms, and depression showed the highest bridge expected influence, indicating they connect the physical and psychological symptom clusters in the network.
Depression showed its strongest association among all physical symptom domains with neurological symptoms, such that higher depression levels were linked to greater neurological symptom severity.
Lack of self-efficacy showed moderate associations with anxiety and COVID-19-related traumatic stress within the network.
Female gender was positively associated with gastrointestinal symptom severity in the long COVID network.
Higher age was associated with more pronounced cardiologic and respiratory symptoms in the network.
Sensory symptoms occupied a peripheral position in the network, showing only weak associations with neurological symptoms and depression.
Psychological and physical symptoms in long COVID are not isolated but form a closely interconnected, integrated symptom system, with cohesive physical and psychological symptom clusters.

Depression is highly prevalent in long COVID, affecting up to 13% of individuals across post-acute stages, and is associated with greater symptom-related impairment, according to cited prior meta-analytic and cohort data.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher incidence of subacute thyroiditis than the general population, with the hazard ratio increasing over time.
SAT risk after COVID-19 was greater in hospitalized patients than in outpatients, suggesting a severity-dependent effect.
A cohort study found a 6.8% incidence of SAT within three months of COVID-19 recovery, with painless SAT presenting earlier and more severely than painful SAT.
Painless SAT patients had higher CRP, IL-6, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratios, and lower lymphocyte counts, than painful SAT patients following COVID-19.

A case series of 10 post-COVID thyroid dysfunction patients proposed cytokine release syndrome and immune hyperactivity as mechanisms, noting a possible biphasic pattern occurring during acute infection and recovery.
Among 204 COVID-19 survivors, 43 had abnormal thyroid function tests including 13 with subclinical thyrotoxicosis during acute infection, of whom 3 persisted at 3-month follow-up.
In a prospective cohort of 29 patients with COVID-19-related thyrotoxicosis, most became euthyroid over follow-up while thyroid hypoecogenicity on ultrasound correlated with higher TSH levels.
Hyperthyroidism, including subclinical forms, was reported in 23 post-COVID cases, with one cohort finding subclinical hyperthyroidism in 12.3% of COVID-19 patients.
Graves' disease was reported in 6 patients across 5 studies following COVID-19, with proposed mechanisms including molecular mimicry, B-cell activation, and cytokine-driven inflammation.
COVID-19 pneumonia patients had significantly higher TSH and significantly lower T3 levels compared with matched non-COVID-19 pneumonia patients of similar severity.

In post-reproductive women, free T4 levels were significantly higher in COVID-19 patients than in controls and asymptomatic patients, positively correlated with TNF-alpha, and persisted for at least 12 months.
A total of 147 post-COVID-19 cases of hypothyroidism were identified across the included studies, with onset typically delayed by weeks to months after recovery.
A cohort study found subclinical hypothyroidism in 60.53% of patients within 3 months of COVID-19 recovery, persisting in some beyond the acute phase.

In a cohort of 163 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, more than half had thyroid abnormalities (mostly NTIS) on admission, with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies in 8% and anti-TPO antibodies in 15.3% at baseline, new antibody positivity emerging by six months, and higher inflammatory markers/lower lymphocyte counts correlating with thyroid dysfunction.
Among children with long-COVID symptoms, 12% had thyroid autoantibodies and 7% were diagnosed with autoimmune thyroiditis by ultrasound.

A case report described a healthcare worker who developed Hashimoto's thyroiditis with elevated TSH, low free T4, and high anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibody titers six weeks after COVID-19, resolving fully with thyroid hormone replacement.
One case of central hypothyroidism following COVID-19 infection was reported, attributed to possible hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.

Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly increased free T3 levels in post-COVID-19 patients with non-thyroidal illness syndrome, correlating with improved lower extremity strength and exercise tolerance.

Thyroid follicular cells express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors at levels comparable to or higher than lung cells, and autopsy studies have confirmed SARS-CoV-2 RNA within thyroid tissue, supporting direct viral cytopathic damage to the thyroid.

Pro-inflammatory cytokines released during the COVID-19 cytokine storm, particularly IL-6, can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, leading to decreased TSH and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

Molecular mimicry, bystander activation, and epitope spreading are proposed immune mechanisms by which SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers autoimmune thyroid diseases such as Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Across the 28 included studies, 419 patients developed post-COVID-19 thyroid disorders, including 235 with elevated thyroid hormones, 173 with low thyroid hormones, and 11 with unspecified thyroid conditions.
Across the 28 included studies, a total of 80 cases of subacute thyroiditis (SAT) were reported following COVID-19 infection, including 5 painless and 6 painful cases.
The included studies reported 35 patients with thyrotoxicosis occurring either during active COVID-19 infection or after recovery.
The review identified 23 post-infection cases of hyperthyroidism, appearing often in the subacute recovery phase.
Included studies reported 85 patients with isolated high T3 and 6 patients with isolated high T4 post-COVID-19, without always clarifying the underlying diagnosis.
147 post-infection cases of hypothyroidism (including Hashimoto's disease) were identified across the included literature, typically with delayed onset weeks to months after recovery.

Graves' disease was reported in six post-COVID cases across five studies, with pathogenesis involving thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins binding the TSH receptor and possible triggering by molecular mimicry, B-cell activation, and cytokine-driven inflammation.

Malik et al. found that patients with COVID-19 pneumonia had significantly higher TSH levels and significantly lower T3 levels than non-COVID-19 pneumonia patients of similar severity, and sick euthyroidism was not observed in the COVID-19 cohort.

Semenova et al. found that free T4 levels correlated positively with TNF-α levels in post-reproductive women 12 months after moderate COVID-19, with fT4 remaining significantly higher than in controls and asymptomatic patients.
Adhikari and Singh found subclinical hypothyroidism in 60.53% of patients within 3 months of COVID-19 recovery, with elevated TSH and normal T3/T4 persisting in some beyond the acute phase.

In the Alphan Uc cohort of 163 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, more than half had thyroid abnormalities on admission (most commonly NTIS), anti-thyroid antibodies were present in 8% (anti-Tg) and 15.3% (anti-TPO), with new antibody positivity developing in some patients by six months, and higher inflammatory markers and lower lymphocyte counts correlated with thyroid dysfunction.

Feghali et al. reported a 38-year-old healthcare worker who developed hypothyroid symptoms and thyroid enlargement six weeks after COVID-19, with severely elevated TSH, low free T4, and high titers of anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; histology confirmed autoimmune thyroiditis, and hormone replacement led to full resolution.
Garai et al. found that 12% of children with long-COVID symptoms had thyroid autoantibodies, and 7% were diagnosed with autoimmune thyroiditis by ultrasound.

Bhatt et al. described a case of autoimmune thyroiditis occurring within the context of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in adults (MIS-A), indicating post-infectious immune activation may target the thyroid as part of a broader inflammatory response.

Croce et al. found that post-COVID inpatients undergoing pulmonary rehabilitation showed a significant increase in free T3 levels after 3 months, correlated with improved lower extremity strength and exercise tolerance, suggesting rehabilitation helps reverse non-thyroidal illness syndrome.

Elhadd et al. reported one case of central hypothyroidism among 10 cases of post-COVID thyroid dysfunction in Qatar, suggesting a possible biphasic pattern of thyroid dysfunction occurring during both acute infection and recovery.
Burekovic et al. described a 38-year-old patient who developed new-onset hypothyroidism six weeks after COVID-19 recovery, illustrating delayed-onset disease in a previously healthy individual.

Thyroid follicular cells express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 at levels comparable to or higher than lung cells, and autopsy studies have confirmed SARS-CoV-2 RNA within thyroid tissue, supporting a mechanism of direct cytopathic viral damage to the thyroid.

The cytokine storm of severe COVID-19 releases high levels of IL-6, which can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, decreasing TSH and impairing peripheral conversion of T4 to T3; historical SARS 2003 data showed apoptosis of anterior pituitary TSH-producing cells, suggesting coronaviruses can cause central endocrine disruption.

COVID-19-related widespread endothelial dysfunction, microvascular thrombosis, and coagulopathy can impair perfusion of the thyroid gland, potentially leading to ischemic injury and contributing to glandular dysfunction, particularly during severe systemic illness.
Polymorphisms in the SOD2 gene were associated with long COVID disease progression in a clinically confirmed cohort of patients with mild or asymptomatic acute infection.
Polymorphisms in the EPHX1 gene were associated with long COVID disease progression in patients with mild or asymptomatic acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Polymorphisms in GSTP1, SELENOS, and CAT genes did not show the same significant association with long COVID progression as SOD2 and EPHX1.
Pre-existing thyroid disease was identified as a significant aggravating factor for long COVID disease progression.
Acute-phase symptom severity during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection was a significant aggravating factor for developing long COVID.
A machine learning analysis combining genetic and clinical data produced a 10-factor predictive model for long COVID with balanced accuracy over 0.74, released as an open-access risk rating webtool.
The authors argue that antioxidant genetic capacity plays a role in long COVID consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction and viral persistence hypotheses.
Urinary levels of the bacteria-derived metabolite 4-hydroxyphenylpropionic acid (HPHPA) were significantly elevated in Long COVID patients.
The bacteria-derived metabolite tryptamine was significantly elevated in urine of Long COVID patients.

Hippuric acid emerged as a unique urinary metabolite marker that, along with other metabolite patterns, distinguished Long COVID patients from healthy controls and ME/CFS patients, with 64% of Long COVID patients showing elevation of at least one metabolite.
Long COVID patients show T cell exhaustion as part of broader immune abnormalities.
Increased neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation was identified as part of the immune abnormalities present in Long COVID.
Chronic activation of memory B cells was identified as a component of persistent immune dysfunction in Long COVID.

COVID-19 vaccination was reported to improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in patients with non-small cell lung cancer, significantly improving progression-free and overall survival in advanced stages.

A broad-spectrum receptor-binding domain vaccine candidate (M5-RBD) incorporating key SARS-CoV-2 mutation sites and a novel CpG adjuvant (HP007) induced durable T cell responses and broad-spectrum neutralizing antibodies, including against Omicron BA.2, and reduced viral replication and tissue damage in K18-hACE2 mice.
Plasma extracellular vesicles expressing CD169+ and HLA-DR+ were persistently elevated in individuals with Long COVID.

CD169+/HLA-DR+ extracellular vesicles correlated with abnormal coagulation function and elevated inflammatory markers such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, and D-dimer, particularly in medium-to-large EVs (240-500 nm and >500 nm).
Patients recovering from mild COVID-19 with ongoing dyspnea and fatigue had significantly higher plasma sCD25 levels (60-74% higher) during the 6-18 month follow-up period.
Patients reporting memory problems after mild COVID-19 showed increased plasma sLAG-3 levels during the 18-month follow-up.
A correlation between sCD25 levels and neutralizing antibody titers was identified exclusively in symptomatic Long COVID patients, not in asymptomatic recovered individuals.
The patient had markedly elevated serum autoantibodies against G protein-coupled receptors prior to treatment.
High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, combined with cognitive stimulation, was associated with normalisation of fatigue scores after the first infusion.
Neurocognitive performance returned to normal values following IVIG treatment and cognitive stimulation.
Quality of life, assessed via the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0, improved after the first IVIG infusion and fully recovered within 1 year.
The patient showed an inverted CD4 to CD8 T-cell ratio that persisted throughout follow-up despite clinical recovery.
A pathogenic CD8+ T cell-monocyte complex (cellular synapse) was identified in the patient's immunological profile before treatment.
Spontaneous IFNγ release was observed in the patient's immune cells prior to IVIG treatment.
IVIG therapy was associated with a significant reduction in pathogenic CD8+ T cell-monocyte complexes.
High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin treatment was associated with a significant reduction in the pathogenic CD8+ T cell-monocyte complexes present at baseline.
Spontaneous IFNγ production was significantly reduced following intravenous immunoglobulin therapy.
Spontaneous TNF production was significantly reduced following intravenous immunoglobulin therapy.
Markers of endothelial inflammation decreased significantly following intravenous immunoglobulin therapy.
Circulating titres of autoantibodies against G protein-coupled receptors decreased significantly following intravenous immunoglobulin therapy.
The patient also underwent a cognitive stimulation intervention in parallel with IVIG treatment, potentially contributing to the observed neurocognitive recovery.
Older adults with Long COVID showed significantly higher levels of depression compared to age-matched healthy controls.
Older adults with Long COVID showed significantly higher levels of fatigue compared to age-matched healthy controls.

In a subset of high-affinity TSPO binders, [18F]FEPPA PET imaging showed significantly higher TSPO binding (a marker of neuroinflammation) in Long COVID participants compared to healthy controls across multiple brain regions.
Among 88 patients with Long COVID symptoms, fatigue was the most prevalent complaint, reported by 67% of affected patients.

Aminopeptide nutritional supplementation was associated with a significantly higher rate of overall Long COVID symptom remission compared with controls, and multivariate regression showed an 8.46-fold increase in remission likelihood.

Aminopeptide supplementation was associated with significantly greater improvement in Long COVID-related fatigue compared with controls, with a 9.19-fold increase in fatigue improvement odds on multivariate analysis.
Peripheral blood CD3+ T cell levels significantly increased after aminopeptide treatment.
Peripheral blood CD8+ T cell levels significantly increased after aminopeptide treatment.
Fatigue was the most commonly documented condition in clinical notes, present in 85% of pediatric long-COVID patients.
Headache was documented in 75.2% of pediatric long-COVID patients' clinical notes.
Dizziness was documented in 64.5% of pediatric long-COVID patients, suggestive of autonomic dysfunction/orthostatic intolerance.
Anxiety was documented in 62.1% of pediatric long-COVID patients' clinical notes.
Abdominal pain and nausea were documented in 38.8% and 59.3% of patients respectively, indicating substantial GI symptom burden.

Pacing, an evidence-based energy/activity management technique from the ME/CFS community, was recommended to 65.9% of patients and has demonstrated effectiveness for fatigue, pain, post-exertional malaise, and brain fog.
Diet changes were the most commonly recommended intervention, given to 81.8% of patients, alongside pacing (65.9%), sleep hygiene (61.2%), and self-care/trigger point practices (46.7%).
Ondansetron was the most commonly prescribed medication, used in 35% of patients, followed by ibuprofen (29.4%) and fludrocortisone (27.6%).
Supplements recommended included multivitamins (47.7%), probiotics (36%), vitamin D (34.1%), magnesium (32.7%), and melatonin (31.8%).
Pediatric long-COVID patients reported markedly reduced (worse) fatigue scores on the PedsQL Multidimensional Fatigue Scale compared with a published healthy pediatric reference sample.
Pediatric long-COVID patients had worse (lower) PedsQL fatigue scores than published cohorts with chronic pain, active cancer treatment, type 1 diabetes, and sickle cell disease.
Pediatric long-COVID patients reported elevated PROMIS sleep disturbance and sleep-related impairment scores compared with national norms and other pediatric clinical populations.
Pediatric long-COVID patients reported elevated PROMIS anxiety and depression scores relative to national norms and comparison adolescent populations.

In a self-report symptom survey of 85 patients, the most frequently endorsed symptoms were fatigue/tiredness (89.4%), post-exertional symptom worsening (87.1%), dizziness/light-headedness (84.7%), and difficulty concentrating (82.4%).
On the PedsQL General Well-Being scale, most patients rated their health as bad or fair (63.5% combined), with only 2.4% reporting very good health.

Findings are consistent with other pediatric long-COVID studies (Gross et al; Montealegre Sanchez et al) showing worse PROMIS scores among children with clinical long-COVID/higher PASC index than uninfected peers, particularly in pain, fatigue, global health, physical functioning, cognitive functioning, and sleep disturbance.
Active taVNS (sub- or supra-threshold stimulation) did not significantly reduce fatigue severity as measured by the MFI-20 compared with sham stimulation over 4-8 weeks.
The compliance/acceptance primary endpoint was met, with mean stimulation of 236 minutes/day and at least 80% of participants achieving at least 80% (192 min) of the prescribed 4-hour daily target.
Depressive symptoms improved over time in most groups but showed no significant between-group differences attributable to active taVNS versus sham.

SF-36 domains generally improved across visits in all groups, with several intragroup improvements reaching significance, but no significant between-group (Pdiff) differences were observed between active taVNS and sham.
The post-COVID symptom score improved over time in all groups, but neither within-group changes nor between-group differences reached statistical significance.

taVNS was generally safe and well tolerated, with skin irritation and vertigo each reported by 7% of patients, tiredness by 4%, and headache, palpitation, and rhinitis each by 2%; no serious adverse events occurred.
28.9% of patients (13/45) reported contact issues with the ring electrode used for taVNS delivery, likely influenced by individual anatomical factors.
At baseline, all treatment groups had markedly worse MFI-20 fatigue scores and SF-36 quality-of-life scores compared with normative values from the general German population.
The only clinical characteristic shared across the heterogeneous long COVID fatigue cohort was a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, present in 13.3% of patients.
Consistent with known long COVID epidemiology, substantially more women (33) than men (12) were enrolled in this fatigue trial.
In adjusted (ANCOVA) analyses, neither age, sex, nor vaccination status (single vs. mixed vaccine types) significantly influenced fatigue, depression, or quality-of-life questionnaire outcomes.

Citing Townsend et al., the authors note that long COVID-related fatigue has previously been found to have no association with autonomic dysfunction or with initial COVID-19 severity/serum markers, consistent with this study's failure to find a taVNS-specific effect.

The authors note that, in contrast to their null finding in long COVID, taVNS has significantly improved fatigue in autoimmune diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus, suggesting long COVID fatigue may not share the same pathophysiology.

The overall discontinuation rate in this trial was 8.9%, higher than the 2.9% reported in previous taVNS studies, which the authors attribute to the more demanding and heterogeneous patient population.

Across the 44 patients, treatment with dipyridamole and/or L-arginine produced a statistically significant overall symptom improvement at 6 weeks, but the improvement was no longer statistically significant by 6 months.
Combination therapy with dipyridamole and L-arginine showed sustained symptom response at both 6 weeks (68.8%) and 6 months (62.5%).
Dipyridamole monotherapy showed a high early response rate (80%) at 6 weeks but markedly reduced efficacy (20%) by 6 months.
Statistical comparisons between combination therapy and monotherapy groups did not show a significant difference, which the authors attribute to limited sample sizes.

In a patient-reported outcomes subset (n=9) assessed ~2 years after treatment initiation, combination therapy was associated with the lowest symptom burden for fatigue, dyspnea, and depression, and the highest functional capacity, compared with monotherapy.

In the patient-reported outcomes subset, combination therapy with dipyridamole and L-arginine was associated with the lowest symptom burden for fatigue, dyspnea, and depression and the highest functional capacity.
Dipyridamole's antiplatelet and anti-inflammatory effects are proposed to reduce microvascular dysfunction and microthrombosis underlying Long COVID endothelitis.
L-arginine is proposed to enhance nitric oxide production, thereby supporting endothelial function and vascular homeostasis in Long COVID patients.

Both dipyridamole and L-arginine were reported to have favorable safety profiles, supporting their use as reasonable treatment options for Long COVID endothelitis in the absence of validated alternatives.
The authors propose that dipyridamole's antiplatelet and anti-inflammatory properties may reduce microvascular dysfunction and microthrombosis underlying Long COVID endothelitis.
The authors propose that L-arginine enhances nitric oxide production, supporting endothelial function and vascular homeostasis in Long COVID endothelitis.
Patients on combination dipyridamole and L-arginine therapy reported the highest functional capacity among treatment groups on patient-reported outcome surveys.

Both dipyridamole and L-arginine were reported to have favorable safety profiles, supporting their use as reasonable treatment options for Long COVID endothelitis in the absence of validated alternatives.

Among long COVID-19 patients with neuropsychological sequelae, fatigue was the most common symptom (48%), followed by headache (47%), anxiety (28%), depression (25%), psychosocial distress (20%), discomfort (20%), cognitive impairment (13%), and dizziness (10%).
Serum IL-6 protein levels (ELISA) were notably elevated in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients across headache, anxiety, cognitive, and psychological symptom domains.
Substance P (SP) protein levels were elevated in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients, higher than in asymptomatic patients, suggesting a link to complication severity.
IL-10 protein levels were less elevated than other cytokines in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients, indicating a limited anti-inflammatory response.

ELISA-measured biomarker levels (IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα, IL-10, SP) did not differ significantly by gender, age, or duration of long COVID-19, apart from slightly higher levels in males, those over 40, and shorter-duration cases.
IL-6 mRNA expression was significantly increased in both asymptomatic (7-fold) and symptomatic (6-fold) long COVID-19 patients relative to healthy controls.
IL-1β mRNA expression was increased 5-fold in asymptomatic and 4-fold in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients compared with controls.
TNFα mRNA expression was increased 11-fold in both asymptomatic and symptomatic long COVID-19 groups relative to controls.
IL-10 mRNA expression was increased 16-fold in asymptomatic and 13-fold in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients relative to controls.

TAC1 (Substance P precursor gene) mRNA expression was increased 13-fold in asymptomatic and 9-fold in symptomatic long COVID-19 patients relative to controls, reflecting escalated pain and neuroinflammatory pathways.

In the study's overall conclusion, IL-1β levels did not differ significantly across symptomatic, asymptomatic, and control groups, in contrast to significantly higher TAC1, IL-6, TNFα, and IL-10 expression in symptomatic individuals.
TNFα, IL-10, and TAC1 mRNA levels were significantly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, and eating disorders in long COVID-19 patients.

Asymptomatic long COVID-19 individuals showed moderate elevations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα alongside regulatory IL-10 and tightly controlled Substance P signaling, contrasting with more pronounced dysregulation in symptomatic patients, suggesting a controlled immune response preserving clinical wellbeing.
The study's own analysis confirmed a significant association between Substance P levels and long COVID-19 sequelae.

In initial molecular docking screening of nine FDA-approved ligands against NK1R, indacaterol showed the highest binding affinity (-8.3 kcal/mol), followed by alosetron, netupitant, and lanepitant, but subsequent molecular dynamics simulations revealed indacaterol formed the least stable NK1R complex.

Aprepitant, an FDA-approved NK1R antagonist, demonstrated the most stable NK1R binding in molecular dynamics simulations, favorable ADMET properties including blood-brain barrier permeability, and low predicted toxicity, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for long COVID-19 neuropsychological sequelae.

N-acetyl-L-tryptophan (NAT) showed stable binding to NK1R with favorable molecular dynamics and ADMET profile, and is reported to exert neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects partly through NK1R antagonism.
TNFα, IL-10, and TAC1 mRNA levels were significantly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, and eating disorders in long COVID-19 patients.
IL-10 signals through heterotetrameric IL-10RA/IL-10RB receptors, activating JAK1 and STAT2 pathways that inhibit T-cell activation, contributing to inflammation resolution in long COVID-19.

Asymptomatic long COVID-19 individuals are not immunologically inert, showing moderate elevations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα alongside regulatory IL-10 and tightly controlled SP-mediated neuroimmune signaling.
Metformin, which activates AMPK and has antiviral-like and metabolic-stabilizing effects, is reported to reduce long COVID-19 incidence by 40%-60% when given early during acute COVID-19 infection.
A phase II clinical trial found nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was not beneficial for treating long COVID-19 compared with placebo-ritonavir.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (100% oxygen) produced significant improvement in long COVID-19-related fatigue but is limited by risks of fire hazard and oxygen free radical-induced toxicity.

In a case study of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome, aprepitant produced rapid symptomatic improvement in fatigue and cognitive complaints, suggesting NK1R blockade modulates neuroimmune crosstalk without broad immunosuppression.

Preclinical ALS and Alzheimer's-like models show N-acetyl-L-tryptophan reduces neuroinflammation, improves cognitive performance, and preserves neuronal integrity, suggesting it may counteract neuronal stress and synaptic dysfunction seen in long COVID-19.
As a tryptophan derivative, N-acetyl-L-tryptophan supports neuronal rescue in neurodegenerative models, reducing neuroinflammation and cerebral edema in traumatic brain injury models.
Administration of N-acetyl-L-tryptophan in an Alzheimer's disease model improved cognitive decline and neuroinflammatory pathways.

In silico ADMET profiling predicted that both aprepitant and N-acetyl-L-tryptophan have good absorption, blood-brain barrier permeability, and low toxicity, supporting their drug-like and safety profiles.

ProTox-III toxicity screening showed aprepitant and N-acetyl-L-tryptophan had no predicted hepatotoxicity, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, immunotoxicity, or cytotoxicity, while indacaterol was predicted mutagenic and alosetron was not tested.

Biomarker (IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα, IL-10, SP) levels showed no significant differences by gender, age, or duration of long COVID-19, except for slightly higher levels in males, those over 40 years, and shorter-duration cases.

IL-6 and Substance P were notably elevated across headache, anxiety, cognitive, and psychological symptom groups, with IL-6 higher in asymptomatic cases and SP higher in symptomatic cases, linking both to complication severity.
Among five predicted binding pockets of NK1R identified via CB-docking and Fpocket, site C1 was selected as the best/primary binding pocket for docking studies.
Individuals homozygous for the GG genotype of ADIPOQ rs1501299 had about twice the risk of developing Long-COVID sequelae compared to T allele carriers.
The ADIPOQ rs1501299 GG genotype was specifically associated with an increased risk of fatigue as a Long-COVID symptom.
The association between ADIPOQ rs1501299 GG genotype and Long-COVID risk remained significant after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, comorbidities, and severity of acute infection.
The association between ADIPOQ rs1501299 GG genotype and fatigue remained significant after multivariable adjustment.
Blood adiponectin levels measured 3 months post-infection were correlated with obesity status in this cohort.
Blood adiponectin levels were correlated with the severity of the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Circulating adiponectin levels were not significantly associated with the presence of Long-COVID symptoms.
ADIPOQ rs2241766 was not significantly associated with development of Long-COVID syndrome, unlike rs1501299.
ADIPOR2 rs16928751 was not significantly associated with development of Long-COVID syndrome.
PPARA rs1800206 was not significantly associated with development of Long-COVID syndrome.
PPARG rs1801282 was not significantly associated with development of Long-COVID syndrome.
Circulating adiponectin levels measured 3 months after acute COVID-19 were correlated with obesity status.
Circulating adiponectin levels measured 3 months after acute COVID-19 were correlated with the severity of the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Adiponectin levels were not significantly correlated with Long-COVID symptoms.

In this Long-COVID cohort, obstructive sleep apnea diagnosed by polysomnography was highly prevalent, with a median AHI of 17.2 events/h and mild, moderate, and severe OSA seen in 27.4%, 24.6%, and 31.5% of patients respectively.
Objective questionnaires identified poor sleep quality and fatigue as the most prevalent persistent symptoms in the Long-COVID cohort, with daytime sleepiness being the least prevalent.
Self-reported symptoms were common in Long-COVID patients, with dyspnea, fatigue, and insomnia being the most frequently reported.
Insomnia was the only symptom that correlated with OSA severity in this Long-COVID cohort, while other objective and subjective symptoms did not correlate with OSA severity.
84.9% of the long COVID sample reported fatigue.
Cognitive difficulties were reported by 55.3%-74.3% of the long COVID sample depending on domain.
51.8% of the long COVID sample had a psychiatric history.
Over half (56.8%) of the long COVID sample expressed interest in rehabilitation psychology services, including individual (50.2%) and group (32.1%) formats.
Not having a current mental health provider was associated with greater interest in individual rehabilitation psychology services.
Greater depression symptoms were associated with increased interest in individual rehabilitation psychology services.

Interest in individual rehabilitation psychology services was associated with not having a mental health provider, greater depression and anxiety symptoms, poorer sleep, and lower cognitive functioning.
Interest in group rehabilitation psychology services was associated with a psychiatric history, greater anxiety, lower cognitive and social functioning, and better physical functioning.
Patients who experienced SARS-CoV-2 reinfection had a significantly higher proportion of abnormal fatigue at the 4-year follow-up than those who were not reinfected.
Reinfected survivors had a higher proportion of medium-to-high respiratory symptom burden (CAT score ≥10) at 4 years than non-reinfected survivors.
Reinfected survivors had a higher proportion of clinically significant depressive symptoms (HADS-D ≥8) than non-reinfected survivors at 4 years.
There was no significant difference in the proportion of clinically significant anxiety symptoms (HADS-A ≥8) between reinfected and non-reinfected survivors at 4 years.

Over one-third of the 4-year follow-up cohort experienced confirmed COVID-19 reinfection during the prespecified December 2022-April 2023 observation window, with a small subset developing pneumonia or requiring hospitalisation.
In multivariable analysis, older age was independently associated with a lower risk of reinfection.
Persistent smoking was associated with reinfection risk in univariable analysis but was not retained as an independent risk factor in the multivariable model.
Older age was an independent risk factor for abnormal fatigue at the 4-year follow-up.
Greater disease severity during the index hospitalisation was an independent risk factor for abnormal fatigue at the 4-year follow-up.
Having a tumour/cancer comorbidity was an independent risk factor for abnormal fatigue at the 4-year follow-up, with the largest effect size among identified risk factors.
Reinfection was independently associated with more than a two-fold increased risk of abnormal fatigue at the 4-year follow-up after adjusting for age, disease severity, and comorbidities.

Among survivors who did not experience reinfection, the proportion reporting sequelae declined substantially and significantly over successive follow-up years, from 57.7% at 2 years to 15% at 4 years.
The incidence of sequelae one year after reinfection was markedly lower than the incidence of sequelae one year after the initial infection.

The spectrum of acute-phase symptoms differed significantly between initial infection and reinfection, with fatigue, chest tightness, cough and shortness of breath more common during initial infection, while sore throat was more common during reinfection.

Patients with long-COVID symptoms at the 3-year follow-up showed a higher incidence of fever and myalgia during subsequent reinfection than those without prior long COVID, suggesting a heightened inflammatory response.
There was no significant difference in the overall incidence of sequelae one year after reinfection between patients with versus without long-COVID symptoms at the 3-year follow-up.
Cough was the only specific sequela that significantly increased following reinfection, and was more frequent among patients without prior long COVID than those with prior long COVID.
Across the full cohort of 395 patients, global PSQI scores improved (decreased) after completing 60-session HBOT compared to baseline.
In patients treated for long COVID, global PSQI score improved from 8.4±3.6 at baseline to 7.7±3.3 after 60-session HBOT.
In the healthy aging subgroup, global PSQI improved from 7.1±3.3 at baseline to 6.5±3.0 post-HBOT.
In the PTSD subgroup, global PSQI improved from 12.1±3.5 at baseline to 10.9±3.6 post-HBOT.
The sleep disturbances component of the PSQI improved significantly after HBOT across the full cohort.
Subjective sleep quality component of the PSQI improved significantly after HBOT.
Sleep latency component of the PSQI improved significantly after HBOT.
Daytime dysfunction component of the PSQI improved significantly after HBOT.
Mean sleep duration score remained numerically unchanged after HBOT, though a modest shift in the paired score distribution reached borderline significance.
No significant change was observed in the habitual sleep efficiency component of the PSQI after HBOT.
No significant change was observed in self-reported sleep medication use after HBOT.
Effect sizes for global PSQI improvement ranged from moderate to large across the three study populations, indicating a clinically meaningful treatment effect.

In a multivariable regression model, baseline PSQI score was the strongest independent predictor of post-treatment PSQI score, while age, sex, and treatment indication were not independently predictive after adjustment.
Among patients with elevated baseline PSQI (disturbed sleep, PSQI>5, n=332), overall sleep quality improved significantly after HBOT.
Among patients with disturbed baseline sleep, the sleep duration component significantly improved after HBOT, unlike in the full cohort.

The authors note that prior studies using shorter HBOT protocols (10 sessions) failed to demonstrate sleep improvements in long COVID and cerebral palsy, whereas longer protocols (20-40 sessions) were effective, suggesting a dose-response relationship between cumulative oxygen exposure and sleep benefit.
Children and adolescents with FXS directed their gaze less toward socially relevant information, particularly faces and eyes, compared with both the ASD and TD groups.
The attentional gap between the FXS and TD groups in implicit emotion recognition narrowed when conflicting, rather than congruent, multisensory emotional information was presented.
The FXS group showed a diminished pupillary (autonomic arousal) response to conflicting emotional information compared with the ASD group.
The FXS group showed greater difficulties with Theory of Mind compared with both the ASD and TD groups.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutation of the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, which encodes the FBN1 protein essential for extracellular matrix microfibril integrity.
FBN1 mutations disrupt sequestration of TGF-β, promoting aberrant tissue remodeling in the aortic media in Marfan syndrome.

The patient's clinical findings yielded a systemic score of 8 points on the revised Ghent nosology, above the threshold of 7, providing definitive clinical confirmation of Marfan syndrome in the absence of genetic testing.

Physical examination revealed positive Steinberg (thumb) and Walker-Murdoch (wrist) signs along with extreme ligamentous laxity, classic external manifestations of the systemic connective tissue laxity in Marfan syndrome.
Echocardiography and CT angiography demonstrated severe aneurysmal dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta with complete loss of the sinotubular junction.

Severe aortic regurgitation was documented, with a central jet occupying 68% of the left ventricular outflow tract and multiple severity markers, secondary to aortic root dilation and loss of coaptation.
An 11 mm ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunt was incidentally detected on echocardiography in this patient with Marfan syndrome.
The patient showed reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% with generalized hypokinesia and increased end-diastolic/systolic diameters, indicating significant LV remodeling.

The authors describe a 'double impact' phenomenon whereby concurrent severe aortic regurgitation (left ventricular overload) and an ASD (right ventricular/pulmonary overload) synergistically worsened biventricular cardiac remodeling in this young Marfan patient.

The patient underwent a Bentall-Bono procedure with mechanical valved conduit replacement of the aortic root and coronary reimplantation, combined with surgical closure of the ASD using a pericardial patch due to friable atrial tissue.

Following surgery the patient improved clinically from NYHA class IV to NYHA class II, with resolution of congestion and independent performance of activities of daily living, indicating functional/hemodynamic recovery.

The authors note that in Marfan syndrome, FBN1 deficiency makes the atrial septum prone to distension, and percutaneous ASD closure devices carry reported risk of tissue erosion or device migration due to lack of firm tissue anchorage, making surgical closure the safer option.
The insular cortex receives interoceptive input and is anatomically connected with sensory, limbic, and autonomic systems, positioning it to integrate bodily signals with social cognition.
Oxytocin receptors (OXTR) are expressed in the insular cortex in rodents.

Neuroimaging studies in individuals with autism spectrum disorder report atypical insular cortex activity during social and affective tasks, with some studies showing increased and others reduced or context-dependent engagement.
Several studies report lower peripheral oxytocin levels in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, though the relation to central OXT signaling is unclear.
Insular cortex activity increases both when individuals experience pain themselves and when they observe others in pain.
Lesions of the insular cortex reduce sensitivity to others' pain, supporting a causal role in empathy for pain.
The insular cortex is activated during facial expression imitation and during both experience and observation of disgust.
Electrical stimulation of the insular cortex can induce affiliative behaviors in rhesus monkeys, indicating a causal role in social affiliation.
The insular cortex is required for emotion recognition and for detecting conspecifics undergoing inflammatory states in rodents.
Both excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons, including parvalbumin-positive and VIP-positive interneurons, respond to social cues in the mouse insular cortex.
Repeated interactions with the same conspecific reduce the proportion of IC 'social cells' that respond to social interaction, suggesting IC encoding of familiarity.

Suppression of insular cortex activity impairs the ability of mice to discriminate between novel and familiar conspecifics, though it does not strongly affect baseline novel-object vs conspecific preference.
After social isolation, manipulation of insular cortex neurons markedly reduces social approach behavior, indicating a state-dependent role of the IC.
OXTR expression is reported in subsets of GABAergic neurons in the insular cortex, suggesting oxytocin acts partly via modulation of local inhibitory microcircuits.
Pharmacological blockade of OXTR in the insular cortex impairs social affective functions, including emotion-recognition abilities, in rats.

Blocking OXTR within the insular cortex enhances pain responses toward socially excluded individuals, suggesting a role for oxytocin in representing others' emotional states under socially challenging conditions.
Intranasal oxytocin administration has been reported to reduce insular cortex responses during socio-emotional tasks including emotional perception and embarrassment-related processing in humans.

Other studies reported increased left insular cortex activity in response to socially salient stimuli such as infant crying following oxytocin administration, contrasting with reports of reduced IC activity in other tasks.
Postmortem and transcriptomic studies in humans suggest OXTR expression in cortical regions including the insular cortex is relatively sparse and variable, unlike more consistent rodent findings.
AVPR1a expression in the insular cortex is relatively high compared with other cortical regions in mice.
In rats, AVPR1a expression in the insular cortex has been reported to be lower relative to OXTR expression.

OXTR activation engages Gq/11-PLC signaling and downstream Ca2+- and PKC-dependent modulation of membrane function, altering excitability of OXTR-expressing neurons including IC principal neurons in a PKC-dependent manner.
In mouse models of autism spectrum disorder, reduced GAD65 expression has been reported in the insular cortex, suggesting an excitation-inhibition imbalance in local circuits.
In mouse models of autism spectrum disorder, reduced parvalbumin expression has been reported in the insular cortex, suggesting an excitation-inhibition imbalance in local circuits.

Deep-brain stimulation of the insular cortex improves social deficits in valproic acid-treated rats, an animal model of autism, indicating a causal contribution of IC activity to autism-like behavioral phenotypes.
The OXTR single-nucleotide polymorphism rs2254298A has been associated with reduced gray matter volume in the insular cortex.
Higher OXTR polygenic risk scores have been associated with reduced gray matter volume in the insular cortex.
Increased methylation of the OXTR gene has been linked to heightened insular cortex activity during social tasks, suggesting altered OXT signaling influences IC processing in autism.
A subset of paraventricular nucleus (PVN) oxytocin neurons projects directly to the insular cortex, while direct supraoptic nucleus (SON) projections to IC have not been firmly established.
Intranasal oxytocin administration has been reported to reduce insular cortex responses during socio-emotional tasks such as emotional perception and embarrassment-related processing.
In contrast to studies showing reduced activity, oxytocin administration increased activity in the left insular cortex in response to socially salient stimuli such as infant crying.
Postmortem and transcriptomic studies indicate that oxytocin receptor expression in human cortical regions, including the insular cortex, is relatively sparse and variable.
Oxytocin receptor activation engages Gq/11-phospholipase C signaling and downstream calcium- and PKC-dependent modulation of membrane function.
Oxytocin receptor signaling modulates the excitability of principal neurons in the insular cortex via a PKC-dependent mechanism.

Neuroimaging studies in individuals with autism spectrum disorder report atypical insular cortex activity during social and affective tasks, with some studies showing increased responses and others showing reduced or context-dependent engagement, indicating substantial heterogeneity.

Mouse models of autism spectrum disorder show reduced expression of the inhibitory markers GAD65 and parvalbumin in the insular cortex, suggesting an excitation-inhibition imbalance within local circuits.

Deep-brain stimulation of the insular cortex improved social deficits in valproic acid-treated rats, a rodent model of autism, suggesting that altered insular cortex activity may causally contribute to autism-related behavioral phenotypes rather than being merely correlated.

Several studies have reported lower peripheral oxytocin levels in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, although the relationship between peripheral measures and central OXT signaling remains unclear.
The OXTR single-nucleotide polymorphism rs2254298A has been associated with reduced gray matter volume in the insular cortex.
Higher OXTR polygenic risk scores have been associated with reduced gray matter volume in the insular cortex.

Increased methylation of the OXTR gene has been linked to heightened insular cortex activity during social tasks, suggesting altered OXT signaling may influence IC processing in autism spectrum disorder.

Oxytocin-based interventions in autism spectrum disorder have shown modest and variable effects on social behavior, possibly reflecting heterogeneity in insular cortex function, OXTR expression, or baseline internal state.
Marfan syndrome results from mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21, which encodes fibrillin-1 and leads to abnormal connective tissue structure and function when mutated.

The patient exhibited cataracta pulverulenta, a fine dust-like opacity of the embryonic/fetal lens nucleus, as an atypical ocular manifestation of Marfan syndrome in the absence of the classical finding of ectopia lentis.
The patient had an arm span-to-height ratio of 1.35, along with arachnodactyly, high-arched palate, and pectus excavatum, supporting a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome per revised Ghent criteria.
Echocardiography showed trace tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation and a small 9 mm atrial septal defect, consistent with the cardiovascular involvement seen in Marfan syndrome.
Manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS) with posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation resulted in a favorable postoperative outcome with best-corrected visual acuity of 6/6.

The patient developed a presumed recurrent episode of MEWDS in the right eye, with symptom onset two weeks after a second serologically confirmed COVID-19 infection, following an earlier presumed episode after her first COVID-19 infection.
Laboratory workup showed an incidentally elevated rheumatoid factor that was deemed non-contributory to the MEWDS diagnosis.

Without any corticosteroid treatment, the patient's photopsias decreased in frequency and fundus autofluorescence lesions resolved by four-week follow-up, consistent with the typically self-limiting course of MEWDS.

The authors hypothesize that persistent photopsias following COVID-19 infection may reflect long COVID-associated chronic low-grade inflammation affecting the retina, mediated by persistent cytokine release, though this was purely speculative and unconfirmed by biomarker testing in this case.

Other published case reports describe recurrent MEWDS occurring after repeated immunologic stimulation, including after a first dose and booster of COVID-19 vaccination in one patient, and after vaccination followed by subsequent COVID-19 infection in another patient.

Multimodal retinal imaging demonstrated punctate hyperautofluorescent spots on fundus autofluorescence, early hyperfluorescent spots on fluorescein angiography, hypofluorescent spots on indocyanine green angiography, and focal ellipsoid zone disruption on OCT, findings characteristic of MEWDS and used to exclude alternative white dot syndromes.

Pre-existing endocrine/metabolic and/or gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary conditions were independently associated with a 3.5-fold increase in the odds of belonging to the high-burden neuroPASC cluster in multivariable logistic regression.
Participants in the high-burden neuroPASC cluster were significantly older than those in the low-burden cluster, and all participants under 30 years fell into the low-burden group.
The high-burden neuroPASC cluster had higher Charlson Comorbidity Index and Framingham Risk Score than controls and low-burden neuroPASC, though the difference lost significance after age-matching.

Individuals with high-burden neuroPASC had a longer cumulative history of alcohol use and earlier age of drinking onset than controls and low-burden neuroPASC, with the drink-years difference reduced to trend-level after age-matching.
High-sensitivity CRP was significantly elevated in neuroPASC compared with controls after adjustment for BMI and inclusion of a group×BMI interaction term, though not with age/sex adjustment alone.
High-sensitivity CRP levels were higher in participants who had been hospitalized during acute COVID-19 compared with both controls and non-hospitalized neuroPASC participants.
IL-6 levels were higher in participants who had been hospitalized during acute COVID-19 compared with both controls and non-hospitalized neuroPASC participants, even after adjusting for BMI.

hsCRP increased more steeply with increasing BMI among hospitalized participants than among non-hospitalized and control participants, indicating a hospitalization×BMI interaction effect on inflammation.

Inflammatory markers (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) and neurodegeneration/amyloid biomarkers (Aβ42/40, pTau181, NfL, GFAP, APOE ε4 allele presence) did not differ significantly between the overall neuroPASC and control groups.

Nearly all neuroPASC participants (93%) remained seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibody approximately 2 years post-infection, compared with 51% of controls, suggesting prolonged antibody persistence or repeated exposure in neuroPASC.
Among control participants without neuroPASC, those seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibody scored lower on verbal fluency tests than seronegative controls, after adjusting for age and sex.

The high-burden neuroPASC cluster performed worse than controls on cognitive screening (MoCA), verbal learning/memory (HVLT-R), response inhibition (Stroop), and processing speed (SDMT), while the low-burden cluster only showed impaired response inhibition.
The high-burden neuroPASC cluster scored lower than the low-burden cluster on delayed verbal memory recall and cognitive flexibility (verbal fluency switching).

Both neuroPASC clusters reported higher fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression and anxiety than controls, with the high-burden cluster showing greater severity than the low-burden cluster and the largest effect sizes vs. controls.

The high-burden neuroPASC cluster had a higher proportion of individuals exhibiting objective neurological exam abnormalities—reduced hearing, reduced upper-extremity strength, reduced lower-extremity sensation, and abnormal gait—than controls and low-burden neuroPASC.

Acute COVID-19 severity indicators (hospitalization rate and need for oxygen therapy) were not different between the low-burden and high-burden neuroPASC clusters, indicating symptom burden was not associated with acute illness severity.
Low COVID-19 vaccination rate prior to infection and higher BMI were associated with development of neuroPASC overall, but not specifically with high-burden neuroPASC severity.

Unsupervised K-means clustering of self-reported symptom frequency identified two robust neuroPASC subgroups (low-burden and high-burden), supported by a majority of internal clustering validity indices.
The high-burden neuroPASC cluster had a higher proportion of individuals unable to work than both controls and the low-burden neuroPASC cluster.

Endocrine/metabolic and gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary conditions were significantly more prevalent in the high-burden neuroPASC cluster than in the low-burden cluster, and this elevated prevalence persisted when compared with controls aged 30 or older.

The association between high-burden neuroPASC and neurological exam signs (gait, sensory deficits, hearing loss) remained significant even after adjusting for age, endocrine conditions, and alcohol use, which are established risk factors for those signs.

Pre-existing psychiatric conditions were more prevalent in the overall neuroPASC group than controls but were not more prevalent in high-burden than low-burden neuroPASC, suggesting symptom burden differences are not driven by psychiatric comorbidity.
The high-burden neuroPASC cluster scored lower on the MoCA cognitive screening test than controls.
High-burden neuroPASC participants scored lower on verbal learning and memory (HVLT-R total and delayed recall) than controls.
Both low-burden and high-burden neuroPASC clusters showed impaired response inhibition on Stroop testing relative to controls, but only high-burden also showed deficits on other domains.
The high-burden neuroPASC cluster scored lower on HVLT-R delayed recall and verbal fluency category switching than the low-burden cluster.
After age-matching by excluding participants younger than 30, the high- vs low-burden differences in HVLT-R delayed recall and Fruit/Furniture scores persisted but fell to trend-level significance.

Control participants who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibodies (indicating prior asymptomatic infection) had lower verbal fluency (COWA-FAS and Fruit/Furniture) scores than antibody-negative controls.
Participants with high-burden neuroPASC were significantly older than those with low-burden neuroPASC, and all high-burden participants were older than 30 years.
The high-burden neuroPASC group had higher Charlson Comorbidity Index and Framingham Risk Score than both controls and low-burden neuroPASC, though the effect attenuated after age-matching.
High-burden neuroPASC participants had greater cumulative alcohol use, reflected by higher drink-years and earlier age of drinking onset, compared to controls and low-burden neuroPASC.

Pre-existing endocrine/metabolic (48%) and gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary (44%) conditions, individually or combined (63%), were significantly more prevalent in high-burden neuroPASC than in low-burden neuroPASC (34%) and controls (26%), even after restricting to controls ≥30 years (35%).

In a multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, education, BMI, CCI, FRS, vaccination, hospitalization, and alcohol use, pre-existing endocrine/metabolic and/or gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary conditions were independently associated with a 3.5-fold increase in odds of high-burden neuroPASC.

Although pre-existing psychiatric conditions (depression, anxiety, ADHD) were more prevalent in the overall neuroPASC group than controls, they were not more prevalent in high-burden than low-burden neuroPASC or controls, and adjusting for them did not change results.

Days since infection, hospitalization rate, oxygen therapy during hospitalization, and BMI were not different between low-burden and high-burden neuroPASC clusters, indicating acute COVID-19 severity was not associated with symptom burden.

Quality-of-life scores and cognitive deficits did not differ between hospitalized and non-hospitalized neuroPASC participants, except that hospitalized participants showed larger effect sizes on MoCA and Stroop Interference.

Approximately 20% of high-burden neuroPASC participants exhibited gait abnormalities and 30% showed lower-extremity sensory deficits, remaining significant after adjusting for age, endocrine conditions, and alcohol use.
IL-6 and TNF-alpha, previously reported elevated in neuroPASC, were not different between neuroPASC and controls in this cohort, possibly due to the long ~2 year interval since infection.
hsCRP did not differ significantly between the low-burden and high-burden neuroPASC clusters.
Low vaccination rates and high BMI were associated with development of neuroPASC overall, but were not associated with distinguishing high-burden from low-burden neuroPASC.
Tobacco use, a previously reported risk factor for long COVID, was low overall in the COVID-BRAIN cohort, limiting the ability to detect an association with high-burden neuroPASC.
Neurocognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms occur in roughly 40% of long COVID patients, contributing to functional impairment, workplace difficulty, and increased healthcare use.
Long COVID has been linked to serious neurological complications including encephalitis, stroke, seizures, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Despite the high neurological burden of long COVID, very few treatments have been described in the literature, and existing ones are often poorly defined, leaving a gap in standardized clinical protocols.
Circulating NET components including cell-free DNA, MPO-DNA complexes, and citrullinated histone H3 are elevated in the plasma of patients with severe COVID-19.
Single-cell RNA sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from COVID-19 patients revealed upregulated expression of NET-formation-associated genes, particularly in severe cases.
HBV induces expression of the calcium-binding protein S100A9 in hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines, where it acts as a potent neutrophil activator that triggers NET formation.
NET levels were higher in hepatocellular carcinoma patients with high HBV-DNA loads compared with those with lower viral loads.

Severe COVID-19 is associated with elevated levels of immature/low-density neutrophils (LDNs) that secrete more proinflammatory cytokines and interferons, show reduced phagocytosis, enhanced ROS production, and spontaneous NET release while evading macrophage clearance.

In patients with HBV-related liver failure, neutrophils showed impaired phagocytosis, increased degranulation, and augmented NET formation, predisposing to tissue injury and secondary bacterial infection.

HBV core (HBc) and envelope (HBe) proteins suppress phosphorylation/activation of ERK1/2, p38 MAPK, and mTOR signaling, pathways required for ROS-dependent NET formation, thereby dampening neutrophil antimicrobial responses.
NET-derived full-length histones H3 and H4 form multivalent bridging interactions with the SARS-CoV-2 spike S2 domain and host cell sialic acid residues, enhancing viral attachment and infectivity.

Post-acute COVID-19 (long COVID) patients show an increased incidence of autoimmune diseases including SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and polymyositis, many linked to neutrophil hyperactivation and excessive NET release.

Long COVID patients show coordinated elevation of multiple interferon subtypes (IFN-α2, IFN-β, IFN-γ, type III IFNs), with biological IFN activity strongly correlating with serum anti-dsDNA antibody levels, suggesting an eDNA-driven interferon amplification loop resembling lupus pathophysiology.

Persistent exposure to NET components in tissues is proposed as a driver of chronic immune activation and long-term tissue remodeling in post-acute sequelae of viral infections, including post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (long COVID).
Severe COVID-19 patients display elevated low-density neutrophils that release NETs enriched in HMGB1-DNA complexes, which may potentiate fibroblast activation and lung fibrosis progression.

Neutrophils colocalize with SPP1+ profibrotic macrophages in a spatially organized niche that reinforces fibrogenic signaling, with elevated SPP1+ macrophage signatures reported in patients with severe COVID-19.

In HBV-related acute-on-chronic liver failure with decompensated cirrhosis, increased absolute neutrophil counts positively correlated with risk of death, accompanied by transcriptomic upregulation of degranulation, NET-formation, and ECM-remodeling genes (including MMP8/9).
Plasma D-dimer and von Willebrand factor antigen levels are elevated in COVID-19 patients compared with healthy individuals, supporting a role for immunothrombosis.
COVID-19 severity correlates with elevated platelet-neutrophil aggregate counts, which contribute to microvascular thrombosis and endothelial injury in lung tissue.
Portal vein thrombosis patients with HBV cirrhosis show elevated plasma levels of cell-free DNA and histone-DNA complexes, which are potential risk factors for disease outcome.

Clinical trials of inhaled dornase alfa in hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed reductions in sputum NET content, improved oxygenation, and decreased inflammatory markers, with preliminary results suggesting shortened hospital stay and reduced mechanical ventilation need when combined with corticosteroids.
PAD4 inhibitors such as Cl-amidine and GSK484 suppress NET formation by blocking histone citrullination and have shown protective effects in animal models of sepsis, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.
NET-associated miR-let-7b complexes with HMGB1 and is expressed at higher levels in low-density neutrophils from lupus patients, where it acts as a TLR7 agonist driving type I interferon production.
Citrullinated histones synergize with NET DNA to enhance TLR4 activation in primary human monocytes, driving IL-1β production and linking extracellular histones directly to atherogenesis.
Neutrophil elastase promotes lung tissue injury and facilitates extracellular release of HMGB1, which acts as a potent TLR4 ligand triggering NF-κB-dependent inflammatory signaling.

In COVID-19-associated pulmonary fibrosis, neutrophils colocalize with SPP1+ profibrotic macrophages, and neutrophil-secreted MMP8/MMP9 proteolytically activate latent TGF-β1 to drive fibroblast differentiation and matrix deposition.
M2-like macrophages localize within fibrotic liver regions in acute/chronic HBV infection and correlate with liver disease severity/failure, paralleling patterns seen in severe COVID-19.
In alcohol-induced hepatitis models, clearance-resistant, defective low-density neutrophils accumulate and exacerbate liver injury while markedly increasing susceptibility to sepsis.
Neutrophil surface TLR2 and TLR4 recognize viral envelope/glycoproteins such as SARS-CoV-2 spike and RSV fusion proteins, triggering MyD88-SYK-MAPK-NF-κB signaling that promotes NET formation.
SARS-CoV-2 immune complexes engage FcγRIIA (CD32) and FcγRIIIB (CD16B) on neutrophils, triggering SYK- and PKC-dependent signaling that potentiates NET formation.
Cytosolic RIG-I-like receptors (RIG-I, MDA5) sense viral RNA and signal through MAVS and IRF3/7 to promote interferon production, amplifying neutrophil antiviral responses and NETosis tendency.
Severe COVID-19 is associated with elevated CXCL8 expression from monocytes and macrophages, correlating with the high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios seen in critically ill patients.
