During HBV infection, IL-15 and IL-7 produced by hepatic stellate cells and hepatocytes enhance T cell activation and license T cells to secrete CXCL8, indirectly amplifying neutrophil recruitment in the liver.
Influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus have been reported to induce robust NET formation that contributes to severe lung injury.
Arboviruses including dengue and chikungunya viruses can induce NET-dependent vascular and inflammatory pathology.
Picornaviruses and retroviruses such as CVB3 and HIV-1 modulate NET formation and clearance, contributing to chronic inflammation and organ dysfunction.

N-acetylcysteine reduces NET formation by replenishing glutathione and scavenging peroxides, inhibiting MPO and neutrophil elastase activation, and lowers circulating NET components and inflammatory cytokines in autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Tempol, a superoxide dismutase mimetic, reduces vascular NET accumulation, thrombosis, and endothelial dysfunction in animal models of oxidative stress-driven vascular and autoimmune inflammation.

Edaravone neutralizes hydroxyl radicals and suppresses mitochondrial ROS generation, blocking PAD4 activation and chromatin decondensation, reducing NET-driven vascular and neuronal damage in stroke and ischemia-reperfusion models.
SYK inhibitors fostamatinib and R406 effectively block NET induction, and p38 MAPK inhibitors diminish NET formation in response to inflammatory cytokines and viral infections.
PAD4 inhibitors Cl-amidine and GSK484 suppress NET formation through blockade of histone citrullination and have shown protective effects in animal models of sepsis, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.

Clinical trials of inhaled dornase alfa (recombinant human DNase I) in hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed reduced sputum NET content, improved oxygenation, and decreased inflammatory markers, with preliminary data from trial NCT04359654 suggesting shortened hospital stay and reduced mechanical ventilation needs when combined with corticosteroids.

Entecavir and Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate are currently recommended treatments for chronic hepatitis B due to their inhibition of viral replication, and combining these with NET clearance strategies could reduce both viral replication and immune-mediated hepatocellular injury.
The overall proportion of total MDSC-like cells among CD33+ myeloid cells did not differ significantly across the three IM study visits.
Total MDSC-like cell frequency was positively associated with markers of systemic inflammation, including presence of fever, anemia, and elevated C-reactive protein.
Presence of clinical warning signs of immune dysregulation (GARFIELD criteria, including recurrent fever) was associated with lower total MDSC-like cell proportions.

A prior history of travel to the Far East was associated with higher total MDSC-like cell frequency, whereas family history of autoimmune disease was associated with lower total MDSC-like cell frequency.
The frequency of PMN-like MDSC among CD33+ myeloid cells significantly decreased from the early phase of IM (V1) to later visits (V2 and V3).
M-like MDSC frequency among CD33+ myeloid cells decreased from V1 to V2 and then increased from V2 to V3 over the course of IM.
e-like MDSC frequency among CD33+ myeloid cells significantly increased from the early phase (V1) to the late phase (V3) of IM.
PMN-like MDSC represented nearly half of the total MDSC-like population at IM onset and its proportional contribution declined substantially over the disease course.
M-like MDSC's proportion of total MDSC-like cells remained stable from V1 to V2 but rose substantially by V3.
e-like MDSC's proportion of total MDSC-like cells increased markedly between V1 and V2 and remained elevated through V3.
Relative monocyte count was not significantly associated with M-like MDSC frequency, arguing against M-like MDSC dynamics being a simple proxy for routine monocyte count shifts.
Relative neutrophil count was not significantly associated with PMN-like MDSC frequency, arguing against PMN-like MDSC dynamics being a simple proxy for routine neutrophil count shifts.
The laboratory IM complexity score significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of PMN-like, M-like, and e-like MDSC subpopulations.
The laboratory IM severity score significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations.
Presence of neurological symptoms during IM significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations.
Presence of hepatitis during IM significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations.
Absolute leucocyte count significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations.
Relative lymphocyte count significantly influenced the compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations.

Dirichlet regression modeling of the compositional trajectory over the disease course showed the mean MDSC-like composition shifting from 35.7% PMN-like/31.0% M-like/33.3% e-like MDSC at day 1 after onset to 16.3% PMN-like/42.9% M-like/40.8% e-like MDSC by day 214.

The compositional dynamics of PMN-like, M-like, and e-like MDSC were significantly influenced by IM laboratory complexity, with PMN-like MDSC proportions rising and e-like MDSC proportions falling as complexity increased, while M-like MDSC was lower at higher complexity but rose with time since onset.

Compositional dynamics of the MDSC-like subpopulations were significantly associated with IM laboratory severity, with PMN-like MDSC proportions rising with severity while e-like MDSC proportions fell and M-like MDSC dipped at medium severity before rising again at higher severity.

Presence of neurological symptoms during IM was associated with a significant shift in MDSC-like composition, with higher PMN-like MDSC proportions and lower M-like and e-like MDSC proportions in patients with neurological symptoms.
Presence of hepatitis during IM was associated with a significant compositional shift, with higher PMN-like MDSC and lower M-like and e-like MDSC proportions in patients with hepatitis.
Higher absolute leucocyte counts were associated with increased PMN-like MDSC proportions and decreased e-like MDSC proportions, while M-like MDSC proportions remained stable.

Higher relative lymphocyte counts were associated with decreased PMN-like MDSC proportions and increased e-like MDSC proportions, with M-like MDSC showing an early positive relationship with lymphocyte count that attenuated later in disease.
Higher ferritin levels were associated with increased PMN-like MDSC proportions and decreased e-like MDSC proportions, while M-like MDSC proportions remained stable across ferritin levels.

Proportions of PMN-like and M-like MDSC measured at earlier visits (V1 and V2) did not significantly predict later clinical outcomes at V3, including other airway symptoms, neurological symptoms, chronic fatigue, or IM protraction.

MDSC-like subpopulation proportions measured concurrently at V3 were not significantly associated with other airway symptoms, neurological symptoms, chronic fatigue, or IM protraction at that same visit.

In individual (non-compositional) linear regression, PMN-MDSC frequency was significantly associated with absolute leucocyte count, relative lymphocyte count, ferritin level, diphtheria toxoid titer, asthma, McIsaac score, number of ELVIS primary-immunodeficiency warning signs, and the ELVIS sign of increased minor infections.

In individual linear regression, M-MDSC frequency was significantly associated with C-reactive protein elevation, the GARFIELD sign of eczema/neurodermatitis, positive EBV EA-p138 IgG status, and neurodermatitis in the family.

In individual linear regression, e-like MDSC frequency was significantly associated with hepatitis, HHV-6 DNA load, travel to the Far East within the last 6 months, the ELVIS sign of multiple infection localization, and a relapsing course of infection.
EBV reactivation was significantly overrepresented in both critical/severe and moderate COVID-19 patients at hospital admission.
HHV-6A DNA was not detected in any of the enrolled COVID-19 patients.
CMV reactivation prevalence was low and not significantly different between critical/severe and moderate COVID-19 patients.
HHV-6B reactivation prevalence was low and not significantly different by severity, but all 8 HHV-6B-positive patients were male.
In patients with critical or severe COVID-19, higher EBV viral load was negatively associated with the frequency of CD4+ central memory T cells, an association not seen in moderate COVID-19.
In patients with critical or severe COVID-19, higher EBV viral load was negatively associated with the frequency of CD8+ effector memory T cells, an association not seen in moderate COVID-19.
There was a non-significant tendency toward higher EBV viral load in patients with critical or severe COVID-19 compared to moderate disease.

Lymphocyte counts were weakly but significantly lower in critical/severe COVID-19 patients than in moderate patients after adjusting for age and sex, with age but not sex being a significant predictor.
Lymphocyte counts did not differ between patients with and without EBV reactivation, regardless of COVID-19 severity.
No differences were found in the frequencies of major immune cell populations (NK, NKT, CD19+ B cells, CD3+, CD4+, CD8+ T cells) between patients with and without EBV reactivation.
CD4+ and CD8+ T cell memory subset distributions (Naive, Central memory, Effector memory, TEMRA) were not associated with EBV reactivation status.
Patients positive for HHV-6B showed a decrease in NK cell frequency and an increase in regulatory T cells compared to HHV-6B-negative patients.
CMV-positive patients had significantly reduced central memory populations in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells compared to CMV-negative patients.
EBV reactivation was associated with a decreased frequency of highly CD11a-expressing (CD11a++) CD4+ T cells, but not CD8+ T cells.
EBV reactivation was associated with a decreased frequency of CD28-expressing cells among both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
Among CD28-expressing CD8+ T cells, the per-cell degree of CD28 expression was decreased in patients with EBV reactivation.
There was a non-significant tendency toward increased CD57 expression in patients with EBV reactivation.
Boolean gating revealed a non-significant tendency toward increased CD11a++CD28−CD57+ frequency among both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in EBV-reactivated patients.

CD8+ T cells co-expressing CD11a++CD28+CD57− (a recently-activated, non-senescent phenotype) were significantly decreased in EBV-reactivated patients, with a similar non-significant tendency in CD4+ T cells.
CD8+ T cells with a CD11a−CD28−CD57+ terminally-differentiated/exhausted phenotype were significantly increased in EBV-reactivated patients, with a slight increase also in CD4+ T cells.
The altered CD11a/CD28/CD57 T-cell activation phenotype observed with EBV reactivation was not seen with CMV or HHV-6B reactivation.
At initial assessment, the Alpha/Delta group performed significantly worse than population norms on the RBANS Immediate Memory index.
The Alpha/Delta group performed significantly better than expected on the RBANS Visuospatial/Constructional index compared to population norms.
The Omicron group also performed significantly worse than population norms on RBANS Immediate Memory at initial assessment.
The Omicron group performed significantly worse than normative expectations on Trail Making Test Part A, a measure of processing speed and simple attention.
There were no significant differences in overall neuropsychological test scores between Alpha/Delta and Omicron groups at initial assessment, aside from TMT-A.
Individuals infected with Alpha/Delta numerically reported higher rates of clinically significant fatigue than the Omicron group, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Both Alpha/Delta and Omicron groups showed higher rates of clinically significant depressive symptoms compared to general population prevalence estimates, regardless of variant.
At follow-up, the Alpha/Delta group scored significantly above average norms on the Stroop Color-Word test.
At follow-up, the Omicron group showed no persistent significant differences from normative values on any neuropsychological test.

Time since acute infection predicted RBANS Delayed Memory performance at follow-up (improvement over time for both groups), and a significant variant-by-time interaction indicated the Alpha/Delta group showed greater improvement over time than the Omicron group.
Participants infected with Alpha/Delta had a significantly greater number of medical comorbidities than those infected with Omicron.
Participants infected with Alpha/Delta reported significantly more severe acute COVID-19 illness than those infected with Omicron.

Across both variant groups, cognitive performance improved between initial and follow-up assessment, and no neuropsychological test scores in either group remained significantly below population norms at follow-up, with no participant showing worsening performance over time.

There were no significant differences between Alpha/Delta and Omicron groups in mean symptom measures for depression, anxiety, PTSD, or fatigue, or in proportions meeting criteria for clinically significant symptoms, at either initial assessment or follow-up.
Dyspnea was reported in 41.3% of 765 Long-COVID patients evaluated at a mean of six months after COVID-19.
Fatigue was reported in 41.6% of the 765 Long-COVID patients evaluated at a mean of six months after COVID-19.

Low-DLCO dyspnea (DLCO <80% predicted) was significantly associated with female sex, anxiety, longer hospitalisation duration, corticosteroid use, and use of monoclonal neutralizing antibodies, with risk decreasing as time since acute infection increased.
Dyspnea occurring with normal DLCO (≥80% predicted) was instead associated with younger age and obesity rather than COVID-19 severity markers.
Low-DLCO fatigue was significantly associated with female sex, heart failure, anxiety, and corticosteroid use.
Fatigue occurring with normal DLCO was not significantly associated with any demographic factor, comorbidity, or COVID-19 severity measure.
For both dyspnea and fatigue, the low-DLCO phenotypes had significantly lower 6-minute walk distance compared with the normal-DLCO phenotypes.
Pooled analysis of four independent studies estimated that 24% of all Nipah virus infection survivors experienced residual neurological deficits after acute infection.
The prevalence of residual neurological deficits was significantly higher among survivors of Nipah encephalitis (45%) than among total Nipah virus infection survivors (24%).
In a single study of survivors of relapsed or late-onset Nipah encephalitis, 61% experienced residual neurological deficits, similar to the rate seen in primary encephalitis survivors.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among total Nipah virus infection survivors, with a pooled prevalence of 48% across two studies.
Cognitive impairment was the most commonly reported symptom among Nipah encephalitis survivors, with a pooled prevalence of 46% across two studies.

Survivors of acute Nipah encephalitis had a numerically higher prevalence of persistent neurological deficit than those with non-encephalitic acute infection, though this trend was imprecise across pooled studies.

In one study, empiric treatment received during acute Nipah infection (including acyclovir, antibiotics, corticosteroids) was identified as a statistically significant risk factor for residual neurological deficits, raising the possibility that treatment rather than infection itself contributed to deficits.

In the single controlled study, residual neurological deficits, fatigue, and daytime somnolence were significantly more common in Nipah survivors than in seronegative household controls 10 years after infection, while 11 other symptoms showed no significant difference.

The prevalence of fatigue among Nipah virus survivors declined sharply over time, from 68% at 6 months to 14% at 2 years post-infection, with a median duration of fatigue of 5 months among those who recovered within 2 years.

In Tan et al., 2002, half of patients with late-onset or relapsing Nipah encephalitis experienced their first episode by a median of 8.4 months after acute infection, and 14% experienced a second episode on average 7.6 months after the first.
Two of five cases of major depressive disorder among Nipah survivors had a delayed onset of approximately one year after the acute infection.

A substantial minority of Nipah encephalitis survivors with neurological deficits required caregiver assistance, with proportions of 15% and 50% reported within 5 months of acute infection, and 15% still requiring assistance at 10 years.

No significant persistent neurological deficits were detected among a total of 41 asymptomatic or non-encephalitic febrile Nipah survivors, though similar brain lesions seen in these individuals as in encephalitis survivors may indicate potential subclinical brain infection even without encephalitis.

More than half of Malaysian Nipah survivors received the antiviral ribavirin during acute hospitalisation, but its relationship to persistent neurological deficits was not investigated in the included studies.
In Ong et al., 2025, one third of Nipah infection survivors with post-acute sequelae recovered from their symptoms within one year of the acute infection.
After 12 weeks of Kyungok-go administration, the primary outcome FSS score improved significantly compared to baseline.
The Fatigue VAS score showed a statistically significant reduction after 12 weeks of Kyungok-go treatment.
ChFS scores improved significantly in the physical domain, mental health domain, and total score after treatment.
Sleep quality, measured by PSQI, showed a slight improvement after Kyungok-go treatment.
Quality of life as measured by EQ-5D-5L improved following Kyungok-go treatment.
Depressive symptoms measured by BDI showed a modest improvement after treatment.
K-MoCA score improved only slightly and Digit Span Forward/Backward tests showed no significant change after Kyungok-go treatment.
Overall CNT scores showed no significant improvement after treatment, except for the trail-making test subscore, which improved significantly.
Physical performance measured by SPPB did not change significantly after 12 weeks of Kyungok-go treatment.

The trial achieved full enrollment of 100 participants within 5 months, with only 6 dropouts and medication adherence ranging from 97.5% to 99.7%, indicating the study design and Kyungok-go administration were feasible.

Most adverse events were mild; only two moderate AEs (shoulder pain, tendinitis) and one severe AE (osteoporosis) occurred, all judged unrelated to Kyungok-go, and no adverse drug reactions were attributed to the medication.
Minor and clinically insignificant deviations in BUN, creatinine, AST, and ALT were observed after Kyungok-go administration, suggesting no hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic effect.

Although 14 ECG abnormalities were recorded after treatment, none were serious (no QT prolongation, ventricular fibrillation, or atrial fibrillation), indicating no clinically significant cardiac safety signal.
Monthly tracking of VAS, FSS, and ChFS total scores from baseline showed all three fatigue measures improved significantly over the 12-week treatment period.
A prior smaller study of 15 Long COVID patients found Kyungok-go was associated with a 53% response rate for fatigue relief and no major safety concerns.

A cited systematic review found fatigue to be the most frequently reported symptom across follow-up in post-COVID patients, persisting at similar or increasing rates over 3 months to 2 years, suggesting fatigue does not resolve substantially with the natural course of Long COVID.
Frequencies of the four major immune cell lineages (T cells, B cells, NK cells, myeloid cells) did not differ between LC, RC, FC and HC groups.
CD56lo CD16lo NK cells were significantly increased in fatigued controls compared to healthy controls and recovered convalescents, but the increase did not reach significance in the Long COVID group.
Both Long COVID and fatigued control groups showed higher frequencies of terminal (CD56lo CD16hi) NK cells than healthy controls.
Early NK and effector NK cell frequencies were significantly lower in the fatigued control and Long COVID groups than in healthy controls.

Recovered convalescents showed an intermediary NK cell phenotype, with terminal NK cells more abundant than in healthy controls and CD56lo CD16lo NK cells reduced compared to fatigued controls, positioning RC between HC and the fatigued groups.
No NK cell subset frequency differed between the Long COVID group and the fatigued control group, indicating shared NK phenotype irrespective of infectious trigger.
PCA of terminal NK cell marker expression showed that separation of LC/FC from HC/RC along PC2 was driven by higher activation marker HLA-DR and lower inhibitory marker CD161 expression.

Upon PMA/ionomycin stimulation, terminal NK cells from Long COVID and fatigued control participants showed higher polyfunctionality scores (multi-cytokine production) than recovered convalescents and healthy controls.
Naive, effector memory, and activated regulatory CD4+ T cell subsets showed no differences between the four study groups.
The Long COVID group showed higher frequencies of naive regulatory T cells compared to recovered convalescents.
The Long COVID group showed lower frequencies of memory regulatory T cells and CD4+ central memory T cells compared to recovered convalescents.

A trend of increased effector CD4+ T cell frequencies was observed in both fatigue groups compared to healthy controls and recovered convalescents, reaching statistical significance only for the FC-versus-RC comparison.

CD4+ T cells from recovered convalescents showed significantly enhanced polyfunctional cytokine response after PMA/ionomycin stimulation compared to healthy controls, while both fatigued groups resembled healthy controls.
Recovered convalescents had significantly higher abundances of CD8+ regulatory T cells compared to both fatigued control and Long COVID groups.
No differences in CD8+ T cell polyfunctionality score in response to PMA/ionomycin stimulation were found between any of the four groups.
No statistically significant differences in gamma-delta T cell subsets were found between the four study groups.
A non-significant trend toward decreased transitional B cell frequencies was observed in fatigued control and Long COVID groups compared to healthy controls.
Marginal Zone B cells were decreased in both the Long COVID and fatigued control groups compared to healthy controls.

Double Negative B cells were increased in both the Long COVID and fatigued control groups compared to healthy controls, consistent with reports in Long COVID and autoinflammatory conditions such as SLE.

An initial Random Forest classifier using immune cell subset frequencies achieved 80.8% prediction accuracy for fatigued cases, with terminal NK cell frequency the most important feature, but performed poorly for healthy and convalescent classes (46% correct for healthy individuals).
A final L1-penalized Linear SVC model achieved 67% classification accuracy for fatigued cases and 67.5% for non-fatigued individuals, with agreement from Logistic Regression and Random Forest models.

Across three independent machine learning models, frequencies of terminal, early and double-negative NK cell subsets, along with memory Tregs and double-negative B cells, were identified as the most important shared predictive features of a general fatigue state.

The authors conclude that Long COVID and unspecific persistent fatigue share an essentially identical peripheral immune cell subset signature, suggesting Long COVID is a subtype of post-infective fatigue syndrome (PIFS) rather than a distinct condition.

Depression symptoms significantly improved from baseline through 3- and 12-month follow-up after the micro-choice-based rehabilitation intervention.

Passive transfer of purified IgG from long COVID patients into mice caused a significant decrease in hind paw withdrawal latency in the Hargreaves thermal test compared to IgG from healthy controls.
Mice receiving IgG from long COVID patients showed a significant transient decrease in paw withdrawal threshold in the Von Frey mechanical allodynia test compared to healthy control IgG recipients.
Paw withdrawal latency in the hot plate test did not differ between mice receiving IgG from long COVID patients versus healthy controls.
The percentage of mice with an abnormal Facial Grimace Scale score was significantly higher in the long COVID IgG group on day 1 post-injection.
General well-being and motivation, measured by nest-building score, did not differ between mice injected with LC versus HC IgG.

Thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity induced by native LC IgG were abolished in mice receiving IgG-depleted serum or papain-digested IgG, confirming intact IgG is required for the pronociceptive effect.
Spatial long-term memory, assessed with the Barnes maze, did not differ between mice injected with LC versus HC IgG.

Short-term spatial working memory (Y-maze spontaneous alternation) and locomotor activity did not differ between mice receiving LC versus HC IgG, including when restricted to donors with cognitive impairment.
Anxiety-like behavior, measured by time in closed arms of the Elevated-plus maze and time in the dark compartment of the Light/Dark box, did not differ between mice receiving LC versus HC IgG.
Depressive-like behavior, measured by immobility time at the tail suspension test, did not differ between mice injected with LC versus HC IgG.
Microglial density (Iba1+ cells) in brain and spinal cord regions did not differ between mice receiving LC versus HC IgG, indicating no overt neuroinflammation.
Astrocyte density (GFAP+ cells) and GFAP/Iba1 mRNA expression in whole brain or DRG did not differ between mice receiving LC versus HC IgG.
The proportion of NeuN+ sensory neurons co-labeled with human IgG in mouse dorsal root ganglia was significantly higher after transfer of LC IgG compared to HC IgG.
Human IgG transferred into mouse DRG did not colocalize with satellite glial cells (glutamine synthetase-positive), in contrast to the neuronal targeting observed with LC IgG.

When applied ex vivo to human post-mortem DRG tissue, IgG from LC patients showed a significant increase in punctate immunoreactivity per neuronal soma compared to HC IgG, localizing specifically to sensory neuron cell bodies.
Anti-HSPA5/GRP78 autoantibody levels were nearly doubled in LC patient serum compared to healthy controls, approaching but not reaching statistical significance.
Anti-NOVA1 and anti-RBPJ autoantibody levels showed a downward trend in LC patient serum relative to healthy controls.
Human LC IgG preferentially colocalized with NF200+ (Aβ/Aδ fiber) DRG neurons more than with peripherin+ or cGRP+ C-fiber-associated neurons in mice.
Colocalization of human IgG with sensory neurons in mouse DRG was lost when mice received IgG-depleted serum or papain-digested IgG instead of purified native LC IgG.
Serum biomarkers of neuronal and glial damage (Nf-L, UCH-L1, GFAP) did not differ significantly between LC patients and healthy controls.
All 13 long COVID patients in the cohort reported cognitive impairment, pain, and fatigue at the time of blood sampling, whereas none of the healthy controls reported such symptoms.
Most long COVID patients presented with depression (9/13) and anxiety (10/13) by HADS/Beck assessment, compared with none reporting depression and only 2/10 reporting anxiety among healthy controls.
Eight of 13 long COVID patients met DN4 questionnaire criteria for neuropathic pain.
The study found a 47.3% incidence of Long COVID among hospitalized and ambulatory children in Jamaica.
Acute vomiting during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
Acute abdominal pain during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
Acute ageusia (loss of taste) during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID and also appeared as a multivariable composite predictor.
Acute anosmia (loss of smell) during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
Acute fatigue during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
Acute confusion during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
Acute brain fog during initial COVID-19 illness was univariately associated with development of Long COVID in children.
A multivariable composite model combining multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, vomiting, and ageusia during acute illness predicted development of Long COVID in this pediatric cohort.
Long COVID incidence was 47.3% among hospitalized and ambulatory children in this Jamaican cohort, highlighting the need for improved care in resource-constrained settings.
Females had approximately twice the odds of developing long COVID compared to males over the one-year follow-up.
Among patients with long COVID, females were less likely than males to recover from persistent symptoms by 12 months.
In females, baseline hypertension was the only factor independently and inversely associated with development of long COVID.
In males, acute COVID-19 severity was independently associated with increased odds of developing long COVID.
In males, higher baseline body mass index was associated with increased odds of developing long COVID.
In males, older age was associated with reduced odds of developing long COVID, acting as a protective factor.
Fatigue was the most prevalent persistent symptom in females, present in 36% at 3 months and 24% at 12 months, with most cases beginning during acute infection.
Dyspnea was the third most prevalent symptom in females and second in males, mainly experienced during acute infection with a 30% recovery rate in females.
Memory loss was the second most common persistent symptom in females and had the lowest recovery rate among major symptoms, mostly appearing after infection.
Hair loss was significantly more common in females than males at 3 months but had the highest recovery rate of all symptoms in both sexes.
In both sexes, long COVID patients who recovered by 12 months had lower rates of severe acute COVID-19 than those who did not recover.
History of thrombosis was present only among females with long COVID who did not recover at 12 months, and was absent in those who recovered.
There was no association between hospital admissions within 24 months of COVID-19 diagnosis and long COVID status, in either sex, even after adjusting for COVID-19 severity.
Chronic fatigue in long COVID has been linked in the literature to inflammatory and immune dysregulation involving cytokines including IL-6 and IL-1β, shared genetic pathways, and microRNA profiles.
Dysregulation of endothelin-1 has been observed in patients with persistent fatigue, suggesting endothelial dysfunction contributes to symptom persistence in long COVID.
Higher testosterone levels were negatively associated with long COVID in both sexes in a cited study, supporting an immunoendocrine dysregulation hypothesis for sex-specific long COVID risk.
Among patients with severe acute COVID-19, a higher proportion of females than males went on to develop long COVID.
Females reported a greater overall number of persistent symptoms than males.
Overall, 57% of the study population reported persistent symptoms at 3 months post-infection, declining to 41% at 1 year, corresponding to an overall recovery rate of 27.5%.
Quality of life (EQ-VAS) scores were significantly lower in the Long-COVID group than the Control group at all three follow-up visits over two years.
A higher proportion of patients in the Long-COVID group had clinically abnormal FSS, mMRC, and CAT scores at each follow-up time point.
Total CAT scores declined over time in both groups but remained consistently higher in the Long-COVID group across all three follow-up visits.

Specific CAT items — chest tightness, breathlessness climbing stairs/hills, activity limitation at home, confidence leaving home, sleep, and energy — were worse in the Long-COVID group, especially at the 1-year and 2-year (winter) visits, while cough and phlegm scores were similar between groups.
Only 20.6% of the Long-COVID group were free from adverse health outcomes (hospitalization or ED visits) over 2 years, versus 50.0% of the Control group.
A significantly higher percentage of the Long-COVID group experienced three or more adverse health outcomes compared to the Control group.
At the 1-year follow-up, FEV1% pred, PEF% pred, MEF75% pred, MEF50% pred, and MVV% pred were significantly lower in the Long-COVID group compared to Controls.
At the 1.5-year follow-up, FEV1/FVC% pred and MEF75/25% pred were additionally significantly lower in the Long-COVID group, on top of the five parameters already differing at 1 year.
At the 2-year follow-up, MVV% pred remained significantly lower in the Long-COVID group, indicating persistent impairment of pulmonary ventilation function reserve.
RV/TLC ratio increased gradually over time in both the Long-COVID and Control groups across the follow-up period.

DLco% pred and DLco/VA% pred were consistently slightly lower in the Long-COVID group at all three follow-ups, but the difference did not reach statistical significance, possibly due to small sample size and heterogeneity.

Serum proteomic analysis at the 2-year follow-up identified 77 differentially expressed proteins between the Long-COVID and Control groups, with 26 up-regulated and 51 down-regulated in the Long-COVID group.
Up-regulated serum proteins in the Long-COVID group were enriched in platelet aggregation, blood coagulation/fibrin clot formation, cell-matrix adhesion, and angiogenesis pathways.
KEGG pathway enrichment of up-regulated proteins in the Long-COVID group showed involvement of ECM-receptor interaction, platelet activation, and focal adhesion pathways.
FLNA (filamin A) was identified as a hub protein up-regulated in the serum proteome of the Long-COVID group at 2 years.
ITGB3 (integrin subunit beta 3) was identified as a hub protein up-regulated in the Long-COVID group's serum proteome at 2 years, consistent with a role in COVID-19-related thrombosis.
FGB (fibrinogen beta chain) was identified as a hub protein up-regulated in the Long-COVID group's serum proteome at 2 years.

ITGA2B (integrin subunit alpha 2b) was identified as a hub protein up-regulated in the Long-COVID group's serum proteome, consistent with prior transcriptomic reports of ITGA2B up-regulation in severe COVID-19.
FN1 (fibronectin 1) was identified as a hub protein up-regulated in the Long-COVID group's serum proteome, consistent with a reported role in COVID-19-related thrombosis.
Comparing 1-year and 2-year proteomes within each group, 349 DEPs were found in the Long-COVID group and 316 in the Control group, of which 76 DEPs were unique to the Long-COVID group.
The 76 DEPs unique to the Long-COVID group between 1- and 2-year follow-up were enriched in the complement and coagulation cascades KEGG pathway.
GO-BP enrichment of the 76 DEPs unique to the Long-COVID group identified seven significant terms primarily related to complement activation and immune response.
C8A (complement C8 alpha chain) was a hub protein up-regulated at the 2-year versus 1-year follow-up within the Long-COVID group, consistent with prior reports linking C8A to COVID-19 deterioration.
C8B (complement C8 beta chain) was a hub protein up-regulated at the 2-year versus 1-year follow-up within the Long-COVID group.

CFH (complement factor H) was a hub protein up-regulated at the 2-year versus 1-year follow-up in the Long-COVID group, consistent with a prior report of persistently elevated CFH at 12 months post-infection.
VTN (vitronectin) was a hub protein down-regulated at the 2-year versus 1-year follow-up within the Long-COVID group.
A multi-scale machine learning model combining EHR, survey, and genomic data achieved higher predictive performance for long COVID identification than an EHR-only model.
Active-duty military service status was among the most informative survey-based predictors in the long COVID identification model.
Self-reported fatigue was among the most informative survey-based predictors in the long COVID identification model.

Following low-dose intranasal SARS-CoV-2 infection, brain viral RNA peaked at 6 days post-infection and remained detectable through 90 dpi, in contrast to peripheral tissues which cleared to near baseline by 60-90 dpi.

Brain levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines including CCL2, CXCL10, IL-6, and TNF-α were robustly induced at 6 dpi, coinciding with peak viral load, then returned toward baseline by 15-30 dpi.
Unlike other cytokines, IL-1β levels remained modestly elevated through 30 dpi before declining, indicating more prolonged inflammatory signaling for this cytokine.
Whole-brain Rbfox3 (NeuN) mRNA was transiently downregulated at 6 dpi following SARS-CoV-2 infection and recovered by 30 dpi.

Despite mRNA recovery, immunohistochemistry revealed persistent, spatially heterogeneous focal loss of NeuN immunoreactivity in the cerebral cortex through at least 60 dpi, sparing the olfactory bulb and hippocampus.

Nissl staining of NeuN-depleted cortical areas showed largely preserved neuronal density, though neurons often exhibited shrunken or condensed morphology, suggesting NeuN loss reflects neuronal stress rather than death.

Hcrt (hypocretin/orexin) was the top downregulated transcript in the neuropeptide signalling category at 6 dpi and functioned as a central hub co-suppressed with Ucn, Avp, and Npvf, suggesting coordinated collapse of hypothalamic homeostatic circuits.
RT-qPCR confirmed Hcrt mRNA was markedly reduced at 6 dpi and restored to mock levels by 15 dpi in K18-hACE2 mice.
Orexin immunohistochemistry showed profoundly diminished orexin-positive neuron staining in the lateral hypothalamus at 6 dpi, re-emerging from 15 dpi onward.

Double immunofluorescence revealed that orexin signal was minimal specifically within viral nucleocapsid-rich regions of the hypothalamus, while adjacent NP-negative regions retained orexin staining, suggesting local viral infection drives orexin neuron loss.

Hcrt mRNA suppression tracked with brain viral burden across SARS-CoV-2 variants: expression fell to ~15-20% of mock at 4 dpi and below 2% by 6 dpi with ancestral and Beta variants, and to ~25% of mock with Omicron KP.3 at 6 dpi, indicating conserved variant-independent Hcrt suppression.

Vaccination with a recombinant RBD subunit protein reduced brain viral RNA ~10,000-fold and preserved Hcrt mRNA near mock levels (~90%) at 6 dpi, compared to a drop to ~3.5% in PBS controls, and improved survival to 88% versus 14% in controls.
Pooled analysis across experimental cohorts (n=56 paired samples) showed a strong inverse correlation between brain viral RNA burden and Hcrt mRNA abundance.

In wild-type BALB/c mice infected with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 (MA10), cortical Rbfox3 mRNA was reduced ~30% at 6 dpi, and immunohistochemistry showed persistent focal NeuN-depleted cortical regions up to 90 dpi, sparing olfactory bulb and hippocampus.
MA10 infection of wild-type BALB/c mice caused ~40% reduction in hypothalamic Hcrt transcripts at 6 dpi that persisted through 14 dpi, longer than the recovery seen in K18-hACE2 mice by 15 dpi.

Despite comparable brain viral RNA levels to MA10 infection, influenza A virus (H1N1 PR8) infection did not alter Rbfox3 mRNA, NeuN immunoreactivity, Hcrt mRNA, or orexin protein levels, indicating that the neuropathological signature is specific to SARS-CoV-2 rather than a generic consequence of brain-detectable viral RNA or systemic inflammation.

Human iPSC-derived glutamatergic neurons (lacking microglia/astrocytes and endogenous orexin signalling) supported productive SARS-CoV-2 infection but did not show reduced NeuN expression at 72 hpt, indicating direct viral infection alone is insufficient to cause NeuN loss.

Treatment of infected iPSC-derived glutamatergic neurons with recombinant orexin-A/B increased NeuN protein abundance by ~1.7-fold compared with mock, an effect reduced by pretreatment with the dual orexin receptor antagonist suvorexant, indicating receptor-dependent action.
Dose-response analysis showed that 10 nM and 100 nM γORX-A/B increased NeuN levels by ~2.3-fold and ~2.8-fold, respectively, in infected iPSC-derived neurons.

In MA10-infected BALB/c mice, daily intranasal γORX-A/B treatment from 0-5 dpi increased whole-brain NeuN protein abundance by ~1.8-fold relative to mock at 6 dpi without altering brain viral load, while endogenous Hcrt mRNA remained suppressed by ~40% in both treated and vehicle groups.

Brain IL-1β protein remained modestly elevated through 30 days post-infection even as most other induced cytokines/chemokines returned toward baseline by 15–30 dpi, indicating a more protracted inflammatory signature for this cytokine.

Gene Ontology enrichment of downregulated transcripts at 6 dpi highlighted neuropeptide signalling pathway and neurotransmitter receptor activity terms, indicating impaired synaptic/neuropeptide transmission during acute infection.

Network analysis showed Hcrt acted as a central node in the suppressed neuropeptide module with functional connectivity to Ucn (urocortin), Avp (vasopressin), and Npvf (neuropeptide VF), suggesting a coordinated collapse of hypothalamic homeostatic circuits rather than isolated orexin loss.

The acute 6 dpi immune transcriptional program was time-restricted, with most genes returning to mock-like levels by 15 dpi, whereas Hcrt expression showed only a trend toward recovery throughout the post-acute phase.

Double immunofluorescence showed orexin signal was minimal within nucleocapsid-rich (viral-infected) hypothalamic regions but retained in adjacent NP-negative regions, suggesting orexin loss results from local viral infection rather than diffuse systemic inflammation.

Two-dose intramuscular RBD subunit vaccination prior to SARS-CoV-2 challenge markedly improved survival (88% vaccinated vs 14% PBS controls) and reduced brain viral RNA by approximately 10,000-fold at 6 dpi compared with PBS controls.

Vaccination preserved Hcrt mRNA near mock levels (~90%) at 6 dpi following challenge, in contrast to PBS controls in which Hcrt mRNA fell to ~3.5% of mock levels, linking vaccine-mediated control of brain viral burden with preservation of orexin expression.
Pooled across all experimental cohorts (n=56 paired samples), brain viral RNA load showed a strong inverse correlation with Hcrt mRNA abundance.

Pretreatment with the dual orexin receptor antagonist suvorexant reduced the NeuN-inducing effect of recombinant orexin-A/B in SARS-CoV-2-infected human iPSC-derived glutamatergic neurons, indicating the effect is orexin receptor-dependent.

Dose-response analysis in infected iPSC-derived neurons showed 10 nM and 100 nM recombinant orexin-A/B increased NeuN levels by approximately 2.3-fold and 2.8-fold, respectively, compared with mock controls.

In vivo intranasal γORX-A/B treatment during MA10 SARS-CoV-2 infection did not alter brain viral load compared with vehicle at 6 dpi, indicating orexin's effect on NeuN is not mediated through antiviral activity.

Limited TUNEL-positive apoptotic signal was observed in the cortex at 6 dpi and did not clearly correspond with focal NeuN-low regions, suggesting the NeuN-low phenotype is not primarily explained by widespread apoptotic neuronal death.

Nissl staining of cortical regions with reduced NeuN immunoreactivity showed that overall neuronal cell density remained largely intact, though neurons often exhibited a shrunken or condensed morphology, indicating NeuN loss reflects altered neuronal state rather than cell loss.

The study used only male mice, which the authors note as an important limitation given that Long COVID risk appears higher in females in human cohorts and that neuroimmune responses and the orexin/hypocretin system show sex-dependent features.

Unlike K18-hACE2 mice, which showed orexin recovery by 15 dpi, wild-type BALB/c mice infected with mouse-adapted MA10 SARS-CoV-2 showed more prolonged hypothalamic orexin suppression persisting through 14 dpi and persistent cortical NeuN loss up to 90 dpi, indicating the neuropathology is not an artifact of transgenic ACE2 overexpression.
Among 118 Long-COVID patients assessed at a mean of 259 days post-COVID-19, mean MoCA score was 25.5, with 32.2% scoring below the cognitive impairment threshold of 24.
72.0% of patients presented persisting symptoms, most commonly fatigue (35.6%), dyspnea (28.8%), and cognitive symptoms (24.6%).
Older age was significantly associated with having a MoCA score below 24 among Long-COVID patients.
Hospitalization during the acute phase of COVID-19 was significantly associated with a MoCA score below 24 in Long-COVID patients.
Female sex was significantly associated with a MoCA score below 24 among Long-COVID patients.
Individuals with persisting subjective cognitive symptoms had significantly lower MoCA scores than those without, with a mean difference of 1.4 points.
Anxiety and depression symptoms were not significantly associated with lower MoCA scores, unlike subjective cognitive symptoms.
In 66 patients re-evaluated at a mean of 959 days post-COVID-19, mean MoCA score decreased by 1.3 points compared to baseline follow-up.
Individuals with persisting subjective cognitive symptoms had significantly lower MoCA scores than those without such symptoms, with a mean difference of 1.4 points.
Anxiety and depression symptoms were not significantly associated with lower MoCA scores among Long-COVID patients.
In a follow-up evaluation at an average of 959 days post-COVID-19 among 66 individuals, mean MoCA scores declined further by 1.3 points compared to the earlier assessment.
The proportion of individuals with a MoCA score below 24 increased from 25.8% to 36.4% at long-term follow-up, though this trend did not reach statistical significance.
The prevalence of subjectively reported cognitive symptoms significantly increased from 27.3% to 53.0% between the first and long-term follow-up evaluations.
In a meta-analysis of seven observational cohort studies, exercise-based pulmonary rehabilitation improved functional exercise capacity measured by the 6-Minute Walk Test.
A meta-analysis of four observational cohort studies showed improved lower-limb functional performance after exercise-based pulmonary rehabilitation, measured by the 30-second Sit-to-Stand Test.
Sensitivity analysis excluding a study with younger participants reduced heterogeneity in the 30″SST meta-analysis, suggesting age influences functional test performance and response.
Two RCTs showed improved physical quality of life after exercise-based pulmonary rehabilitation compared with control groups.
Two RCTs showed improved mental quality of life after exercise-based pulmonary rehabilitation compared with control groups, suggesting an indirect psychological benefit of physical training.
Two observational cohort studies showed improvement in quality of life measured by the EQ visual analog scale after exercise-based rehabilitation.
Pulmonary function measured by FVC did not significantly change after exercise-based rehabilitation compared with control in a meta-analysis of two RCTs.
FEV1 did not significantly change after exercise-based rehabilitation compared with control in a meta-analysis of two RCTs.
The FEV1/FVC ratio did not significantly change after exercise-based rehabilitation compared with control in a meta-analysis of two RCTs.
A meta-analysis of two RCTs showed exercise-based rehabilitation reduced the impact of dyspnea on activities of daily living, as measured by the mMRC scale, compared with control.
A meta-analysis of two observational cohort studies showed a reduction in exertional dyspnea assessed by the Borg scale after exercise-based rehabilitation.

Fatigue, though not a pre-specified outcome, was reduced following exercise-based pulmonary rehabilitation in two RCTs and six observational cohort studies, based on heterogeneous self-report instruments.
Several individual studies found no post-intervention improvement in quality of life, assessed by EQ-5D, SF-12 domains, or the mental domain of SF-36.
Two individual RCTs found no significant improvement in dyspnea after exercise-based rehabilitation, assessed by mMRC or the Dyspnea-12 instrument.
Among three studies reporting adverse events, only one observational cohort study identified a case of post-exertional malaise related to exercise-based rehabilitation.

Individual studies using alternative sit-to-stand test formats (not pooled in meta-analysis) also demonstrated significant improvement in functional exercise capacity after exercise-based rehabilitation.

Latent class analysis of 15 binary symptoms identified two distinct symptom profiles among long COVID patients: a low-burden class (36.6%) with lower overall symptom endorsement and a high-burden multisystem class (63.4%) with widespread endorsement across systems including dyspnoea, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, palpitations, dizziness and digestive symptoms.

Cluster analysis of the six LC-6D-QoL domains identified three QoL profiles among long COVID patients: High QoL (13.2%), Medium QoL (34.2%), and Low QoL (52.6%), with more than half of participants in the most impaired group.
High symptom burden (high-burden multisystem class) was strongly associated with membership in the Low QoL cluster compared with the High QoL cluster.
In a model restricted to demographic and clinical factors, increasing age showed a borderline, small positive association with Medium QoL cluster membership relative to High QoL.
Compared with actively employed participants, unemployed participants had 86% lower odds of belonging to the Low QoL cluster.

Participants on sick leave or with recognized work incapacity had 95% lower odds of belonging to the Low QoL cluster compared with active workers, an unexpected pattern where those who remained employed reported poorer outcomes.
Age, sex, education, and household income were not significantly associated with QoL cluster membership in the full multinomial regression model once symptom burden was accounted for.

Social support showed the smallest differentiation among QoL clusters, and participants in the High QoL group unexpectedly reported lower perceived social support than those in the Medium and Low QoL groups.
The three QoL clusters differed significantly on a global QoL index derived from all LC-6D-QoL items, confirming the internal validity of the cluster solution.
Cognitive dysfunction—particularly difficulties with attention, memory, and mental speed—was common among participants and appeared to contribute to reduced work-related quality of life.

Most participants had lived with long COVID for over three years (82.9%), indicating a prolonged, chronic disease course in this cohort, likely reflecting selection of more chronic/severe cases via online recruitment.
Nearly one-third of participants (30.6%) reported having a recognized disability status related to long COVID.
In a meta-analysis of 24 studies (1,080 patients), MSC therapy combined with standard care significantly reduced all-cause mortality in COVID-19 patients compared with standard care or placebo.
Subgroup analysis showed MSC therapy significantly reduced mortality in patients with severe or critical COVID-19, while no significant benefit was seen when moderate cases were included.
Intravenous administration of MSCs was associated with a significant mortality reduction, though data for non-IV routes were too scarce for comparison.
Subgroup comparison of RCTs versus NRCTs found no significant difference in mortality outcomes between study designs, supporting robustness of the primary mortality finding.
GRADE assessment of 13 RCTs (n=705) showed moderate-certainty evidence that mortality was significantly lower in the MSC group compared with control.

In the 11 NRCTs (n=375), MSC therapy showed no statistically significant mortality difference compared with control, and this moderate-certainty evidence was considered less robust due to confounding.
Meta-analysis of adverse events across 7 comparative studies found no significant increase in AE incidence with MSC therapy compared with control.

Meta-analysis of serious adverse events across 5 comparative studies found no significant difference between MSC and control groups overall, and one study reported significantly fewer SAEs in the MSC group.
One study reported a significantly lower incidence of hypertension as an adverse event in the MSC group compared with control.

Among 18 studies reporting symptom outcomes, most found no significant between-group difference, but four studies reported faster clinical recovery with MSC therapy, including greater relief of dyspnea and cough.
Among 16 studies reporting hospital/ICU stay duration, most showed no between-group difference, but one study (Adas et al.) reported significantly shorter ICU stay with MSC therapy.
Among 17 studies assessing pulmonary function, four reported improved oxygenation or respiratory indices after MSC therapy, though high variability limited definitive conclusions.
Of 13 studies with lung imaging data, five reported greater resolution of inflammatory lesions, consolidation, or severity scores with MSC therapy.

Two individual trials found that MSC therapy increased anti-inflammatory markers (IL-10, IL-1Ra, IL-1β, TGF-β) and growth factors (VEGF, KGF, NGF) relative to control, suggesting an immunomodulatory mechanism.
Infection-related markers including MMP-9, MMP-3, and procalcitonin were reduced in MSC-treated patients relative to controls in two included trials.
At one-year follow-up, a significantly higher proportion of MSC-treated patients had normalized chest CT scans compared with controls.
MSC-treated patients had lower numerical rating scale pain scores than controls at long-term follow-up.
At 3 months, MSC-treated patients had lower (better) St George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores and less wheezing than controls.
At 1 year, MSC-treated patients reported less fatigue and had better pulmonary function (FEV1% predicted and FEV1/FVC) than controls.
MSC-treated patients showed higher SF-36 general health scores at 18 months and a smaller proportion with below-normal 6-minute walk distance at 2 years compared with controls.
One trial found shorter ICU stay duration in critical COVID-19 patients treated with MSCs compared with controls.
One trial reported a lower incidence of hypertension as an adverse event in the MSC group compared with controls.
In one trial, serious adverse events were significantly less frequent in the MSC group than in the control group, with none attributed to MSC infusion.
One trial reported greater relief of dyspnea and cough symptoms with MSC treatment.
Excluding one high-risk-of-bias non-randomized trial from the mortality meta-analysis in a sensitivity analysis did not materially change the pooled mortality estimate.
Most people with Long COVID did not actively engage with the digital patient-reported outcome measure app, with 61% in stage 1 and 70% in stage 2 not actively using it.
Non-registered/paper-completing patients (Group 1) tended to be older and have a narrower age range compared to those who used the app once (Group 2) or repeatedly (Group 3).
Patients living in more deprived areas (higher Index of Multiple Deprivation decile) were more likely to belong to the group that did not register or use the app digitally.
Non-users of the app (Group 1) had a substantially higher unemployment rate than single-use (Group 2) or repeat-use (Group 3) groups.
Gender did not appear to significantly affect uptake of the DPROM app among people with Long COVID.
Sixty percent of Stage 2 respondents were aware of the DPROM app's existence, but only 40% felt they had received enough information to use it.
Most Stage 2 respondents (60%) felt that symptom tracking would be useful for managing their Long COVID.

Among active app users (Group 3), half were aware of the app's radar graph feature and most of those aware found it clear to understand, whereas single-use participants (Group 2) had mixed views on its clarity.
Qualitative analysis identified usability problems with the app, including clunky functionality, confusing navigation, and design that did not feel patient-centred, as barriers to sustained use.
Low digital literacy and negative emotional responses (fear, discomfort, unease) toward the technology were identified as major barriers to app engagement among people with Long COVID.

Participants who used the app valued its symptom-tracking function, reporting it helped them notice patterns and gradual improvement in their Long COVID symptoms that they might otherwise not have recognised.

Participants reported insufficient onboarding and organisational support for the app, including unclear initial instructions, login/access difficulties, and limited awareness of features such as the symptom-tracking radar graph.
Patients with PPS and PCC had substantially greater somatic symptom burden and symptom-related distress than age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
52.2% of patients with persistent physical symptoms exceeded the combined SSD-12 and PHQ-15 threshold indicating high somatic symptom burden and symptom-related distress.
48.0% of patients with post COVID-19 condition exceeded the combined SSD-12 and PHQ-15 threshold indicating high somatic symptom burden and symptom-related distress.

Joint factor analysis of SSD-12 and PHQ-15 items identified a four-factor structure: a dominant cognitive-affective distress factor, a narrower persistence-worry factor, and two symptom clusters reflecting pain/gastrointestinal and autonomic-neurological symptoms.

Participants exceeding the somatic symptom burden and distress threshold had poorer quality of life, lower resilience, and more comorbidities and symptoms than those below threshold, across both cohorts.
Joint factor analysis of the SSD-12 and PHQ-15 items identified a dominant cognitive-affective distress factor common to both patient cohorts.
A narrower persistence-worry factor was identified alongside the dominant distress factor in the joint factor analysis.
A distinct symptom cluster combining pain and gastrointestinal symptoms emerged from the joint factor analysis of PPS and PCC patients.
A distinct symptom cluster reflecting autonomic-neurological symptoms emerged from the joint factor analysis of PPS and PCC patients.
Despite differing clinical entry points, the persistent physical symptoms cohort and the post-COVID-19 condition cohort showed broadly similar symptom-related dimensions.
Patients above the combined SSD-12/PHQ-15 threshold had more comorbidities and more symptoms than those below threshold across both cohorts.
Patients who had acute neurological symptoms during COVID-19 showed significantly higher (worse) IQCODE cognitive decline scores at 2-year follow-up than those without acute neurological symptoms.
After adjusting for confounders, presence of acute neurological symptoms remained significantly associated with a higher IQCODE score at 2-year follow-up.
Older age was an independent risk factor for cognitive decline (IQCODE ≥3.5) at 2-year follow-up.
Chronic kidney disease was an independent risk factor for cognitive decline at 2-year follow-up in COVID-19 survivors.
A greater number of SARS-CoV-2 reinfections was an independent risk factor for cognitive decline at 2-year follow-up.
Higher educational attainment was a protective factor against cognitive decline at 2-year follow-up.
Overall presence of acute neurological symptoms during COVID-19 was independently associated with increased odds of cognitive decline at 2-year follow-up.

Within patients who had neurological symptoms, those with CNS involvement (delirium, brain fog, headache, dizziness, or acute ischemic stroke) had significantly higher risk of cognitive decline than those without CNS involvement.
Current cognitive status (TICS-40 score) did not differ significantly between patients with and without acute neurological symptoms.
After adjustment for covariates, the presence of neurological symptoms was still not significantly associated with TICS-40 score.
Older age, hyperlipidemia, and severe COVID-19 during acute infection were significant risk factors for current cognitive impairment (TICS-40 ≤20) at 2-year follow-up.
Higher education level and a greater number of COVID-19 vaccination doses were protective factors against current cognitive impairment.
Patients with acute CNS symptoms had a significantly higher risk of current cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up after adjusting for confounders.
Acute delirium during COVID-19 was a strong independent risk factor for both cognitive decline and cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
Acute-phase brain fog was a strong independent risk factor for both cognitive decline and cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
Acute ischemic stroke during COVID-19 infection was a significant independent risk factor for both cognitive decline and cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
Acute numbness during COVID-19 infection was a strong independent risk factor for both cognitive decline and cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
Acute facial paralysis during COVID-19 infection was a strong independent risk factor for both cognitive decline and cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
Acute headache was associated with cognitive decline but not with current cognitive impairment at 2-year follow-up.
During acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, fatigue, myalgia, and headache were the most commonly reported neurological symptoms in this cohort.
At 2-year follow-up, most acute neurological symptoms had markedly declined in prevalence, but fatigue and brain fog remained relatively common.

Among patients with acute neurological symptoms, a higher proportion of women was observed in the subgroup with persistent (residual) neurological symptoms at 2-year follow-up compared to those without residual symptoms.
Distribution of COVID-19 vaccination doses differed significantly between patients with residual neurological symptoms and those without.
Patients with acute neurological symptoms had a significantly higher incidence of new-onset symptoms overall at 2-year follow-up compared to those without acute neurological symptoms.
Insomnia was the most common new-onset symptom after SARS-CoV-2 infection and was significantly more frequent in the neurological symptom group than in the non-neurological symptom group.

Patients who developed new-onset stroke after COVID-19 were generally older, predominantly male, and more frequently had hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and liver disease, consistent with traditional vascular risk factors.
New-onset depression after COVID-19 was more common among patients with lower education level and hyperlipidemia, suggesting an interplay of metabolic and psychosocial determinants.

New-onset insomnia after COVID-19 was more frequent among older patients, women, and those with fewer vaccine doses, implying demographic and immunization status may influence susceptibility to sleep disturbances.

Fibromyalgia is characterized as a chronic pain syndrome of unclear etiology marked by increased pain sensitivity, with symptoms including widespread chronic pain, fatigue, sleep disturbances, mood changes, and in some cases cognitive impairment.

Fibromyalgia lacks objective laboratory or imaging tests, so diagnosis relies solely on clinical evaluation of patient-reported symptoms, which can create diagnostic uncertainty and underestimation of complaints by clinicians, especially in forensic contexts.

The substantial rise in autism spectrum disorder diagnoses over the past three decades is attributed largely to increased clinical vigilance, expanded diagnostic criteria (introduction of Asperger disorder in DSM-IV and the spectrum concept in DSM-5), reduced stigma, and social/identity factors, rather than a true increase in underlying prevalence.

Because ASD is a spectrum with highly heterogeneous functional repercussions, automatically classifying the diagnosis as a disability without individualized functional assessment is considered inappropriate, particularly for adults diagnosed later in life who may have developed adaptive strategies and successful trajectories.

Individuals with high social anxiety showed selectively reduced left posterior STS activation during mentalizing scenes relative to both pain and control scenes, despite otherwise preserved engagement of the canonical theory of mind network.

Bayesian analyses showed evidence against group differences in the right temporoparietal junction, precuneus, and medial prefrontal cortex during mentalizing scenes, indicating largely preserved theory of mind engagement outside the pSTS.

During the first two-thirds of the film, participants with high social anxiety showed reduced intersubject neural alignment in superior parietal and bilateral temporal regions compared with low-SA participants.

During the final third of the film, participants with high social anxiety showed reduced neural alignment in supplementary motor, medial prefrontal, and precentral regions compared with low-SA participants.
Across much of the film, participants with high social anxiety showed increased neural alignment in occipital, inferior frontal, and superior temporal cortices relative to low-SA participants.
The spatial overlap between the group-difference intersubject correlation clusters and the canonical theory of mind network was limited, with no cluster exceeding 20% overlap.
Within the high-SA group, intersubject correlation alignment values in the group-difference clusters were not associated with individual pSTS activation during mentalizing events.

A neural alignment cluster showing reduced alignment in high-SA participants (supramarginal, inferior temporal, anterior midcingulate, precuneus) spatially overlapped ~60% with a cluster previously reported as showing increased alignment in autistic individuals using the same movie paradigm, indicating that anatomically overlapping regions support opposite directions of neural alignment change in social anxiety versus autism.
Mean heart rate and movie-driven heart rate alignment (intersubject correlation) did not differ between high- and low-SA groups during film viewing, indicating comparable autonomic arousal.
Pupil diameter varied by event type (greatest during pain events) but showed no main effect of group or group-by-event interaction, indicating comparable attentional engagement across groups.
Movie-driven alignment of pupil diameter fluctuated over time but showed no group differences at any time point or in mean intersubject correlation.
High- and low-SA groups did not differ in the proportion of mental state terms or overall emotion-related language used in postviewing plot summaries.

Contrary to predictions, participants with high social anxiety used a lower proportion of negatively valenced emotion words in their postviewing plot summaries than low-SA participants, indicating a more positive emotional framing of the narrative.

Several maternal diagnoses (obstetric codes, injury codes, personality disorders, epilepsy) showed a significant association with autism in both cross and parallel cousins with a consistent effect direction, interpreted as evidence of direct genetic (pleiotropic) effects shared regardless of maternal vs paternal lineage.

Maternal obstetric diagnoses were associated with a lower likelihood of autism in the cousins, contrasting with the positive association between these maternal diagnoses and child autism previously reported in a mother-child design.

Maternal obstetric diagnoses (abnormal product of conception, multiple gestation, false labor) and psychiatric diagnoses (recurrent major depressive disorder, other anxiety disorders) were associated with higher autism likelihood specifically in parallel cousins (offspring of the mother's sister) and not equally in cross cousins, consistent with indirect genetic effects operating prenatally.

Maternal diagnosis of systemic involvement of connective tissue (a category including Sjögren syndrome and hypermobility syndromes) was associated with higher autism likelihood in parallel cousins compared with cross cousins, suggesting an indirect genetic effect linking maternal connective-tissue disease liability to offspring autism risk.

Maternal multiple gestation diagnosis was not associated with autism in cross cousins but was associated with lower autism likelihood in parallel cousins, mirroring the direction seen in the authors' prior direct mother-child analysis.

Additionally adjusting for the maternal aunt's own diagnosis did not meaningfully change the parallel-cousin associations, providing no evidence that the maternal diagnosis-autism associations were driven by shared non-genetic familial factors.

For several maternal psychiatric/substance-related diagnoses, fecundity was disproportionately lower in the index mother's brothers than sisters (relative to unaffected siblings), with the largest sex-differential fecundity effects (>10%) seen for alcohol use, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, persistent mood disorders, and psychotropic drug poisoning.

Maternal postpartum hemorrhage, along with other childbirth complications, OCD, eating disorders, and personality disorders, was associated with lower fecundity in both brothers and sisters of affected index mothers, with postpartum hemorrhage showing the largest decrease.

Maternal malignant breast neoplasm and essential hypertension were both associated with higher fecundity in both brothers and sisters of the index mother, plausibly because these conditions occur later in life after peak childbearing.

The authors' prior sibling-comparison analyses showed that effects of recurrent depression, false labor, and systemic connective tissue involvement (including hypermobility syndromes) were attenuated by more than 60% relative to population-based maternal-autism estimates, exceeding the attenuation expected from 50% shared direct genetic effects alone and supporting an indirect genetic effect interpretation.

For OCD and obesity, prior sibling analyses showed over 80% attenuation of the maternal-autism association, yet the current cousin-based design found no significant evidence of indirect genetic effects, a discrepancy the authors attribute to possible methodological differences or cohort heterogeneity.

The authors' prior work found that paternal anxiety disorder had a weaker association with child autism than maternal anxiety disorder, consistent with (though not decisively confirming) an indirect genetic effect operating via the maternal prenatal environment, albeit with overlapping confidence intervals between maternal and paternal estimates.

For diagnoses such as epilepsy and asthma, direct and indirect genetic effects may act in opposite directions, which can increase the estimated association in cross cousins relative to parallel cousins and complicate interpretation of the cousin-comparison design.

Mast cells show a conserved perivascular distribution in the thalamus, hypothalamus, choroid plexus, and circumventricular organs, largely within the blood-brain barrier, positioning them to interact with neurons, glia and endothelium.

Autoantibodies against brain epitopes have been found in mothers of children with ASD and in many affected children, associated with allergic manifestations and possible blood-brain barrier disruption.
In a rat model of ADHD, the traditional Chinese decoction An Shen Ding Zhi Ling reduced hyperactivity and impulsivity, potentially via inhibition of mast cell activation.

In a maternal allergen-induced inflammation rat model, offspring fetal brains showed upregulated microglia and increased mast cell numbers at birth, followed by abnormal social behavior and hyperlocomotion.
Mast cells and microglia are sensitive to sex steroid hormones, suggesting sex-dependent differences in offspring response to maternal inflammation contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders.
Degranulation of meningeal mast cells is positively associated with motor activity in animal studies.
Chemically intolerant women were hypothesized to have a higher likelihood of having children with ADHD or autism.
Toxicant exposure may alter mast cells through epigenetic modifications, triggering chronic including brain inflammation and increasing ADHD risk.
Maternal allergies or autoimmune diseases were associated with increased risk of ADHD in offspring.
The link between maternal allergies and neurodevelopmental disorders may also extend to autism spectrum disorder.

In a gender-affirming primary care clinic sample over 16 years old, 2.7% met diagnostic criteria for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome versus an estimated 0.02% in the general population; among this EDS-positive group, 16.9% also had a mast cell activation disorder and 47.5% met criteria for ADHD.
NK1 receptor knockout mice, lacking the substance P receptor, exhibit locomotor hyperactivity, a phenotype also seen in wild-type mice treated with an NK1R antagonist.
Hyperactivity in NK1R knockout mice was observed predominantly in males, consistent with the higher prevalence of hyperactive symptoms in boys with ADHD.
Methylphenidate was more effective in wild-type mice than in NK1R knockout mice, in which it could even exacerbate ADHD-like symptoms.
Human genetic studies indicate that variations in the TACR1 gene may increase susceptibility to ADHD.
Approximately 10% of individuals with ASD present comorbid atopic dermatitis, with autism prevalence increasing with dermatitis severity.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, frequently comorbid with autism, has also been associated with mast cell activation syndrome.
NGF levels correlated positively with serotonin levels in autistic patients, and autistic children showed NGF levels above the normal range, potentially contributing to neurogenic inflammation.

Tachykinin 1-expressing neurons in the periaqueductal gray send excitatory projections to oxytocin-producing neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus, promoting social behaviors that are impaired in autism spectrum disorder.
A traditional Chinese herbal decoction reduced hyperactivity and impulsivity in a rat model of ADHD, possibly by inhibiting mast cell activation.
In a maternal allergen-induced inflammation rat model, offspring fetal brains showed increased microglia and mast cell numbers at birth, followed by abnormal social behavior and hyperlocomotion.
Degranulation of meningeal mast cells was positively associated with motor activity in animal studies.

In a gender-affirming primary care clinic sample, 2.7% met diagnostic criteria for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vs ~0.02% general population), and among these, 16.9% also had a mast cell activation disorder and 47.5% met criteria for ADHD.
NK1R knockout mice, lacking the substance P receptor, displayed locomotor hyperactivity, a phenotype also seen in wild-type mice treated with an NK1R antagonist.
Hyperactivity in NK1R knockout mice was observed predominantly in males, consistent with the higher prevalence of hyperactive symptoms in boys with ADHD compared to girls.
Methylphenidate was more effective in wild-type mice than in NK1R knockout mice, in which it could even exacerbate hyperactivity symptoms.
Translational human research indicated that variations in the TACR1 gene may increase susceptibility to ADHD.
Approximately 10% of individuals with autism spectrum disorder have comorbid atopic dermatitis, with autism prevalence increasing with dermatitis severity.
Autistic children showed NGF levels above the normal range, positively correlated with serotonin levels released by mast cells, potentially contributing to neurogenic inflammation.

Tachykinin 1-expressing neurons in the periaqueductal gray project to oxytocin-producing neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus to promote social behaviors that are impaired in autism spectrum disorder.

A positive linear relationship was found among serum mercury levels, neurokinin A, and Childhood Autism Rating Scale scores, suggesting mercury-induced neuroinflammation with elevated tachykinin A may contribute to ASD pathogenesis.
Children with allergic rhinitis had a 76% increased risk of developing epilepsy, with an additional 21% increase in boys compared to girls, and a younger age at epilepsy diagnosis.
Epileptic subjects exhibit altered immune profiles with increased activated mast cells, associated with key genes FGD3 and SSH2.
A correlation was observed between EGFR levels and infiltration of immune cells, including mast cells, in epilepsy.
Histamine, TNF-α, and IL-2 may contribute to seizures in children, and modulation of mast cell activation may exert neuroprotective effects.
In an animal model, mast cell degranulation exerted an anticonvulsant effect, possibly mediated by serotonin (5-HT), contrasting with reports of mast cells promoting epileptogenesis.
Substance P is thought to contribute to seizure induction via the NK1 receptor, while paradoxically protecting against seizures when activating NK1 receptors on specific hippocampal interneurons.
In 125 individuals with mast cell activation syndrome, depression was more common among younger participants, with severity increasing proportionally to illness intrusiveness.
Children, adolescents, and young adults with food allergies exhibit higher rates and more severe forms of anxiety.
In youths aged 8-17 with irritable bowel syndrome, increased mast cell numbers in the descending colon and rectosigmoid were associated with anxiety and depression.
In children and adolescents with functional gastrointestinal disorders, nausea was associated with increased mast cell density and higher self-reported anxiety and depression.

An insect-derived product traditionally used to treat epilepsy alleviated atopic dermatitis symptoms in a mouse model, reducing mast cell infiltration, IgE, and histamine, potentially via NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition.

A three-generation family carries a heterozygous 22q13.1 deletion spanning TNRC6B exons 2-23, causing gene haploinsufficiency associated with variable neurodevelopmental and behavioral phenotypes across four affected members.
Chromosomal microarray on the proband identified a 0.25 Mb 22q13.1 deletion encompassing TNRC6B exons 2-23 with no other genes included in the deleted region.

Multiple affected family members (proband, sister, father, grandmother) exhibited joint laxity of varying severity, consistent with a connective-tissue phenotype associated with TNRC6B haploinsufficiency.
The paternal grandmother required surgery for craniosynostosis in childhood, a previously under-recognised feature proposed to expand the TNRC6B phenotypic spectrum.

Cardiac valve anomalies (mitral valve prolapse in the father) were observed in this family, paralleling aortic root dilation reported in two patients from a prior TNRC6B cohort, suggesting TNRC6B may influence valvular/vascular development.
