Among 17 individuals with heterozygous TNRC6B variants, high frequencies of speech delay, autism/autistic traits, ADHD, and hypotonia were reported.

Joint hypermobility or other connective tissue-like features were observed in 8 of 17 individuals with TNRC6B variants in Granadillo et al.'s cohort, consistent with joint laxity seen in the present family.

Genotype-phenotype analysis suggested N-terminal TNRC6B variants affecting the Argonaute-binding domain associate with macrocephaly, whereas C-terminal variants affecting the silencing domain associate with microcephaly.
23% of pathogenic TNRC6B variants in the Granadillo et al. cohort were inherited rather than de novo, indicating variable expression among carriers.
Dysregulated miRNA networks have been implicated in ASD pathogenesis by targeting genes involved in synaptic function, metabolism, and immune response.
In an exome sequencing study of 362 probands with non-syndromic tetralogy of Fallot, one individual carried a de novo heterozygous TNRC6B variant.
Loss-of-function TNRC6B variants have been reported in patients with childhood apraxia of speech and other developmental language disorders.
Functional studies showed a synonymous TNRC6B variant can disrupt RNA splicing, illustrating a distinct molecular mechanism contributing to disease.
A de novo pathogenic TNRC6B variant was identified in a 31-year-old woman with infantile-onset epilepsy and autism spectrum disorder without intellectual disability.

Two unrelated Chinese patients with de novo TNRC6B variants presented with developmental delay/intellectual disability, delayed speech, ADHD, behavioural abnormalities, short stature, café-au-lait spots, metabolic abnormalities, and facial dysmorphism.
Disease-causing variants in AGO1 and AGO2, other RISC components, have also been linked to intellectual disability and autism.
Intronic TTTCA and TTTTA repeat expansions in the paralogous gene TNRC6A are implicated in benign familial myoclonic epilepsy.

In brothers with a chromosome 22 pericentric inversion disrupting both TNRC6B and TCF20, craniosynostosis was attributed to TCF20 rather than TNRC6B, contrasting with the possible TNRC6B-craniosynostosis link proposed in the present family.
De novo frameshift and nonsense TNRC6B variants were first identified in the DDD study's exome sequencing of over 2500 simplex autism families.
Prior diagnoses of postviral and related fatigue syndromes were significantly more common in people with HPPD than in population controls, psychedelic-using controls, and visual symptom controls.
A pre-existing diagnosis of postviral and related fatigue syndrome was associated with almost double the hazard of subsequently developing HPPD among psychedelic users.
Fibromyalgia diagnoses prior to index were significantly more common in the HPPD cohort than in population controls, psychedelic-using controls, and visual symptom controls.
Pre-existing fibromyalgia was not significantly associated with the hazard of developing HPPD after psychedelic use once corrected for multiple comparisons.
Irritable bowel syndrome diagnoses were more common in the HPPD cohort than in population controls and psychedelic-using controls, but less common than in visual symptom controls.
Pre-existing IBS was not significantly associated with the hazard of developing HPPD following psychedelic use.

Migraine diagnoses were more common in the HPPD cohort than in population controls and psychedelic-using controls, but less common than in visual symptom controls, an inconsistent pattern the authors suggest points to distinct pathophysiology from visual snow syndrome.
Pre-existing migraine was not significantly associated with the hazard of developing HPPD after psychedelic use.
A pre-existing diagnosis of anxiety disorder was associated with a 1.5-fold increased hazard of developing HPPD among psychedelic users.

Individuals diagnosed with HPPD had approximately double the risk of subsequently developing functional somatic syndromes (composite group including fibromyalgia, IBS, migraine, chronic pain, and postviral fatigue) compared with psychedelic-using controls.

Autism diagnoses were less frequent in the HPPD cohort than in psychedelic-using controls (significant), with non-significant lower rates also seen versus population controls and visual symptom controls after correction for multiple comparisons.
Chronic pain diagnoses were significantly more common in the HPPD cohort compared with population controls, psychedelic-using controls, and visual symptom controls.

Functional neurological disorder diagnoses prior to index were more common in the HPPD cohort than in population controls and visual symptom controls, but not significantly different from psychedelic-using controls.
Pre-existing somatoform disorder was not significantly associated with the hazard of developing HPPD after psychedelic use.
People who developed HPPD were more likely than psychedelic-using controls to subsequently develop anxiety, depression, pain disorders, fatigue, functional neurological disorder, and PTSD.
Increased fibrinogen contribution to clot strength (FIBTEM MCF on ROTEM) showed a direct, linear association with risk of PASC in adjusted analyses.
Elevated fibrinogen-driven clot strength (FIBTEM MCF) was similarly associated with patient-reported moderate or greater post-exertional malaise (PEM).
Elevated fibrinogen-driven clot strength (FIBTEM MCF) was similarly associated with patient-reported fatigue.
Fibrinogen-driven clot strength (FIBTEM MCF) was not significantly associated with brain fog.
At 15 months after hospitalization for COVID-19 ALI/ARDS, 24% of survivors met criteria for PASC, 43% reported PEM, 27% reported fatigue, and 20% reported brain fog.
Fractional anisotropy in the fornix was significantly reduced in participants with N-PASC relative to controls after FDR correction.
Mean, radial, and axial diffusivity were elevated in the fornix among N-PASC participants relative to controls.
Correlational tractography identified bilateral, permutation-significant white matter diffusion abnormalities in the forceps minor associated with N-PASC status.
Lower whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy was strongly associated with greater fatigue among N-PASC participants.
Lower whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy was associated with greater executive impairment among N-PASC participants.
Lower whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy was associated with mood disorder among N-PASC participants.
Fractional anisotropy within the core tractography-defined ROI showed an even stronger association with N-PASC status than whole-brain metrics.
The strong association between core-ROI FA and N-PASC status was driven primarily by fatigue.
Among N-PASC participants, whole-brain white matter FA, AD, MD, and RD were significantly correlated with visual memory performance.
Whole-brain white matter FA was negatively associated with working memory performance among N-PASC participants.
Participants with N-PASC scored significantly lower on measures of working memory and verbal fluency compared with controls.
No significant differences in white matter diffusion metrics were found between COVID-19-recovered controls and never-infected controls, supporting combining them into a single control group.
In a small PET substudy of N-PASC participants, whole-brain white matter FA was positively correlated with TSPO distribution volume, a marker of glial activation.
There was no statistically significant correlation between time since COVID-19 infection and white matter diffusion markers.
Among N-PASC participants, brain fog and fatigue formed the most common co-occurring symptom pattern, with a median of two neurological symptoms reported.
Higher frequency of post-exertional malaise was significantly correlated with lower EQ-5D index scores in Long COVID patients.
Higher frequency of post-exertional malaise was significantly correlated with lower EQ-VAS self-rated health scores.
Participants with daily PEM had the lowest HRQoL, whereas those with PEM less than monthly had the highest HRQoL scores, with significant differences across all PEM frequency categories.
Higher fatigue severity (FAS score) was significantly correlated with lower EQ-5D index HRQoL.
Higher fatigue severity was significantly correlated with lower EQ-VAS self-rated health scores.

In multivariable regression adjusting for age, sex, employment, comorbidities, PEM frequency, and social status, each one-point increase in fatigue severity was independently associated with a 0.98-point decrease in EQ-5D index, but not significantly associated with EQ-VAS.
In adjusted regression, monthly PEM (versus daily PEM) was associated with significantly higher (better) EQ-VAS self-rated health scores.
Weekly PEM (versus daily PEM) showed only a borderline, non-significant association with better EQ-VAS scores in the adjusted model.
Unemployed participants reported significantly lower HRQoL than employed participants on both the EQ-5D index and EQ-VAS.
Older age was positively associated with EQ-5D index scores but showed no significant association with EQ-VAS.
Gender (female vs. male) was not a significant predictor of HRQoL in the adjusted regression models.
The large majority of participants reported at least some pain or discomfort, with most reporting moderate problems.
Most participants reported impairment in usual activities, with over a third reporting severe impairment.
Mobility problems were common, affecting more than half of the sample.
Self-care impairment was relatively uncommon compared to other EQ-5D domains.
About a third of participants reported anxiety/depression problems, mostly moderate in severity.
Overall HRQoL in this Long COVID cohort with PEM was low, with mean EQ-5D index and EQ-VAS scores comparable to those reported for other serious chronic illnesses such as dementia and PTSD.
Weekly PEM was the most commonly reported frequency, occurring in over half of participants with Long COVID and PEM.

The most frequent diagnoses recorded in electronic health records for Long COVID patients were respiratory conditions, joint pain, cardiovascular issues, malaise and fatigue, and ear/nose/throat issues.

Journal entries from the same Long COVID patients highlighted symptoms similar to EHR diagnoses, including tiredness/fatigue, pain, respiratory challenges, mental health concerns, and cardiovascular issues.

Compared to EHR diagnoses, patient journal entries placed greater emphasis on subjective and functional symptoms such as fatigue, brain fog, and mental health, and captured the impact of Long COVID on daily, work, and social activities that EHRs did not capture.
Manual review of 10 randomly selected cases with co-occurring EHR and journal entries showed limited to no overlap in symptom description between the two data sources for the same encounter periods.

The study concludes that neither EHR data nor patient-reported journal data alone fully captures the Long COVID experience, suggesting integration of both data types is needed for complete understanding and treatment.
Long covid is now a recognised condition affecting up to 60% of COVID-19 cases, with 41% having persisting symptoms after 1 year and 19% after 2 years.

A cited systematic review and meta-analysis found a 16% reduction in 6-minute walk test distance compared with age- and gender-matched norms, and a 59% return-to-employment rate, within 6 months of COVID-19 hospitalisation.
A cited Swedish cohort study found that 9% of COVID-19 cases were on sick leave four months after infection.
The number of people economically inactive due to long-term sickness has risen by over 400,000 to more than 2.5 million since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
In a prior cohort study of a rehabilitation programme, only half of participants who completed the programme successfully returned to work, with little exploration of factors affecting success.

Phase 1 interviews found that most participants had difficulties returning to work, primarily due to fatigue and breathlessness, with symptom heterogeneity between and within individuals complicating return-to-work, and lack of colleague/manager understanding leading to premature return and relapse.
Employer flexibility (role/task adaptation, ability to work from home) and family support outside work were identified by participants as fundamental to successful return-to-work.

In the feasibility case series (n=6), no changes were observed between baseline and follow-up on measures of fatigue, disability, illness perceptions, generalised anxiety or trauma following the long covid vocational rehabilitation intervention.
Group median PHQ-9 scores improved from moderate to mild depression following the long covid vocational rehabilitation intervention.
Group median Work and Social Adjustment Scale scores improved, indicating reduced functional limitation/psychopathology affecting work and social participation after the intervention.

Following the intervention, 10 of 17 participant-set vocational goals were rated as achieved (4 'a lot more achieved', 5 'achieved as expected'), three were partially achieved, and one was unchanged; all participants achieved at least one goal.

Following the intervention, five of six participants remained in work; changes in working hours varied (one increased, two decreased, two unchanged), and one participant sought a reduction to 60% whole-time-equivalent hours instead of retiring.

Qualitative acceptability interviews identified three themes (emotional restoration, resources/practical benefits, distinctive service configuration involving employer negotiation) and participants overwhelmingly found the intervention beneficial despite initial apprehension.
Despite high pre-intervention levels of depression and anxiety, and mood improving for some, anxiety levels remained high following the intervention.
Consistent with other research, breathlessness and fatigue were identified as the symptoms most affecting work ability in people with long covid.

Some employers did not implement suggested workplace adjustments, citing lack of funding or requiring input from their own occupational health services rather than the treating occupational therapist.

Occupational therapists concluded that the long covid vocational rehabilitation intervention constituted specialist Tier 3 support, due to the complexity, chronicity, and specialist knowledge required (e.g., employment legislation, negotiation, fatigue management).

Dealing with non-work-related 'current issues' such as claiming disability benefits and processing bereavement/COVID-19 experiences consumed the most intervention time, ahead of work-focused vocational rehabilitation activities.
The feasibility sample was predominantly women, who may face additional pressures such as homeschooling alongside work, limiting representativeness of the broader long covid population.

Occupational therapists observed 'boom-and-bust' cycles of activity and fatigue in participants, similar to those seen in other chronic fatigue conditions, requiring patients to accept their diagnosis and limitations to enable sustainable work adjustments.
Accepting that they may be unable to resume their pre-COVID-19 role without adjustment or modified duties has been identified (in cited prior work) as a predictor of return to work.
Among 1071 patients with COVID-19 in the cohort, 66.7% developed long COVID, defined as at least one symptom persisting ≥3 months after initial infection.
Among respondents with long COVID, fatigue and runny nose were the most commonly reported symptoms, each reported by about 32%.
20%-24% of long COVID respondents reported headache, cough, nasal congestion, and sore throat.
The restricted mean resolution time for long COVID symptoms was slightly longer for women (323.9 days) than for men (311.1 days).
Younger individuals were more likely than older patients to experience long COVID.
Patients who were overweight, obese, or underweight reported long COVID more frequently than patients with normal body weight.
Patients with pre-existing psychological disorders showed a higher risk of long COVID than those without.
Patients with pre-existing psychological disorders had a higher risk of developing long COVID compared to those without such disorders.
Patients with pre-existing seasonal allergies had a higher risk of developing long COVID compared to those without seasonal allergies.
Participants with long COVID reported physical and mental health scores approximately one standard deviation lower than U.S. adult population norms on the PROMIS Global Health measure.
Most participants reported being either physically inactive or insufficiently active according to national aerobic PA guidelines.
Nearly all participants reported engaging in less physical activity than they did before the COVID-19 pandemic began.
Most participants perceived that physical activity worsened their long COVID symptoms.
A minority of participants reported that physical activity improved their long COVID symptoms.
About one-fifth of participants perceived that physical activity had no effect on their long COVID symptoms.
Fatigue or exhaustion during and/or following physical activity was the most frequently endorsed worsened symptom.
Participants reported crashing or feeling worse (post-exertional malaise) following physical activity, driving a distinct theme in the data.
A substantial proportion of participants reported worsened symptoms the day following physical activity.

Undesirable heart rate changes, including tachycardia, were noted with physical activity among a subset of participants, with the authors noting POTS as a documented long COVID comorbidity in which exercise can act as a trigger.
About a third of participants believed physical activity was beneficial for their health, motivating them to attempt it despite symptom concerns.

Worsened mental health themes emerged around perceived external control over physical activity, a forced inactive lifestyle, and loss of former abilities/identity, which the authors interpret through self-determination theory (competence, autonomy, relatedness) as contributing to psychological distress.
Improved mental health themes emerged including a sense of accomplishment, improvements in PA abilities, and increased hope, particularly among those experiencing symptom improvement.
Among 128 COPD patients with Long COVID, the most prevalent symptoms were cough/sputum (100%), fatigue/weakness (90.6%), and dyspnea (88.3%).
The newly developed LCSSI demonstrated excellent internal consistency in COPD patients with Long COVID, with a Cronbach's alpha of .88.
LCSSI scores correlated positively with the COPD Assessment Test, supporting convergent validity.
LCSSI scores correlated negatively with the 15D Health-Related Quality of Life scale, indicating worse quality of life with higher symptom severity.
Mean LCSSI total and core symptom scores were significantly higher in GOLD Group E COPD patients compared to other GOLD groups, supporting construct validity.
Older age was associated with more than double the odds of belonging to the highest-burden versus lowest-burden long COVID symptom cluster.
Female sex was associated with higher odds of belonging to the highest-burden versus lowest-burden long COVID symptom cluster.
Having a pre-existing mental health disorder was associated with higher odds of belonging to the highest-burden versus lowest-burden long COVID symptom cluster.
Immunodeficiency was associated with more than four-fold higher odds of belonging to the highest-burden versus lowest-burden long COVID symptom cluster.
Longitudinal K-means clustering of self-reported symptoms identified three distinct long COVID symptom burden trajectories over 12 months: highest, moderate, and lowest burden.
The moderate-burden long COVID cluster peaked at a median of 3 concurrent symptoms during follow-up, compared with 6 symptoms in the highest-burden cluster.
The lowest-burden long COVID cluster maintained a median of only 1 symptom throughout the 3-12 month follow-up period.

Within the highest-burden cluster, hierarchical clustering identified three distinct symptom phenotypes: multisystemic dysfunction, psychiatric/neurological dysfunction, and physical/respiratory dysfunction.

The highest-burden cluster was characterized by persistent multisystem symptoms including fatigue, concentration difficulty, post-exertional malaise, myalgia, sleep disturbance, gastrointestinal symptoms, headache, irritability, and mobility limitations, peaking at a median of 6 symptoms at 6-9 months.

Among 1,787 SARS-CoV-2 infected cohort participants, 511 (about 29%) met criteria for long COVID with at least one new symptom and concurrent activity limitation persisting 3-12 months post-infection.
Patients with low IGF-I SD scores had significantly higher fatigue (FAS) scores than those with normal IGF-I SD scores.
Patients with low IGF-I SD scores had significantly higher depression (SDS) scores than those with normal IGF-I SD scores.
No significant differences were found in gastrointestinal symptom scores (FSSG) or quality of life (EQ-5D VAS) among IGF-I SD groups.
Serum IGF-I SD values were negatively correlated with ferritin levels in long COVID patients.
Serum IGF-I SD values were negatively correlated with TSH levels.
Serum IGF-I SD values were positively correlated with albumin levels.
Serum IGF-I SD values were positively correlated with free thyroxine (FT4) levels.
Serum growth hormone levels were positively correlated with IGF-I SD values, consistent with a physiological linkage in the GH/IGF-I axis.
Multivariable linear regression showed IGF-I SD was independently and inversely associated with fatigue (FAS) scores after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, albumin, ferritin, thyroid function, and CH50.

Multivariable linear regression showed IGF-I SD was independently and inversely associated with depression (SDS) scores after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, albumin, ferritin, thyroid function, and CH50.
Follow-up duration to recovery trended longer in the low IGF-I SD group compared with normal and high IGF-I SD groups, though the difference was not statistically significant.
Among patients under 50 years old, the low IGF-I SD group had a significantly longer follow-up duration to recovery than other groups.
The proportion of patients achieving recovery during the observation period differed significantly among IGF-I SD groups, with the normal IGF-I group having the highest recovery rate.
Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that the low IGF-I SD group had a significantly longer time to recovery compared with the high IGF-I SD group.
In patients under 50 years old, Kaplan-Meier analysis showed a significant delay in recovery in the low IGF-I SD group compared with the high IGF-I SD group.
Cognitive symptoms such as memory impairment appeared more frequent in the low IGF-I SD group compared with other groups, based on descriptive symptom distribution.
The unadjusted incidence of long COVID symptoms differed significantly by vaccination schedule, being lowest in the S1 (two-dose) group and higher in the S2 and S3 (three-dose) booster groups.
Overall reported COVID-19 infection symptoms during the December 2022-April 2023 wave did not significantly differ among the three vaccination schedule groups.
Male sex was associated with significantly lower odds of symptomatic COVID-19 infection compared with female sex.
Male sex was associated with significantly lower odds of developing long COVID compared with female sex.
Age group (60-69 vs 70-80 years) was not significantly associated with COVID-19 infection or long COVID risk.
BMI category (<24.0 vs ≥24.0) was not significantly associated with COVID-19 infection or long COVID risk.

In multivariable analysis, vaccination schedule showed only a borderline, non-significant association with long COVID risk, with the S2 (three doses at 1-month intervals) schedule trending toward higher odds relative to S1.
Muscular soreness during acute COVID-19 infection differed significantly by vaccination schedule, being most common in the two-dose (S1) group.
Runny nose during acute COVID-19 infection differed significantly by vaccination schedule, being least common in the two-dose (S1) group.
Fatigue, the most reported long COVID symptom, did not differ significantly in frequency across vaccination schedules despite a numerically higher rate in the three-dose schedules.
Pharyngeal discomfort as a long COVID symptom was reported only in the three-dose schedule groups and differed significantly between them.
A third booster dose administered 4-6 months after the second dose (S3 schedule) produced the highest neutralizing antibody titers at 1 month post-vaccination for both inactivated vaccines.
Neutralizing antibody titers declined progressively over the 12-month follow-up in all vaccination schedules, though the extended-interval booster (S3) maintained the highest titers at 12 months.

None of the vaccination schedules or vaccine types elicited any detectable neutralizing activity against the Omicron variant at 1 month post-vaccination, in contrast to robust neutralization of the wild-type strain.

Across all vaccine schedules, neutralization inhibition was consistently ranked wild-type strain greater than Delta variant greater than Omicron variant, reflecting progressive immune escape by newer variants.
CoronaVac recipients in the S3 schedule had a significantly higher incidence of vaccine-related adverse reactions than Covilo recipients in the same schedule.

The authors conclude that booster vaccination reduces long COVID risk in older adults and that optimized (extended) booster intervals may further reduce this risk, consistent with a multi-country study but extending it to older populations with schedule optimization.
The median PHQ-9 depression score among long-term survivors of severe COVID-19 was 4.0, indicating generally mild symptom burden with wide variability.
Using a PHQ-9 cutoff of ≥7, over a third of long-term survivors of severe COVID-19 screened positive for depressive symptoms.
Using the more conservative PHQ-9 cutoff of ≥10, about one-fifth of long-term survivors of severe COVID-19 screened positive for depressive symptoms.
Women in this severe COVID-19 survivor cohort were significantly more likely than men to screen positive for depressive symptoms at both PHQ-9 cutoffs.
The single-factor structure of the PHQ-9 showed better internal consistency than the two-factor (somatic vs affective-cognitive) structure in this severe COVID-19 survivor cohort.

Confirmatory factor analysis showed that two-factor PHQ-9 models (theory-driven and two published alternative specifications) did not fit significantly better than a single-factor model, and interfactor correlations were near-unity or inadmissible, indicating the somatic and cognitive-affective dimensions were not empirically separable.

The fatigue item of the PHQ-9 showed the weakest item-total correlation and lowest standardized factor loading of all items in this severe COVID-19 survivor cohort, suggesting fatigue behaves differently from core depressive symptoms in long COVID.

Sensitivity analysis using oblique (promax and oblimin) rotations of the two-factor EFA solution yielded moderate, not near-unity, interfactor correlations but similar loadings/variance to the orthogonal solution, supporting the unidimensional interpretation of the PHQ-9.

Using the EPILOC PCS case definition, post-COVID-19 syndrome was much less prevalent after infection during the Omicron era (14.5%) than during the early pandemic (29.6%), with an adjusted relative risk of about 0.50.

Applying the externally developed COVIDOM PCS case definition also showed lower prevalence in the Omicron cohort (13.4%) than the early pandemic cohort (20.4%), with a less pronounced risk reduction than the EPILOC definition.
When PCS was defined simply as any new moderate-to-strong symptom, prevalence was 41.5% in the early pandemic cohort versus 24.6% in the Omicron cohort, a 40% relative risk reduction.
The moderate-to-strong fatigue symptom cluster was about half as prevalent following Omicron infection (12.3%) as following early pandemic infection (23.1%).
The neurocognitive impairment symptom cluster showed about half the risk after Omicron infection compared to early pandemic infection.
The chest symptoms cluster showed the greatest relative reduction among common clusters, with roughly 53% lower risk after Omicron infection.
The smell or taste disorder symptom cluster showed the largest reduction of all clusters examined, with an 83% lower relative risk after Omicron infection.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) lasting beyond 14 hours after physical or mental exertion was reported by 14.8% of EPILOC-Omicron participants; this symptom was not assessed in the earlier EPILOC cohort so no comparison could be made.

PCS cases had markedly lower physical and mental health-related quality of life than PCS-negative participants, by about 11-12 SF-12 points, and this magnitude of impairment was similar in both pandemic-period cohorts.

Consistent predictors of PCS case status across both pandemic-period cohorts and all case definitions included treatment for acute infection, female sex, lower education, current smoking, obesity, and pre-existing diseases.
Certain acute-phase symptoms (sore throat, cough, fever, hoarseness, chills, and myalgia) were more frequently reported during acute infection in the Omicron era than during the early pandemic.

Certain acute-phase symptoms (altered smell, altered taste, chest pain, chronic fatigue, diarrhea, anxiety, depressive mood, and memory disturbance) were more common during acute infection in the early pandemic than during the Omicron era.

No post-COVID-19 symptom was more common after Omicron-era infection than after early-pandemic infection; the largest absolute risk differences favoring lower Omicron-era prevalence were for altered smell, altered taste, shortness of breath, rapid physical exhaustion, concentration difficulties, chronic fatigue, and memory disturbance.
More than half of participants with available early follow-up reported at least one persistent symptom 1-2 years after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Persistent symptoms at 1-2 years occurred in 57.6% of hospitalised participants.
Persistent symptoms at 1-2 years occurred in 53.0% of non-hospitalised participants, a rate similar to hospitalised patients.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported persistent symptom in both hospitalised and non-hospitalised participants.
Only a small proportion of participants had a formal long COVID diagnosis recorded in their medical records, despite the high prevalence of self-reported persistent symptoms.
Female sex was associated with persistence of post-COVID symptoms.
Chest pain during the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with subsequent symptom persistence.
Smoking was associated with persistence of post-COVID symptoms.
At five-year follow-up, 14.3% of the total cohort (19.0% of those with early follow-up) sought healthcare for symptoms compatible with post-COVID conditions.

Healthcare encounters at five-year follow-up for symptoms compatible with post-COVID conditions were not formally attributed to prior SARS-CoV-2 infection in the medical records, suggesting under-recognition of long-term post-COVID symptom burden in routine clinical practice.

In Long COVID patients, lung function parameters (FEV1, PEF) improved within the untreated control group but not in the speleotherapy intervention group, with FEV1 significantly better in controls than in the intervention group at T2.
Dysfunctional breathing, measured by the Nijmegen Questionnaire, decreased significantly in the Long COVID speleotherapy group at T2 compared with controls, and fatigue (FAS) was reduced at T3.

Fatigue severity, measured by the Fatigue Assessment Scale, was reduced in the Long COVID intervention group at 3-month follow-up, though the median change fell slightly below the proposed minimal clinically important difference.

Maximal inspiratory pressure, an indicator of diaphragmatic strength, improved significantly in the Long COVID intervention group, though this effect did not remain significant after Bonferroni-Holm correction for multiple comparisons.

The Long COVID intervention group showed significant improvements over controls in three of fourteen Long COVID Questionnaire domains-dyspnoea, problems with stair climbing/muscle exertion, and anxiety/sleep disturbances-at T2, with the dyspnoea improvement persisting at 3 months.

Speleotherapy showed a favorable safety profile across the combined asthma, COPD, and Long COVID cohort: two intervention-group participants developed upper respiratory tract infections possibly related to therapy, and no serious adverse events were observed.

Fractional exhaled nitric oxide, the pre-defined primary endpoint for the asthma subgroup, did not change significantly with speleotherapy in either arm, indicating no measurable effect on type 2 airway inflammation.

In asthma patients, speleotherapy significantly improved lung function (FVC, PEF, and FEV1 in those under 70), respiratory muscle strength (MIP, MEP), asthma control (ACT), and asthma-related quality of life (AQLQ) compared with controls, with ACT and AQLQ improvements meeting established minimal clinically important difference thresholds.

In COPD patients, speleotherapy significantly improved COPD Assessment Test (CAT) scores relative to controls, meeting or exceeding the minimal clinically important difference, despite no measurable improvement in lung function or respiratory muscle strength.
During a single therapy session inside the cave, end-tidal CO2 (PetCO2) increased significantly while respiratory rate decreased significantly during and immediately after cave exposure.

Participants treated in higher-CO2 caves (Bindweide/Ennepetal) showed significantly higher PetCO2 and blood pCO2 at T2 than those treated in lower-CO2 caves (Bodenmais/Prettau), though the difference was no longer significant at 3 months.

The authors hypothesize that the cool, still, underground speleotherapy environment may exert vagotonic effects contributing to reduced respiratory rate and improved dysfunctional breathing, complementing direct effects on bronchial mucosal oedema.

Across the total cohort of patients with asthma, COPD, and Long COVID, dysfunctional breathing (NQ) decreased significantly in the speleotherapy group at T2 and T3 versus controls, and respiratory muscle strength improved only in the intervention group.
Intake of ultra-processed foods did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
Sugary product intake did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
PRES diet quality scores did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
TNF-α levels did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
TGF-β levels did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
IL-6 levels did not differ significantly among control, acute PACS, and chronic PACS groups.
Among women with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome, poorer diet quality was associated with greater symptom burden, particularly in fatigue, memory, mental health, circulatory, and skin symptom domains.
Principal component analysis indicated that post-acute COVID-19 syndrome reflects a convergence of genomic instability, systemic inflammation, and low diet quality.
Overall, only a limited number of associations were observed among diet quality, health index, and biological (inflammatory, neurotrophic, DNA damage) markers.
The WHO estimates that 10-15% of COVID-19 survivors worldwide develop post-COVID-19 condition (PCC).
Cognitive dysfunction is one of the most common PCC symptoms, affecting approximately 22% of the post-COVID-19 population.

Cognitive symptom burden in PCC appears to worsen over time, increasing from 6 months to 2-3 years after infection onset, with both worsening of pre-existing symptoms and emergence of new-onset symptoms.
Objective neuropsychological testing shows PCC patients have deficits across multiple cognitive domains including attention, memory, executive function, language, and visuospatial ability.
Multiple prior studies found decreased fractional anisotropy and axial diffusivity in white matter of PCC patients.
Prior studies found increased mean diffusivity and radial diffusivity in white matter of PCC patients.
White matter microstructural changes in PCC patients were related to impaired performance in verbal fluency, concentration, and information processing speed.

Resting-state fMRI studies reported disrupted functional connectivity between the hippocampus and parietal areas, between prefrontal regions and cerebellum/occipital lobes, and between bilateral parahippocampal regions in PCC patients.
Enhanced functional connectivity was reported between the striatum and parietal cortex, and between the cerebellum and resting-state networks, in PCC patients.
Altered functional connectivity involving the cerebellum and hippocampus was associated with performance in memory, cognitive control, and working memory tasks among PCC patients.

Graph theoretical analysis revealed altered regional topological measures (nodal, betweenness, and closeness centrality) in nodes such as the olfactory gyrus, orbitofrontal and cingulate cortices, and thalamus in PCC patients relative to healthy people, linked to divided attention and verbal memory performance.

In mild traumatic brain injury patients with postconcussion symptoms, 14 sessions of acupuncture significantly increased FA values in several white matter tracts compared with sham acupuncture, and the FA increase was associated with improvement of postconcussion symptoms.
Acupuncture at bilateral Zusanli (ST36) increased global network efficiency of the functional brain network in healthy subjects.

A systematic review of 44 rs-fMRI studies found that acupuncture increased default mode network and sensorimotor network connectivity with pain-, affective-, and memory-related brain areas, and increased connectivity between periaqueductal gray, anterior cingulate cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, insula, limbic/paralimbic regions, and precuneus compared with sham acupuncture, across healthy people and patients with nervous system, motor system, and other diseases.

In patients with mild cognitive impairment, acupuncture-induced increases in resting-state functional connectivity between cognition-related regions (insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, inferior parietal lobule, anterior cingulate cortex) were positively associated with improved cognitive performance.
Two case reports indicated that acupuncture treatment significantly improved cognitive symptoms in patients with post-COVID-19 condition.

Receiving an autism diagnosis provided participants with an explanatory framework for previously unarticulated social differences, producing a sense of relief and reducing self-blame or guilt for past negative experiences.

Participants described that autism diagnosis can also introduce or reinforce negative stereotypes, with some perceiving public perceptions of autism as polarized between 'non-functional' and 'genius' extremes, and worrying that mistakes would be misattributed to their autism.

Some participants constructed a positive 'Asperger's/Yǎsī' identity associated with traits such as intelligence and honesty, influenced by public figures such as Ko Wen-je and Greta Thunberg who publicly disclosed autistic traits.

After diagnosis, participants used autism-related knowledge (obtained from research, online communities, and peer stories) as a 'guidebook' to increase self-awareness of autistic traits and to self-initiate modification of social behaviors to reduce social difficulties.
The autism diagnosis acted as a gateway to connecting with other autistic peers (online and in person), reducing feelings of isolation and fostering a sense of belonging and shared identity.

Participants used their autism diagnosis to explain their difficulties to non-autistic peers, teachers, and family, which improved others' understanding and empathy and validated their previously invisible struggles.
A formal autism diagnosis was used by adolescents to negotiate with the Taiwanese educational system, resulting in increased teacher flexibility, tolerance, and accommodation of atypical behaviors.

Formal autism diagnosis provided practical access to educational resources including disability certification, special education eligibility, group therapy/counseling, and individualized sensory accommodations (e.g., a quiet room).

The study sample skewed toward female participants and later age at autism diagnosis (8–18 years) compared to the broader autistic population, likely reflecting that participation required high self-awareness, verbal ability, and self-advocacy.
The myogenic gene ASB15 was downregulated 2.18-fold in paraspinal muscle of patients who developed proximal junctional failure compared to those who did not.
The fatty acid metabolism gene FABP4 was significantly upregulated (1.42-fold) in paraspinal muscle of patients who developed proximal junctional failure compared to those who did not.
FABP4 gene expression positively correlated with multifidus functional cross-sectional area measured on MRI.
No significant differences in histologic muscle morphology or fiber size were found between PJF and non-PJF patients.
Higher continuous autism traits (SRS) were associated with reduced gaze inter-subject correlation magnitude across all four naturalistic video paradigms in separate dimensional models.
Higher continuous autism traits (SRS) were associated with attenuated shared pupillary (autonomic arousal) synchrony during The Present, Despicable Me, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid.
Continuous ADHD traits (SWAN) showed no significant independent association with gaze or pupillary synchrony after FDR correction in separate dimensional models.

Continuous trait severity (SRS and SWAN) did not significantly predict absolute gaze phase divergence in any video paradigm after FDR correction, indicating idiosyncratic spatial locking is not linearly related to trait severity.
In joint models controlling for shared variance with ADHD traits, autistic traits uniquely predicted reduced gaze synchrony across all four video contexts.
In joint models, autistic traits retained unique predictive power over attenuated pupillary synchrony during The Present and Diary of a Wimpy Kid, independent of ADHD traits.
In joint models, ADHD traits (SWAN) had no unique explanatory power for physiological synchrony once autistic traits were accounted for.

The continuous SRS × SWAN interaction term showed no significant effect on any physiological synchrony metric across any video, indicating no synergistic effect of comorbid trait severity at the dimensional level.
In the categorical 2x2 ANCOVA, an isolated ASD diagnosis produced severe main-effect reductions in gaze synchrony across all four video stimuli relative to comparison groups.
An isolated ADHD diagnosis (without ASD) also showed significant main-effect reductions in gaze synchrony during Despicable Me, Diary of a Wimpy Kid, and Fun with Fractals.

A significant, non-additive ASD × ADHD interaction was found for gaze synchrony during socially/dynamically complex videos: comorbid ASD+ADHD children showed less severe gaze decoupling than the isolated-ASD group, though this buffering was absent for the abstract Fractals video.
Isolated ASD diagnosis showed strong main effects of increased absolute gaze phase divergence (idiosyncratic spatial locking) during the dynamic Despicable Me and Diary of a Wimpy Kid videos.

A significant negative ASD × ADHD interaction on absolute gaze phase divergence showed that comorbid children's spatial error was pulled back toward the normative trajectory relative to isolated ASD during dynamic videos.
Isolated ASD diagnosis showed significant main-effect reductions in pupillary (autonomic) synchrony during Despicable Me and Diary of a Wimpy Kid.

A significant positive ASD × ADHD interaction on Pupil ISC during Diary of a Wimpy Kid indicates comorbid ADHD partially normalizes autonomic arousal responses that are typically decoupled in isolated autism.

A sensitivity check found that the isolated-ASD group actually had significantly milder autism trait severity than the comorbid ASD+ADHD group, ruling out the possibility that comorbid buffering was simply due to lower baseline autism severity.

A robust regression sensitivity analysis (Huber's T norm) confirmed that the ASD × ADHD buffering interaction on gaze synchrony remained highly significant in narrative video contexts, ruling out an outlier-driven artifact.
Acute stimulant medication use on the day of testing was rare (1.09% of the full sample) and did not account for or alter the ASD × ADHD buffering interaction when included as a covariate.
Across the full cohort, narrative-driven videos elicited stronger gaze inter-subject correlation than the abstract, non-social Fractals video, confirming context-dependent baseline entrainment.
Pupillary synchrony was highest during socially salient narrative videos and lower during action-oriented or abstract media across the full cohort.
Of 36 COVID-19 patients without pre-existing glucose metabolism disorders, 24 developed de novo insulin resistance by 4 months post-infection, while 12 maintained normal glucose metabolism.
Blood glucose levels at 4 months post-COVID-19 did not differ significantly between patients who developed insulin resistance and those without glucose metabolism disorders.
Circulating insulin levels were significantly higher in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to those without glucose metabolism disorders.
HOMA-IR index was significantly elevated in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to patients without glucose metabolism disorders, confirming the IR diagnosis.
Serum IL-6 was significantly increased in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to patients without glucose metabolism disorders.
Serum IL-8 was significantly increased in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to patients without glucose metabolism disorders.
Serum CXCL-9 was significantly increased in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to patients without glucose metabolism disorders.
Serum CXCL-10 was significantly increased in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to patients without glucose metabolism disorders.

Liver enzymes AST, ALT and alkaline phosphatase were significantly elevated in patients who developed post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to those without glucose metabolism disorders, suggesting hepatic/pancreatic involvement.
Circulating miR-495-3p, previously linked to diabetes complications, was upregulated in the post-COVID-19 insulin resistance group compared to controls.
Pre-existing glucose metabolism disorders (before COVID-19) predisposed patients to acute-phase ARDS, but the development of insulin resistance after COVID-19 was not associated with acute ARDS.
Basal (unstimulated) NETosis was significantly increased in neutrophils isolated from patients with post-COVID-19 insulin resistance compared to the other patient groups.

Stimulation with IL-6 and TNF-α produced a greater increase in NETosis in neutrophils from patients with pre-existing GMDs or post-viral insulin resistance compared to patients with no metabolic alteration.
Intracellular TLR7 and TLR8 expression in isolated neutrophils did not differ significantly between patient groups.

Neutrophils from patients with post-COVID-19 insulin resistance failed to show the significant NETosis increase seen in non-GMD patients upon stimulation with TLR7/8 agonists imiquimod, R848, and CL075, indicating a blunted antiviral TLR7/8 response, while TLR8-selective agonists ssRNA40/41 produced no differences in either group.

Plasma from patients with post-COVID-19 insulin resistance induced greater NETosis in healthy donor neutrophils than plasma from patients without glucose metabolism disorders, at 1, 5, and 6 hours of exposure.

Acute-phase plasma, despite containing higher cytokine levels than 4-month plasma, did not induce a significant increase in NETosis in healthy neutrophils, suggesting cytokines alone are not the main driver of the observed NETosis effect.
NETosis percentage positively correlated with insulin levels and HOMA-IR index in the insulin-resistant group, but showed no correlation with blood glucose.

In vitro, healthy neutrophils exposed to glucose plus insulin showed significantly greater NETosis than those exposed to glucose alone at physiological glucose concentrations; glucose alone only increased NETosis at a non-physiological 25 mM concentration.
Confocal microscopy confirmed that insulin exposure markedly increased NETosis (Sytox Green positivity) in healthy neutrophils compared with glucose alone.

In the DISCOVER pediatric cohort, a substantial proportion of children with mild acute COVID-19 later developed persistent multisystem symptoms, most commonly fatigue, respiratory issues, and somatic complaints.
Vaccination was associated with reduced risk of subsequent gastrointestinal sequelae in children with pediatric PASC.
Vaccination was associated with preserved pulmonary function by mitigating small airway resistance in children with pediatric PASC.

Advanced diagnostic modalities, including impulse oscillometry and deep learning-assisted echocardiography, detected subclinical organ dysfunction that conventional methods often missed in children with pediatric PASC.
Symptom severity in pediatric PASC was closely linked to elevated anti-nucleocapsid antibody titers.
Higher symptom severity in pediatric PASC was associated with elevated anti-nucleocapsid antibody titers.
Markers of T-cell exhaustion indicated persistent immune dysregulation in pediatric PASC rather than ongoing viral replication.
A preliminary single-center RCT within the cohort found that vitamin D supplementation may reduce overall symptom burden in children with PASC.
Vitamin D supplementation was reported to modulate pro-inflammatory cytokine profiles in children with PASC.
Participants who completed 4 weeks of community-delivered hyperbaric oxygen therapy reported improved fatigue.
Participants who completed 4 weeks of community-delivered hyperbaric oxygen therapy reported improved breathlessness.
Quality of life improved among participants who completed 4 weeks of community-delivered hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
Attending regular HBOT sessions was often difficult for participants due to the ongoing challenges associated with long COVID.
Individuals with severe long COVID showed poorer functional performance on the 30-second sit-to-stand test compared to matched healthy controls at 18 and 24 months post-infection.
Self-reported fatigue measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale was significantly higher in the severe long COVID group compared to controls at 18 and 24 months post-infection.
Rate of force development, a measure of neuromuscular function, was significantly lower in the severe long COVID group compared to controls at 18 and 24 months post-infection.
Ultrasound-derived muscle thickness did not differ significantly between the severe long COVID group and healthy controls.
Ultrasound-derived muscle echogenicity, a marker of muscle quality, did not differ significantly between the severe long COVID group and healthy controls.

A commentary highlights that two independent studies found autoantibodies present in a subset of long COVID patients that may directly cause symptoms such as pain, fatigue, and neurocognitive problems.
Long COVID commonly presents with fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, including impaired memory, attention deficits ('brain fog'), and executive dysfunction.
Brain fog and anxiety were reported significantly more often in patients infected with the Alpha variant compared to the wild-type Wuhan variant.
SARS-CoV-2 shows neurotropic potential, with viral proteins and RNA detected in brain tissue and neural cell cultures.
Neuroimaging in Long COVID patients shows reduced gray matter thickness and overall brain volume, likely mediated by chronic neuroinflammation.
Persistent elevation of the cytokine CCL11 and microglial activation may suppress neurogenesis and contribute to prolonged neuroinflammation post-infection.
Sustained endothelial dysfunction and abnormal von Willebrand factor levels persist months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A large proportion of adult and pediatric Long COVID patients meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, with 58.7% of adults and 40% of pediatric COVID cases developing ME/CFS.
Elevated IL-6 is implicated in the neuroinflammation shared between Long COVID and ME/CFS.
Elevated IL-1β is implicated in the neuroinflammation shared between Long COVID and ME/CFS.
Endothelin-1 dysregulation in Long COVID correlates with exertion intolerance, mirroring the pattern seen in ME/CFS.
Retinal microvascular damage and abnormal endothelial markers such as von Willebrand factor persist post-infection in Long COVID/ME-CFS patients.
Persistent fatigue in the Saudi Arabian Long COVID population was assessed using the Chalder Fatigue Scale, consistent with global reports of fatigue as a dominant symptom.
43.4% of patients experienced ongoing dyspnea two months after COVID-19 infection.
About 24% of Long COVID patients had dyspnea and dry cough after acute illness in a cohort study.
Elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8) correlate with persistent dyspnea and may contribute to pulmonary fibrosis in Long COVID.
A multinational study of 56 countries found that 86.04% of Long COVID patients experienced chest pain, palpitations, or fainting.
A cohort of over 150,000 COVID-19 survivors showed elevated cardiovascular risks at 12 months post-infection, including arrhythmias, inflammatory heart disease, and ischemic heart disease.
About 30% of Long COVID patients were reported to develop postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

Acute-phase cardiac injury in COVID-19 may involve troponin elevation, with microvascular thrombosis found in a large proportion of autopsy studies, implicating ACE2-mediated viral toxicity and cytokine-driven endothelial injury.

Chronic cardiovascular symptoms in Long COVID are thought to stem from persistent viral reservoirs detected beyond four months or autoimmunity, including antibodies against ACE2, beta2-adrenoceptor, and M2 receptor.
Contrary to the belief that cardiovascular effects relate to COVID vaccination or variant differences, studies found no association between cardiovascular events and vaccines or SARS-CoV-2 variants.

Cardiovascular symptoms such as chest discomfort, palpitations, and exercise intolerance were observed in Saudi Long COVID patients across several observational studies, but without detailed cardiac evaluation.
An international survey of 56 countries found 20.5% of Long COVID patients experienced chronic diarrhea and 13.7% reported appetite loss even seven months post-infection.

In a study of 749 COVID-19 survivors, 29% continued to experience gastrointestinal issues six months after initial recovery, most commonly acid reflux, constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and nausea/vomiting.
Proposed mechanisms behind gastrointestinal symptoms in Long COVID include viral persistence in the gut and dysregulation of the gut microbiome.

Two Saudi studies reported differing prevalence of GI manifestations in Long COVID: 28.5% (Al Argan et al.) versus 13.2% (Alzahrani et al.), likely reflecting differences in study design rather than true prevalence variation.
Women with Long COVID commonly experience menstrual irregularities, and altered follicular fluid composition with reduced IL-1β and VEGF levels has been suggested as a marker of ovarian dysfunction.
Other research found no direct ovarian impairment from COVID-19, suggesting menstrual irregularities may instead result from systemic inflammation or stress rather than direct ovarian damage.
In men, COVID-19 is associated with reduced sperm quality and production, potentially due to viral damage or immune responses.
A large retrospective study of 486 men found increased risks of ejaculatory dysfunction, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction following COVID-19 infection.
Persistent erectile issues in Long COVID may stem from SARS-CoV-2 remnants in penile tissue disrupting vascular function.
ME/CFS patients with Long COVID often exhibit reproductive issues such as menstrual abnormalities and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
One Saudi cross-sectional study reported changes in menstrual cycle characteristics, including alterations in cycle length, flow, and regularity, following COVID-19 infection.
The Linköping COVID-19 Study found that 28.5% of Long COVID participants reported limb weakness and 10.5% experienced generalized muscle weakness.
Another study found that 18.59% of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors developed joint pain and 15.09% experienced myalgia six months after infection.
SARS-CoV-2 may directly infect musculoskeletal tissue because skeletal muscle cells express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the key proteins used by the virus for cell entry.

Musculoskeletal complaints including muscle pain, joint pain, and generalized weakness were commonly reported in Saudi Long COVID patients, notably as the most prevalent symptom in one study and a significant contributor to post-COVID discomfort in the Ha'il region.

A Saudi web-based survey of 979 recovered COVID-19 patients (mean age 37.7, 53% male) found fatigue/weakness in 73%, headache in 64%, mood changes in 41%, insomnia in 39%, loss of smell in 64% (62% severe, mean duration 13.9 days), cough in 47%, dyspnea in 43%, appetite loss in 42%, and diarrhea in 53%, with age over 40 linked to prolonged weakness, insomnia, and loss of smell/taste.

A Saudi cross-sectional study of 744 recovered COVID-19 patients using the C19-YRS tool found 47.5% reported persistent symptoms (fatigue 25.4%, headache 15.9%, myalgia 8.5%, anxiety 13.2%, depression 9.5%, dyspnea 6.9%, cough 11%), lasting >6 months in 47.2%, with age >50 and comorbidities as risk factors but no significant association with gender or disease severity.

A Saudi cross-sectional study of 486 COVID-19 survivors found 61% reported persistent symptoms (fatigue 56%, breathlessness 47%, loss of smell 44%, muscle aches 40%); comorbidities were not significantly linked to most symptoms except chest pain and tachycardia, and 37% took over a year to recover.

A Saudi study of 327 adults found 49.1% reported persistent symptoms (anosmia 22.6%, ageusia 19.2%, cough 11.6%, fatigue 9.1%, alopecia 7.3%), with females reporting significantly higher rates of anosmia, ageusia, and hair loss, and hospitalization/ICU admission and oxygen use significantly associated with persistence.

A Hail comparative cross-sectional study of 292 adults found both short-term (≤1 year) and long-term (>1 year) COVID groups had significantly lower social functioning on SF-36, with no significant psychological outcomes on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale.
A Saudi study found that vaccinated subjects exhibited significantly higher IgG levels against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein compared to naturally infected patients, regardless of disease severity.

In Riyadh, anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG antibodies induced by BNT162b2 and ChAdOx1 vaccines were detected in most subjects after the prime dose, peaked after a booster, remained elevated for six months, declined after one year, and increased again after a third dose, with previously infected and younger subjects showing higher titers.
A Sakaka City cross-sectional seroprevalence study found statistically significant correlations between vaccination status—especially after a second dose—and IgM/IgG positivity.
Women with long COVID commonly report menstrual irregularities, suggesting an effect on reproductive hormonal cycles.
Some studies suggest ovarian dysfunction in long COVID is reflected by reduced interleukin-1β and VEGF levels in follicular fluid.
Other research found no direct ovarian impairment in long COVID patients, suggesting menstrual irregularities may result from systemic inflammation or stress rather than direct ovarian damage.
In men, COVID-19 is associated with reduced sperm quality and production, potentially due to direct viral damage or immune responses.
A large retrospective study of 486 men found increased risks of ejaculatory dysfunction, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction following COVID-19.
Persistent erectile dysfunction may stem from SARS-CoV-2 remnants in penile tissue disrupting vascular function.
ME/CFS patients with long COVID often exhibit reproductive issues such as menstrual abnormalities and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
A Saudi cross-sectional study found alterations in menstrual cycle length, flow, and regularity following COVID-19 infection.
The Linköping COVID-19 Study found that 28.5% of long COVID participants reported limb weakness and 10.5% experienced generalized muscle weakness.
A study found that 18.59% of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors developed joint pain and 15.09% experienced myalgia six months after infection.
SARS-CoV-2 may directly infect musculoskeletal tissue since skeletal muscle cells express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the key proteins the virus uses for cell entry.

Muscle pain, joint pain, and generalized weakness are commonly reported musculoskeletal complaints among Saudi long COVID patients, being among the most prevalent symptoms in the Garout et al. study and a significant contributor to post-COVID discomfort in a Ha'il region study.
A Saudi cross-sectional web-based survey of 979 COVID-19 recovered individuals found that 73% reported fatigue and weakness of moderate severity with a mean duration of 7-8 days.
In the same Saudi survey, loss of smell was reported by 64% of participants, with 62% describing it as severe and a mean duration of 13.9 days.
Participants older than 40 years in the Saudi survey were associated with prolonged weakness, insomnia, and loss of smell/taste.

A Saudi cross-sectional survey of 744 recovered COVID-19 patients using the C19-YRS tool found that 47.5% reported persistent symptoms, most commonly fatigue (25.4%), headache (15.9%), myalgia (8.5%), anxiety (13.2%), depression (9.5%), dyspnea (6.9%), and cough (11%).
In the Garout et al. Saudi study, age over 50 years and comorbidities were significantly associated with persistent long COVID symptoms.
No significant association was found between gender or COVID-19 severity/hospitalization status and persistent symptom development in the Garout et al. Saudi cohort.

A Saudi cross-sectional study of 486 COVID-19 survivors found that 61% reported persistent symptoms, most commonly fatigue (56%), breathlessness (47%), loss of smell (44%), and muscle aches (40%); the study population was 71% female and 43% aged 18-30.
In the Almalag et al. Saudi cohort, comorbidities were not significantly linked to most long COVID symptoms, with the exceptions of chest pain and tachycardia.
Ovarian dysfunction in Long COVID has been suggested via altered follicular fluid composition with reduced IL-1β and VEGF levels.

Other research found no direct ovarian impairment in Long COVID, suggesting reported menstrual irregularities may instead result from systemic inflammation or stress rather than direct ovarian damage.
COVID-19 is associated with reduced sperm quality and production in men, potentially due to viral damage or immune responses.
A large retrospective study of 486 men found increased risks of ejaculatory dysfunction, decreased libido, and erectile dysfunction following COVID-19.
Persistent erectile dysfunction in Long COVID may stem from SARS-CoV-2 remnants in penile tissue disrupting vascular function.
ME/CFS patients with Long COVID often exhibit reproductive issues such as menstrual abnormalities and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
A Saudi cross-sectional study found alterations in menstrual cycle characteristics, including cycle length, flow, and regularity, following COVID-19 infection.
The Linköping COVID-19 Study reported that 28.5% of Long COVID participants had limb weakness and 10.5% had generalized muscle weakness.
Among hospitalized COVID-19 survivors, 18.59% developed joint pain and 15.09% experienced myalgia six months after infection.
Skeletal muscle cells express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the key proteins SARS-CoV-2 uses for cell entry, suggesting a mechanism for direct viral infection of musculoskeletal tissue.
A regional study in the Ha'il region of Saudi Arabia identified muscle pain as a significant contributor to post-COVID discomfort.
Studies have shown no association between cardiovascular events in Long COVID and either vaccination or SARS-CoV-2 variant species, contrary to prior beliefs.
In a Saudi study, vaccinated individuals had significantly higher IgG levels against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein compared to naturally infected hospitalized patients, regardless of disease severity.

In Riyadh, anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG antibodies from BNT162b2 and ChAdOx1 vaccines peaked after a booster dose, remained elevated for six months, declined by one year, and increased again following a third dose, with higher titers noted in previously infected and younger individuals.
A cross-sectional seroprevalence study in Sakaka City found statistically significant correlations between vaccination status, especially after a second dose, and IgM/IgG positivity.

A 2025 study found enduring elevation of IgG and IgA antibodies over a six-month period following a third dose of an mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine in healthy Saudi individuals, indicating swift and durable immune activation.
In healthcare workers, both Pfizer (BNT162b2) and AstraZeneca (ChAdOx1) vaccines showed declining neutralizing antibodies after six months, but T-cell responses persisted.

A Phase 2 multicenter open-label trial (NCT04915300) is investigating oral apabetalone for Long COVID, assessing functional capacity via 6-minute walk test and symptoms such as fatigue and cognitive impairment, with Saudi Arabia as a key recruitment site; results have not yet been published.

Diagnosis and management of Long COVID face significant challenges due to symptom variety, unclear pathophysiology, and the lack of standardized biomarkers, with diagnosis currently based solely on clinical history.
Potential biomarkers for Long COVID, such as micro-clots, immune dysregulation, and viral persistence, remain to be fully explored and validated.
Because of overlapping symptoms, clinicians must be cautious in differentiating Long COVID from ME/CFS, dysautonomia (including POTS), and mast cell activation syndrome.

A Hail, Saudi Arabia comparative study found both short-term (≤1 year) and long-term (>1 year) COVID groups had significantly lower social functioning on the SF-36 quality-of-life scale, with no significant differences in psychological outcomes measured by the Hamilton Anxiety Scale.
In the Jabali et al. Jeddah study, female sex was significantly associated with higher rates of persistent anosmia, ageusia, and hair loss compared to males.
In the Jabali et al. study, hospitalization, ICU admission, and oxygen requirement (in 20.8% of participants) were significantly associated with persistent Long COVID symptoms.
Long COVID videos on Bilibili had significantly higher median Global Quality Score and modified DISCERN scores than videos on TikTok.
Long COVID videos produced by professional sources showed significantly higher quality scores than those from non-professional sources.
In multivariate linear regression, professional source was the strongest independent predictor of both GQS and mDISCERN scores for long COVID videos.
Video duration and number of shares were weakly but significantly associated with GQS score, while other engagement metrics showed no significant association.

Among respondents infected at least once with SARS-CoV-2, 16.1% (n=520) reported symptoms lasting at least 2 months after infection that impacted their work or home life 'a lot' or 'extremely', meeting the WHO definition of long COVID.
Among infected respondents, 61.4% reported at least one persistent symptom lasting more than 2 months post-infection, and 25.2% reported four or more such symptoms.
The most commonly reported persistent symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection were fatigue and lack of energy, followed by reduced physical capacity and muscle and joint pain.
In multivariate logistic regression, respondents aged 50–64 had the highest likelihood of developing long COVID among infected respondents.
People engaging in risky stress behaviour (frequent stress combined with poor coping) had twice the odds of developing long COVID compared to those who did not.
Respondents classified as at risk of a depressive disorder (via WHO-5 well-being score) were the group most likely to develop long COVID, emerging as the second most significant factor overall.
The number of SARS-CoV-2 infections was associated with risk of long COVID, with those infected 3 or more times having the highest risk.
Vaccinated individuals had a higher risk of developing long COVID than those who were not vaccinated, did not intend to be, or could not be vaccinated for health reasons.

Respondents who experienced at least one severe episode of COVID-19 had four times higher odds of developing long COVID compared to those with mild or asymptomatic illness, the strongest factor identified.

People with at least one chronic disease (diabetes, asthma, hypertension/cardiovascular disease, COPD/other pulmonary disease, or chronic headache/migraine) had higher odds of developing long COVID than those without.
In bivariate comparison, more women were among those who developed long COVID, but gender was not statistically significant in the adjusted multivariate regression model.

Respondents infected at least once with SARS-CoV-2 were more often younger, more educated, employed, without chronic diseases, and had poorer mental well-being compared with never-infected respondents.

The overall multivariate logistic regression model for long COVID (age, risky stress behaviour, well-being, number of infections, vaccination, severity, chronic disease) was statistically significant and explained 18.9% of variance.
Symptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals had lower maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP) than asymptomatic individuals.
Symptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals had lower sustained maximal inspiratory pressure (SMIP) than asymptomatic individuals.
Symptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals had a lower inspiratory fatigue index (FIT) than asymptomatic individuals.
Total pulmonary aerosol deposition measured by 99mTc-DTPA scintigraphy was reduced in symptomatic compared with asymptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals.
Total lung perfusion measured by 99mTc-MAA scintigraphy was reduced in symptomatic compared with asymptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals.
Symptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals had worse (higher) Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores, indicating poorer sleep quality, than asymptomatic individuals.
Symptomatic post-COVID-19 individuals had worse (higher) Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores, indicating greater daytime sleepiness, than asymptomatic individuals.
The inspiratory fatigue index (FIT) was strongly correlated with total pulmonary aerosol deposition measured by scintigraphy in post-COVID-19 individuals.
Serum IL-6 concentrations were significantly elevated in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls at all follow-up time points (3, 6, and 9 months).
IL-2 was significantly elevated in long COVID patients relative to healthy controls at 3, 6, and 9 months.
IL-17A was significantly elevated in long COVID patients relative to healthy controls at 3, 6, and 9 months.
CXCL9 was significantly elevated in long COVID patients relative to healthy controls at all time points, but this was largely attributable to age.
TNF-α was significantly elevated in long COVID patients relative to healthy controls at all time points.
IFN-γ was significantly elevated in long COVID patients relative to healthy controls at 3, 6, and 9 months.
CXCL10 showed a transient elevation compared with healthy controls only at 3 months, then declined to control levels.
CCL5 showed a transient elevation compared with healthy controls at 6 months, peaking then declining by 9 months.
IL-10 was significantly elevated compared with healthy controls at 3 and 6 months, and increased progressively over follow-up.
CXCL8 did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
CCL2/MCP-1 did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
IL-4 did not differ significantly overall between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
In the severe disease subgroup, IL-2 was significantly higher at 3 months compared with the moderate disease group.
D-dimer levels were significantly lower in the severe disease group compared with the moderate group at 3 and 9 months.
Overall, long-term immune parameters showed only limited differentiation by initial COVID-19 severity, suggesting long-term immune profiles are not strongly determined by initial disease severity.
Presence of any comorbidity was associated with a higher frequency of long COVID symptoms at 3 months, but not at later time points.
Metabolic comorbidities (diabetes mellitus and abdominal obesity) were associated with a significantly higher prevalence of long COVID symptoms only at 3 months.
At 6 months, higher IL-17A, IgM, and platelet counts were associated with symptom persistence in long COVID patients.
At 9 months, patients with persistent symptoms had higher platelet counts, IgM, procalcitonin, and white blood cell counts than asymptomatic patients.
Vaccinated individuals had a significantly lower prevalence of any symptom at 3 and 6 months post-infection compared with unvaccinated individuals, but no difference remained at 9 months.

IL-6 demonstrated good diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing long COVID patients from healthy controls (AUC > 0.82) and remained the only marker independently associated with long COVID status after adjusting for age.
CXCL9's apparent diagnostic ability for long COVID was attenuated after adjusting for age, indicating its discriminatory performance was largely age-driven rather than disease-specific.

No cytokine-cytokine correlations, including IL-6-CXCL9, were observed in the long COVID group, whereas healthy controls exhibited numerous and stable inter-marker relationships, suggesting a loss of coordinated immune regulation after COVID-19.

Prevalence of cough, fatigue, and dyspnea significantly declined over the 9-month follow-up, with the most pronounced improvement between 3 and 6 months and a plateau thereafter; fatigue remained the most common residual symptom at 9 months (23%).
IL-10 concentrations increased significantly across follow-up (3 to 6 and 3 to 9 months), diverging progressively further from healthy control levels.
IFN-γ concentrations decreased significantly over follow-up, between 3 and 6 months and between 3 and 9 months.
CXCL8 concentrations decreased progressively over follow-up (3 to 6 and 6 to 9 months), approaching healthy control levels.
Presence of comorbidities was associated with significantly elevated CXCL8, CXCL9, IL-2, and monocyte percentage at 3 months post-discharge.
Vitamin D deficiency is common in long COVID and is associated with neurocognitive symptoms, delayed recovery, and poor physical performance, particularly in older adults.
Insulin resistance markers are consistently correlated with fatigue, mood disturbances, and myalgia, suggesting a distinct metabolic long COVID phenotype.
Lower cortisol levels frequently correlate with fatigue, sensory disturbances, and neurocognitive symptoms in long COVID.

Alterations in cortisol/ACTH, growth hormone, prolactin, and gonadotropins suggest possible hypothalamic-pituitary axis involvement in long COVID, though these changes are often transient, dynamic, or nonsignificant.
Some long COVID patients exhibit low free triiodothyronine (T3) levels, which are associated with fatigue.
No significant incidence of thyroid dysfunction or autoimmunity was found to be associated with long COVID.
Activation of the kynurenine pathway, with increased kynurenine levels, is observed in long COVID and is associated with fatigue, neurocognitive symptoms, and depressive symptoms.
Increased quinolinic acid, a downstream product of the kynurenine pathway, is associated with fatigue, neurocognitive symptoms, and depressive symptoms in long COVID.
Emerging metabolites related to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid metabolism alterations have been reported in long COVID but require further validation.

Telehealth and online rehabilitation platforms for long COVID typically combined cognitive training, physical exercise, and mental health support delivered via weekly video calls and digital resources.
mHealth tools used in included studies included an immersive VR-based app integrating mindfulness and cognitive training, along with mobile apps and wearable monitoring tools.
VR interventions showed benefits in physical recovery and emotional well-being in long COVID patients, though some users reported side effects such as dizziness and headaches.
A cognitive video game intervention designed to enhance cognitive function led to improvements in processing speed and executive function in long COVID patients.

Digital psychotherapy approaches identified for long COVID included trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy delivered online and telehealth group CBT incorporating verified COVID-19 information and peer support.

A blended multicomponent digital rehabilitation program combining web-based exercise classes, symptom education, and in-person community support, involving over 600 participants, was associated with improved quality of life, mental health, and physical activity.
Remotely supervised transcranial direct current stimulation was reported to improve fatigue and depression in a small case series of long COVID patients.
Across included trials, digital interventions were associated with cognitive improvements including enhanced processing speed and attention, global cognition, and memory performance.
Cognitive effects of digital interventions were not consistent across all studies, with some reporting no significant cognitive gains.
Digital interventions were associated with psychological benefits including reductions in depression and anxiety and improvements in emotional well-being among long COVID patients.
Physical outcomes improved in several digital intervention trials, including enhanced sleep quality, decreased breathlessness, and increased physical activity.
Included studies showed an overrepresentation of women, with digital tool acceptance reported to be higher among women and those with prior digital experience.

Older adults, individuals from low-income households, and those in rural areas were significantly less likely to have consistent access to internet-enabled devices or the digital literacy needed to engage with digital long COVID interventions.
Global mental health status was among the top predictors of whether patients returned to work after COVID-19 infection.
