Global physical health status was among the strongest predictors of return-to-work status following COVID-19 infection.
Emotional distress was one of the top individual symptom predictors of return-to-work status among long COVID symptoms, alongside global mental/physical health.
Number of recovery days was among the top variables predicting return-to-work outcomes after COVID-19 infection.
Back pain was one of the top individual symptom predictors of return-to-work status, alongside emotional distress.

Among employed participants, most returned to usual work duties within about three weeks, a subset resumed work under modified conditions after a longer recovery, and a smaller group could not return to work due to persistent long COVID symptoms.
Acute SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers de novo production of diverse, functional autoantibodies that remain elevated in individuals with long COVID.
Individuals with long COVID who had neurocognitive symptoms showed increased autoantibodies against central and peripheral nervous system proteins compared with those without such symptoms.
Purified IgG from individuals with long COVID reacted with human locus coeruleus, thalamus, adrenal gland, and thyroid tissue.
IgG from individuals with long COVID cross-reacted with mouse sciatic nerve and meninges tissue.
CNS-reactive autoantibodies correlated with several neurological symptoms in individuals with long COVID.
IgG targeting MED20 from patients with long COVID showed enhanced antibody-dependent phagocytosis.

Passive transfer of IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice caused fatigue-like behavior, loss of balance/coordination, thermal hyperalgesia, small fiber nerve damage, and increased pain-related neuronal activity, recapitulating patient symptoms.
Purified IgG from individuals with long COVID cross-reacted with mouse meninges, suggesting CNS-directed autoantibody binding.
CNS-reactive autoantibodies correlated with the presence of several neurological symptoms in individuals with long COVID.
IgG autoantibodies targeting MED20 from long COVID patients showed enhanced antibody-dependent phagocytosis.
Passive transfer of IgG from long COVID patients into mice induced fatigue-like behavior.
Passive transfer of IgG from long COVID patients into mice induced loss of balance and coordination.
Passive transfer of purified IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice induced fatigue-like behavior.
Passive transfer of purified IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice induced loss of balance and coordination.
Passive transfer of purified IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice induced thermal hyperalgesia.
Passive transfer of purified IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice caused small fiber nerve damage.
Passive transfer of purified IgG from individuals with long COVID into mice increased pain-related neuronal activity.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were significantly more frequent in internally displaced children with COVID-19 than in the local population.
Respiratory symptoms during COVID-19 were significantly more common in the local population than in internally displaced children.
Severe fatigue during acute COVID-19 predominated in the local population compared with internally displaced children.
Internally displaced children experienced a more severe clinical course of COVID-19 than local children.
Internally displaced children had a significantly longer duration of hospital stay for COVID-19 than local children.
Serum zinc levels were significantly lower in internally displaced children than in the local population.
Internally displaced children with COVID-19 reported higher total quality-of-life scores than local children, indicating better perceived health status.
IDP children scored higher on the physical functioning domain of quality of life compared to local children.
IDP children scored higher on the psychosocial functioning domain of quality of life compared to local children.
IDP children scored higher on the school functioning domain of quality of life compared to local children.
The overall frequency of long COVID did not differ significantly between internally displaced and local children.
Among children under 6 years of age, long COVID was significantly more frequent in the internally displaced group than in the local population.
Among children aged 6 years and older, long COVID was significantly more common in the local population than in internally displaced children.
The pattern of long COVID symptoms differed by age group between internally displaced and local children.
Self-reported worsening of health was reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
Memory problems were reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
Concentration problems were reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
Dyspnea was reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
Fatigue was reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
Changes in smell or taste were reported more frequently 3-35 months after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test than before infection.
The overall prevalence of long COVID symptoms decreased over the course of the pandemic, being lower at the end of 2022 than in 2020.

Individuals who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 during the Omicron-dominated period reported a lower prevalence of long COVID symptoms than those who tested positive during the period dominated by earlier variants.
COVID-19 autopsy heart, kidney, liver, and lymph node tissues showed prolonged inhibition of OXPHOS transcripts that persisted despite the absence of detectable viral transcripts.
In autopsy lymph nodes, immune gene transcription decreased while the RAAS pathway was markedly upregulated, coinciding with histological scarring.
In autopsy lung tissue, OXPHOS transcripts recovered but immune activation was the highest among all examined tissues, with significantly elevated mitochondrial immune and stress responses.

In the acute-phase (3 dpi) PCS hamster model, mitochondrial ribosomal genes and biogenesis signatures were upregulated in heart, lung and kidney, alongside robust innate immune activation via mtdsRNA and mtDNA signaling across all tissues, most pronounced in lung.

By the post-acute phase (31 dpi) in PCS hamsters, lung OXPHOS transcripts normalized but immune/mitochondrial stress remained elevated, whereas heart and kidney continued to show suppressed OXPHOS expression.

Hamster skeletal muscle showed OXPHOS downregulation with immune/mitochondrial stress activation at 3 dpi that remained suppressed through 31 and 61 dpi, accompanied by extracellular matrix remodeling and later HIF/mTOR pathway upregulation.

Human skeletal muscle biopsies from both PCS-associated chronic fatigue syndrome (PCS-CFS) and Type IIb fiber atrophy CFS (T2bFA-CFS) patients showed downregulated OXPHOS and elevated HIF signaling relative to controls, but PCS-CFS uniquely showed heightened integrated stress response, unfolded protein response, and innate/adaptive immune signaling.
PCS-CFS muscle samples showed significant downregulation of mitochondrial and contraction-related pathways, resembling the pathology seen in hamster muscle at 61 dpi.

At 3 dpi, all sensory tissues (olfactory epithelium, olfactory bulb, trigeminal ganglia) showed robust mitochondrial stress and innate immune activation, with the olfactory bulb and trigeminal ganglia showing strong tissue damage/PANoptosis induction along with suppression of OXPHOS and peroxisomal metabolism.

By 31 dpi, the olfactory epithelium showed persistent HIF activation and suppressed fatty acid oxidation, while trigeminal ganglia immune signaling largely resolved and OXPHOS/mitophagy pathways were upregulated, indicating regeneration.

Sustained suppression of neuronal signaling and synaptic function was observed in the olfactory epithelium and olfactory bulb from 3 to 31 dpi, providing a proposed mechanistic basis for persistent anosmia in PCS.

At 3 dpi, all deep brain regions (mPFC, striatum, thalamus, cerebellum) showed upregulated innate immunity and mitochondrial stress; mPFC and cerebellum showed reduced OXPHOS while striatum and thalamus showed elevated OXPHOS transcripts.

By 31 dpi, the mPFC uniquely worsened with stronger repression of OXPHOS transcripts, while striatum and thalamus showed reduced OXPHOS and cerebellum showed upregulation, indicating heterogeneous regional recovery.

Human COVID-19 autopsy frontal cortex showed pronounced OXPHOS inhibition, increased HIF/mTOR signaling, and widespread immune activation without compensatory mitochondrial stress response, coinciding with suppressed neuronal/synaptic signaling.
In contrast to frontal cortex, the substantia nigra displayed elevated OXPHOS-associated transcripts with minimal immune activation, suggesting regional metabolic resilience.

In PBMCs from patients with severe acute COVID-19, early recovery phase samples showed coordinated downregulation of mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS transcripts across complexes I, III, IV, and V in most immune cell types, a weaker effect seen in mild cases.
Mild COVID-19 patients showed partial metabolic recovery with increased nDNA- and mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS transcripts in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells.

Late-phase (4-12 months) severe COVID-19 patients showed persistent broad suppression of mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS genes across nearly all PBMC subsets, with isolated exceptions such as MT-CO2 and MT-CO3, along with similarly downregulated nDNA-encoded OXPHOS pathways, independent of symptom stratification.

A prior serum metabolomics/biochemical study observed elevated lactate and IL-17 in PCS patients, consistent with increased glycolytic activity and immune dysfunction, which was corroborated by this paper's re-analysis.

Early-phase (acutely hospitalized) COVID-19 patient serum showed elevated glycolytic intermediates (glucose, lactic acid) and decreased TCA cycle intermediates (glutamic acid, citric acid) relative to healthy controls, reflecting a shift toward glycolysis and reduced OXPHOS.

At 20-24 months post-infection, PCS patients retained persistently elevated glucose and reduced glutamic acid, while COVID-recovered individuals also had elevated glucose but to a lesser extent than PCS patients.
Both COVID-recovered and PCS patients showed elevated kynurenine, a tryptophan-derived metabolite linked to chronic inflammation, IDO activation, and NAD+ pathway remodeling.
Participants with Long COVID and post-exertional malaise (LC-PEM) showed significantly reduced glucose metabolism in the left sensorimotor cortex on 18F-FDG PET compared to those without PEM.
The left superior parietal region showed a trend toward reduced metabolism in LC-PEM versus non-PEM participants, but this did not reach statistical significance.
Bilateral primary visual cortex hypometabolism was significantly greater in LC-PEM participants compared to those without PEM.

Cerebral hypometabolism on 18F-FDG PET-CT persisted in Long COVID patients well beyond 6 months post-infection, with scans performed up to 149 weeks (~2 years) after initial symptoms, far exceeding the previously reported longest duration of 155 days.
The majority of the Long COVID cohort (29/40, 73%) exhibited fatigue with post-exertional malaise as a predominant phenotype.
There was no significant difference in the time elapsed from initial COVID-19 symptoms to PET scan between the LC-PEM and non-PEM groups.
Parents of children with autism spectrum disorder reported the highest level of child's challenging behaviour compared with parents of children with other chronic conditions.
Parents of children with type 1 diabetes showed lower stress resistance compared with parents of children with other chronic conditions.
Child's challenging behaviour was significantly associated with higher parental stress across the parent groups studied.
Child's challenging behaviour was significantly associated with reduced parental stress resilience.
Child's challenging behaviour was significantly associated with higher advanced glycation end products in parents, consistent with increased oxidative stress.
Child's challenging behaviour was significantly associated with a longer mean interval between heartbeats in parents.
Advanced glycation end product levels in parents were associated with parental age.
Advanced glycation end product levels in parents were associated with nonsmoking status.
Advanced glycation end product levels in parents were associated with the heart rate variability time-domain parameter pNN50.
Parents of children with chronic conditions showed increased sympathetic activity and impaired sympathovagal balance relative to what would be expected in unaffected adults.
Arterial tortuosity syndrome is caused by biallelic (homozygous) pathogenic variants in SLC2A10, which encodes the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT10, confirmed in all three patients.

The neonatal patient with homozygous SLC2A10 variant exhibited a severe early-onset phenotype with respiratory symptoms, significant feeding dysfunction, congenital heart defects (VSD, PFO), and widespread arterial tortuosity affecting systemic and pulmonary circulations.
The neonate scored 1 on the Dysphagia Outcome and Severity Scale, indicating unsafe oral feeding and need for continued nasogastric tube nutrition.
The 15-month-old infant, carrying the same homozygous SLC2A10 variant, showed a milder phenotype with isolated vascular tortuosity, preserved cardiac function, and no feeding or respiratory symptoms.

Despite identical homozygous SLC2A10 molecular diagnoses, the three patients differed markedly in age at presentation, symptom burden, and extent of vascular involvement, demonstrating broad phenotypic variability of ATS.
Case 3 showed systemic connective tissue involvement beyond the vasculature, including an inguinal hernia and a Morgagni-type diaphragmatic hernia, alongside diffuse arterial tortuosity.
ATS may be associated with systemic connective tissue features such as skin laxity, joint hypermobility, and hernia defects, as noted in the broader literature.

ATS can mimic other heritable connective tissue disorders including Loeys-Dietz syndrome and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, but is distinguished by predominant arterial tortuosity relative to aneurysm formation.
Polyhydramnios in the pregnancy of Case 3 may serve as an early prenatal clinical red flag for arterial tortuosity syndrome.
Whole-body MRI was particularly valuable as a radiation-sparing imaging method for evaluating systemic arterial involvement in the neonatal ATS patient.

CT and MR angiography depict hallmark ATS imaging findings including marked aortic elongation, tortuosity of supra-aortic trunks, and an early bifurcation 'inverted V' pattern of the pulmonary arteries, useful for raising diagnostic suspicion.

Across both autistic and non-autistic children, simultaneous audiovisual stimulation attenuated pupil constriction relative to visual-only stimulation, indicating cross-modal modulation of the pupil light reflex.

During the 500-1000 ms post-stimulus window, autistic children showed significantly more positive baseline-corrected pupil responses than non-autistic children across all sensory conditions, reflecting less constriction in visual/audiovisual trials and greater dilation in auditory-only trials.
Autistic and non-autistic children did not differ significantly in peak pupil constriction or constriction latency within visual-only conditions, contrary to the study's hypothesis.
Over 94% of autistic adults report sensory hyperreactivity, 40% report sensory seeking, and 30% report hyporeactivity.
Autistic adults self-report significantly more sensory needs than informants report for adults with intellectual disabilities, suggesting under-recognition of sensory needs via informant report.

Sensory reactivity differences occur beyond autism: 50% of children with attention disorders and 30% of children with additional needs show sensory reactivity differences, with 5-15% of kindergarteners overall affected.

Using the SP3-D observational measure, autistic youth showed elevated and more variable sensory responsivity than typically developing peers, with hyperreactivity persisting through adolescence, while parent-reported and observed measures did not correlate.
Alsaedi et al. reported elevated sensory processing difficulties across multiple sensory modalities in children with autism in the Gulf region.
Worthley et al. found that early sensory responsivity profiles predicted later adaptive functioning, with sensory hypersensitivity predicting lower socialisation.

Rossow et al. using the SAND found that hyperreactivity was associated with internalising problems (anxiety, depression) in autistic children, while sensory seeking was linked to externalizing symptoms.

Qualitative work describes autistic adults experiencing sensory environments as overwhelming, distressing, or painful, and autistic mothers reporting sensory overload as a source of emotional exhaustion and social withdrawal.
Autistic adults perceive sensory hyperreactivity as preceding anxiety, while sensory seeking is perceived more as an effect (coping strategy) of anxiety rather than its cause.
In autistic males, higher sensory seeking (measured with the Sensory Profile) was associated with poorer sustained attention performance.
Kadlaskar et al. reported that young autistic children with elevated sensory hyperreactivity also demonstrated lower adaptive functioning and increased attentional problems.

In an Egyptian sample using the Short Sensory Profile, affective reactivity differences were common in autistic children and were associated with other autistic behaviours including stereotypic behaviours.
Using the German Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire, Jakob et al. found higher affective reactivity in autistic adults.
A case study documented a successful CBT-based intervention for noise hypersensitivity in an autistic teenager.
Autistic individuals show higher flutter (low-frequency) tactile thresholds and reduced adaptation to sustained stimuli applied to the fingers.
Differences in social (affective) touch perception have been observed in autism.
Higher tactile perceptual thresholds have been linked to increased sensory reactivity as measured by questionnaires, suggesting perceptual differences contribute to higher-order sensory reactivity.

Reduced GABA and increased glutamate levels correlate with tactile perceptual differences in both autistic children and adults, though the relationship with excitation-inhibition balance is not straightforward.

Drift diffusion modelling with EEG showed autistic children demonstrate typical or enhanced integration of motion information, with motion coherence differences reflecting reduced noise exclusion rather than impaired signal integration.
A meta-analysis confirmed that global motion processing differences in autism, while reliable, show only small effect sizes with substantial individual variability.
Autistic children show a different developmental trajectory in contrast sensitivity, with continued development at high spatial frequencies beyond typical ages.
Recent meta-analytic evidence supports enhanced pitch perception in autism, particularly with simple tones and among individuals with a history of language delay.
Dumont and colleagues found that enhanced pitch discrimination in autistic children was most pronounced in those who had unexpectedly acquired a second language through screen exposure.
Chan and colleagues replicated elevated auditory temporal-order thresholds using online assessment, with autistic children requiring substantially longer intervals to accurately judge temporal order.

Meta-analytic work confirms wider cross-modal temporal binding windows in autism, and Ainsworth and Bertone found that binding windows were negatively correlated with age only in autistic participants, with group differences diminishing by adolescence.
Jertberg and colleagues found McGurk susceptibility in autistic adults is similar to non-autistic adults, with susceptibility increasing with age in both groups.
Zhou and colleagues found that reduced visual temporal acuity correlated with sensory avoidance specifically in adolescents with higher autistic traits.
Taylor and colleagues used a revised Sensory Perception Quotient scoring to demonstrate greater hypersensitivity in autistic females, supporting enhanced perceptual functioning accounts.

Green and colleagues identified a subgroup of autistic children with elevated parent-reported and observed Sensory Over Responsivity who also exhibited heightened sympathetic arousal, suggesting behavioural responsivity may be underpinned by autonomic dysregulation.
Matsushima et al. demonstrated increased vagal activity in response to less controllable sensory stimuli, indicating behavioural rigidity may be linked to atypical physiological modulation.

A subgroup of autistic children with elevated parent-reported and observed sensory over-responsivity also showed heightened sympathetic arousal, suggesting behavioural responsivity may be underpinned by autonomic dysregulation.
Increased vagal activity was demonstrated in response to less controllable sensory stimuli, suggesting behavioural rigidity may be linked to atypical physiological modulation.
Autistic individuals exhibit increased postural sway and reduced gait adaptability under sensory and attentional load, reflecting diminished sensorimotor integration and behavioural flexibility.

Bumetanide, a pharmacological intervention targeting neural excitability, showed preliminary efficacy in reducing irritability associated with sensory processing difficulties, potentially via GABAergic mechanisms.
Preliminary data suggest that upregulating the parasympathetic nervous system through cranial electrotherapy stimulation reduces sensory sensitivity, anxiety, and improves emotional regulation.

Diffusion Tensor Imaging has repeatedly shown reduced white matter organization in posterior and interhemispheric (corpus callosum) tracts, which correlates with sensory reactivity and emotional regulation.

Cortical excitation-inhibition imbalance has been recognized as early as 6 weeks of age in infants at risk for autism, persists across the lifespan, and is associated with restricted and repetitive behaviour and sleep differences.
EEG studies support differences in sensory gating and adaptation processes in autistic children and adults, including responses to GABAergic intervention across developmental stages.

In a resting-state fcMRI study, children with directly measured sensory over-responsivity exhibited reduced long-range functional connectivity across all brain networks compared to children without sensory over-responsivity.

Sensory reactive children showed decreased local functional connectivity in exogenous (outside-input) networks but increased connectivity in endogenous (internally processing) networks, whereas children without sensory reactivity showed the opposite, mirrored pattern.

Sensory reactive children who were emotionally resilient showed a balanced pattern of equal and opposite turning down of exogenous and turning up of endogenous network connectivity, whereas sensory reactive but emotionally dysregulated children showed no difference between exogenous and endogenous network connectivity, suggesting balance between the two systems is critical for resilience.

Across structural and functional models of sensory processing, the brainstem, cerebellum, subcortical structures, and primary/multisensory sensory cortices are repeatedly implicated as core links in the sensory processing chain in autism.
Serum amyloid A, an amyloidogenic plasma protein, interacts with fibrinogen to form circulating procoagulant fibrinaloid microclot complexes (FMCs).
Fibrinogen interacts with cellular debris, microparticles, and immune complexes such as neutrophil extracellular traps to form heterogeneous circulating procoagulant fibrinaloid microclot complexes.

During inflammation or cell death, phosphatidylserine externalization exposes negatively charged, amyloidogenic membrane surfaces that recruit coagulation factors and generate catalytic sites for prothrombinase assembly.
Neutrophil extracellular traps, as immune complexes, interact with fibrinogen and contribute to formation of procoagulant fibrinaloid microclot complexes.

Fibrinaloid microclot complexes are distinct from canonical fibrin clots, displaying beta-sheet-rich amyloid features, Thioflavin T binding, and resistance to fibrinolysis, implicating them in vascular pathology of inflammatory and post-viral syndromes.
Damage to glycosaminoglycans of the glycocalyx during inflammation contributes to exposure of negatively charged amyloidogenic surfaces that promote thrombo-inflammatory complex formation.
Children with post-COVID syndrome had significantly wider central retinal arteriolar equivalent (CRAE) than matched healthy controls, independent of blood pressure and hospitalisation status.
Children with post-COVID syndrome had significantly wider central retinal venular equivalent (CRVE) than matched healthy controls, independent of blood pressure and hospitalisation status.
The arteriolar-to-venular ratio (AVR) was significantly higher in the PCS group than in matched healthy controls, reflecting a disproportionate arteriolar contribution to vessel dilation.
Higher diastolic blood pressure was inversely associated with the arteriolar-to-venular ratio in the PCS cohort, consistent with known haemodynamic effects on retinal vessel calibre.
Higher systolic blood pressure was associated with narrower central retinal arteriolar equivalent in the PCS cohort.
Hospitalisation during the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, used as a proxy for disease severity, did not explain the observed retinal microvascular alterations in the PCS cohort.

Across the PCS cohort, no significant group-level change occurred in static or dynamic retinal vessel parameters between baseline and follow-up (median 14 weeks later), despite substantial inter-individual variability.
Children with wider venular diameter (CRVE) at baseline were more likely to show a decrease in venular calibre over time, suggesting partial normalisation or regression to the mean.
Higher AVR values at baseline were associated with a subsequent reduction in AVR over the follow-up period.
Children with lower baseline flicker light-induced vasoreactivity (arteriolar dilation, arteriolar constriction, venular dilation) showed greater increases in these parameters at follow-up.
A longer interval between baseline and follow-up examinations was associated with a greater reduction in venular diameter (CRVE) over time.

Children who reported a reduction in symptom burden (decrease in MLCSQ score) between visits showed a corresponding increase in AVR, a pattern the authors interpret cautiously as possible partial microvascular normalisation during clinical recovery.

In a subgroup of PCS patients (n=19) with elevated blood pressure at baseline, CRAE and CRVE were reduced compared to the rest of the cohort, but this difference did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Total symptom burden measured by the MLCSQ did not change significantly between baseline and follow-up in the PCS cohort.
Retinal vascular parameters showed no significant association with patient age or gender within the PCS cohort.

The patient's serology showed positive EBV VCA IgG and EBV nuclear antigen IgG with negative VCA IgM, a pattern consistent with prior EBV infection rather than active or reactivated disease, in a patient newly diagnosed with fibromyalgia.
A cited study (Reshkova et al.) found that elevated EBV IgG antibody levels correlated with pain severity and related clinical symptoms in fibromyalgia patients.

In a study of 50 primary fibromyalgia patients, a substantial proportion had symptoms resembling chronic EBV infection, including adenopathy, persistent cough, recurrent rash, sore throat, and low-grade fevers, and over half reported an abrupt viral syndrome-like onset.
A subset of chronic fatigue syndrome patients showed increased blood expression of the EBV-induced gene 2 (EBI2).

The patient's inflammatory and muscle enzyme markers (CRP, ESR, IL-6, creatine kinase) were all within normal reference ranges, arguing against active inflammatory or autoimmune disease as the cause of her pain.
Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibody were all negative, excluding autoimmune connective tissue disease and rheumatoid arthritis as causes of the patient's pain.

Elevated white blood cell and neutrophil counts were noted, consistent with a concurrent bacterial infection (pneumonia) that confounded the clinical picture rather than reflecting active EBV disease.
The patient was started on meloxicam 15 mg as needed for fibromyalgia-related pain, along with patient education, which provided sufficient reassurance.
Physical therapy was initiated three months after diagnosis to improve mobility, strength, and reduce fear of instability.
Low-dose sertraline was reported to improve the patient's overall condition.
Higher levels of anxiety and depression noted in women have been linked to a greater incidence of fibromyalgia in women.
Fibromyalgia has been associated with various infections including hepatitis C, Lyme disease, Coxsackievirus, Parvovirus B19, HIV, and Epstein-Barr virus.
The case patient had comorbid mixed irritable bowel syndrome, generalized anxiety disorder (managed with buspirone), and obesity alongside her fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Fibromyalgia-related pain is similar to that seen in temporomandibular disorder and irritable bowel syndrome, and these conditions are commonly comorbid in many patients.
Fibromyalgia prevalence varies by population, reported as approximately 5.4% in the UK, 2.1% in Japan, and a pooled global prevalence of 1.78% from a large meta-analysis.
Some fibromyalgia patients have circulating autoantibodies targeting gangliosides, TRPV1, serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, GABA receptors, or fibroblast growth factor 3.

Transplantation of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into mice induced hyperalgesia, with IgG deposition observed in the dorsal root ganglia, suggesting an IgG-mediated mechanism contributes to FM symptoms in some patients.
Cohort studies from Sweden and Canada reported that fibromyalgia patients with elevated anti-satellite glial cell IgG antibodies exhibit more severe symptoms.

Levels of autoantibodies against various nerve- and tissue-specific antigens correlate with the severity of fatigue, bodily pain, depression, anxiety, and physical and mental health-related quality of life in fibromyalgia.
Phosphorus-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies demonstrated mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced oxygen utilization in the skeletal muscle of fibromyalgia patients.

Studies of peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed that mitochondrial function is impaired in fibromyalgia patients and correlates with symptom severity, contributing to lactate/pyruvate accumulation and enhanced peripheral nociceptive input.
Fibromyalgia patients have elevated concentrations of substance P in cerebrospinal fluid and serum.
Fibromyalgia patients have elevated concentrations of CGRP in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, promoting vasodilation, plasma extravasation, and mast cell activation contributing to local hyperalgesia.

Fibromyalgia patients show reduced muscle capillary density and blood perfusion, suggesting reduced oxygen supply, particularly during exercise, which may amplify peripheral pain signals via local hypoxia.

Microneurography and skin biopsy findings revealed hyperexcitability of C nociceptors and reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density in some fibromyalgia patients, supporting a role of peripheral ischemia and small fiber pathology in perpetuating peripheral sensitization.
First-degree relatives of fibromyalgia patients have up to an eightfold increased risk of developing FM, supporting a genetic component to disease clustering in families.
Genetic association studies have identified polymorphisms in the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) associated with fibromyalgia, implicating pain and mood regulation pathways.
Genetic association studies have identified polymorphisms in the catechol-O-methyltransferase gene (COMT) associated with fibromyalgia, implicating pain and mood regulation pathways.
Genetic association studies have identified polymorphisms in the dopamine receptor D4 gene (DRD4) associated with fibromyalgia, implicating pain and mood regulation pathways.
There is no evidence that fibromyalgia is caused by a single gene mutation, supporting the view that FM is polygenic/multifactorial rather than monogenic.

Compared with healthy controls, fibromyalgia patients exhibit hypo-methylation in pathways such as signal transduction, calcium signaling, the MAPK pathway, immune response, and cellular stress/oxidative stress response.
An epigenome-wide association study in healthy monozygotic twins found that higher methylation status of the TRPA1 promoter region was associated with higher pain sensitivity.

Small fiber neuropathy has been detected in up to 40-60% of fibromyalgia patients, supported by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy and abnormal corneal confocal microscopy findings.
A recent meta-analysis reported that approximately half of fibromyalgia patients had small fiber dysfunction.
Skin biopsies have demonstrated a significant reduction in unmyelinated C fibers in patients with fibromyalgia.

Elevated nerve growth factor (NGF) levels have been reported in fibromyalgia and other chronic pain conditions, potentially promoting pain transmission via TrkA receptor signaling and increased Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and TRPV1 expression.

Tolerance at mu-opioid receptors on inhibitory interneurons of the descending pain inhibitory system (e.g., periaqueductal gray) can cause opioid-induced hyperalgesia that clinically resembles fibromyalgia.
Resting-state functional MRI studies have shown dysfunction of the descending pain inhibitory system in patients with fibromyalgia.
PET imaging in fibromyalgia patients showed increased TSPO binding in frontal and parietal cortical regions, indicating widespread microglial activation.

Neuroinflammation in fibromyalgia is heterogeneously distributed, with increased signal in motor/somatosensory and parietal/frontal cortices and decreased signal in the medulla, superior temporal gyrus, and amygdala.

Diffusion kurtosis imaging revealed decreased kurtosis parameters in the dorsolateral prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices of fibromyalgia patients, with amygdala changes correlating with pain severity.
